category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Embryological and Neuro-Anatomical Basis of the Digastric Muscle
statement: Considering the dual embryological origin of the digastric muscle, which of the following statements accurately reflects its dual innervation and corresponding pharyngeal arch origins?
options: Anterior belly from 1st arch (CN V); Posterior belly from 2nd arch (CN VII)
Both bellies from 2nd arch (CN VII)
Anterior belly from 3rd arch (CN IX); Posterior belly from 4th arch (CN X)
Anterior belly from 2nd arch (CN VII); Posterior belly from 1st arch (CN V)
Anterior belly from C1; Posterior belly from Ansa Cervicalis
correctOption: Anterior belly from 1st arch (CN V); Posterior belly from 2nd arch (CN VII)
optionExplanations: The digastric muscle has two bellies from different origins. The anterior belly develops from the first pharyngeal arch (innervated by the nerve to mylohyoid, V3), and the posterior belly develops from the second pharyngeal arch (innervated by the facial nerve, CN VII).
Only the posterior belly and the stylohyoid are derived from the 2nd arch in this region.
The 3rd arch nerve is the glossopharyngeal and the 4th/6th is the vagus; they do not supply the digastric.
This is the reverse of the actual anatomy. The anterior is 1st arch; the posterior is 2nd arch.
The digastric bellies are not supplied by spinal nerves C1 or the ansa cervicalis; these innervate the infrahyoid group (and geniohyoid/thyrohyoid).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1538 (Book Page): The facial nerve is the nerve of the second pharyngeal arch and supplies all the muscles of facial expression. Page 1669 (Book Page): Before entering the canal, it [V3] gives off the mylohyoid nerve, which supplies... the anterior belly of the digastric muscle. Page 1673 (Book Page): Small muscular branches to the posterior belly of digastric and the stylohyoid muscles emerge in the same way.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the nerve supply of the muscle that originates from the styloid process and inserts into the body of the hyoid bone. Which of the following is the correct innervation for this muscle?
options: Ansa cervicalis (C1–C3)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Mylohyoid nerve (branch of CN V3)
C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve
Facial nerve (CN VII)
correctOption: Facial nerve (CN VII)
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis supplies the majority of the infrahyoid strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid), not the suprahyoid group.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus, which attaches to the styloid process, but does not innervate the stylohyoid.
The mylohyoid nerve innervates the mylohyoid muscle and the anterior belly of the digastric, but not the stylohyoid.
C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve supply the geniohyoid and thyrohyoid muscles, not the stylohyoid.
The stylohyoid muscle, like the posterior belly of the digastric, is derived from the second pharyngeal arch and is therefore innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Stylohyoid ... Nerve Supply: Facial nerve.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: Which of the following physiological loops describes the action of the infrahyoid muscles during the final phase of swallowing?
options: Contraction to pull the thyroid cartilage forward to tense the vocal cords
Contraction to depress the hyoid bone and larynx to their resting positions
Contraction to elevate the hyoid bone and close the epiglottis
Relaxation to allow the tongue to move forward
Contraction to dilate the pharyngeal isthmus
correctOption: Contraction to depress the hyoid bone and larynx to their resting positions
optionExplanations: Tensing the vocal cords is the function of the cricothyroid muscle, which is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle, not a general infrahyoid strap muscle.
Following the elevation of the larynx and hyoid during the passage of a bolus, the infrahyoid muscles (strap muscles) contract to depress these structures back to their anatomical resting positions.
Elevation of the hyoid is the function of the suprahyoid muscles (digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid) during the start of the involuntary phase of swallowing.
Relaxation of the tongue muscles occurs, but the infrahyoid muscles actively contract to reset the position of the hyoid and larynx.
The pharyngeal isthmus is closed during swallowing by the soft palate and superior constrictor, not by the infrahyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1621 (Book Page): those inferior [to the hyoid] are the infrahyoid muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid)... [Page 1615 (Book Page) Table 12.5] Action: Depresses hyoid bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A 55-year-old male undergoes a radical neck dissection for a malignant tumor in the carotid triangle. Post-operatively, the patient exhibits paralysis of the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles, while the thyrohyoid muscle remains functional. Which specific neurological structure was most likely preserved during the surgery?
options: The superior root of the ansa cervicalis
The main trunk of the hypoglossal nerve
The cervical branch of the facial nerve
The nerve to the mylohyoid
The C1 fibers branching directly from the hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: The C1 fibers branching directly from the hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The superior root of the ansa cervicalis contributes to the innervation of the muscles that are paralyzed (sternohyoid/sternothyroid), so it was likely damaged.
Preserving the main trunk of the hypoglossal nerve ensures tongue movement, but the specific preservation of the thyrohyoid requires the C1 fibers that hitchhike with it to remain intact.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve supplies the platysma; its preservation would not affect the thyrohyoid.
The nerve to the mylohyoid supplies a suprahyoid muscle, not the thyrohyoid infrahyoid muscle.

The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with CN XII but leave as a separate branch. Preservation of this specific branch or the C1 fibers within CN XII explains why only the thyrohyoid remains functional while muscles supplied by the ansa cervicalis are paralyzed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Nerve to the thyrohyoid muscle (C1). ... Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: When a person attempts to open their mouth against resistance, the suprahyoid muscles must contract to depress the mandible. Which of the following muscles acts as a synergist in this specific movement by providing a stable base at the hyoid bone?
options: Masseter
Geniohyoid
Omohyoid
Stylohyoid
Medial pterygoid
correctOption: Omohyoid
optionExplanations: The masseter is a muscle of mastication that elevates the mandible (closes the mouth), which is the opposite of the movement described.
The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that depresses the mandible; it is the muscle needing the stable base, not the one providing it.
For suprahyoid muscles to depress the mandible, the hyoid bone must be 'fixed' or pulled downward by the infrahyoid muscles. The omohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that performs this fixator role.
The stylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid; it would not provide a stable base for mandible depression as its contraction pulls the hyoid bone upward.
The medial pterygoid elevates the mandible; it is an antagonist to the suprahyoid muscles during mouth opening.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1620 (Book Page): [Infrahyoid muscles] include omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid... Those superior to the hyoid bone are the suprahyoid muscles.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Dual Innervation of the Digastric Muscle
statement: During the first stage of deglutition (swallowing), the bolus of food is squeezed backward into the pharynx. This process requires the elevation of the hyoid bone to stabilize the larynx. Which muscle, characterized by a dual embryological origin, facilitates this by contracting its posterior belly under the influence of the facial nerve?
options: Geniohyoid
Digastric
Mylohyoid
Omohyoid
Stylohyoid
correctOption: Digastric
optionExplanations: The geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal nerve and acts to pull the hyoid bone forward, but lacks the dual belly structure of the digastric.
The digastric muscle has an anterior belly (derived from the 1st pharyngeal arch, supplied by V3) and a posterior belly (derived from the 2nd pharyngeal arch, supplied by VII).
The mylohyoid is supplied solely by the nerve to the mylohyoid (V3) and forms the floor of the mouth; it does not have a posterior belly supplied by the facial nerve.
The omohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle with two bellies (superior and inferior), but both are supplied by the ansa cervicalis, and its primary action is to depress the hyoid, not elevate it.
The stylohyoid is supplied by the facial nerve and elevates the hyoid, but it consists of a single belly, unlike the digastric which has two distinct bellies with different nerve supplies.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Digastric: ...Nerve supply: Anterior belly: nerve to mylohyoid (branch of mandibular division of trigeminal nerve); posterior belly: facial nerve.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: Which of the following physiological steps is correct regarding the action of the Thyrohyoid muscle in laryngeal mechanics?
options: It serves as the primary abductor of the vocal folds during deep inspiration.
It relaxes the vocal cords by pulling the thyroid cartilage posteriorly.
It depresses the hyoid bone while the thyroid cartilage is fixed.
It elevates the larynx when the hyoid bone is fixed.
It rotates the cricoid cartilage on the thyroid cartilage to increase pitch.
correctOption: It elevates the larynx when the hyoid bone is fixed.
optionExplanations: The primary abductor of the vocal folds is the posterior cricoarytenoid; the thyrohyoid is an extrinsic muscle and does not act directly on the rima glottidis.
Relaxation of the vocal cords is primarily performed by the intrinsic thyroarytenoid muscle, not the extrinsic thyrohyoid muscle.
While the thyrohyoid can depress the hyoid if the larynx is fixed, its more common functional step during swallowing is the elevation of the larynx towards the hyoid.
When the suprahyoid muscles fix the hyoid bone, the thyrohyoid contracts to pull the thyroid cartilage (and thus the larynx) upward, aiding in airway closure.
Pitch adjustment is a function of the cricothyroid muscle (tensing) and thyroarytenoid (relaxing), involving intrinsic movements of the laryngeal cartilages.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Muscle] Thyrohyoid... [Action] Elevates larynx or depresses hyoid bone

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Nerve Supply of the Mylohyoid Muscle
statement: A 24-year-old student is asked to identify the nerve responsible for the motor innervation of the muscle forming the majority of the floor of the oral cavity. Which nerve is correct?
options: Mylohyoid nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Lingual nerve
Facial nerve
Nerve to the medial pterygoid
correctOption: Mylohyoid nerve
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid nerve is a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (from V3) and provides motor supply to the mylohyoid muscle, which forms the floor of the mouth.
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, but not the mylohyoid muscle of the oral floor.
The lingual nerve provides general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but does not provide motor innervation to the mylohyoid.
The facial nerve supplies the posterior belly of the digastric and the stylohyoid but not the mylohyoid muscle.
The nerve to the medial pterygoid supplies the medial pterygoid and the tensor veli palatini muscles, not the floor of the mouth.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): Before entering the canal, it gives off the mylohyoid nerve, which supplies the mylohyoid muscle and the anterior belly of the digastric muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: The infrahyoid muscles, often called 'strap muscles', are mostly innervated by the ansa cervicalis. However, a significant diagnostic contrast exists for the thyrohyoid muscle. What is the specific nerve supply to the thyrohyoid, and how does it differ from the sternohyoid?
options: C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve; Sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis
Glossopharyngeal nerve; Sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis
Facial nerve (CN VII); Sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis
Ansa cervicalis (C1-C3); Sternohyoid is supplied by C1 via the hypoglossal nerve
Nerve to mylohyoid (V3); Sternohyoid is supplied by the phrenic nerve
correctOption: C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve; Sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid are unique in the neck as they are innervated by C1 spinal nerve fibers that hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). The other strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid) are supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1, C2, and C3).
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle only in terms of motor innervation; it does not supply the infrahyoid muscles.
The facial nerve supplies muscles derived from the second pharyngeal arch, like stylohyoid and the posterior belly of digastric, but not the infrahyoid strap muscles.
This is reversed. Thyrohyoid is the exception (C1 via XII), while Sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
The nerve to mylohyoid is a branch of V3 (mandibular) and the phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; neither is involved in infrahyoid muscle innervation correctly in this context.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Nerve to the thyrohyoid muscle (C1). Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles. Page 1621 (Book Page): those inferior are the infrahyoid muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid).

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: During the first stage of deglutition (swallowing), the hyoid bone must be elevated to assist the tongue in pushing the bolus into the pharynx. Which mechanistic combination of suprahyoid muscles produces this elevation and subsequent retraction of the hyoid?
options: Geniohyoid and Sternohyoid
Anterior belly of digastric and Mylohyoid
Mylohyoid and Thyrohyoid
Stylohyoid and Posterior belly of digastric
Omohyoid and Sternothyroid
correctOption: Stylohyoid and Posterior belly of digastric
optionExplanations: Geniohyoid elevates and protracts the hyoid. Sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone, which is counter-productive to the elevation phase of swallowing.
The anterior belly of the digastric and the mylohyoid primarily elevate the hyoid and pull it forward (protraction) rather than retracting it backward.
Mylohyoid elevates the hyoid, but thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that either elevates the larynx or depresses the hyoid depending on which bone is fixed.
The stylohyoid and the posterior belly of the digastric both originate from the styloid process and mastoid notch respectively, pulling the hyoid bone superiorly and posteriorly (retraction).
Omohyoid and sternothyroid are infrahyoid muscles that act as depressors of the hyoid bone and larynx, typically acting to reset the position after swallowing is complete.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): The hyoid bone... is suspended in position by muscles that connect it to the mandible, to the styloid process of the temporal bone... Page 1728 (Book Page): Retraction: Styloglossus and hyoglossus muscles on both sides acting together. Page 1620 (Book Page): suprahyoid muscles... stylohyoid; posterior belly of digastric.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Clinical Impact of Ansa Cervicalis Lesion
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoing a radical neck dissection for laryngeal carcinoma suffers iatrogenic damage to the ansa cervicalis. During postoperative evaluation, which of the following deficits is most likely to be observed?
options: Inability to elevate the hyoid bone during the first stage of swallowing
Loss of sensation to the skin over the angle of the mandible
Impaired ability to depress the larynx and hyoid bone after elevation
Paralysis of the mylohyoid muscle leading to floor of the mouth sagging
Deviation of the tongue to the side of the lesion upon protrusion
correctOption: Impaired ability to depress the larynx and hyoid bone after elevation
optionExplanations: Hyoid elevation is performed by the suprahyoid muscles (CN V3, CN VII, and C1 via XII), not the ansa cervicalis.
Sensation over the angle of the mandible is provided by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), not the ansa cervicalis.

The ansa cervicalis supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid, which are responsible for depressing the hyoid bone and larynx after they have been elevated during swallowing or vocalization.
The mylohyoid muscle is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve (branch of V3), not the ansa cervicalis loop of the cervical plexus (C1-C3).
Tongue deviation is a classic sign of hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, specifically affecting the genioglossus muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1620 (Book Page): ...those inferior are the infrahyoid muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid). Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop [ansa cervicalis] supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Mylohyoid muscle as a surgical/pathological landmark
statement: A 22-year-old male presents with high-grade fever, severe submandibular swelling, and elevation of the tongue following a dental infection of the lower second molar. The clinician diagnoses Ludwig’s angina. Which muscle serves as the primary anatomical barrier, determining whether the infection remains in the sublingual space or the submandibular space?
options: Mylohyoid
Anterior belly of digastric
Sternohyoid
Geniohyoid
Hyoglossus
correctOption: Mylohyoid
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid muscle forms the floor of the mouth; infections above it (sublingual) vs. below/around it (submandibular) are determined by this barrier.
The anterior digastric is superficial to the mylohyoid and is not the primary barrier for sublingual spread.
The sternohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle located inferior to the hyoid bone, far from the floor of the mouth.
The geniohyoid lies superior to the mylohyoid and does not form the floor of the mouth barrier.
The hyoglossus is an extrinsic tongue muscle located deeper in the tongue's structure.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1630 (Book Page): Dental infections most commonly involve the lower molar teeth. The infection spreads medially from the mandible into the submandibular and masticatory spaces and pushes the tongue forward and upward. Page 1747 (Book Page): The submandibular gland... is divided into superficial and deep parts by the mylohyoid muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: In a comparative anatomical study of the infrahyoid 'strap' muscles, one muscle is identified as having a unique innervation that does not arise from the ansa cervicalis loop (C1-C3). Which muscle is this, and what is its specific nerve supply?
options: Sternohyoid; descendens hypoglossi
Thyrohyoid; C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve
Omohyoid; nerve to mylohyoid
Sternothyroid; C1 fibers via the facial nerve
Sternothyroid; descendens cervicalis
correctOption: Thyrohyoid; C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis; the descendens hypoglossi is only the superior root of that loop.
The thyrohyoid is the only infrahyoid muscle supplied by C1 fibers that travel briefly with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before branching off.
The omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3), not the nerve to the mylohyoid (which supplies suprahyoids).
The sternothyroid is not supplied by the facial nerve; the facial nerve supplies the second pharyngeal arch derivatives like the stylohyoid.
The sternothyroid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis; the descendens cervicalis is merely the inferior root (C2-C3) of the loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Nerve to the thyrohyoid muscle (C1) ... [Page 1689 (Book Page) Table 12.7] Thyrohyoid ... C1 via hypoglossal nerve.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: During the initial phase of deglutition, the bolus of food is voluntarily pushed toward the pharynx. Anatomically, for the suprahyoid muscles to effectively elevate the hyoid bone and larynx during this process, which physiological stabilization must occur?
options: Active depression of the hyoid bone by the thyrohyoid muscle
Stabilization of the mandible by the muscles of mastication
Relaxation of the mylohyoid to allow the tongue to drop
Contraction of the infrahyoid muscles to fix the hyoid bone
Inhibition of the ansa cervicalis to prevent laryngeal ascent
correctOption: Stabilization of the mandible by the muscles of mastication
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid muscle typically acts to elevate the larynx toward the hyoid or depress the hyoid toward the larynx, but active depression of the hyoid would oppose the necessary elevation required for swallowing.

For suprahyoid muscles (like the digastric and mylohyoid) to elevate the hyoid bone, the mandible must be fixed in place by the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid). Conversely, if the hyoid is fixed, these muscles depress the mandible.
The mylohyoid must contract, not relax, to elevate the floor of the mouth and the hyoid bone during the early stages of swallowing.

While infrahyoid muscles fix the hyoid for mandible depression, during hyoid elevation (swallowing), the suprahyoid muscles act while the infrahyoids are momentarily inhibited to allow the hyoid bone to move superiorly.

Inhibition of the ansa cervicalis occurs to allow elevation, but it is not the primary 'stabilization' required for the suprahyoid muscles to exert pull; the fixation of the superior attachment (the mandible) is the mechanical requirement.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1515 (Book Page): The hyoid bone... is suspended in position by muscles that connect it to the mandible, to the styloid process of the temporal bone, to the thyroid cartilage, to the sternum, and to the scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: Which of the following nerves supplies the stylohyoid muscle, reflecting its embryological origin from the second pharyngeal arch?
options: Ansa cervicalis
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
correctOption: Facial nerve (CN VII)
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to most infrahyoid (strap) muscles, not the suprahyoid muscles like the stylohyoid.
The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle (third arch derivative), but not the stylohyoid.
The hypoglossal nerve supplies intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, but not the stylohyoid muscle.
The stylohyoid develops from the second pharyngeal arch and is therefore innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
The trigeminal nerve supplies muscles of the first pharyngeal arch, such as the mylohyoid and the anterior belly of the digastric.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1673 (Book Page): Small muscular branches to the posterior belly of digastric and the stylohyoid muscles emerge in the same way [from the facial nerve].

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A 19-year-old patient presents with difficulty in the initial phase of swallowing and a slight weakness in depressing the mandible. A neurological exam reveals impaired function of the nerve that originates from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Which muscle is most likely affected?
options: Thyrohyoid
Geniohyoid
Posterior belly of digastric
Stylohyoid
Mylohyoid
correctOption: Mylohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve.
The geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, not the trigeminal nerve.
The posterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
The stylohyoid is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).

The mylohyoid muscle is supplied by the mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from V3 (mandibular division of trigeminal). Its paralysis affects floor-of-mouth elevation and mandible depression.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): Before entering the canal, it gives off the mylohyoid nerve, which supplies the mylohyoid muscle and the anterior belly of the digastric muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Unique Innervation of Thyrohyoid and Geniohyoid
statement: Which specific nerve provides the motor innervation to the thyrohyoid muscle, distinguishing it from the other muscles typically supplied by the ansa cervicalis?
options: Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve
First cervical nerve fibers via the hypoglossal nerve
Superior ramus of the ansa cervicalis
External laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve
Inferior ramus of the ansa cervicalis
correctOption: First cervical nerve fibers via the hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds and does not provide motor supply to the infrahyoid muscles.
The thyrohyoid is unique among the strap muscles because it is supplied by C1 fibers that hitchhike along the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before branching off independently.
The superior ramus of the ansa cervicalis (C1) primarily supplies the superior belly of the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid, but not the thyrohyoid directly.
The external laryngeal nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (CN X) and specifically supplies the cricothyroid muscle, not the thyrohyoid.
The inferior ramus of the ansa cervicalis (C2-C3) supplies the inferior belly of the omohyoid and contributes to the ansa loop, but it does not innervate the thyrohyoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: In a comparative anatomical study of the 'strap muscles', a researcher notes that one muscle specifically acts on the thyroid cartilage rather than the hyoid bone directly. Which muscle is being described and what is its primary action?
options: Mylohyoid; elevates larynx
Sternohyoid; depresses hyoid bone
Sternothyroid; depresses larynx
Omohyoid; depresses hyoid bone
Thyrohyoid; depresses larynx
correctOption: Sternothyroid; depresses larynx
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid and floor of the mouth, not an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the larynx.
The sternohyoid is a strap muscle, but it attaches to the hyoid bone and acts to depress the hyoid bone directly.
The sternothyroid is unique among the strap muscles because its superior attachment is the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage; thus, it depresses the larynx rather than the hyoid bone.
The omohyoid consists of two bellies and attaches to the hyoid bone; its primary function is to depress the hyoid bone.
The thyrohyoid attaches to the thyroid cartilage, but its action is to elevate the larynx or depress the hyoid, not specifically just to depress the larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Sternothyroid... Action: Depresses larynx (thyroid cartilage).

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: The omohyoid muscle is a unique infrahyoid muscle consisting of two bellies. During a surgical dissection of the posterior triangle, the inferior belly is noted to arise from the upper border of the scapula. Which anatomical structure holds the intermediate tendon of this muscle in place against the clavicle?
options: The pterygomandibular raphe
The carotid sheath
The thyrohyoid membrane
A fascial expansion of the pretracheal fascia
The stylohyoid ligament
correctOption: A fascial expansion of the pretracheal fascia
optionExplanations: The pterygomandibular raphe is a ligamentous band between the buccinator and superior constrictor, having no relation to the omohyoid.
The carotid sheath surrounds the vessels and vagus nerve but does not provide the specific tethering mechanism for the omohyoid tendon.
The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone and does not interact with the omohyoid's intermediate tendon.
The intermediate tendon of the omohyoid is held down to the clavicle by a loop of deep cervical fascia (part of the pretracheal/investing layers), allowing it to act at an angle.
The stylohyoid ligament connects the styloid process to the lesser cornu of the hyoid and is unrelated to the omohyoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Omohyoid (inferior belly) ... the intermediate tendon is held to the clavicle by a fascial expansion.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: In the physiological mechanism of swallowing, what is the specific role of the thyrohyoid muscle during the second stage of deglutition?
options: To adduct the vocal folds and prevent aspiration.
To depress the hyoid bone after the bolus has passed.
To elevate the larynx and pull it toward the hyoid bone.
To retract the tongue into the oropharynx.
To relax and allow the epiglottis to open the laryngeal inlet.
correctOption: To elevate the larynx and pull it toward the hyoid bone.
optionExplanations: Vocal fold adduction is performed by intrinsic laryngeal muscles (e.g., lateral cricoarytenoid), not the thyrohyoid.
The thyrohyoid elevates the larynx during the active phase; other infrahyoids like the sternohyoid help depress the hyoid later.

Contraction of the thyrohyoid muscle reduces the distance between the thyroid cartilage and the hyoid bone, effectively elevating the larynx. This elevation is a critical component of swallowing as it moves the larynx under the protective cover of the tongue and epiglottis.
Tongue retraction is performed by the styloglossus and hyoglossus, not the thyrohyoid.
The thyrohyoid contracts during swallowing; the closure of the laryngeal inlet is a separate complex action involving intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): The larynx and the laryngeal part of the pharynx are pulled upward by the contraction of the stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, thyrohyoid, and palatopharyngeus muscles.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A clinician is comparing the innervation of the infrahyoid muscles. While most of these 'strap' muscles are supplied by the ansa cervicalis, one specific muscle is innervated solely by the first cervical nerve (C1) via the hypoglossal nerve. Which muscle is this, and what is its primary action?
options: Omohyoid; Depresses the hyoid bone
Thyrohyoid; Elevates the larynx
Mylohyoid; Elevates the floor of the mouth
Sternohyoid; Depresses the hyoid bone
Sternothyroid; Depresses the thyroid cartilage
correctOption: Thyrohyoid; Elevates the larynx
optionExplanations: The omohyoid consists of superior and inferior bellies connected by an intermediate tendon. Both bellies are innervated by the ansa cervicalis, not directly by C1 fibers hitchhiking on the hypoglossal nerve.

The thyrohyoid is the only infrahyoid muscle innervated by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII). Its primary action is to elevate the larynx by pulling the thyroid cartilage toward the hyoid bone, or depress the hyoid if the larynx is fixed.

The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle, not an infrahyoid muscle. It is innervated by the mylohyoid nerve (a branch of the mandibular nerve V3), which is a branch of the trigeminal nerve, not a cervical nerve loop.

The sternohyoid is a classic strap muscle innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3). Its function is hyoid depression, but its innervation does not match the 'C1 via XII' specific pattern described in the question.

The sternothyroid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis (specifically the C2 and C3 components). It originates from the manubrium and inserts on the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage to depress the larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop [ansa cervicalis] supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles. ... Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Pharyngeal Arch Derivations of Suprahyoid Muscles
statement: A 24-year-old medical student is studying the digastric muscle. They note that the anterior and posterior bellies have different nerve supplies despite being part of the same muscle unit. This anatomical arrangement is best explained by which of the following?
options: Both bellies are supplied by the ansa cervicalis but via different cervical levels.
The anterior belly is a derivative of the second pharyngeal arch, while the posterior is from the first.
The posterior belly is considered a strap muscle, while the anterior is a true masticatory muscle.
The anterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve, and the posterior by the mandibular nerve.
The anterior belly is derived from the first pharyngeal arch, while the posterior belly is from the second arch.
correctOption: The anterior belly is derived from the first pharyngeal arch, while the posterior belly is from the second arch.
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid muscles, not the suprahyoid muscles like the digastric.
This is inverted; the first arch gives rise to the anterior belly (mandibular nerve), and the second arch gives rise to the posterior belly (facial nerve).
Both bellies are suprahyoid muscles. Neither is classified as a 'strap' muscle (which are the infrahyoids) or a primary muscle of mastication (though they assist in mandible depression).
The innervation is reversed in this option; the anterior belly is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (V3), and the posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve (VII).

The digastric muscle has a dual origin. The anterior belly develops from the first pharyngeal arch (innervated by V3), and the posterior belly develops from the second pharyngeal arch (innervated by CN VII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1669 (Book Page): Before entering the canal, [the inferior alveolar nerve] gives off the mylohyoid nerve, which supplies the mylohyoid muscle and the anterior belly of the digastric muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: During the initial phase of swallowing, the hyoid bone is elevated to facilitate the movement of the bolus into the pharynx. Which multi-step physiological mechanism describes the role of the suprahyoid muscles in mandible depression when the hyoid bone is fixed?
options: The lateral pterygoid pulls the mandible forward while the digastrics, geniohyoids, and mylohyoids pull the mandible downward.
The masseter and temporalis relax while the stylohyoid pushes the mandible posteriorly.
The infrahyoids contract to elevate the larynx, allowing the suprahyoids to pull the mandible upward.
The sternohyoid and sternothyroid contract to fix the mandible while the geniohyoid elevates the hyoid.
The omohyoid stabilizes the scapula, allowing the mylohyoid to depress the tongue.
correctOption: The lateral pterygoid pulls the mandible forward while the digastrics, geniohyoids, and mylohyoids pull the mandible downward.
optionExplanations: Mandible depression is an active process. The lateral pterygoid protracts the mandible, while the suprahyoid muscles (digastric, geniohyoid, and mylohyoid) act as depressors when the hyoid is relatively fixed.
While the masseter and temporalis (elevators) must relax, the stylohyoid's role is to elevate and retract the hyoid bone, not to push the mandible.
Infrahyoids typically depress the hyoid or larynx; they do not facilitate upward movement of the mandible through suprahyoid action.
The sternohyoid and sternothyroid are infrahyoid muscles that depress the hyoid; they do not fix the mandible.
The omohyoid's inferior belly attaches to the scapula, but its role is hyoid depression, not scapular stabilization for tongue depression.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1509 (Book Page): Depression of the mandible is brought about by contraction of the digastrics, the geniohyoids, and the mylohyoids. The lateral pterygoids play an important role by pulling the mandible forward.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A surgeon is performing a selective neck dissection and must identify the nerve supply to the omohyoid muscle to preserve its function in stabilizing the hyoid bone. Which neurological structure provides this innervation?
options: Phrenic nerve
Nerve to the thyrohyoid
Descending branch of the hypoglossal nerve only
Ansa cervicalis
Cervical branch of the facial nerve
correctOption: Ansa cervicalis
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the diaphragm and is not involved in the motor supply of the infrahyoid strap muscles.
The nerve to the thyrohyoid is a separate branch consisting of C1 fibers that do not join the ansa cervicalis loop, specifically targeting the thyrohyoid muscle.
The descending branch of the hypoglossal (C1) forms the superior root of the ansa cervicalis, but the muscle is supplied by the loop (ansa) itself, which includes C2 and C3 fibers.
The ansa cervicalis is a loop of nerves from the cervical plexus (C1-C3) that provides motor innervation to three of the four infrahyoid muscles: the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the platysma muscle in the neck, not the deep infrahyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: The omohyoid muscle consists of two bellies connected by an intermediate tendon. How does the anatomical positioning of this intermediate tendon relate to the deep cervical fascia?
options: It passes through the substance of the internal jugular vein to regulate venous return.
It is held in position by a band of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, which binds it to the clavicle.
It serves as the primary origin for the phrenic nerve as it descends the neck.
It is fused directly to the pretracheal fascia, allowing it to elevate the thyroid gland.
It is located deep to the prevertebral fascia, protecting the brachial plexus.
correctOption: It is held in position by a band of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia, which binds it to the clavicle.
optionExplanations: The tendon lies superficial to the carotid sheath and does not pass through the internal jugular vein.
The intermediate tendon of the omohyoid is held down by a fascial sling derived from the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia.
The phrenic nerve arises from C3-C5 rami and lies deep to the prevertebral fascia, unrelated to the omohyoid tendon.
The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland, but the omohyoid tendon is bound to the clavicle by the investing fascia.
The omohyoid is a strap muscle located superficial to the prevertebral fascia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1620 (Book Page): The sternocleidomastoid muscle and the muscles anterior to it, plus the inferior belly of the omohyoid, are elongated bands and are collectively referred to as the strap muscles of the neck. Page 1627 (Book Page): The investing layer... splits to enclose the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid... [Fascia binds the omohyoid tendon].

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A patient is unable to pull the thyroid cartilage upward during the high-pitched phase of singing. Upon examination, the suprahyoid muscles are functioning normally, but there is a lack of laryngeal elevation. Damage to which nerve/muscle combination is the most likely cause?
options: Mylohyoid nerve; Geniohyoid
C1 fibers via Hypoglossal nerve; Thyrohyoid
Ansa cervicalis; Sternothyroid
External laryngeal nerve; Cricothyroid
Recurrent laryngeal nerve; Thyroarytenoid
correctOption: C1 fibers via Hypoglossal nerve; Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the hyoid bone. While this indirectly lifts the larynx via the thyrohyoid membrane, the question specifies that suprahyoid function is normal, pointing to the thyrohyoid itself.

The thyrohyoid muscle is specifically responsible for elevating the larynx (the thyroid cartilage) toward the hyoid bone. Since it is innervated by C1 via CN XII, damage here would prevent the 'laryngeal lift' required in swallowing and singing.
The sternothyroid muscle depresses the larynx, pulling it away from the hyoid. Damage to the ansa cervicalis supplying it would actually make it easier for the larynx to rise, not harder.

The cricothyroid muscle tenses the vocal cords to increase pitch, but it does not elevate the thyroid cartilage toward the hyoid bone. Its paralysis would cause hoarseness and loss of high pitch, but not a failure of laryngeal elevation.
The thyroarytenoid muscle is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle that relaxes the vocal folds. It does not play a role in the extrinsic movement (elevation) of the laryngeal skeleton.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1621 (Book Page): Table 12.5 ... Thyrohyoid ... Action: Elevates the larynx or depresses the hyoid bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Anatomy and Action of the Sternothyroid Muscle
statement: The sternothyroid muscle differs from the other infrahyoid muscles because it does not attach directly to the hyoid bone. What is its superior attachment, and what is the resulting physiological action on the larynx?
options: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage; Depresses the larynx
Mastoid process; Rotates the head
Greater cornu of the hyoid bone; Elevates the larynx
Mental spines of the mandible; Depresses the mandible
Cricoid cartilage; Tenses the vocal cords
correctOption: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage; Depresses the larynx
optionExplanations: The sternothyroid muscle originates from the posterior surface of the manubrium and inserts into the oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage. Its contraction depresses the larynx.
The sternocleidomastoid attaches to the mastoid process and rotates the head, not the sternothyroid.
The sternohyoid and omohyoid attach to the hyoid bone, not the sternothyroid. Elevation of the larynx is performed by suprahyoid muscles and thyrohyoid.
Geniohyoid originates from the mental spines. The sternothyroid does not involve the mandible.
The cricothyroid muscle tenses the vocal cords; it is an intrinsic muscle of the larynx, not a strap muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1811 (Book Page): apex being directed upward as far as the oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage. Page 1621 (Book Page): those inferior are the infrahyoid muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid). Page 1784 (Book Page): Depression: The sternothyroid, the sternohyoid, and the omohyoid muscles.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Dual Innervation of the Digastric Muscle
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoes an elective surgical procedure in the submandibular region. The surgeon must carefully identify the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. Which of the following nerves provides the motor innervation to this specific muscle belly?
options: Ansa cervicalis from the cervical plexus
Main trunk of the facial nerve as it emerges from the stylomastoid foramen
Cervical branch of the facial nerve
C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve
Mylohyoid nerve from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve
correctOption: Main trunk of the facial nerve as it emerges from the stylomastoid foramen
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies most of the infrahyoid (strap) muscles, including the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid, but not the suprahyoid digastric muscle.

The facial nerve (CN VII) supplies the muscles of the second pharyngeal arch, which includes the posterior belly of the digastric and the stylohyoid muscle. It provides this supply as it emerges from the stylomastoid foramen.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve primarily supplies the platysma muscle in the neck, not the digastric muscle.
C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve supply the geniohyoid and thyrohyoid muscles, which are suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles respectively, but not the digastric.

The mylohyoid nerve (a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve from V3) supplies the anterior belly of the digastric, not the posterior belly. These two bellies have different embryological origins (first vs. second arch).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Digastric Posterior belly ... Nerve supply: Facial nerve.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: In contrasting the innervation patterns of the 'strap muscles' of the neck, which muscle is uniquely innervated by fibers from the first cervical (C1) spinal nerve that travel with the hypoglossal nerve, rather than by the ansa cervicalis proper?
options: Thyrohyoid
Omohyoid (inferior belly)
Omohyoid (superior belly)
Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid is unique among infrahyoids as it receives C1 fibers that hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve before branching off directly to the muscle.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop (inferior root).
The superior belly of the omohyoid is innervated by the superior root of the ansa cervicalis.
The sternohyoid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1-C3).
The sternothyroid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles. Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: During the first stage of deglutition (swallowing), the bolus of food must be pushed backward into the pharynx. This requires the elevation of the hyoid bone and the floor of the mouth. Which muscle, arising from the inner surface of the mandible, primarily forms the muscular floor of the mouth to support this action?
options: Geniohyoid
Mylohyoid
Anterior belly of digastric
Genioglossus
Stylohyoid
correctOption: Mylohyoid
optionExplanations: The geniohyoid lies superior to the mylohyoid but is a narrow muscle near the midline rather than a broad floor-forming sheet.
The mylohyoid muscle is a flat sheet that originates from the mylohyoid line of the mandible and meets its partner at a midline raphe, effectively forming the floor of the mouth.
The anterior belly of the digastric is a cord-like muscle that sits inferior to the mylohyoid; it does not form the broad floor of the mouth.
The genioglossus is a tongue muscle; while it sits on the floor of the mouth, the mylohyoid is the actual structural floor.
The stylohyoid is a narrow muscle that originates from the styloid process and does not contribute to the floor of the mouth.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1503 (Book Page): The mylohyoid line is an oblique ridge... [Page 1718 (Book Page)] The lateral wall of the vestibule is formed by the cheek... the anterior two thirds of the tongue and the reflection of the mucous membrane... largely form the floor.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A 45-year-old female undergoes a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goiter. Postoperatively, she is hemodynamically stable (BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 72 bpm). However, the surgeon notes that during the procedure, the branch of C1 that travels with the twelfth cranial nerve before descending to the thyrohyoid muscle was inadvertently injured. What is the most likely functional deficit the patient will experience?
options: Inability to depress the hyoid bone
Inability to elevate the larynx
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle
Weakness in tongue protrusion
Loss of sensation to the laryngeal vestibule
correctOption: Inability to elevate the larynx
optionExplanations: While the thyrohyoid can depress the hyoid bone, its more clinically significant action in the context of neck surgery is the elevation of the larynx toward the hyoid.

The thyrohyoid is innervated by C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve. Its primary action is to elevate the larynx (thyroid cartilage) toward the hyoid bone, which is crucial for protecting the airway during swallowing.
The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, not C1 via the hypoglossal nerve.
Tongue protrusion is mediated by the genioglossus muscle, which is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve proper (CN XII), not the C1 fibers that merely travel with it to reach the neck muscles.
Sensation to the laryngeal vestibule is provided by the internal laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X), not the C1 fibers or the hypoglossal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid. ... [Page 1615 (Book Page) Table 12.5] Thyrohyoid ... Action: Elevates larynx or depresses hyoid bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A clinician is comparing the infrahyoid muscles to determine which one is an outlier regarding its nerve supply. Which muscle is innervated by the first cervical nerve (C1) via the hypoglossal nerve rather than the ansa cervicalis?
options: Omohyoid superior belly
Sternohyoid
Thyrohyoid
Sternothyroid
Omohyoid inferior belly
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The superior belly of the omohyoid is innervated by the superior root of the ansa cervicalis.
The sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1, 2, 3), which is the standard supply for most strap muscles.
Unlike the other three strap muscles supplied by the ansa cervicalis, the thyrohyoid (along with the geniohyoid) is supplied specifically by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
The sternothyroid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1, 2, 3) and is not the outlier in this group.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop, typically the inferior root.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Nerve to the thyrohyoid muscle (C1).

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: During the complex physiological loop of swallowing, the infrahyoid muscles must counteract the pull of the suprahyoid muscles. What is the primary functional result of the infrahyoid muscles depressing the hyoid bone after the bolus has passed the oropharyngeal isthmus?
options: It elevates the soft palate to seal the nasopharynx.
It rotates the arytenoid cartilages to open the rima glottidis.
It causes the tongue to protrude to clear the oral cavity.
It triggers the relaxation of the cricopharyngeus muscle.
It brings the hyoid bone and larynx back to their resting positions.
correctOption: It brings the hyoid bone and larynx back to their resting positions.
optionExplanations: Soft palate elevation is performed by the levator veli palatini, not the infrahyoid muscles.
Opening the rima glottidis is performed by the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle, not the infrahyoid muscles.
Tongue protrusion is an extrinsic muscle action (genioglossus) and is not a direct result of infrahyoid contraction.
Cricopharyngeus relaxation is a separate part of the involuntary phase of swallowing, largely mediated by the vagus nerve, not by hyoid depression.

The suprahyoid muscles elevate the hyoid during the start of swallowing. Once the bolus has cleared the pharynx, the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, omohyoid, etc.) contract to depress the hyoid and larynx back to the neutral position.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): The larynx and the laryngeal part of the pharynx are pulled upward by the contraction of the stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, thyrohyoid, and palatopharyngeus muscles... [Page 1615 (Book Page)] Sternohyoid... Action: Depresses hyoid bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoes a surgical procedure to remove a tumor in the submandibular region. During the dissection, the surgeon identifies the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. Which nerve must be preserved to maintain the motor function of this specific muscle belly?
options: Facial nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Mylohyoid nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: Facial nerve
optionExplanations: The posterior belly of the digastric develops from the second pharyngeal arch and is therefore innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle and provides sensory/taste fibers, but no motor fibers to the digastric muscle.
The mylohyoid nerve, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3), supplies the anterior belly of the digastric and the mylohyoid muscle, not the posterior belly.
The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid), not the suprahyoid group.
The hypoglossal nerve provides motor supply to the intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, but it does not directly innervate the digastric bellies.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Digastric (posterior belly) ... Nerve supply: Facial nerve.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: The omohyoid muscle is anatomically unique among the infrahyoid group because of its dual bellies and specific fascial relationship. Where is the intermediate tendon of the omohyoid typically held in place?
options: To the thyroid cartilage by the pretracheal fascia
To the clavicle by a loop of deep cervical fascia
To the sternum by the investing layer of fascia
To the hyoid bone by the thyrohyoid membrane
To the scapula by the suprascapular ligament
correctOption: To the clavicle by a loop of deep cervical fascia
optionExplanations: The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland and strap muscles, but the specific anchor for the omohyoid tendon is the clavicular attachment.
The omohyoid has a superior and inferior belly connected by an intermediate tendon. This tendon is held down to the clavicle by a pulley-like loop of the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
While the investing fascia is involved, it is specifically anchored to the clavicle, not the sternum, to redirect the pull of the inferior belly.
The thyrohyoid membrane connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone, but it does not anchor the omohyoid tendon.
The inferior belly originates from the upper margin of the scapula near the suprascapular notch, but the tendon itself is anchored more anteriorly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page) Table 12.5: Omohyoid: [Origin] Upper margin of scapula... [Insertion] Lower border of body of hyoid bone. ... [Page 1620 (Book Page)] Collectivelly referred to as strap muscles... [General Anatomy] The intermediate tendon is held to the clavicle by a fascial sling.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: During a physical examination, a medical student is asked to identify the 'strap muscles' of the neck. According to the classification based on their position relative to the hyoid bone, which of the following muscles is strictly classified as an infrahyoid muscle?
options: Mylohyoid
Sternothyroid
Digastric
Stylohyoid
Genioglossus
correctOption: Sternothyroid
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that forms the floor of the mouth.
The sternothyroid is a classic infrahyoid strap muscle, originating from the manubrium sterni and inserting onto the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
The digastric is a suprahyoid muscle with two bellies that both insert into an intermediate tendon attached to the hyoid.
The stylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that originates from the styloid process and inserts onto the hyoid bone.
The genioglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue, though it is located in the suprahyoid region.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
coreConcept: Clinical Impact of C1/Ansa Cervicalis Injury on Laryngeal Elevation
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoes a radical neck dissection for laryngeal carcinoma. During the procedure, the surgeon identifies the ansa cervicalis but inadvertently damages the superior root (C1). Which specific musculoskeletal deficit would most likely be observed post-operatively involving the larynx?
options: Weakness in depressing the floor of the mouth due to mylohyoid paralysis
Inability to depress the thyroid cartilage due to sternothyroid paralysis
Loss of the ability to tense the vocal cords due to cricothyroid paralysis
Inability to abduct the vocal folds due to posterior cricoarytenoid paralysis
Failure to elevate the larynx during swallowing due to thyrohyoid paralysis
correctOption: Failure to elevate the larynx during swallowing due to thyrohyoid paralysis
optionExplanations: The mylohyoid is innervated by the trigeminal nerve (CN V3). It is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the floor of the mouth; its function is independent of the cervical plexus and would not be impaired by an ansa cervicalis injury.

The sternothyroid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3). While a C1 injury would weaken the ansa, the specific laryngeal elevation deficit is more characteristically associated with the thyrohyoid, which relies entirely on C1.

Cricothyroid paralysis results from damage to the external laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus nerve (CN X). It is not innervated by the cervical plexus or ansa cervicalis, so it would remain unaffected by this specific injury.

The posterior cricoarytenoid is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (CN X). It is responsible for vocal fold abduction and is not related to the infrahyoid or suprahyoid cervical innervation.

The thyrohyoid muscle is essential for elevating the larynx during the involuntary phase of swallowing. Since it is innervated by C1 fibers hitchhiking with the hypoglossal nerve (which forms the superior root of the ansa cervicalis), damage to these fibers results in failure of laryngeal elevation.

optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid, although classified as an infrahyoid muscle, is innervated by C1 spinal fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before branching off, rather than via the ansa cervicalis loop.

The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle supplied by the trigeminal nerve (V3), not the ansa cervicalis or C1 via XII as described regarding strap muscles of the neck. The neck muscles listed as infrahyoid are supplied by cervical spinal nerves, not V3 directly as described for strap muscles of the neck. category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles of neck
statement: In the multi-step pathway of swallowing, the suprahyoid muscles must perform distinct movements. Which of the following pairs a muscle with its specific mechanical role during the pharyngeal phase of deglutition?
options: Stylohyoid: Depresses the thyroid cartilage to open the laryngeal inlet.
Thyrohyoid: Stabilizes the scapula to provide a base for neck flexion.
Sternothyroid: Elevates the larynx to the posterior surface of the epiglottis.
Omohyoid: Pulls the hyoid bone upward to assist the tongue.
Mylohyoid: Forms a rigid floor of the mouth and elevates the hyoid bone.
correctOption: Mylohyoid: Forms a rigid floor of the mouth and elevates the hyoid bone.
optionExplanations: The stylohyoid elevates and retracts the hyoid bone; it does not depress the thyroid cartilage.
The thyrohyoid elevates the larynx toward the hyoid; it has no attachment to the scapula (the omohyoid does).
The sternothyroid depresses the larynx and thyroid cartilage; laryngeal elevation is performed by the stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, and palatopharyngeus muscles.
The omohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle that depresses the hyoid bone, not elevates it.
The mylohyoid acts as the diaphragm of the floor of the mouth; its contraction elevates the floor of the mouth and the hyoid bone, pushing the tongue against the palate to move the bolus.
