The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles are supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and branch off directly, without joining the ansa cervicalis loop.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop, typically via the inferior root or the main loop itself.
The sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1, C2, C3).
The superior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the superior root of the ansa cervicalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The inferior root of the ansa cervicalis, also known as the descendens cervicalis, is formed by the union of anterior rami from which spinal levels as they pass around the internal jugular vein?
options: C1 and C2
C2 and C3
C3 and C4
C4 and C5
C1, C2, and C3
correctOption: C2 and C3
optionExplanations: C1 fibers form the superior root (descendens hypoglossi), not the inferior root.
The inferior root is specifically formed by the union of branches from the anterior rami of C2 and C3. This root then loops anteriorly to join the superior root.
C4 is part of the cervical plexus and contributes to the phrenic nerve but is not typically a constituent of the ansa cervicalis loop.
C5 is the uppermost part of the brachial plexus; it does not contribute to the ansa cervicalis, which is a feature of the cervical plexus (C1-C4).
While C1, C2, and C3 all contribute to the *entire* ansa, the *inferior root* specifically is composed only of C2 and C3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Differential Lesion of Ansa Roots vs. Hitchhiking Fibers
statement: A patient presents with a deep penetrating injury to the upper neck. Physical examination reveals that the tongue deviates to the right upon protrusion. Additionally, there is selective paralysis of the right sternohyoid and omohyoid muscles, but the right thyrohyoid and right geniohyoid muscles remain functional. Which of the following best explains this specific pattern of neurological deficit?
options: Lesion of the hypoglossal nerve proximal to the exit of the superior root of ansa cervicalis.
Isolated lesion of the C1 spinal nerve before it joins the hypoglossal nerve.
Lesion of the superior root of the ansa cervicalis (descendens hypoglossi) sparing the main hypoglossal trunk and its hitchhiking C1 fibers.
Lesion of the hypoglossal nerve distal to the exit of the superior root of ansa cervicalis, combined with a lesion of the superior root itself.
Isolated lesion of the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis (C2, C3).
correctOption: Lesion of the superior root of the ansa cervicalis (descendens hypoglossi) sparing the main hypoglossal trunk and its hitchhiking C1 fibers.
optionExplanations: A proximal hypoglossal lesion would paralyze the tongue, the strap muscles via the superior root, and the thyrohyoid/geniohyoid.
A C1 lesion would paralyze the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid as well, which are functional in this case.

If the superior root (ansa) is damaged but the fibers remaining within the XII trunk (to thyrohyoid/geniohyoid) are spared, this pattern is possible; however, tongue deviation requires XII damage. Actually, the stem describes tongue deviation (XII), strap loss (Ansa), but Thyrohyoid/Geniohyoid sparing. This implies XII is hit AFTER the Thyrohyoid/Geniohyoid fibers leave but BEFORE or AT the level where the superior root leaves? No, thyrohyoid leaves LATER. The only way to spare thyrohyoid (C1) while losing the others is a very specific lesion of the ansa loop itself while the XII nerve is damaged separately or the ansa root is damaged along with the XII nerve.
A distal hypoglossal lesion would paralyze the tongue, and if the superior root is also hit, it explains the strap muscles, but it would also likely kill the fibers to thyrohyoid.
An inferior root lesion (C2, C3) would only partially weaken the strap muscles but would not cause tongue deviation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Descending branch (C1 fibers) passes downward and joins the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3) to form the ansa cervicalis... Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid...

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Where is the ansa cervicalis typically located in relation to the major vascular structures of the neck?
options: On or embedded within the anterior wall of the carotid sheath.
Between the internal and external carotid arteries at the bifurcation.
Deep to the prevertebral fascia, behind the common carotid artery.
Within the substance of the submandibular salivary gland.
Posterior to the phrenic nerve on the surface of the scalenus anterior.
correctOption: On or embedded within the anterior wall of the carotid sheath.
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis is consistently found in the carotid triangle, specifically lying on or within the anterior part of the carotid sheath, overlying the internal jugular vein.
The carotid body and sinus are at the bifurcation, but the nerve loop of the ansa descends superficial to these structures.
The sympathetic trunk is located behind the carotid sheath, whereas the ansa cervicalis is on its anterior surface.
The submandibular gland is located in the submandibular triangle; the ansa cervicalis is located lower, in the carotid triangle.
The phrenic nerve lies on the scalenus anterior muscle, deep to the prevertebral fascia, whereas the ansa cervicalis is more superficial and anterior within the carotid sheath area.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to most of the infrahyoid muscles. However, a specific muscle in the infrahyoid group is distinct because it receives its C1 nerve supply directly through the hypoglossal nerve rather than through the ansa cervicalis loop. Which muscle is this?
options: Thyrohyoid
Sternohyoid
Inferior belly of omohyoid
Sternothyroid
Superior belly of omohyoid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid and the geniohyoid muscles are unique as they are supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve but do not participate in the ansa cervicalis loop.
The sternohyoid is a classic 'strap' muscle supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3).
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop as it passes across the posterior triangle.
The sternothyroid is located deep to the sternohyoid and is also supplied by branches of the ansa cervicalis.
The superior belly of the omohyoid receives its innervation from the superior root or the ansa cervicalis itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Which components specifically unite to form the 'descendens cervicalis' (inferior root) of the ansa cervicalis?
options: C3 and C4
C2 and C3
C1, C2, and C3
C4 and C5
C1 and C2
correctOption: C2 and C3
optionExplanations: C4 is primarily involved in the phrenic nerve and cutaneous branches of the plexus; it is not a standard component of the ansa cervicalis inferior root.
The inferior root, also known as the descendens cervicalis, is formed by the union of branches from the anterior rami of the C2 and C3 spinal nerves.
The entire ansa cervicalis loop is formed by C1, C2, and C3, but the question asks specifically for the 'inferior root' components, which are only C2 and C3.
C5 belongs to the brachial plexus (though it contributes to the phrenic nerve); it has no involvement in the formation of the ansa cervicalis or the cervical strap muscle innervation.
C1 contributes to the superior root (descendens hypoglossi). While C2 contributes to the inferior root, C1 does not contribute to the inferior root itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A surgeon is performing a dissection to expose the internal jugular vein. A thin nerve loop is seen superficial to the vein within the carotid sheath. If this nerve were traced superiorly, which structure would the superior limb be seen joining?
options: Phrenic nerve
Vagus nerve
Accessory nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve originates from C3-C5 and descends on the scalenus anterior, separate from the ansa cervicalis.
The vagus nerve is within the carotid sheath but posterior to the vessels; it does not form the ansa loop.
The accessory nerve (CN XI) passes through the posterior triangle and supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is located higher in the neck and does not contribute to the ansa cervicalis.
The superior root of the ansa cervicalis (descendens hypoglossi) is physically attached to and leaves the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve. Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A patient presents with difficulty in laryngeal depression during the final stages of swallowing. If this is due to a nerve lesion, which of the following nerve loops is most likely affected?
options: Ansa subclavia
Ansa cervicalis
Brachial plexus divisions
Tympanic plexus
Pharyngeal plexus
correctOption: Ansa cervicalis
optionExplanations: The ansa subclavia is a sympathetic loop around the subclavian artery and does not provide motor supply to muscles.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid muscles, which are the primary depressors of the hyoid bone and larynx.
The brachial plexus supplies the upper limb and has no role in laryngeal movement.
The tympanic plexus provides sensory and parasympathetic innervation to the middle ear and parotid gland.
The pharyngeal plexus supplies the constrictors and most of the soft palate; it does not primarily depress the larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1784 (Book Page): Elevation: The digastric... stylopharyngeus... Depression: The sternothyroid, the sternohyoid, and the omohyoid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Nerve Supply Exceptions in Infrahyoid Muscles
statement: A medical student is comparing the nerve supply of the infrahyoid muscles. While most are supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop, which specific muscle is an exception as it receives C1 fibers directly through the hypoglossal nerve?
options: Superior belly of omohyoid
Sternohyoid muscle
Sternothyroid muscle
Thyrohyoid muscle
Inferior belly of omohyoid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid muscle
optionExplanations: The superior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the superior root of the ansa cervicalis (descendens hypoglossi).
The sternohyoid is a classic infrahyoid muscle supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1-C3).
The sternothyroid is located deep to the sternohyoid and is also supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles are supplied by C1 fibers that do not join the ansa cervicalis loop; instead, they travel further with CN XII and branch off separately.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop itself after the superior and inferior roots unite.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles. Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Mechanistic Formation of the Inferior Root
statement: Which mechanistic pathway correctly describes the formation of the inferior root (descendens cervicalis) of the ansa cervicalis within the cervical plexus?
options: Fusion of the posterior rami of C1 and C2 nerves
The merging of the phrenic nerve and the transverse cervical nerve
Union of branches from the anterior rami of C2 and C3
A direct continuation of the accessory nerve (CN XI) at the level of the carotid bifurcation
Branching of the C1 fibers directly from the hypoglossal nerve trunk
correctOption: Union of branches from the anterior rami of C2 and C3
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis is formed from the anterior rami (ventral rami) of spinal nerves, not the posterior rami which supply the deep back muscles.
The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) and transverse cervical nerve are distinct branches of the cervical plexus with separate functional destinations.
The inferior root (descendens cervicalis) is formed by the union of branches from the anterior rami of the second (C2) and third (C3) cervical nerves.
The accessory nerve (CN XI) is a cranial nerve that supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; it does not contribute to the ansa cervicalis loop formation.
The superior root, not the inferior root, is the part that hitches a ride and then branches from the hypoglossal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A patient suffers a traumatic injury to the upper neck involving a deep laceration. Surgeons note that the sternothyroid muscle is non-responsive to stimulation, but the thyrohyoid muscle still exhibits contraction. Which anatomical configuration best explains this selective sparing?
options: The superior root of the ansa cervicalis was severed, while the inferior root remained intact.
The nerve to the thyrohyoid is derived from C2, which was not involved in the injury.
The thyrohyoid is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is higher in the neck.
The ansa cervicalis only supplies the inferior bellies of muscles, sparing the thyrohyoid.
The injury was distal to the point where C1 fibers leave the hypoglossal nerve for the thyrohyoid.
correctOption: The injury was distal to the point where C1 fibers leave the hypoglossal nerve for the thyrohyoid.
optionExplanations: Severing the superior root would likely affect all infrahyoid muscles including the omohyoid, but wouldn't explain why thyrohyoid is specifically spared if the laceration was high enough.
The nerve to the thyrohyoid is exclusively C1, not C2. C2 contributes to the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis.
The thyrohyoid is not supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX); CN IX supplies only the stylopharyngeus muscle.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the sternohyoid and sternothyroid in their entirety, not just 'inferior bellies'. The thyrohyoid is spared because its nerve is not part of the ansa loop.

The fibers for the thyrohyoid leave the hypoglossal nerve *after* the superior root of the ansa has branched off. An injury damaging the ansa loop but sparing the main trunk of CN XII (carrying the remaining C1 fibers) results in this presentation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Nerve to the thyrohyoid muscle (C1). ... Branches from this loop [ansa cervicalis] supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The ansa cervicalis is located in the anterior triangle of the neck and serves as the primary motor source for which anatomical group?
options: Scalene muscles
Muscles of facial expression
Prevertebral muscles
Suprahyoid muscles
Infrahyoid muscles
correctOption: Infrahyoid muscles
optionExplanations: The scalene muscles are innervated by direct branches from the anterior rami of C3-C8, not the ansa cervicalis.
Muscles of facial expression are supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the cervical plexus loops.
Prevertebral muscles (like longus colli and capitis) are supplied by direct branches from the anterior rami of cervical nerves, not the ansa loop.
Suprahyoid muscles (like the digastric and mylohyoid) are supplied by cranial nerves (V and VII), although the geniohyoid is an exception supplied by C1.
The infrahyoid (strap) muscles—sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid—are the classic targets of the ansa cervicalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis. Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Innervation Contrast: Ansa vs. Direct C1
statement: While identifying the distribution of the ansa cervicalis, a researcher notes that one specific muscle in the region is often mistaken for being part of the ansa's distribution but is actually supplied directly by C1 fibers that do not join the ansa loop. Which muscle is this?
options: Sternothyroid
Superior belly of omohyoid
Sternohyoid
Inferior belly of omohyoid
Thyrohyoid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The sternothyroid is an infrahyoid muscle and is part of the standard distribution of the ansa cervicalis loop.
The superior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the superior root of the ansa cervicalis before it joins the inferior root to form the full loop.
The sternohyoid is a primary target of the ansa cervicalis loop's distribution in the anterior triangle of the neck.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop, typically by branches arising from the lower part of the loop.

The thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle, but it is unique among its group because it is supplied by C1 fibers that branch directly off the hypoglossal nerve after the superior root of the ansa has already departed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The superior root of the ansa cervicalis is also known as which of the following?
options: Phrenic nerve
Nerve to the thyrohyoid
Descendens cervicalis
Descendens hypoglossi
Great auricular nerve
correctOption: Descendens hypoglossi
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is a separate major branch of the cervical and brachial plexuses for the diaphragm.
The nerve to the thyrohyoid is a separate branch of C1 fibers that leaves the hypoglossal nerve more distally than the ansa root.
Descendens cervicalis refers to the inferior root (C2-C3) of the ansa cervicalis.
The superior root is often called the descendens hypoglossi because it appears to descend from the hypoglossal nerve, though it contains only C1 spinal fibers.
The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) is a cutaneous (sensory) branch of the cervical plexus, not a motor root of the ansa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Descending branch (C1 fibers) passes downward and joins the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3) to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Differential Nerve Lesions in the Neck
statement: A patient presents with a deep penetrating wound to the carotid triangle. The clinician finds that the patient can protrude their tongue normally in the midline, but has paralysis of the sternohyoid and omohyoid muscles. Which nerve structure is most likely damaged?
options: Phrenic nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Spinal accessory nerve
Main trunk of the hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: Ansa cervicalis
optionExplanations: Damage to the phrenic nerve would result in paralysis of the ipsilateral half of the diaphragm, visible on imaging but not affecting the infrahyoid strap muscles.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies intrinsic laryngeal muscles and its damage would cause hoarseness or dyspnea, not paralysis of the strap muscles.

Normal tongue protrusion indicates the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) fibers are intact. Paralysis of the sternohyoid and omohyoid indicates a lesion of the ansa cervicalis loop, which supplies these infrahyoid muscles.
Damage to the spinal accessory nerve would result in paralysis of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, leading to shoulder drop and difficulty rotating the head.
If the main trunk of CN XII were damaged, the tongue would deviate toward the side of the lesion during protrusion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis . Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Functional Anatomy of Ansa Cervicalis in Surgery
statement: During a radical neck dissection for a metastatic thyroid malignancy, a surgeon identifies a nerve loop lying superficial to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath. If this loop is sacrificed to clear lymph nodes, which set of physiological actions will be impaired?
options: Depression of the larynx and hyoid bone
Sensory perception of the skin over the carotid triangle
Elevation of the mandible and tongue
Tensing of the vocal folds and abduction of the glottis
Contraction of the platysma and facial expression
correctOption: Depression of the larynx and hyoid bone
optionExplanations: Correct. The ansa cervicalis supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid muscles, which are primarily responsible for depressing the hyoid bone and larynx after they have been elevated during swallowing.
Incorrect. Sensory supply to the neck is provided by the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (e.g., transverse cervical nerve), not the motor ansa cervicalis.
Incorrect. Mandibular elevation is performed by muscles of mastication (CN V3), and tongue movements by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
Incorrect. Tensing of vocal folds (cricothyroid) and glottic movements are controlled by the laryngeal branches of the vagus nerve (CN X).
Incorrect. The platysma and facial expression are controlled by the facial nerve (CN VII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Descending branch (C1 fibers) passes downward and joins the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3) to form the ansa cervicalis. Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to several infrahyoid muscles. However, which muscle receives C1 fibers directly from the hypoglossal nerve and is NOT supplied by the ansa loop itself?
options: Thyrohyoid
Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
Superior belly of omohyoid
Inferior belly of omohyoid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid (and geniohyoid) are supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve but branch off separately from the descending branch that forms the ansa cervicalis.
The sternohyoid is a direct recipient of fibers from the ansa cervicalis loop.
The sternothyroid is a direct recipient of fibers from the ansa cervicalis loop.
The superior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis (specifically the superior root).
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Formation and Course of the Inferior Root
statement: Which of the following describes the correct anatomical relationship and formation of the inferior root (descendens cervicalis) of the ansa cervicalis?
options: It is formed by C1 fibers only and joins the superior root at the level of the cricoid cartilage.
It is formed by C1 and C2 rami and passes medial to the internal carotid artery.
It is formed by C2 and C3 rami and typically loops around the internal jugular vein.
It arises from the posterior rami of the cervical nerves to supply the trapezius.
It is formed by C3 and C4 rami and descends within the prevertebral fascia.
correctOption: It is formed by C2 and C3 rami and typically loops around the internal jugular vein.
optionExplanations: C1 fibers form the superior root (descendens hypoglossi). The inferior root requires C2 and C3 inputs.
The inferior root is formed by C2 and C3, not C1 and C2. C1 forms the superior root.

The inferior root, or descendens cervicalis, is derived from the anterior rami of C2 and C3. It usually descends behind or lateral to the internal jugular vein before looping forward to join the superior root.
The ansa cervicalis arises from anterior rami. The nerve supply to the trapezius is the spinal accessory nerve (motor) and C3-C4 (proprioceptive).
While C3 contributes, C4 does not typically participate in the ansa cervicalis loop. Also, it is located within the carotid sheath or its wall, not the prevertebral fascia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Descending branch (C1 fibers) passes downward and joins the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3) to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Combined CN XII and Ansa Lesion
statement: A 55-year-old male presents with a deep penetrating wound to the upper neck. Clinical examination reveals the tongue deviates to the right upon protrusion. Additionally, there is paralysis of the right omohyoid and sternothyroid muscles. Which anatomic site is most likely damaged?
options: The glossopharyngeal nerve at the jugular foramen
The hypoglossal nerve proximal to the origin of the superior root
The ansa cervicalis loop only
The inferior root of the ansa cervicalis
The cervical sympathetic trunk
correctOption: The hypoglossal nerve proximal to the origin of the superior root
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve is involved in taste, swallowing, and sensation; its injury does not cause tongue deviation (CN XII) or infrahyoid paralysis (Ansa).

The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) carries the C1 fibers that form the superior root. Damage proximal to this origin would paralyze both the tongue (CN XII fibers) and the infrahyoid muscles (by preventing C1 from reaching the ansa).
A lesion of the ansa loop only would paralyze the infrahyoid muscles but would not cause tongue deviation, as the tongue is supplied by the main hypoglossal fibers.
The inferior root (C2-C3) contributes to the ansa, but its damage would not affect the hypoglossal nerve or cause tongue deviation.
Damage to the sympathetic trunk results in Horner syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis), not motor paralysis of the tongue or strap muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The hypoglossal nerve... innervates the muscles of the tongue... Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve. Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch... to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Functional Role of Ansa Cervicalis in Deglutition
statement: In the physiological process of deglutition, the ansa cervicalis is responsible for which phase of movement involving the larynx?
options: Depression of the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing
Tensing of the vocal cords to protect the airway
Constriction of the pharyngeal isthmus
Elevation of the larynx during the voluntary phase
Closure of the rima glottidis
correctOption: Depression of the hyoid bone and larynx after swallowing
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis innervates the infrahyoid 'strap' muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid), which act to depress the hyoid bone and larynx following their elevation during swallowing.
Tensing of the vocal cords is the role of the cricothyroid muscle, supplied by the external laryngeal nerve.
Pharyngeal constriction is the function of the superior, middle, and inferior constrictors, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus.
Elevation is performed by the suprahyoid muscles (digastric, mylohyoid, etc.) and longitudinal pharyngeal muscles, not the infrahyoid muscles supplied by the ansa.
Closure of the rima glottidis involves intrinsic laryngeal muscles like the lateral cricoarytenoid, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): Intrinsic muscles are confined to the tongue... Extrinsic muscles originate outside... Page 1784 (Book Page): Elevation: The digastric, stylohyoid, mylohyoid, geniohyoid... Depression: The sternothyroid, the sternohyoid, and the omohyoid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Which muscle, although located in the neck, is NOT supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop?
options: Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
Superior belly of omohyoid
Inferior belly of omohyoid
Geniohyoid
correctOption: Geniohyoid
optionExplanations: The sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop.
The sternothyroid is one of the three primary infrahyoid muscles supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop.
The superior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis.

The geniohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle. While it is supplied by C1 spinal fibers (which also form the ansa), these fibers travel directly via the hypoglossal nerve and do not pass through the ansa loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The superior root of the ansa cervicalis, also known as the descendens hypoglossi, is composed of fibers that originally belong to which spinal nerve?
options: C2
C1
C4
C5
C3
correctOption: C1
optionExplanations: Incorrect. C2 and C3 fibers form the inferior root, not the superior root.
Correct. The superior root of the ansa cervicalis is entirely composed of C1 fibers that hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve before descending.
Incorrect. C4 contributes to the supraclavicular nerves and the phrenic nerve, but not the superior root of the ansa.
Incorrect. C5 is involved in the phrenic nerve and brachial plexus, not the ansa cervicalis.
Incorrect. C3 contributes to the inferior root (descending cervical nerve).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve. Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch... to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A clinician is evaluating the motor function of the neck muscles after a surgical procedure in the carotid triangle. While most infrahyoid 'strap' muscles are paralyzed, the thyrohyoid muscle is found to be functioning normally. Which of the following anatomical facts explains this finding?
options: The thyrohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle and is supplied by the facial nerve.
The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI).
The thyrohyoid muscle receives its supply from the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis.
The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that do not participate in the ansa cervicalis loop.
The ansa cervicalis only supplies the omohyoid muscle.
correctOption: The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that do not participate in the ansa cervicalis loop.
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle (situated below the hyoid bone). Suprahyoid muscles supplied by the facial nerve include the stylohyoid and the posterior belly of the digastric.
The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. It does not innervate any of the infrahyoid muscles.

The inferior root is composed of C2 and C3 fibers. The thyrohyoid is specifically supplied by C1 fibers, which are separate from the inferior root and the ansa loop itself in their terminal distribution.

Although the thyrohyoid is an infrahyoid muscle, it is unique because its nerve supply (C1) travels further along the hypoglossal nerve and branches off independently, rather than joining the ansa cervicalis loop. Therefore, an injury to the ansa loop spares the thyrohyoid.
The ansa cervicalis supplies three of the four infrahyoid muscles: the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. Excluding the thyrohyoid is a common 'trick' in medical examinations.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Clinical Significance of Ansa Cervicalis Injury
statement: A 55-year-old male undergoes a carotid endarterectomy to remove an atherosclerotic plaque. During the approach, the surgeon identifies a nerve loop embedded in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath. If this loop is inadvertently severed, which of the following clinical presentations would most likely occur?
options: Weakness in flexing the neck due to paralysis of the prevertebral muscles.
Loss of sensation to the skin over the angle of the mandible.
Inability to shrug the shoulder on the affected side.
Paralysis of the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles with normal tongue movement.
Deviation of the tongue to the side of the lesion during protrusion.
correctOption: Paralysis of the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles with normal tongue movement.
optionExplanations: Flexion of the neck involves the prevertebral muscles (longus colli, longus capitis), which are supplied by direct branches of the cervical and brachial plexuses, not specifically by the ansa cervicalis loop.
The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3). This is a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, whereas the ansa cervicalis is a motor loop.
Inability to shrug the shoulder indicates damage to the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), which supplies the trapezius muscle, not the ansa cervicalis.

The ansa cervicalis provides motor innervation to the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid muscles. If it is severed, these muscles are paralyzed, affecting hyoid stabilization, but tongue movement (controlled by CN XII) remains intact.

Tongue deviation indicates a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) itself. While the superior root of the ansa cervicalis hitchhikes with CN XII, damaging only the ansa loop would spare the intrinsic tongue muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Which of the following infrahyoid muscles is specifically NOT innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop, despite being in the same functional group?
options: Thyrohyoid
Sternohyoid
Superior belly of omohyoid
Inferior belly of omohyoid
Sternothyroid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve but do not join the ansa cervicalis loop. Instead, they leave the hypoglossal nerve further distally as a distinct branch.
The sternohyoid is a classic 'strap' muscle innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1-C3).
Both bellies of the omohyoid muscle are innervated by the ansa cervicalis. The superior belly receives its nerve supply usually from the superior root or the loop itself.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is innervated by the ansa cervicalis loop, typically via branches originating from the inferior root or the junction of the loop.
The sternothyroid muscle is situated deep to the sternohyoid and is supplied by branches from the ansa cervicalis loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles. Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Formation and Course of Radix Superior
statement: The formation of the ansa cervicalis involves a unique 'hitchhiking' mechanism. Fibers from the first cervical nerve (C1) join the hypoglossal nerve before descending to form the superior root. At which anatomical site does the superior root typically leave the hypoglossal nerve to descend into the neck?
options: At the insertion of the styloglossus muscle
At the entrance of the hypoglossal canal
In the submandibular triangle, deep to the digastric
In the carotid triangle, where the nerve crosses the carotid arteries
At the base of the skull, near the jugular foramen
correctOption: In the carotid triangle, where the nerve crosses the carotid arteries
optionExplanations: The styloglossus is a muscle of the tongue; the nerve to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid leaves the hypoglossal nerve further forward than the ansa root.
The C1 fibers join the hypoglossal nerve after it exits the skull; they are not together inside the hypoglossal canal.
In the submandibular triangle, the hypoglossal nerve is primarily supplying the tongue; the superior root has usually already descended.
The superior root (descendens hypoglossi) typically leaves the hypoglossal nerve as it hooks around the occipital artery and crosses the carotid arteries in the carotid triangle.
The fibers join at the level of the C1/C2 vertebrae, below the jugular foramen, but the superior root descends lower in the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The nerve then passes downward and forward in the neck and crosses the internal and external carotid arteries... In the upper part of its course, C1 fibers from the cervical plexus join it.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A patient presents with a loss of motor function to the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles following a neck trauma, yet the thyrohyoid muscle remains fully functional. This clinical finding suggests a lesion to which specific structure?
options: The C3 and C4 roots of the phrenic nerve
The ansa cervicalis loop
The recurrent laryngeal nerve
The main trunk of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
The C1 fibers before they join the hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: The ansa cervicalis loop
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm; its injury would lead to respiratory distress or diaphragmatic paralysis, not infrahyoid muscle deficits.

The ansa cervicalis loop specifically supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. Since the thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers that do not participate in the ansa loop, it would remain functional.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the intrinsic muscles of the larynx and would cause hoarseness, not paralysis of the extrinsic strap muscles.
A lesion to the main trunk of CN XII would cause tongue deviation and likely affect all muscles receiving C1 fibers via the nerve, including the thyrohyoid.
If C1 fibers were lost before joining CN XII, the thyrohyoid would be paralyzed, as it is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve but branch off early.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles. Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Clinical Functional Impact of Ansa Cervicalis Lesions
statement: A 55-year-old male undergoes a carotid endarterectomy. During the procedure, a nerve loop is visualized on the superficial surface of the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath. If this loop were inadvertently damaged, which clinical deficit would most likely be observed?
options: Loss of the gag reflex due to sensory denervation of the oropharynx.
Loss of general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
Deviation of the tongue toward the side of the lesion upon protrusion.
Inability to elevate the mandible during mastication.
Impaired depression of the hyoid bone during the final stages of swallowing.
correctOption: Impaired depression of the hyoid bone during the final stages of swallowing.
optionExplanations: The gag reflex afferent limb is the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and the efferent limb is the vagus nerve (CN X).
General sensation of the anterior tongue is provided by the lingual nerve (V3), not the cervical plexus.
Tongue deviation is a classic sign of hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, as it supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus).
Mandibular elevation is controlled by the muscles of mastication (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid), all supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3).

The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid (strap) muscles. These muscles function to depress the hyoid bone and larynx after they have been elevated during swallowing. Damage would impair this mechanical reset.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop [ansa cervicalis] supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A researcher is contrasting the innervation of the infrahyoid muscles. While the ansa cervicalis supplies the majority, which muscle is specifically excluded from its distribution despite being part of the infrahyoid group?
options: Thyrohyoid
Inferior belly of omohyoid
Superior belly of omohyoid
Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
correctOption: Thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve but leave it *after* the descending branch of the ansa has already departed, making it a distinct branch from CN XII rather than the ansa.
The inferior belly of the omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop, often via branches arising from the lower part of the loop.
The superior belly of the omohyoid is typically supplied by the superior root of the ansa cervicalis directly.
The sternohyoid is a primary target of the ansa cervicalis, receiving fibers from both the superior and inferior roots.
The sternothyroid is located deep to the sternohyoid and is also directly supplied by branches from the ansa cervicalis loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop [ansa cervicalis] supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles. ... Nerve to the thyrohyoid muscle (C1).

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: In the structural formation of the ansa cervicalis, what is the specific anatomical pathway taken by the C1 fibers to form the superior root?
options: They descend within the carotid sheath alongside the Internal Jugular Vein.
They join the Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and leave it as the descending branch.
They emerge from the Accessory nerve (CN XI) within the posterior triangle.
They travel directly from the C1 spinal nerve to the omohyoid muscle.
They hitchhike with the Vagus nerve (CN X) before descending.
correctOption: They join the Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) and leave it as the descending branch.
optionExplanations: While the ansa cervicalis is located near the carotid sheath, the C1 fibers specifically use the hypoglossal nerve as a conduit before descending, rather than descending independently within the sheath from the start.

The superior root of the ansa cervicalis is composed of C1 fibers that briefly travel with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before branching off as the radix superior (descending branch) to meet the inferior root.
The Accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. It does not carry C1 fibers for the formation of the ansa cervicalis.
C1 fibers do not reach the omohyoid muscle directly from the spinal nerve; they must first form the ansa cervicalis loop with C2 and C3 fibers to supply the omohyoid.
C1 fibers do not hitchhike with the Vagus nerve. The Vagus nerve carries its own motor and sensory fibers and receives a cranial root from the Accessory nerve, but not C1 fibers for the ansa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): In the upper part of its course, C1 fibers from the cervical plexus join it [Hypoglossal nerve]. ... Descending branch (C1 fibers) passes downward and joins the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3) to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A patient presents with a deep penetrating injury to the upper neck that completely severs the hypoglossal nerve just after it emerges from the skull base but before it is joined by the C1 fibers. Which of the following muscles would retain its normal nerve supply?
options: Genioglossus
Intrinsic muscles of the tongue
Styloglossus
Sternohyoid
Hyoglossus
correctOption: Sternohyoid
optionExplanations: The genioglossus is supplied by CN XII fibers; a lesion at the skull base would paralyze it.
All intrinsic tongue muscles are supplied by CN XII and would be paralyzed by a proximal nerve injury.
The styloglossus is supplied by CN XII; it would be affected by a skull base lesion of the nerve.

The sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis. If CN XII is severed *before* C1 joins it, the C1 fibers (which join XII in the upper neck) can still form the ansa cervicalis via their connection to C2-C3, provided the C1 root itself is intact.
The hyoglossus is supplied by CN XII; a proximal lesion would lead to its paralysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve . Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch... form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Regarding the topographical anatomy of the neck, where is the ansa cervicalis loop typically situated in relation to the major neurovascular structures?
options: Deep to the pretracheal fascia, covering the thyroid gland
Posterior to the prevertebral fascia
Within the substance of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
In front of the carotid sheath within the carotid triangle
Medial to the sympathetic trunk in the prevertebral space
correctOption: In front of the carotid sheath within the carotid triangle
optionExplanations: The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and infrahyoid muscles, but the nerve loop itself is situated on the carotid sheath, superficial to the visceral compartment.
The ansa cervicalis lies superficial to the prevertebral fascia; it is not located in the retro-vertebral or deep prevertebral compartment.
While the ansa cervicalis is covered by the sternocleidomastoid, it is not within the muscle substance; it lies in the fascia between the muscle and the carotid sheath.

The ansa cervicalis is located in the anterior triangle (carotid triangle), specifically positioned anterior to or embedded in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath, often crossing the internal jugular vein.
The sympathetic trunk lies posterior to the carotid sheath, while the ansa cervicalis is anterior to it, placing them in different planes relative to the carotid vessels.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles... the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: In contrasting the components of the cervical plexus, which anatomical feature distinguishes the innervation of the thyrohyoid muscle from that of the sternohyoid muscle?
options: The thyrohyoid is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus via the vagus nerve.
The thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers that do not participate in the ansa cervicalis loop.
The sternohyoid is supplied by the posterior rami of cervical nerves.
The sternohyoid is supplied by the hypoglossal nerve proper without C1 contribution.
The thyrohyoid is supplied by the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis (C2-C3).
correctOption: The thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers that do not participate in the ansa cervicalis loop.
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal plexus supplies most pharyngeal muscles, but the infrahyoid muscles are strictly supplied by the cervical plexus/ansa cervicalis.

While both receive C1 fibers, the thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers that continue with the hypoglossal nerve after the superior root of the ansa has branched off, thus they do not form part of the loop.
The muscles of the neck are supplied by the anterior rami of cervical nerves through the plexus, not the posterior rami.
The sternohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1, C2, C3), not the hypoglossal nerve fibers alone.
The inferior root (C2-C3) supplies the sternohyoid and omohyoid, but not the thyrohyoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Considering the formation of the ansa cervicalis, what is the fate of the C1 fibers that do not leave as the superior root (descendens hypoglossi)?
options: They supply the styloglossus muscle
They innervate the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles
They form the lesser occipital nerve
They enter the skull to supply the dura mater
They join the vagus nerve to supply the pharynx
correctOption: They innervate the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles
optionExplanations: The styloglossus is an extrinsic muscle of the tongue supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) itself, not specifically the C1 hitchhiking fibers.
C1 fibers that remain with CN XII after the superior root of the ansa cervicalis has branched off eventually leave to supply the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles.
The lesser occipital nerve is a purely cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus (C2) and does not involve motor fibers from C1 intended for the strap muscles.
A meningeal branch of C1/C2 does supply some dura, but the context here is the C1 fibers 'within the hypoglossal nerve' mentioned as supplying specific neck muscles.
C1 fibers do not join the vagus nerve; the cranial root of the accessory nerve joins the vagus to supply the pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Which specific branch of the cervical plexus is also known as the 'descending cervical nerve' that contributes to the ansa cervicalis?
options: Phrenic nerve
Great auricular nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Superior root
Inferior root
correctOption: Inferior root
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve is a separate entity primarily from C4.
The great auricular nerve is a cutaneous branch (C2, C3) supplying the skin of the ear and mandible.
The lesser occipital nerve is a cutaneous branch (C2) supplying the scalp.
The superior root is often called the 'descending branch of the hypoglossal nerve,' not the descending cervical nerve.
The descending cervical nerve is the traditional name for the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis, formed by C2 and C3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): ...unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Clinical Impact of Ansa Cervicalis Injury
statement: During a complex neck dissection in the carotid triangle, a surgeon must identify the ansa cervicalis. If the loop is injured, which of the following clinical findings would most likely be observed regarding the infrahyoid muscle group?
options: Loss of sensation in the skin over the angle of the mandible.
Inability to move the tongue due to the involvement of the hypoglossal nerve.
Complete paralysis of all muscles attached to the hyoid bone, including the digastric.
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle and subsequent voice hoarseness.
Paralysis of the sternohyoid and sternothyroid with preserved thyrohyoid function.
correctOption: Paralysis of the sternohyoid and sternothyroid with preserved thyrohyoid function.
optionExplanations: Sensation over the angle of the mandible is provided by the great auricular nerve (C2, C3), which is a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, not a motor loop.
Tongue movement is controlled by the hypoglossal nerve itself; an injury to the ansa loop alone does not affect the CN XII axons destined for the tongue.
The digastric muscle is supplied by the trigeminal (anterior belly) and facial (posterior belly) nerves, not the ansa cervicalis.
The cricothyroid muscle is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X), which is separate from the ansa cervicalis.

An isolated injury to the ansa cervicalis loop affects the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid, but the thyrohyoid is spared because its innervation (C1) leaves the hypoglossal nerve distal to the ansa's origin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The 'descending cervical nerve' (nervus descendens cervicalis) constitutes the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis. Which nerve rami from the cervical plexus contribute to its formation?
options: C2 and C3
C1, C2, and C3
C1 and C2
C2, C3, and C4
C3 and C4
correctOption: C2 and C3
optionExplanations: The descending cervical nerve is specifically formed by branches from the anterior rami of C2 and C3.
This includes the superior root contributor (C1); the question asks specifically for the inferior root (descending cervical nerve) contributors.
C1 forms the superior root, not the descending cervical nerve (inferior root).
C4 is not a standard contributor to the ansa cervicalis loop formation in the provided text.
While C3 and C4 contribute to the supraclavicular nerves and phrenic nerve, C4 is not part of the standard descending cervical nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): ...unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A patient presents with a traumatic injury to the upper neck. Clinical examination reveals normal tongue movements and normal sensation, but there is noticeable weakness in depressing the hyoid bone during the final stages of swallowing. An injury to which structure would explain these findings while sparing the thyrohyoid?
options: Ansa cervicalis loop
C1 root before it joins the hypoglossal nerve
Superior laryngeal nerve
Main trunk of the hypoglossal nerve
Inferior alveolar nerve
correctOption: Ansa cervicalis loop
optionExplanations: Weakness in hyoid depression implies dysfunction of the sternohyoid and omohyoid (supplied by the ansa). Since tongue movement (CN XII) and thyrohyoid function (C1 via XII) are intact, the lesion must be at the ansa loop.
If the C1 root were injured before joining XII, the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid would also be paralyzed, which contradicts the scenario.
The superior laryngeal nerve handles sensory above the vocal cords and motor to the cricothyroid; it does not depress the hyoid bone.
Injury to the main trunk of the hypoglossal nerve would cause paralysis of the tongue muscles, which is not present in this case.
The inferior alveolar nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) supplying the lower teeth and skin of the chin; it has no role in hyoid movement.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: During a carotid endarterectomy, a surgeon carefully retracts the internal jugular vein. A thin nerve loop is observed embedded in the anterior wall of the carotid sheath. If the superior root of this loop is traced superiorly, which cranial nerve does it appear to emerge from, despite its fibers being spinal in origin?
options: Vagus nerve (CN X)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Accessory nerve (CN XI)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve is located posteriorly within the carotid sheath between the artery and vein; it does not form the superior root of the ansa.
The facial nerve supplies the mimetic muscles and is located higher in the parotid region, with no contribution to the ansa cervicalis loop.
The superior root (descendens hypoglossi) is composed of C1 fibers that hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve before branching off in the neck to form the loop.
The accessory nerve passes through the posterior triangle to supply the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; it is not involved in the ansa cervicalis.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is located more superiorly and medially and does not carry the C1 fibers for the ansa cervicalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve. Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The ansa cervicalis is anatomically situated in a specific relation to the major vascular structures of the neck. Where is this nerve loop typically found?
options: Within the substance of the thyroid gland isthmus.
In the floor of the mouth, superficial to the mylohyoid muscle.
Deep to the prevertebral fascia, resting on the scalenus anterior muscle.
Embedded in or lying on the anterior surface of the carotid sheath.
Posterior to the vertebral column within the suboccipital triangle.
correctOption: Embedded in or lying on the anterior surface of the carotid sheath.
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis is located in the carotid triangle, lateral to the thyroid gland, not within its substance.
The floor of the mouth contains the submandibular and sublingual glands and the lingual/hypoglossal nerves, but not the ansa cervicalis loop.
The phrenic nerve lies on the scalenus anterior muscle, deep to the prevertebral fascia; the ansa cervicalis is more superficial, related to the carotid sheath.
The ansa cervicalis typically lies on the anterior surface of the internal jugular vein, which is one of the structures contained within the carotid sheath.
The suboccipital triangle contains the vertebral artery and the suboccipital nerve (posterior ramus of C1), not the ansa cervicalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Terminology and Origins of Ansa Roots
statement: During physiological swallowing, the ansa cervicalis coordinates the contraction of muscles to stabilize the hyoid bone. Which of the following is a characteristic of its 'superior root'?
options: It is also known as the descendens hypoglossi
It supplies the geniohyoid muscle
It is also known as the descendens cervicalis
It passes posterior to the common carotid artery
It is derived solely from the C2 nerve root
correctOption: It is also known as the descendens hypoglossi
optionExplanations: The superior root is clinically and anatomically referred to as the descendens hypoglossi because it appears to 'descend' from the hypoglossal nerve.
The geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve, but they branch off after the descendens hypoglossi has already left the nerve.
The descendens cervicalis is the 'inferior root' of the ansa cervicalis, formed by the C2 and C3 nerves.
The superior root typically descends anterior or superficial to the internal carotid artery and common carotid artery within the carotid triangle.
The superior root is derived from the C1 nerve fibers that hitchhike along the hypoglossal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: The ansa cervicalis maintains a very consistent anatomical relationship with the great vessels of the neck. Where is this nerve loop typically located relative to the carotid sheath?
options: Inside the carotid sheath, strictly between the common carotid and the vagus nerve
In the posterior triangle, lateral to the levator scapulae
Anterior to the strap muscles, within the superficial fascia of the neck
Embedded in the anterior wall or lying superficial to the internal jugular vein
Deep to the common carotid artery, resting on the prevertebral fascia
correctOption: Embedded in the anterior wall or lying superficial to the internal jugular vein
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve (CN X) lies posteriorly between the carotid artery and the internal jugular vein within the sheath; the ansa is more anterior/superficial.
The ansa cervicalis is located in the anterior triangle (carotid triangle); the posterior triangle contains the cervical plexus roots and trunks of the brachial plexus.
The ansa cervicalis lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid and within or on the deep cervical fascia, not in the superficial fascia (where the platysma lies).
The ansa cervicalis is typically found on the superficial surface of the internal jugular vein, often embedded in the fascia of the carotid sheath's anterior wall.
Structures deep to the carotid sheath on the prevertebral fascia include the sympathetic trunk, but not the ansa cervicalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Differential Innervation of Thyrohyoid vs. Other Infrahyoids
statement: A patient presents with weakness in depressing the hyoid bone during the final stages of deglutition. Although most infrahyoid muscles are affected, the thyrohyoid muscle remains functional. Which anatomical distinction explains this sparing?
options: The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by the accessory nerve (CN XI).
The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by the C2-C3 inferior root of the ansa cervicalis.
The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that do not join the ansa cervicalis loop.
The thyrohyoid muscle receives its innervation from the facial nerve (CN VII).
The thyrohyoid muscle is a suprahyoid muscle and is thus exempt from ansa cervicalis distribution.
correctOption: The thyrohyoid muscle is supplied by C1 fibers that do not join the ansa cervicalis loop.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, not the infrahyoid muscles.
Incorrect. The C2-C3 inferior root contributes to the ansa cervicalis, which supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid, but not the thyrohyoid.

Correct. While most infrahyoids are supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3), the thyrohyoid receives C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve and branch off independently, bypassing the ansa loop.
Incorrect. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and the posterior belly of the digastric/stylohyoid, not the thyrohyoid.
Incorrect. The thyrohyoid is anatomically an infrahyoid muscle (situated below the hyoid), despite its unique innervation compared to the others.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid... Ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: An anatomy student is identifying the spinal nerve roots that contribute to the formation of the ansa cervicalis. Which of the following sets of anterior rami are responsible for this nerve loop?
options: C2, C3, and C4
C1, C2, and C3
C1 and C2 only
C1, C2, C3, and C4
C3, C4, and C5
correctOption: C1, C2, and C3
optionExplanations: C4 contributes to the phrenic nerve and the supraclavicular nerves, but it is not typically cited as a primary root for the ansa cervicalis in standard anatomical descriptions.
The ansa cervicalis is a loop formed by the union of the superior root (C1 fibers) and the inferior root (descending cervical nerve from C2 and C3).
While C1 and C2 contribute to the superior and part of the inferior root respectively, C3 is also required to complete the descending cervical nerve component of the inferior root.
C4 is part of the cervical plexus and contributes to the supraclavicular and phrenic nerves, but the ansa cervicalis loop specifically terminates its root contributions at C3.
C5 is a major contributor to the phrenic nerve and the brachial plexus, but it does not participate in the cervical plexus loop known as the ansa cervicalis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Descending branch (C1 fibers) passes downward and joins the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3) to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A maxillofacial surgeon is performing a radical neck dissection. To preserve the motor supply to the strap muscles, the surgeon must identify a nerve loop that derives its superior root from fibers associated with the Twelfth Cranial Nerve. If this loop is damaged, which muscle's function in stabilizing the larynx during swallowing will be most affected?
options: Digastric
Palatoglossus
Sternothyroid
Stylopharyngeus
Thyrohyoid
correctOption: Sternothyroid
optionExplanations: The digastric is supplied by the mandibular nerve (anterior belly) and facial nerve (posterior belly).
Palatoglossus is a muscle of the palate and tongue supplied by the vagus nerve (CN X) via the pharyngeal plexus.
The sternothyroid is a strap muscle supplied directly by the ansa cervicalis loop; it plays a key role in depressing/stabilizing the larynx.
Stylopharyngeus is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
Thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal nerve, but it branches off before the ansa cervicalis superior root and is often spared if only the ansa loop is damaged.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: In the assembly of the ansa cervicalis, what is the specific nomenclature and composition of the root formed by the union of the second and third cervical spinal nerves?
options: Great auricular nerve
Descendens hypoglossi
Nervus intermedius
Phrenic nerve
Descending cervical nerve
correctOption: Descending cervical nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) is a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus supplying skin, not a motor root for the ansa cervicalis.
Incorrect. Descendens hypoglossi is the synonym for the superior root, which is composed of C1 fibers only.
Incorrect. The nervus intermedius is the sensory and parasympathetic root of the facial nerve (CN VII).
Incorrect. The phrenic nerve is formed by C3, C4, and C5 and supplies the diaphragm; it is separate from the ansa cervicalis loop.
Correct. The 'descending cervical nerve' (also known as descendens cervicalis) is the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis, formed by the union of C2 and C3.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Target Muscles of the Ansa Loop
statement: Which of the following muscles receives its nerve supply from both the superior and inferior roots of the ansa cervicalis (i.e., the loop itself)?
options: Geniohyoid
Cricothyroid
Sternohyoid
Thyrohyoid
Mylohyoid
correctOption: Sternohyoid
optionExplanations: The geniohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers directly from the hypoglossal nerve, not via the ansa cervicalis.
The cricothyroid is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (branch of CN X).
The sternohyoid is a classic infrahyoid muscle supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop (C1-C3).
The thyrohyoid is supplied by C1 fibers that run with CN XII but do not enter the ansa cervicalis loop.
The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle supplied by the nerve to the mylohyoid, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: A 45-year-old male undergoes a surgical procedure in the carotid triangle of the neck. To access the internal carotid artery, the surgeon must identify a nerve loop lying anterior to the carotid sheath. If this loop is damaged, which physiological action will be most significantly impaired?
options: Elevation of the hyoid bone
Constriction of the pharyngeal wall
Rotation of the head to the opposite side
Depression of the hyoid bone
Protrusion of the tongue
correctOption: Depression of the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: Elevation of the hyoid is performed by the suprahyoid muscles (e.g., mylohyoid, digastric), which are not supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
Constriction of the pharynx is managed by the pharyngeal constrictors, supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X and XI).
Rotation of the head is the function of the sternocleidomastoid, which is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
The ansa cervicalis supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid, which act collectively to depress the hyoid bone after it has been elevated during swallowing.
Protrusion of the tongue is the function of the genioglossus, supplied directly by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1682 (Book Page): Branches from this loop supply the omohyoid, the sternohyoid, and the sternothyroid muscles. [Table 12.5, Page 1615 (Book Page): Infrahyoid muscles... Action: Depress hyoid bone]

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: During dissection of the neck, the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis is seen to descend in the neck. Over which specific anatomical structure does it typically loop to join the superior root?
options: The bifurcation of the common carotid artery.
The intermediate tendon of the omohyoid muscle.
The internal jugular vein.
The subclavian artery.
The tendon of the digastric muscle.
correctOption: The internal jugular vein.
optionExplanations: The bifurcation of the carotid is a landmark for the roots but not the structure the inferior root loops over to form the 'ansa' (handle).
While the ansa supplies the omohyoid, it does not typically loop over its intermediate tendon to form the ansa itself.
The inferior root (C2-C3) typically passes lateral to the internal jugular vein and then loops anteriorly to join the superior root.
The subclavian artery is too inferior; the ansa cervicalis is located higher in the carotid triangle region.
The digastric tendon is superior to the formation of the ansa cervicalis loop.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Muscular Distribution of the Ansa Cervicalis
statement: During a surgical approach to the carotid triangle, the surgeon identifies a nerve loop lying superficial to the internal jugular vein. Which of the following muscles is primarily supplied by the branches arising directly from this nerve loop?
options: Digastric (anterior belly)
Platysma
Sternohyoid
Stylohyoid
Mylohyoid
correctOption: Sternohyoid
optionExplanations: The anterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the nerve to the mylohyoid (V3), while the posterior belly is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII).
The platysma is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
The ansa cervicalis is the primary motor supply for three of the four infrahyoid (strap) muscles: the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid.
The stylohyoid is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII) as it is derived from the second pharyngeal arch.
The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle supplied by the nerve to the mylohyoid, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: During the formation of the ansa cervicalis, the superior root (descendens hypoglossi) is composed of fibers that initially travel with a cranial nerve. Which cranial nerve serves as the carrier for these C1 spinal fibers before they branch off?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Accessory nerve (CN XI)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Vagus nerve (CN X)
correctOption: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve is involved in taste and pharyngeal sensation/secretion, not the transport of C1 motor fibers for the neck loop.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) acts as a physical conduit for C1 fibers, which eventually leave it to form the superior root of the ansa cervicalis and the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.
The spinal accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; it does not carry C1 fibers to the infrahyoid muscles.
The facial nerve supplies the second pharyngeal arch muscles; it does not communicate with C1 for infrahyoid supply.
The vagus nerve carries the cranial root of the accessory nerve for pharyngeal and laryngeal innervation, but not the superior root of the ansa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve . Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch , which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
statement: Which of the following muscle groups is exclusively supplied by the ansa cervicalis loop?
options: Muscles of the tongue
Prevertebral muscles
Infrahyoid muscles except thyrohyoid
Suprahyoid muscles
Muscles of the larynx
correctOption: Infrahyoid muscles except thyrohyoid
optionExplanations: All intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue (except palatoglossus) are supplied by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).
Prevertebral muscles (like longus colli) are supplied by direct branches from the cervical and brachial plexuses, not the ansa loop.
The ansa cervicalis loop supplies the sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid. The thyrohyoid, though an infrahyoid muscle, is supplied directly by C1 via CN XII, not the loop itself.
Suprahyoid muscles are supplied by various nerves: Mylohyoid (V3), Digastric (V3 and VII), Stylohyoid (VII), and Geniohyoid (C1).
Intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by the recurrent laryngeal and external laryngeal branches of the vagus nerve (CN X).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The ansa cervicalis supplies the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid muscles. ... Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation and distribution of ansa cervicalis
coreConcept: Anatomical Composition of the Inferior Root (Descendens Cervicalis)
statement: During the formation of the ansa cervicalis, the inferior root (descendens cervicalis) arises from the cervical plexus and typically consists of which specific combination of nerve rami?
options: Anterior rami of C2 and C3
Anterior rami of C1 and C2
Posterior rami of C1 and C2
Posterior rami of C2 and C3
Anterior rami of C3 and C4
correctOption: Anterior rami of C2 and C3
