citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Sternocleidomastoid... Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral part of superior nuchal line.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The sternocleidomastoid muscle has two distinct heads of origin. Which of the following correctly describes these attachments?
options: The sternal head arises from the xiphoid process, and the clavicular head arises from the medial third of the clavicle.
The sternal head arises from the manubrium, and the clavicular head arises from the medial third of the clavicle.
The sternal head arises from the sternal angle, and the clavicular head arises from the acromion.
The sternal head arises from the manubrium, and the clavicular head arises from the lateral third of the clavicle.
The sternal head arises from the first rib, and the clavicular head arises from the coracoid process.
correctOption: The sternal head arises from the manubrium, and the clavicular head arises from the medial third of the clavicle.
optionExplanations: The sternal head arises from the manubrium, not the xiphoid process.
The SCM originates via a rounded tendon from the manubrium (sternal head) and a flat muscular-tendinous head from the medial third of the clavicle.
The sternal angle is the level of the second rib; the SCM originates higher up on the manubrium. The acromion is the insertion site for the trapezius.
The clavicular head arises from the medial third of the clavicle, not the lateral third.
The first rib and coracoid process are associated with the subclavius and pectoralis minor/biceps/coracobrachialis respectively, not the SCM.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Sternocleidomastoid ... Origin: Manubrium sterni and medial third of clavicle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A student is tracing the origin of the trapezius muscle along the vertebral column. Which of the following lists the correct midline structures that provide attachment for this muscle?
options: The mastoid process and the transverse processes of C1-C4
The anterior tubercle of the atlas and the dens of the axis
The coronoid process of the mandible and the hyoid bone
The spines of the lumbar vertebrae and the sacral promontory
The external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of C7 to T12
correctOption: The external occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of C7 to T12
optionExplanations: The mastoid process is an attachment for the SCM, and the transverse processes of C1-C4 are origins for muscles like the levator scapulae and scalenes.
The anterior tubercle of the atlas and the dens are deep structures involved in the atlantoaxial joints and prevertebral muscle attachments, not the superficial trapezius.
The coronoid process is an attachment for the temporalis muscle, and the hyoid bone is for the suprahyoid/infrahyoid muscles.
The trapezius does not extend into the lumbar region or the sacrum; its vertebral origin ends at the T12 level.
The trapezius has a wide origin encompassing the external occipital protuberance, the nuchal ligament, and the spinous processes of all twelve thoracic vertebrae (T1-T12) plus C7.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Trapezius... Origin: External occipital protuberance, medial third of superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of seventh cervical and all thoracic vertebrae.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Regarding the attachments of the trapezius muscle, which of the following bones serves as a site for its lateral insertion?
options: The transverse process of the atlas
The medial third of the clavicle
The spine of the scapula and the acromion
The first rib
The coracoid process of the scapula
correctOption: The spine of the scapula and the acromion
optionExplanations: The transverse process of the atlas (C1) provides attachment for muscles like the levator scapulae or obliquus capitis, not the trapezius.
The medial third of the clavicle is an origin site for the sternocleidomastoid, whereas the trapezius attaches to the lateral third.
The trapezius inserts on the lateral third of the clavicle and the acromion and spine of the scapula.
The trapezius does not attach to the ribs; the scalene muscles and serratus anterior have rib attachments.
The coracoid process provides attachment for the pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, and the short head of the biceps, but not the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Trapezius... Occipital bone, ligamentum nuchae, spines of C7 to T12 ... Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula.]

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles receive dual innervation from both a cranial nerve and spinal nerves. What is the specific functional modality of the branches they receive from the cervical plexus (C2, C3, and C4)?
options: Parasympathetic secretomotor control for local glands.
General somatic motor fibers for voluntary contraction.
Proprioceptive sensory fibers for muscle position sense.
Special visceral afferent fibers for taste perception.
Sympathetic vasomotor fibers for blood flow regulation.
correctOption: Proprioceptive sensory fibers for muscle position sense.
optionExplanations: Parasympathetic fibers in the head and neck are carried by CN III, VII, IX, and X; they are not carried to skeletal muscles like the trapezius via the cervical plexus.
While they are spinal nerves, the primary motor (voluntary contraction) supply for these two muscles is the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
The branches from the anterior rami of C2, C3 (for SCM) and C3, C4 (for Trapezius) carry proprioceptive information, which is essential for coordinating head and neck posture.
Special visceral afferent (SVA) fibers are associated with taste (CN VII, IX, X) and olfaction (CN I), which have no relation to the trapezius.
Sympathetic vasomotor fibers originate from the sympathetic trunk (superior, middle, and inferior cervical ganglia), not directly from the cervical plexus rami.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 3-week-old infant is brought to the clinic because the parents noticed a small, firm lump on the side of the neck and the head is consistently tilted. What is the most likely pathophysiological mechanism for this congenital condition?
options: Fibrous tissue contraction within the sternocleidomastoid muscle following hemorrhage
Hypertrophy of the trapezius muscle due to birth trauma
Ossification of the stylohyoid ligament hindering neck rotation
Idiopathic palsy of the spinal accessory nerve resulting in muscle flaccidity
Bilateral agenesis of the infrahyoid strap muscles
correctOption: Fibrous tissue contraction within the sternocleidomastoid muscle following hemorrhage
optionExplanations: Hemorrhage into the sternocleidomastoid during birth leads to fibrosis; the resulting scar tissue contracts, shortening the muscle and pulling the head into a characteristic tilt and rotation.
While birth trauma is involved, the primary muscle affected is the sternocleidomastoid, not the trapezius, and it involves shortening rather than simple hypertrophy.
Ossification of the stylohyoid ligament is related to Eagle's syndrome and usually affects adults, not infants with tilted heads.
Palsy of the spinal accessory nerve would lead to muscle wasting and weakness (drooping), not the firm, contracted lump and fixed tilt seen in torticollis.
Bilateral agenesis of infrahyoid muscles would affect laryngeal stabilization and swallowing rather than producing a localized neck mass and unilateral tilt.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): [Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.]

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient with a history of chronic neck pain is found to have proprioceptive deficits in the upper neck region. While the motor supply to the sternocleidomastoid is intact, the sensory component is compromised. Which nerve fibers are responsible for carrying proprioceptive information from the sternocleidomastoid?
options: CN XI and CN XII
C1 and C2
C3 and C4
Glossopharyngeal nerve
C2 and C3
correctOption: C2 and C3
optionExplanations: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is the motor supply to the SCM/Trapezius, and the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is the motor supply to the tongue; neither carries the muscle's proprioception.
While C1 fibers are involved in the cervical plexus and travel with the hypoglossal nerve, they do not provide the primary proprioceptive innervation for the SCM.
C3 and C4 provide proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius muscle, but the SCM receives its proprioceptive input from slightly higher levels (C2 and C3).
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory and motor innervation to the pharynx and tongue, but has no role in the innervation of the SCM.

The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) provides only motor innervation to the SCM. Proprioception (sensory feedback) for the SCM is carried by branches from the anterior rami of the second and third cervical nerves (C2, C3).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius muscle is essential for the full abduction of the upper limb. Which specific action does it perform to facilitate the movement of the arm above 90 degrees?
options: Downward rotation of the scapula.
Upward rotation of the scapula by the upper and lower fibers.
Retraction of the scapula toward the midline.
Protraction of the scapula away from the midline.
Depression of the acromion process.
correctOption: Upward rotation of the scapula by the upper and lower fibers.
optionExplanations: Downward rotation is performed by muscles like the rhomboids and levator scapulae, which would hinder abduction above 90 degrees.
The trapezius (upper and lower fibers) and serratus anterior work together to rotate the scapula upward, turning the glenoid cavity superiorly to allow the humerus to move above the horizontal.
Retraction (pulling medially) is done by the middle fibers of the trapezius but is not the primary motion for overhead abduction.
Protraction is primarily the role of the serratus anterior and pectoralis minor, not the trapezius.
Depression of the acromion would occur during downward rotation; full abduction requires elevation and upward rotation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Trapezius ... Upper fibers: elevate scapula; Middle fibers: pull scapula medially; Lower fibers: pull medial border of scapula downward; together with serratus anterior: rotate scapula to allow for abduction of the arm above 90 degrees.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Functional Outcome of CN XI Section
statement: A patient diagnosed with spasmodic torticollis is being considered for surgical intervention after failing conservative therapy. If the surgeon decides to perform a section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve, which combination of muscle actions will be primarily diminished?
options: Contralateral head tilt and jaw depression
Contralateral head rotation and scapular retraction
Ipsilateral shoulder shrugging and tongue deviation
Ipsilateral head rotation and scapular depression
Bilateral neck extension and hyoid elevation
correctOption: Contralateral head rotation and scapular retraction
optionExplanations: Jaw depression is performed by the digastric, mylohyoid, and geniohyoid muscles, none of which are supplied by the accessory nerve.

The spinal accessory nerve supplies the SCM and trapezius. Sectioning it will weaken the SCM (which rotates the head to the *opposite* side) and the trapezius (which retracts the scapula via its middle fibers).
While shoulder shrugging is affected (trapezius), tongue deviation is a symptom of hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, which is not supplied by the accessory nerve.
SCM contraction causes rotation to the *opposite* (contralateral) side, not the same (ipsilateral) side.
Neck extension can involve many posterior muscles, and hyoid elevation is performed by the suprahyoid muscles (CN V and CN VII), not CN XI.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Sternocleidomastoid Action] One muscle: ...rotates the head to the opposite side. [Trapezius Action] ...middle fibers retract the scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Cranial Nerve Lesions at the Jugular Foramen
statement: A 40-year-old woman presents with persistent hoarseness and a weak voice following a procedure involving the jugular foramen. On examination, the uvula deviates to the left, she cannot shrug her right shoulder, and the right sternocleidomastoid shows wasting. Which nerve is completely lesioned in this case?
options: Right vagus nerve only
Right spinal accessory nerve only
Right glossopharyngeal nerve only
Right hypoglossal and right accessory nerves
Right spinal accessory and right vagus nerves
correctOption: Right spinal accessory and right vagus nerves
optionExplanations: Vagus nerve lesion explains the hoarseness and uvula deviation but does not explain the inability to shrug or the sternocleidomastoid wasting.
Accessory nerve lesion explains the shrugging and SCM issues but does not explain the hoarseness or uvula deviation (vagal signs).
Glossopharyngeal lesion would affect the gag reflex and sensation to the posterior tongue but not the motor functions of the shoulder or larynx.
The hypoglossal nerve exits through the hypoglossal canal, not the jugular foramen. Its lesion would cause tongue deviation, which is not mentioned.
A lesion at the jugular foramen commonly involves multiple nerves (CN IX, X, XI). Shoulder drop/SCM wasting (CN XI) plus uvula deviation/hoarseness (CN X) indicates involvement of both.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): The cranial root joins the vagus nerve and is distributed in its branches... The spinal root runs downward... and supply the trapezius muscle... Page 1791 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerves innervate the intrinsic muscles of the larynx... vulnerable during operations.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient is asked to contract only their right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Based on the intermediate physiological mechanics of this muscle, what is the expected movement of the head?
options: The neck is flexed directly forward.
The head is extended at the atlanto-occipital joint.
The chin is pulled directly toward the suprasternal notch.
The face rotates toward the left side.
The face rotates toward the right side.
correctOption: The face rotates toward the left side.
optionExplanations: Direct forward flexion of the neck is the result of bilateral contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscles, not unilateral contraction.

While the SCM can assist in head extension at the atlanto-occipital joint, this is typically a bilateral action or a secondary component of its complex movement, not the primary result of isolated unilateral contraction.
Pulling the chin toward the suprasternal notch is a result of bilateral flexion of the cervical spine, which occurs when both SCM muscles act in unison.

When the right sternocleidomastoid contracts, it pulls the right mastoid process toward the right sternum. Because of the muscle's oblique orientation, this force rotates the atlas on the axis, turning the face to the left.
Rotation toward the same side is incorrect; the unilateral contraction of the SCM pulls the mastoid process anteriorly and inferiorly, causing rotation to the opposite side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The mastoid process is thus pulled down toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side, the cervical spine is flexed, and the face looks upward to the opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: What are the specific points of origin and insertion for the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: Origin: Coracoid process; Insertion: Mastoid process and occipital bone
Origin: Sternal angle; Insertion: Mastoid process and zygomatic arch
Origin: Lateral third of clavicle; Insertion: Mastoid process and superior nuchal line
Origin: Medial third of clavicle; Insertion: Spine of scapula and mastoid process
Origin: Manubrium sterni and medial third of clavicle; Insertion: Mastoid process and lateral half of superior nuchal line
correctOption: Origin: Manubrium sterni and medial third of clavicle; Insertion: Mastoid process and lateral half of superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: Option C is incorrect as the coracoid process is an attachment site for the pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, and short head of biceps brachii.
Option D is incorrect because the origin is specifically the manubrium sterni, and it does not insert onto the zygomatic arch.
Option A is incorrect because the SCM originates from the *medial* third of the clavicle, not the lateral third (which is the origin for the trapezius and deltoid).
Option E is incorrect because the spine of the scapula is an insertion point for the trapezius, not the sternocleidomastoid.

Option B is correct. The SCM has two heads of origin: a sternal head from the manubrium and a clavicular head from the medial third of the clavicle. It inserts onto the mastoid process and the superior nuchal line.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Sternocleidomastoid] Origin: Manubrium sterni and medial third of clavicle; Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral half of superior nuchal line of occipital bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is an essential landmark in the neck. Which of the following correctly describes its anatomical role in defining the cervical triangles?
options: Its posterior border forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle
It lies entirely within the carotid triangle
Its anterior border forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle
Its anterior border forms the lateral boundary of the submental triangle
It forms the floor of the omoclavicular triangle
correctOption: Its posterior border forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle
optionExplanations: The SCM diagonally crosses the neck; its posterior border serves as the anterior limit of the posterior triangle, while its anterior border serves as the posterior limit of the anterior triangle.
The SCM forms one boundary of the carotid triangle but does not lie 'within' it as content; it is a bordering structure.
The *posterior* border of the SCM forms the anterior boundary of the posterior triangle, not the anterior border.
The submental triangle is bounded by the midline, the hyoid bone, and the *anterior belly of the digastric*, not the SCM.
The floor of the posterior triangle (including the omoclavicular part) is formed by prevertebral fascia over muscles like the splenius capitis and levator scapulae, not the SCM itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1626 (Book Page): Posterior Triangle: The boundaries are the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the trapezius muscle, and the clavicle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius is a large, triangular muscle with extensive origins. Which of the following bony landmarks provides the most inferior point of origin for the trapezius fibers?
options: Spinous process of the 12th thoracic vertebra
Lateral third of the clavicle
Spine of the scapula
Spinous process of the 7th cervical vertebra
External occipital protuberance
correctOption: Spinous process of the 12th thoracic vertebra
optionExplanations: The trapezius originates from all thoracic vertebrae (T1 to T12), making the spinous process of T12 its most inferior origin.
The lateral third of the clavicle is an insertion point for the superior fibers of the trapezius, not a point of origin.
The spine of the scapula is an insertion point for the trapezius muscle, not a point of origin.
The spine of C7 is a point of origin in the neck region, but the muscle extends much further down the back to the thoracic region.
The external occipital protuberance is the most superior point of origin for the trapezius, not the inferior point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5... Trapezius... Origin: External occipital protuberance, medial third of superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of 7th cervical and all thoracic vertebrae.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles are both enclosed by which layer of the deep cervical fascia?
options: The prevertebral layer
The pretracheal layer
The investing layer
The carotid sheath
The visceral fascia
correctOption: The investing layer
optionExplanations: The prevertebral layer covers the prevertebral muscles and forms the floor of the posterior triangle.
The pretracheal layer surrounds the thyroid, parathyroid, and infrahyoid muscles, but not the SCM or trapezius.
The investing layer is the most superficial layer of deep fascia; it splits to create 'envelopes' for the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
The carotid sheath contains the carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve, but not the SCM or trapezius muscles themselves.
Visceral fascia is usually associated with the organs (like the pharyngeal or esophageal walls), not the large skeletal muscles of the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1627 (Book Page): [The investing layer is a thick layer that encircles the neck. It splits to enclose the trapezius and the sternocleidomastoid muscles.]

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A newborn is brought to the pediatrician because the parents noticed a small, rounded 'tumor' in the right side of the neck. Over several weeks, the mass becomes fibrous and the child's head is tilted toward the right, with the face looking toward the left side. What is the anatomical basis for this condition?
options: Congenital absence of the spinal accessory nerve on the left side
Rupture of the stylohyoid ligament during labor
A benign neoplasm of the parotid gland compressing the facial nerve
Spasmodic contraction of the trapezius due to nerve irritation
Hemorrhage into the sternocleidomastoid followed by fibrous contraction
correctOption: Hemorrhage into the sternocleidomastoid followed by fibrous contraction
optionExplanations: Absence of the nerve would cause muscle wasting and weakness (flaccid paralysis), not the forceful, fixed postural contraction and shortening seen in torticollis.
The stylohyoid ligament connects the styloid process to the hyoid; its rupture would affect swallowing or hyoid stability but would not cause the classic head tilt and rotation of torticollis.
A parotid tumor would cause facial paralysis (drooping), but it would not cause the neck muscle shortening or the specific head-tilt and face-rotation pattern described, which is muscular in origin.

While torticollis can be spasmodic (usually psychogenic in adults), the presentation of a 'tumor' in a newborn following labor points to a specific musculoskeletal injury rather than a nerve irritation.

Congenital torticollis (wryneck) results from injury to the SCM during birth. The resulting hematoma (the 'tumor') is replaced by fibrous tissue that shrinks, pulling the mastoid toward the sternum (tilting the head to the same side and rotating the face to the opposite side).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): [Congenital Torticollis] Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Proprioceptive Innervation Contrast of Neck Muscles
statement: A researcher is contrasting the proprioceptive pathways of the two largest muscles in the neck. While both receive motor innervation from the same cranial nerve, which of the following correctly identifies the distinct sensory (proprioceptive) contributions for each?
options: Sternocleidomastoid: C3, C4; Trapezius: C4, C5
Sternocleidomastoid: Vagus nerve; Trapezius: Facial nerve
Sternocleidomastoid: Glossopharyngeal nerve; Trapezius: Hypoglossal nerve
Sternocleidomastoid: C2, C3; Trapezius: C3, C4
Sternocleidomastoid: C1, C2; Trapezius: C2, C3
correctOption: Sternocleidomastoid: C2, C3; Trapezius: C3, C4
optionExplanations: These segments are too low for the primary proprioceptive supply of the sternocleidomastoid, though C3/C4 are correct for the trapezius.
The motor supply for both is CN XI (Spinal Accessory), not Vagus or Facial; the sensory supply is via cervical spinal nerves.
Neither CN IX nor CN XII provide the sensory or motor innervation for these superficial neck muscles.
According to the cervical plexus distribution, the sternocleidomastoid receives its proprioceptive fibers from C2 and C3, whereas the trapezius receives fibers from C3 and C4.
The C1 nerve does not have a cutaneous or specific muscle branch to the SCM; the SCM starts at C2.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient presents with 'winging' of the scapula and an inability to shrug the shoulders. Which specific fibers of the trapezius are primarily responsible for the elevation of the scapula observed during a shrug?
options: Lower fibers only
Internal fibers attached to the ribs
Both middle and lower fibers together
Middle fibers only
Upper fibers
correctOption: Upper fibers
optionExplanations: Lower fibers of the trapezius actually depress the scapula or pull its medial border downward, which is the opposite of shrugging.
The trapezius does not have 'internal fibers' attached to the ribs; it is a superficial muscle of the back and neck that attaches to the vertebral column and pectoral girdle.
Together, the middle and lower fibers act to retract and depress the scapula; they cannot elevate it because their vectors of pull are horizontal or inferior.
Middle fibers of the trapezius act primarily to retract (adduct) the scapula toward the midline; they do not significantly contribute to vertical elevation.
The upper fibers of the trapezius (originating from the skull and ligamentum nuchae) are responsible for elevating the scapula, an action clinically tested by shrugging the shoulders.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Trapezius... Action: Upper fibers elevate the scapula; middle fibers pull scapula medially; lower fibers pull medial border of scapula downward.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Origin of the Spinal Accessory Nerve
statement: Regarding the origin of the motor supply to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, where do the cell bodies of the spinal root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) reside?
options: The dorsal root ganglion of C2 and C3
The anterior gray column of the upper five cervical spinal cord segments
The nucleus ambiguus in the medulla oblongata
The superior salivary nucleus of the pons
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain
correctOption: The anterior gray column of the upper five cervical spinal cord segments
optionExplanations: Dorsal root ganglia contain sensory cell bodies, while the spinal accessory nerve root is motor.
The spinal accessory nerve cell bodies are located in the spinal accessory nucleus, situated in the anterior horn of the first five or six cervical cord segments.
The nucleus ambiguus gives rise to the cranial root of the accessory nerve and vagal motor fibers, but the 'spinal root' specifically comes from the cord.
The superior salivary nucleus is the origin of parasympathetic fibers for the facial nerve (CN VII), not motor fibers for CN XI.
The Edinger-Westphal nucleus is parasympathetic for the oculomotor nerve (CN III), regulating pupillary constriction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): The spinal root arises from nerve cells in the anterior gray column (horn) of the upper five segments of the cervical part of the spinal cord.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 55-year-old female presents with a progressive inability to elevate her right arm above the horizontal plane (100 degrees), despite having normal deltoid function and no history of glenohumeral joint trauma. On inspection, there is noticeable wasting of the muscle that forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle of the neck. Which additional finding is most likely present?
options: Inability to flex the neck against resistance.
Weakness in depressing the hyoid bone.
Deviation of the tongue to the right side upon protrusion.
A 'dropped shoulder' on the right side and winging of the scapula during retraction.
Loss of sensation over the angle of the jaw.
correctOption: A 'dropped shoulder' on the right side and winging of the scapula during retraction.
optionExplanations: Option A is incorrect because neck flexion is primarily performed by the sternocleidomastoid and prevertebral muscles (like longus colli), not the trapezius.
Option E is incorrect as hyoid depression is the function of the infrahyoid strap muscles supplied by the ansa cervicalis.
Option D is incorrect because tongue deviation is a hallmark of hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury.

Option C is correct. Paralysis of the trapezius (which forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle) causes a dropped shoulder and loss of upward scapular rotation, preventing overhead arm elevation. It also leads to scapular instability.
Option B is incorrect as sensation over the angle of the jaw is provided by the great auricular nerve (C2,3), not the spinal accessory nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve... the trapezius muscle is paralyzed, the muscle will show wasting, and the shoulder will drop. The patient will experience difficulty in elevating the arm above the head... Page 1626 (Book Page): The boundaries [of the posterior triangle] are the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the trapezius muscle, and the clavicle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A pediatric patient is diagnosed with congenital torticollis. The primary pathophysiological mechanism involves a permanent shortening of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Based on the muscle's unilateral action, how would the patient’s head and face be positioned?
options: The head is tilted away from the affected side, and the face is rotated downward toward the opposite side.
The head is pulled forward into a flexed position, and the face is rotated strictly in the sagittal plane.
The head is tilted toward the affected side, and the face is rotated toward the affected side.
The head is tilted toward the affected side, and the face is rotated upward to the opposite side.
The head is tilted away from the affected side, and the face is rotated toward the affected side.
correctOption: The head is tilted toward the affected side, and the face is rotated upward to the opposite side.
optionExplanations: Option D is incorrect as it describes tilting away from the lesion, which is the opposite of what occurs in muscle shortening or contraction.
Option E is incorrect because strict flexion in the sagittal plane is a result of bilateral SCM contraction, not the unilateral shortening seen in torticollis.
Option B is incorrect because while the head tilts toward the affected side, the rotation of the face is always to the opposite side due to the posterior attachment on the mastoid process.
Option C is correct. The unilateral action of the SCM involves tilting the head to the ipsilateral side and rotating the head so that the face looks toward the contralateral side and upward.

Option A is incorrect because the unilateral contraction of the SCM pulls the mastoid process toward the sternum of the same side, resulting in tilting of the head *toward* the muscle, not away from it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The mastoid process is thus pulled down toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side, the cervical spine is flexed, and the face looks upward to the opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: What are the specific cranial attachments for the insertion of the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: External occipital protuberance and superior nuchal line
Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line
Styloid process and the angle of the mandible
Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral third of the superior nuchal line
Mastoid process and the inferior nuchal line
correctOption: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: The external occipital protuberance is a site of origin for the trapezius, not the insertion for the sternocleidomastoid.
The SCM inserts on the mastoid process and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line. This provides a broad base for its role in head rotation and flexion.
The styloid process is the origin for muscles like the stylohyoid and stylopharyngeus. The angle of the mandible is an attachment for the masseter and the stylomandibular ligament.
While the mastoid process is correct, the attachment extends to the lateral half of the superior nuchal line, not just the lateral third.
The inferior nuchal line is located below the superior nuchal line and serves as an attachment for deep neck extensors like the rectus capitis muscles, not the SCM.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Sternocleidomastoid... Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral half of superior nuchal line of occipital bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Positional anatomy of the SCM and carotid sheath
statement: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is an essential landmark in the neck. Regarding its anatomical relations and clinical significance, which of the following is correct?
options: The internal jugular vein lies superficial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
The muscle is an accessory muscle of inspiration, helping to lift the thoracic cage.
The platysma muscle lies deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
The muscle is derived from the first pharyngeal arch.
The carotid sheath is located posterior to the muscle during neck extension.
correctOption: The carotid sheath is located posterior to the muscle during neck extension.
optionExplanations: The internal jugular vein is deep to the sternocleidomastoid muscle; the external jugular vein is the one that lies superficial to it.
While true physiologically, the provided text does not explicitly detail the SCM's role in inspiration, though it does detail its role in head/neck movement and protection.
The platysma is a superficial muscle embedded in the superficial fascia and lies superficial to the sternocleidomastoid.
The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are associated with the pharyngeal arches (specifically the caudal ones), but the platysma is the one explicitly listed as second arch (Page 1535).
In clinical notes regarding suicide attempts, neck extension causes the carotid sheath and its vessels to slide posteriorly under the protection of the thick sternocleidomastoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Extension of the cervical part of the vertebral column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint cause the carotid sheath with its contained large blood vessels to slide posteriorly beneath the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius muscle has an extensive insertion on the pectoral girdle, allowing it to manipulate the position of the shoulder. Which of the following represents its insertion on the clavicle?
options: The medial third of the clavicle
The sternoclavicular joint capsule
The lateral third of the clavicle
The entire superior surface of the clavicle
The coracoid process of the clavicle
correctOption: The lateral third of the clavicle
optionExplanations: The medial third of the clavicle is the site of origin for the clavicular head of the sternocleidomastoid and the pectoralis major.
The trapezius does not insert into the sternoclavicular joint capsule; that area is related to the origin of the SCM.
The trapezius inserts into the posterior border of the lateral third of the clavicle, as well as the acromion and the spine of the scapula.
The muscle does not attach to the entire clavicle; its clavicular attachment is limited to the lateral portion.
The coracoid process is a part of the scapula, not the clavicle, and serves as an attachment for muscles like the pectoralis minor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Trapezius Insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of Neck Block Dissection
statement: During a 'block dissection' of the neck for metastatic carcinoma, a surgeon must systematically identify and sometimes sacrifice structures. According to anatomical protocols, which of the following is typically removed en bloc along with the deep cervical lymph nodes?
options: The brachial plexus trunks
The submandibular salivary gland
The phrenic nerve
The vagus nerve
The common carotid artery
correctOption: The submandibular salivary gland
optionExplanations: The brachial plexus is located in the floor of the posterior triangle and is a vital structure that surgeons avoid damaging during lymphatic clearance.
Standard block dissection protocol includes removal of the internal jugular vein, cervical fascia, lymph nodes, and the submandibular salivary gland as a single unit.
The phrenic nerve is deep to the prevertebral fascia and is typically preserved to maintain diaphragmatic function.
Like the carotid, the vagus nerve is preserved if possible, though the text notes it may be sacrificed if involved in cancerous deposits.
The carotid arteries are vital structures and are 'carefully preserved' during a block dissection unless absolutely involved.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1657 (Book Page): This procedure involves the removal en bloc of the internal jugular vein, the fascia, the lymph nodes, and the submandibular salivary gland.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which of the following best describes the origin of the Trapezius muscle?
options: External occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of C7 to T12
Medial third of the clavicle and the manubrium sterni
First rib and the costal cartilages
Transverse processes of the atlas and axis
Lower border of the mandible and the parotid fascia
correctOption: External occipital protuberance, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of C7 to T12
optionExplanations: The trapezius is a large, diamond-shaped muscle of the back and neck. It originates from the midline of the skull (occipital bone) and the posterior midline of the spine (C7 through all 12 thoracic vertebrae).
The medial third of the clavicle and the manubrium are the origin sites for the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not the trapezius.
The first rib serves as the insertion for the scalenus anterior and medius and the origin for the subclavius, but it is not an origin for the trapezius.
The transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae are associated with the origins of the scalene muscles and levator scapulae.
The lower border of the mandible and parotid fascia are related to the attachments of the platysma and masseter muscles, respectively.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Trapezius... Origin: External occipital protuberance, superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae, and spines of the seventh cervical and all the thoracic vertebrae.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A clinician is assessing the sensory pathways of the neck. While the spinal accessory nerve provides motor innervation to the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid, the proprioceptive fibers for these muscles are derived from different sources. Which combination correctly identifies the proprioceptive supply?
options: SCM: CN VII; Trapezius: CN X
SCM: C1, C2; Trapezius: C2, C3
SCM: C3, C4; Trapezius: C5, C6
SCM: C2, C3; Trapezius: C3, C4
SCM: CN XI; Trapezius: CN XI
correctOption: SCM: C2, C3; Trapezius: C3, C4
optionExplanations: Cranial nerves VII and X do not provide proprioceptive fibers to these specific muscles; CN VII is for facial expression and CN X is for the pharynx/larynx.
The C1 nerve does not have a cutaneous branch and primarily joins the hypoglossal nerve; it is not the primary proprioceptive source for the SCM.
C5 and C6 are the primary roots of the brachial plexus and do not provide proprioception for the trapezius or SCM.
According to the cervical plexus distribution, proprioception for the sternocleidomastoid is carried by branches from C2 and C3, while the trapezius receives fibers from C3 and C4.
While CN XI provides the motor supply, the sensory (proprioceptive) components travel via the cervical spinal nerves, not the accessory nerve itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Accessory Nerve Vulnerability in the Posterior Triangle
statement: A 28-year-old male presents with a drooping shoulder and difficulty elevating his arm above the horizontal plane following a surgical biopsy of a lymph node in the posterior triangle of his neck. He is still able to rotate his head to the opposite side with full strength. What is the most likely anatomic consequence of this injury?
options: Compression of the brachial plexus roots within the interscalene triangle.
Transection of the spinal accessory nerve distal to the sternocleidomastoid.
Denervation of the sternocleidomastoid due to proximal CN XI injury.
Lesion of the C1 fibers traveling with the hypoglossal nerve.
Injury to the phrenic nerve as it crosses the scalenus anterior.
correctOption: Transection of the spinal accessory nerve distal to the sternocleidomastoid.
optionExplanations: Brachial plexus compression would typically present with sensory loss, pain, or weakness in the upper limb muscles (like the deltoid), not isolated trapezius signs.

The accessory nerve is superficial in the posterior triangle. Injury here paralyzes the trapezius, leading to shoulder drop and loss of scapular rotation needed to elevate the arm above 90 degrees, while sparing the SCM which was innervated earlier.
If the injury were proximal to the SCM, head rotation (SCM function) would be impaired. The fact that he can rotate his head suggests the SCM branch is intact.
C1 fibers supply the infrahyoid strap muscles via the ansa cervicalis; injury there would not cause the trapezius-related signs described.
Phrenic nerve injury would lead to diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory issues, not shoulder drooping or impaired arm elevation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position. It can be injured at operation or from penetrating wounds. The trapezius muscle is paralyzed... The patient will experience difficulty in elevating the arm above the head, having abducted it to a right angle by using the deltoid muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Mechanical actions of the Trapezius fibers
statement: A patient is asked to perform a full abduction of the arm from 0 to 180 degrees. Which portion of the trapezius muscle is primarily responsible for rotating the scapula so that the glenoid cavity faces upward?
options: Middle fibers only
Lower fibers only, acting to depress the scapula
Upper fibers only, acting to elevate the scapula
Upper and lower fibers acting together
The muscle fibers that attach to the medial third of the clavicle
correctOption: Upper and lower fibers acting together
optionExplanations: The middle fibers adduct (retract) the scapula toward the spine but do not rotate it upward.
Lower fibers alone depress the scapula; they require the upper fibers to produce the rotational force on the scapula.
Upper fibers alone elevate the scapula (as in shrugging) but do not produce the necessary rotation for full abduction without the lower fibers.
To rotate the scapula for high abduction, the upper fibers (elevating the outer part) and lower fibers (pulling the inner part down) work together.
The fibers attaching to the lateral third (not medial) of the clavicle are the ones involved in trapezius function.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Trapezius] Action: Upper fibers elevate scapula; middle fibers adduct scapula; lower fibers depress scapula; upper and lower fibers together rotate scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: When both sternocleidomastoid muscles contract simultaneously (bilateral contraction), they produce a complex set of movements. Which of the following is a result of this bilateral action?
options: Abduction of the humerus above 90 degrees
Rotation of the face toward the ceiling
Retraction of the mandible and depression of the hyoid bone
Flexion of the cervical column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
Lateral flexion of the neck to the right
correctOption: Flexion of the cervical column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
optionExplanations: Abduction of the humerus above 90 degrees is the result of the combined action of the trapezius and serratus anterior rotating the scapula; the SCM does not cross the shoulder joint.
While bilateral contraction can extend the head (looking up), the most accurate anatomical description involves the specific combination of cervical flexion and atlanto-occipital extension.
Retraction of the mandible is performed by the temporalis muscle. Depression of the hyoid bone is the function of the infrahyoid muscles, not the SCM.

The SCM muscles together flex the cervical vertebral column (pulling the neck forward) but, because of their insertion on the mastoid process behind the axis of rotation, they also extend the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.
Lateral flexion is the result of unilateral contraction (one muscle acting alone), not bilateral contraction where forces on both sides balance out.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Sternocleidomastoid... Action: ...Both together: Flex the neck; extend the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which specific anatomical structure serves as the primary superior insertion point for the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: The mastoid process of the temporal bone
The lateral third of the superior nuchal line
The styloid process of the temporal bone
The external occipital protuberance
The transverse process of the atlas
correctOption: The mastoid process of the temporal bone
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid inserts primarily on the lateral surface of the mastoid process and extending onto the lateral half of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
The muscle inserts on the lateral half of the superior nuchal line, but the mastoid process is the more prominent and primary insertion point listed.
The styloid process gives origin to the stylohyoid and styloglossus muscles, but it has no direct attachment to the sternocleidomastoid.
The external occipital protuberance is a site of origin for the trapezius muscle, not an insertion for the sternocleidomastoid.
The transverse process of the atlas is not an attachment site for the sternocleidomastoid; it serves as an origin for muscles like the levator scapulae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Muscle] Sternocleidomastoid... [Insertion] Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral half of superior nuchal line.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius muscle is a large, triangular muscle with extensive attachments. Which of the following represents its correct insertion on the pectoral girdle?
options: Medial third of the clavicle, acromion, and coracoid process
The entire superior border of the scapula and the xiphoid process
Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula
Medial border of the scapula and lesser tubercle of the humerus
Lateral third of the clavicle and the bicipital groove
correctOption: Lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula
optionExplanations: The trapezius attaches to the lateral third of the clavicle, not the medial third. The coracoid process is the attachment site for the pectoralis minor, coracobrachialis, and the short head of the biceps brachii.
The xiphoid process is an attachment for abdominal muscles and the diaphragm. The trapezius is a posterior muscle and does not reach the anterior thoracic wall or the xiphoid process.

The trapezius inserts onto the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion process, and the superior border of the spine of the scapula. This lateral placement allows it to effectively move the scapula and rotate the glenoid cavity upward.
The medial border of the scapula is the insertion for the serratus anterior and rhomboid muscles. The lesser tubercle of the humerus is the insertion for the subscapularis muscle.
The bicipital groove (intertubercular sulcus) of the humerus is the insertion site for the 'lady between two majors' (latissimus dorsi, pectoralis major, and teres major), not the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Trapezius... Insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A forensic pathologist is reviewing a case of a failed suicide attempt involving horizontal neck lacerations. The pathologist notes that the carotid sheath remained intact despite deep cuts. How does the anatomical action of the sternocleidomastoid contribute to this protective phenomenon during neck extension?
options: The SCM forms a rigid bony-like shield via calcification of its middle third
Extension causes the carotid sheath to slide posteriorly beneath the thick SCM muscle
The SCM's attachment to the thyroid cartilage pulls the larynx forward to block the knife
Contraction of the SCM causes the carotid sheath to slide anteriorly away from the vertebrae
Unilateral contraction of the SCM rotates the carotid sheath toward the midline
correctOption: Extension causes the carotid sheath to slide posteriorly beneath the thick SCM muscle
optionExplanations: The SCM is a skeletal muscle and does not normally calcify to form a rigid shield; its protection is purely due to its mass and the relative movement of the vessels.

When the neck is extended, the carotid sheath moves posteriorly under the sternocleidomastoid. Because the SCM is a thick, strong muscle, it provides a physical barrier that often protects the underlying neurovascular structures from superficial or horizontal cuts.
The SCM is not attached to the thyroid cartilage; it attaches to the sternum, clavicle, and mastoid process. It does not move the larynx in the manner described.
The carotid sheath slides posteriorly, not anteriorly, during neck extension, which places it in a more protected position.
While unilateral contraction rotates the head, the question concerns the protective effect during extension, which involves the sheath sliding beneath the muscle mass.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Extension of the cervical part of the vertebral column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint cause the carotid sheath with its contained large blood vessels to slide posteriorly beneath the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: An athlete suffers a tear in the superior (upper) fibers of the trapezius muscle. Which of the following scapular movements would be most significantly impaired as a result?
options: Protraction of the scapula
Elevation of the scapula
Depression of the scapula
Rotation of the scapula so that the glenoid cavity faces downward
Adduction (retraction) of the scapula
correctOption: Elevation of the scapula
optionExplanations: Protraction of the scapula is the function of the serratus anterior; the trapezius is an antagonist to this movement as it retracts the scapula.
The upper fibers of the trapezius originate from the skull and ligamentum nuchae and insert onto the lateral clavicle and acromion; their contraction elevates the scapula.
Depression of the scapula is the function of the lower fibers of the trapezius, not the upper fibers.
The trapezius rotates the scapula so the glenoid cavity faces upward (to facilitate abduction). Downward rotation is handled by other muscles like the levator scapulae and pectoralis minor.
Adduction (retraction) of the scapula is primarily the function of the middle fibers of the trapezius and the rhomboids.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page) (Table 12.5): Trapezius... Action: Upper fibers elevate the scapula; middle fibers adduct the scapula; lower fibers depress the scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: While the spinal accessory nerve provides the primary motor stimulus for the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, which nerves are responsible for the proprioceptive feedback from these muscles?
options: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
C2 and C3 for SCM; C3 and C4 for trapezius
C1 and C2 anterior rami
C5 and C6 roots of the brachial plexus
The vagus nerve (CN X)
correctOption: C2 and C3 for SCM; C3 and C4 for trapezius
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve is sensory to the pharynx and posterior tongue, but it does not supply the SCM or trapezius.
According to the cervical plexus distribution, the SCM receives proprioceptive fibers from the C2 and C3 spinal nerves, while the trapezius receives them from C3 and C4.
C1 contributes to the nerve to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid via the hypoglossal nerve, but it is not the main proprioceptive supply for the SCM.
C5 and C6 roots form the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and supply the muscles of the shoulder and arm (e.g., deltoid, biceps), not the SCM.
The vagus nerve provides motor supply to the pharynx and larynx; it is not the source of proprioception for the superficial neck muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page) (Table 12.7): Sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A neonate is brought to the clinic with an abnormal head posture. The child's head is flexed toward the right side, and the face is rotated toward the left. A small, firm, non-tender mass is palpated within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. What is the most likely pathological mechanism for this condition?
options: Fracture of the right clavicle causing muscle splinting
Congenital absence of the mastoid process
Fibrosis and shortening of the SCM following birth trauma
Agenesis of the contralateral trapezius muscle
Idiopathic spasm of the spinal accessory nerve
correctOption: Fibrosis and shortening of the SCM following birth trauma
optionExplanations: A clavicular fracture would cause pain and limited movement (pseudoparalysis), but it does not cause the characteristic fibrotic shortening or rotation seen in torticollis.
The mastoid process is not even present at birth; it develops later due to the pull of the SCM. Its 'absence' at birth is normal and does not cause torticollis.
Congenital torticollis (wryneck) results from hemorrhage and subsequent fibrosis of the SCM. The shortened muscle pulls the head toward the affected side and rotates the face to the opposite side.
Agenesis of the trapezius would cause a drooping shoulder and inability to shrug, but it would not produce the specific rotation/flexion pattern of torticollis or a localized mass in the SCM.
Spasmodic torticollis is usually psychogenic and seen in adults, characterized by chronic contractions, rather than a fibrous mass in a neonate.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Accessory Nerve Lesion and Trapezius Paralysis
statement: A patient undergoes a surgical procedure in the posterior triangle of the neck. Post-operatively, they present with a dropped shoulder and difficulty elevating the arm above the horizontal plane. Upon examination, they can abduct the arm to 90 degrees using the deltoid, but no further. Which nerve was likely damaged, and which muscle is failing to perform its role?
options: Ansa cervicalis; Sternohyoid.
Spinal accessory nerve; Trapezius.
Suprascapular nerve; Supraspinatus.
Long thoracic nerve; Serratus anterior.
Phrenic nerve; Diaphragm.
correctOption: Spinal accessory nerve; Trapezius.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. Damage here causes issues with swallowing/laryngeal movement, not shoulder movement.

Correct. The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is relatively superficial in the posterior triangle. Its injury paralyzes the trapezius, causing the shoulder to drop and preventing the upward rotation of the scapula necessary to elevate the arm above 90 degrees.

Incorrect. Suprascapular nerve damage would affect the initiation of abduction (supraspinatus) and external rotation (infraspinatus), but wouldn't typically cause a dropped shoulder or prevent elevation above 90 if the deltoid is intact.
Incorrect. While serratus anterior damage also affects arm elevation (winging of scapula), the 'dropped shoulder' and 'abduction to 90 degrees' with wasting are classic for trapezius/CN XI injury.
Incorrect. Phrenic nerve injury leads to diaphragmatic paralysis, resulting in respiratory distress, not shoulder drop or arm elevation issues.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The trapezius muscle is paralyzed, the muscle will show wasting, and the shoulder will drop. The patient will experience difficulty in elevating the arm above the head, having abducted it to a right angle by using the deltoid muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: During a physical examination, a patient is asked to rotate their head to the left against resistance. This movement specifically tests the integrity and mechanical action of which of the following muscles?
options: The superior fibers of the left trapezius
The bilateral contraction of the splenius capitis
The inferior fibers of the right trapezius
The right sternocleidomastoid muscle
The left sternocleidomastoid muscle
correctOption: The right sternocleidomastoid muscle
optionExplanations: The superior fibers of the trapezius are primarily involved in elevating the scapula and extending the neck, rather than primary rotation of the face.
Bilateral contraction of the splenius capitis causes extension of the head, not isolated rotation of the face to the opposite side.
The inferior fibers of the trapezius act to depress the scapula and do not participate in face rotation.
The sternocleidomastoid acts unilaterally to tilt the head to the same side but rotate the face to the opposite side. Therefore, rotating the face to the left requires the right SCM.
Contraction of the left sternocleidomastoid would rotate the face to the right, not the left.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): The mastoid process is thus pulled down toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side, the cervical spine is flexed, and the face looks upward to the opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which of the following describes a correct anatomical attachment point for the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: Spine of the scapula
Lateral third of the clavicle
External occipital protuberance
Medial third of the superior nuchal line
Lateral half of the superior nuchal line
correctOption: Lateral half of the superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: The spine of the scapula is an insertion for the trapezius.
The *medial* third of the clavicle is an origin for the SCM; the *lateral* third is an attachment for the trapezius.
The external occipital protuberance is an origin for the trapezius.
The *medial* third of the superior nuchal line is an origin for the trapezius, not the SCM.
The sternocleidomastoid inserts into the mastoid process and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line. This is a high-yield anatomical fact.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Sternocleidomastoid] Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral half of superior nuchal line of occipital bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The origin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle is characterized by two distinct heads. Where are these heads attached?
options: Mastoid process and superior nuchal line
First rib and the transverse process of C1
Styloid process and angle of the mandible
Acromion and the coracoid process
Manubrium sterni and medial third of the clavicle
correctOption: Manubrium sterni and medial third of the clavicle
optionExplanations: The mastoid process and the superior nuchal line are the *insertion* points of the sternocleidomastoid, not its origin. The muscle is named for its origin-to-insertion path.
The first rib is the origin for the subclavius and the insertion for the scalenus anterior/medius. C1 transverse process is an origin for the levator scapulae.
The styloid process is the origin for the stylohyoid and stylopharyngeus muscles. The angle of the mandible is an attachment for the masseter and medial pterygoid.
The acromion and coracoid process are parts of the scapula involved in the attachments of the trapezius, deltoid, and various arm muscles, but not the sternocleidomastoid.
The sternocleidomastoid originates via a rounded sternal head from the manubrium sterni and a wider clavicular head from the superior surface of the medial third of the clavicle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Sternocleidomastoid... Origin: Manubrium sterni and medial third of clavicle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which of the following is a component of the proximal attachment (origin) for the trapezius muscle?
options: Manubrium sterni
First rib
Medial third of the clavicle
Body of the hyoid bone
Ligamentum nuchae
correctOption: Ligamentum nuchae
optionExplanations: The manubrium sterni is an origin for the sternocleidomastoid, not the trapezius.
The first rib is an attachment for the scalene muscles, not the trapezius.
The trapezius inserts into the lateral third of the clavicle; the sternocleidomastoid originates from the medial third.
The hyoid bone is an attachment for the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles, but the trapezius does not attach there.
The trapezius has a wide origin that includes the external occipital protuberance, the ligamentum nuchae, and the spines of C7 down to T12.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Trapezius] Origin: External occipital protuberance, superior nuchal line, ligamentum nuchae, spines of C7 to T12.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius muscle is essential for the full abduction of the upper limb. Which specific action of the trapezius facilitates this by moving the scapula?
options: Fixation of the scapula in a retracted position only
Protraction of the scapula away from the midline
Pure depression of the scapula by the upper fibers
Downward rotation of the scapula
Upward rotation of the scapula by the upper and lower fibers
correctOption: Upward rotation of the scapula by the upper and lower fibers
optionExplanations: While the middle fibers do retract the scapula (pull it medially), this action alone does not facilitate the upward rotation required for high abduction.
Protraction (moving the scapula forward) is primarily the action of the serratus anterior and pectoralis minor, not the trapezius (which retracts).
The upper fibers of the trapezius elevate the scapula; it is the lower fibers that assist in depression and downward pull on the medial border.
Downward rotation would lower the glenoid cavity and inhibit abduction. The trapezius performs upward rotation to facilitate lifting the arm.
To abduct the arm above 90 degrees, the scapula must rotate so the glenoid cavity faces upward. This is achieved by the upper and lower fibers of the trapezius acting as a force couple.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Trapezius... Action: Upper fibers elevate the scapula; middle fibers pull scapula medially; lower fibers pull medial border of scapula downward; together with serratus anterior, rotates scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: While both the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles are motorially innervated by the same cranial nerve, they differ in their sources for proprioceptive sensation. Which spinal nerves provide proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius?
options: C3 and C4
C1 and C2
C5 and C6
C1 through C4
C2 and C3
correctOption: C3 and C4
optionExplanations: Anatomical texts specify that branches from the C3 and C4 ventral rami of the cervical plexus carry proprioceptive information from the trapezius muscle.
C1 does not typically provide cutaneous or proprioceptive branches to these muscles; C2 is involved with SCM but not primarily trapezius proprioception.
C5 and C6 are part of the brachial plexus and do not provide proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius.
While C1-C4 forms the cervical plexus, only the specific branches from C3 and C4 are designated for trapezius proprioception.
C2 and C3 provide proprioceptive fibers to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): [Cervical Plexus] The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A newborn is brought to the clinic with an abnormal head posture. The head is tilted toward the right shoulder, and the face is rotated toward the left side. A small, firm mass is palpated within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Based on the mechanism of congenital torticollis, what is the underlying cause of this presentation?
options: Paralysis of the left spinal accessory nerve
Spasmodic contraction due to psychogenic origin
Idiopathic hypertrophy of the right mastoid process
Agenesis of the contralateral trapezius muscle
Fibrosis and shortening of the muscle following a birth injury
correctOption: Fibrosis and shortening of the muscle following a birth injury
optionExplanations: Paralysis would lead to a lack of tone, not the fixed contracture seen here.
Spasmodic torticollis is usually psychogenic and seen in adults, whereas this is a neonatal presentation with a palpable mass.
The mastoid process develops later in response to SCM pull; it is not the primary cause of the tilt.
Trapezius agenesis would not cause the specific SCM-mediated rotation/tilt pattern described.
Congenital torticollis results from birth trauma (hemorrhage) followed by fibrous contraction of the SCM, pulling the mastoid toward the sternum and rotating the face to the opposite side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient presents with 'winged scapula' and significant weakness in rotating the scapula upward during arm elevation. However, the clinician notes the serratus anterior is functioning normally. A lesion is suspected in the nerve supplying the muscle that originates from the external occipital protuberance and ligamentum nuchae. Where did this nerve most likely sustain damage?
options: Within the carotid sheath
In the mandibular notch
At the stylomastoid foramen
As it crosses the posterior triangle of the neck
In the internal acoustic meatus
correctOption: As it crosses the posterior triangle of the neck
optionExplanations: While the accessory nerve leaves the skull via the jugular foramen and travels near the carotid sheath, its most vulnerable, superficial point where it can be easily injured in isolation is in the posterior triangle.
The mandibular notch is related to the masseteric nerve and artery, far from the course of the spinal accessory nerve.
The stylomastoid foramen is the exit for the facial nerve (CN VII).

The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) emerges from the SCM and crosses the posterior triangle superficially to reach the trapezius. This is a high-risk site for injury during neck surgeries or trauma, leading to trapezius-specific 'winging' (different from serratus anterior winging).
The internal acoustic meatus transmits the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves, not the accessory nerve (XI).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position. It can be injured at operation or from penetrating wounds. The trapezius muscle is paralyzed...

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is a prominent landmark of the neck. Which of the following constitutes its primary motor innervation?
options: The cranial root of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
Ansa cervicalis (C1, C2, and C3)
The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, and C5)
The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
correctOption: The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
optionExplanations: The cranial root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) is considered accessory to the vagus nerve and primarily supplies the muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx, rather than the sternocleidomastoid.
The ansa cervicalis is a loop of the cervical plexus (C1-C3) that supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles, such as the omohyoid and sternothyroid, but not the sternocleidomastoid.

The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) originates from the upper five segments of the cervical spinal cord, enters the skull through the foramen magnum, and exits through the jugular foramen to provide motor supply to both the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
The phrenic nerve provides the sole motor supply to the diaphragm and sensory supply to various serous membranes; it does not innervate the superficial neck muscles like the sternocleidomastoid.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) descends into the neck to supply the platysma muscle, but it does not provide motor innervation to the sternocleidomastoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): The spinal root runs downward and laterally and enters the deep surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which it supplies, and then crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to supply the trapezius muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which of the following describes the correct distal attachment (insertion) of the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and superior nuchal line
Body of the hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage
Coronoid process of the mandible
Transverse processes of C1–C4 vertebrae
Spine of the scapula and acromion
correctOption: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid originates from the sternum and clavicle and inserts into the mastoid process and the lateral part of the superior nuchal line.
These are the attachments of the infrahyoid strap muscles like the thyrohyoid or sternohyoid.
The coronoid process of the mandible is the insertion for the temporalis muscle.
The transverse processes of the upper cervical vertebrae are origin sites for prevertebral muscles like the longus capitis or levator scapulae.
The spine of the scapula and acromion are the insertion sites for the trapezius muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Sternocleidomastoid] Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and superior nuchal line of occipital bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 34-year-old female undergoes a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. Post-operatively, she complains of a 'heavy' shoulder and difficulty combing her hair. Physical exam shows a dropped shoulder and an inability to abduct her arm above the horizontal plane. Which anatomical attachment of the affected muscle explains the loss of overhead abduction?
options: Origin from the medial third of the superior nuchal line
Insertion into the bicipital groove of the humerus
Insertion into the mastoid process of the temporal bone
Origin from the spines of all thoracic vertebrae
Insertion into the lateral third of the clavicle and acromion
correctOption: Insertion into the lateral third of the clavicle and acromion
optionExplanations: The superior nuchal line is an origin for the upper fibers of the trapezius, but the inability to rotate the scapula (the cause of abduction loss) is tied to the forces exerted on the insertion points.
The trapezius does not insert into the humerus. The latissimus dorsi inserts into the bicipital groove.
The mastoid process is the insertion for the sternocleidomastoid, not the trapezius. SCM palsy would cause head rotation weakness, not abduction failure.

While the trapezius originates from the thoracic spines, this origin provides the stable base but doesn't explain the mechanical failure of scapular rotation as directly as the insertion site on the mobile scapula/clavicle.

The patient has suffered an injury to the spinal accessory nerve in the posterior triangle, paralyzing the trapezius. The trapezius inserts into the lateral clavicle, acromion, and scapular spine. Its role in rotating the scapula upward is essential for abducting the arm above 90 degrees; without this rotation, the humerus hits the acromion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Trapezius] Insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula. Action: Upper fibers elevate the scapula; middle fibers retract the scapula; lower fibers depress the scapula; upper and lower fibers together rotate the scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Bilateral contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscles produces a specific movement of the cervical column and head. What is the net result of this bilateral action when the neck is not fixed?
options: Elevation of the scapula and clavicle
