The mechanism involves birth trauma causing hemorrhage into the SCM, followed by fibrosis. The resulting contracture pulls the mastoid process down, causing the head to tilt and the face to rotate to the opposite side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 40-year-old female presents with an inability to pull her scapula medially toward the midline. Physical examination reveals wasting of the muscle that attaches to the ligamentum nuchae and the spines of the thoracic vertebrae. Which nerve is most likely compromised?
options: Suprascapular nerve
Long thoracic nerve
Thoracodorsal nerve
Spinal accessory nerve
Dorsal scapular nerve
correctOption: Spinal accessory nerve
optionExplanations: The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles of the rotator cuff, which act on the glenohumeral joint, not on scapular retraction.
The long thoracic nerve supplies the serratus anterior. Damage to this nerve causes 'winging' of the scapula, not an isolated inability to retract it toward the midline.
The thoracodorsal nerve supplies the latissimus dorsi. This muscle acts on the humerus (adduction, extension, internal rotation) rather than being the primary retractor of the scapula.

The trapezius is responsible for scapular retraction (adduction) via its middle fibers. It is innervated by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), and its paralysis leads to loss of this movement and muscle wasting.

The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the rhomboids, which also retract the scapula. However, the question specifies a muscle attached to the ligamentum nuchae and thoracic spines (Trapezius), which is innervated by CN XI.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5 Trapezius ... Nerve supply: Spinal part of accessory nerve (motor) and C3 and 4 (proprioceptive). ... Action: Upper fibers elevate scapula; middle fibers adduct scapula; lower fibers depress scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Regarding the attachments of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which of the following accurately describes its superior insertion?
options: The zygomatic arch and temporal line
The coronoid process of the mandible
The mastoid process of the temporal bone and superior nuchal line
The spinous process of the axis (C2)
The transverse process of the atlas (C1)
correctOption: The mastoid process of the temporal bone and superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: The zygomatic arch is the origin of the masseter muscle, while the temporal lines provide attachment for the temporal fascia and temporalis muscle.
The coronoid process of the mandible is the insertion for the temporalis muscle, a muscle of mastication.
The sternocleidomastoid inserts superiorly onto the mastoid process and the lateral portion of the superior nuchal line, allowing it to act on the skull.
The spinous process of the axis is an attachment point for various deep neck muscles and the ligamentum nuchae, but not the sternocleidomastoid.
The transverse process of the atlas serves as an attachment for muscles like the levator scapulae or small rotators, but not the sternocleidomastoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5... Sternocleidomastoid... Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral part of superior nuchal line of occipital bone.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient is evaluated for an inability to flex the neck forward against resistance. Which of the following describes the anatomical basis for this movement as performed by the sternocleidomastoid muscles?
options: Unilateral contraction tilting the head to the same side
Unilateral contraction rotating the face to the opposite side
Bilateral contraction extending the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
Bilateral contraction elevating the sternum as an accessory muscle of respiration
Bilateral contraction flexing the cervical part of the vertebral column
correctOption: Bilateral contraction flexing the cervical part of the vertebral column
optionExplanations: Unilateral contraction tilting the head to the same side is a lateral flexion movement, not the forward flexion of the neck tested by resisted forward bowing.
Rotation of the face to the opposite side is a result of unilateral contraction, which occurs when only one SCM is active.
While the SCM can assist in head extension depending on the starting position of the atlanto-occipital joint, 'flexing the neck forward' specifically refers to cervical spine flexion.
Elevating the sternum is an auxiliary action of the SCM used during forced inspiration, but it is not the primary motor description for resisted neck flexion testing in a neurological exam.
When both SCM muscles contract together, they act to flex the cervical spine, drawing the head forward. This is the primary bilateral action of these muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page) (Table 12.5): Action: Bilateral: flex cervical part of vertebral column; extend head. Unilateral: tilts head to same side and rotates it so face looks to opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: While both the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius receive motor innervation from the spinal accessory nerve, they differ in their proprioceptive nerve supply. Which of the following correctly identifies this contrast?
options: Sternocleidomastoid is C1-C2; Trapezius is C2-C3
Sternocleidomastoid is C4-C5; Trapezius is C5-C6
Sternocleidomastoid is C3-C4; Trapezius is C2-C3
Sternocleidomastoid is C2-C3; Trapezius is C5-C6
Sternocleidomastoid is C2-C3; Trapezius is C3-C4
correctOption: Sternocleidomastoid is C2-C3; Trapezius is C3-C4
optionExplanations: The C1 nerve generally has no cutaneous or distinct proprioceptive branch to these muscles. Proprioceptive fibers for the SCM start at C2.
C5 and C6 are components of the brachial plexus, primarily supplying the upper limb muscles (like the deltoid or biceps), not the proprioception for the neck strap or superficial muscles.
This option reverses the correct levels. SCM is supplied by more superior cervical segments (C2,3) than the trapezius (C3,4).
While C2-C3 is correct for SCM, C5-C6 is incorrect for the trapezius, which relies on the C3 and C4 roots for its sensory feedback regarding position and tension.

The cervical plexus provides distinct proprioceptive fibers to these muscles: C2 and C3 for the sternocleidomastoid, and C3 and C4 for the trapezius. This subtle difference is vital for understanding segmental nerve lesions in the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): [Cervical Plexus] The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: During an orthopedic evaluation, a patient is asked to perform 'upward rotation of the scapula' to allow full abduction of the arm. Which coordination of trapezius muscle fibers is necessary to achieve this specific rotation of the glenoid cavity upward?
options: Contraction of the upper fibers only.
Inhibition of all trapezius fibers with isolated serratus anterior activity.
Contraction of the lower fibers only.
Contraction of the middle fibers only.
Contraction of the upper and lower fibers together.
correctOption: Contraction of the upper and lower fibers together.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Isolated contraction of the upper fibers results in simple elevation of the scapula (shrugging), not upward rotation.
Incorrect. While the serratus anterior also rotates the scapula upward, it works in concert with the trapezius, not in its absence, for full range of motion.
Incorrect. Isolated contraction of the lower fibers results in depression of the scapula.
Incorrect. The middle fibers primarily retract the scapula (pull it toward the midline) rather than rotating it upward.
Correct. To rotate the scapula so that the glenoid cavity faces upward (allowing the arm to be raised above the head), the upper and lower fibers of the trapezius must contract in synergy.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Trapezius ... Action: Upper fibers: elevate scapula; middle fibers: retract scapula; lower fibers: depress scapula; upper and lower fibers: rotate scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A newborn is brought to the clinic with the head tilted toward the right shoulder and the face turned upward toward the left. On palpation, a firm, non-tender mass is felt within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism responsible for this permanent positional deformity?
options: Wedge-shaped deformity of the thoracic vertebrae
Acute spasm of the muscle due to psychogenic origin
Congenital absence of the contralateral trapezius muscle
Fibrous tissue invasion and contraction following muscle stretching
Denervation atrophy of the spinal accessory nerve
correctOption: Fibrous tissue invasion and contraction following muscle stretching
optionExplanations: Vertebral wedging is a secondary skeletal change that occurs if the muscular torticollis is left untreated, rather than being the primary cause.
Spasmodic torticollis, not congenital, is often psychogenic and results from repeated chronic contractions rather than fibrous shortening.
Trapezius absence would lead to shoulder drop and inability to shrug, not the characteristic head tilt and rotation of torticollis.
The condition is caused by labor-induced stretching and hemorrhage, which is replaced by contracting fibrous tissue that shortens the muscle, pulling the mastoid toward the sternum.
Denervation would lead to flaccid paralysis and wasting, not the contracted shortening seen in congenital torticollis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page)-1625: Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the Accessory Nerve in the Posterior Triangle
statement: During a surgical biopsy of a lymph node in the posterior triangle of the neck, the surgeon accidentally transects a nerve as it emerges from the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and crosses the triangle. Which functional deficit will be most prominent?
options: Inability to rotate the face toward the opposite side.
Paralysis of the diaphragm on the affected side.
Inability to shrug the shoulder and drop in shoulder height.
Hoarseness due to vocal cord paralysis.
Loss of sensation over the angle of the mandible.
correctOption: Inability to shrug the shoulder and drop in shoulder height.
optionExplanations: Face rotation is a function of the SCM. Since the nerve was cut after emerging from the SCM, the SCM's innervation remains intact.
The phrenic nerve lies deep to the prevertebral fascia and is usually protected unless the dissection is very deep; it is not the superficial nerve crossing the triangle.

The spinal accessory nerve supplies the SCM first and then enters the posterior triangle to reach the trapezius. Transection in the triangle spares the SCM but paralyzes the trapezius, leading to a shoulder drop and inability to shrug.
Vocal cord paralysis results from damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus, which does not cross the posterior triangle.
The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) provides sensation to the angle of the mandible; while it also emerges from the SCM, the question implies a motor/nerve trunk lesion related to CN XI.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position. It can be injured at operation or from penetrating wounds. The trapezius muscle is paralyzed, the muscle will show wasting, and the shoulder will drop.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 22-year-old medical student is studying the muscular boundaries of the neck triangles. She identifies a muscle that originates from the manubrium sterni and the medial third of the clavicle. To which specific anatomical landmarks does this muscle insert?
options: Lateral third of the clavicle and the acromion process
Transverse processes of the upper four cervical vertebrae
Body of the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage
Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the superior nuchal line
Spine of the scapula and the external occipital protuberance
correctOption: Mastoid process of the temporal bone and the superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: This describes the insertion of the trapezius muscle, which attaches to the lateral third of the clavicle and acromion, rather than the sternocleidomastoid.
This describes the origin of the levator scapulae muscle, which is located in the floor of the posterior triangle.
These landmarks are associated with the infrahyoid (strap) muscles such as the thyrohyoid and sternohyoid, not the sternocleidomastoid.

The sternocleidomastoid muscle inserts on the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone, forming the landmark boundary between the anterior and posterior triangles.
These are the origin points for parts of the trapezius muscle, not the insertion of the sternocleidomastoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1620 (Book Page): [Muscle: Sternocleidomastoid] [Insertion:] Mastoid process of temporal bone and superior nuchal line of occipital bone

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient presents with a chronic psychogenic condition resulting in repeated, painful contractions of the Trapezius and Sternocleidomastoid muscles. Which clinical intervention is described as a potential treatment for severe cases of this 'spasmodic' condition?
options: Surgical resection of the C3 and C4 nerve roots
Anesthesia of the great auricular nerve
Ligature of the external jugular vein to reduce muscle congestion
Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve
Bilateral excision of the mastoid processes
correctOption: Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve
optionExplanations: Resecting C3 and C4 would primarily affect proprioception and potentially other cervical plexus functions, but it would not stop the motor spasms driven by CN XI.
The great auricular nerve is purely sensory to the skin over the parotid and angle of the jaw; it has no motor control over the SCM or trapezius.
The external jugular vein is a superficial drainage vessel. Ligating it would not affect the neuro-muscular contractions of the neck muscles and could cause venous congestion.

Because the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the motor drive to both the SCM and the trapezius, surgically cutting (sectioning) this nerve can paralyze these muscles to stop the chronic, painful spasms.
Excising the mastoid processes would destroy the insertion of the SCM but is a radical and inappropriate treatment for a functional/psychogenic movement disorder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): Spasmodic torticollis... results from repeated chronic contractions of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles... Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve may be necessary in severe cases.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient with a suspected Accessory nerve lesion is found to have a drooping shoulder and an inability to elevate the arm above the horizontal plane. What is the physiological role of the trapezius in allowing full abduction above 90 degrees?
options: It rotates the scapula, directing the glenoid cavity upward.
It provides initial abduction of the humerus for the first 15 degrees.
It depresses the clavicle to prevent impingement on the acromion.
It acts as the primary adductor of the scapula to stabilize the glenoid.
It flexes the humerus at the glenohumeral joint to clear the acromion.
correctOption: It rotates the scapula, directing the glenoid cavity upward.
optionExplanations: To lift the arm above the head, the scapula must be rotated by the trapezius and serratus anterior so that the glenoid cavity faces upward; without this rotation, the humerus hits the acromion.
Initial abduction (0-15 degrees) is the role of the supraspinatus muscle.
The trapezius elevates the scapula/clavicle (upper fibers) rather than depressing the clavicle during abduction.
Adduction of the scapula (bringing it toward the midline) is performed by the middle fibers of the trapezius, but this does not directly facilitate arm elevation above 90 degrees.
Flexion of the humerus is primarily performed by the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid, not the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5... Trapezius... Action: Upper fibers elevate the scapula; middle fibers adduct the scapula; lower fibers depress the scapula; upper and lower fibers together rotate the scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: In a clinical examination, a patient is asked to rotate their head to the left against resistance. Which muscle is primarily being tested, and what is its specific unilateral action on the head?
options: Left trapezius; it rotates the head to the opposite side and elevates the shoulder.
Right sternocleidomastoid; it tilts the head to the right and rotates the face to the left.
Bilateral sternocleidomastoids; they produce pure flexion without rotation.
Left sternocleidomastoid; it tilts the head to the left and rotates the face to the left.
Right trapezius; it rotates the head to the same side and retracts the scapula.
correctOption: Right sternocleidomastoid; it tilts the head to the right and rotates the face to the left.
optionExplanations: The trapezius is primarily involved in scapular movements and head extension; while it can assist in rotation, the standard test for head rotation targets the SCM.

The sternocleidomastoid pulls the mastoid process toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side (ipsilateral tilt) while simultaneously rotating the face to the opposite side (contralateral rotation). To rotate the face to the left, the right SCM must contract.
Bilateral contraction of the sternocleidomastoids causes flexion of the neck and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint, rather than isolated rotation.
The left sternocleidomastoid rotates the face to the right, not the left. Unilateral contraction causes ipsilateral tilt but contralateral rotation.
The trapezius acts on the scapula (retraction, elevation, depression) and assists in head extension; it is not the primary muscle tested by head rotation against resistance.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): The mastoid process is thus pulled down toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side, the cervical spine is flexed, and the face looks upward to the opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: During forced inspiration, the sternocleidomastoid muscle is recruited to assist the primary muscles of respiration. By which physiological mechanism does it contribute to increasing thoracic volume?
options: By depressing the first rib and clavicle
By relaxing the diaphragm to allow more air
By pulling the manubrium sterni and clavicle upward
By rotating the thoracic vertebrae laterally
By constricting the laryngeal inlet
correctOption: By pulling the manubrium sterni and clavicle upward
optionExplanations: Depressing the ribs would decrease thoracic volume and facilitate expiration, not inspiration.
SCM does not regulate the diaphragm; the phrenic nerve manages diaphragmatic contraction to increase volume.
When the head is fixed, the SCM acts as an accessory muscle of inspiration by elevating the manubrium and clavicles, thereby lifting the thoracic cage and increasing volume.
The SCM acts on the head and neck, not on the rotation of the thoracic vertebrae themselves during respiration.
The laryngeal inlet is managed by intrinsic laryngeal muscles; SCM is an extrinsic neck muscle with no role in the inlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Sternocleidomastoid... Two heads together flex neck, draw head forward; also accessory muscle of inspiration.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: In the neck, the sternocleidomastoid muscle serves as a critical anatomical landmark. Which of the following describes its insertion most accurately?
options: The transverse processes of the upper four cervical vertebrae.
The acromion process and the spine of the scapula.
The body of the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage.
The mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line.
The manubrium sterni and the medial third of the clavicle.
correctOption: The mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line.
optionExplanations: The transverse processes of cervical vertebrae are the origins for muscles like the scalenes and levator scapulae, not the sternocleidomastoid.
The acromion and scapular spine are insertion sites for the trapezius and origin sites for the deltoid.
The hyoid bone and thyroid cartilage are attachment sites for infrahyoid and suprahyoid muscles, not the sternocleidomastoid.
The sternocleidomastoid inserts superiorly onto the mastoid process and the lateral part of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
These are the origins (sternal and clavicular heads) of the sternocleidomastoid, not its insertion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5... Sternocleidomastoid: Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral half of superior nuchal line.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Differential Proprioceptive Innervation of Neck Muscles
statement: Regarding the sensory and motor innervation of the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles, which of the following statements accurately distinguishes their nerve supply?
options: The sternocleidomastoid is supplied by the phrenic nerve while the trapezius is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve.
The motor supply to the trapezius is from the dorsal rami of C3-C4, whereas the SCM is supplied by the ventral rami of C2-C3.
Proprioceptive fibers for both muscles are exclusively carried within the trunk of the spinal accessory nerve.
Both muscles receive motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve, but SCM receives proprioception from C2 and C3 while trapezius receives it from C3 and C4.
Both muscles receive motor supply from the facial nerve, but proprioception is provided by the cervical plexus (C1-C2).
correctOption: Both muscles receive motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve, but SCM receives proprioception from C2 and C3 while trapezius receives it from C3 and C4.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm. Both SCM and trapezius receive motor supply from CN XI.
Incorrect. The motor supply is CN XI; C3-C4 provide proprioception to the trapezius, but they are not the primary motor nerves.

Incorrect. Proprioceptive fibers reach these muscles through branches of the cervical plexus (C2,3 and C3,4), not through the spinal accessory nerve itself, which is motor in function at the muscles' entry points.

Correct. Both muscles are innervated by the spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor function. However, proprioceptive fibers for the SCM are derived from the anterior rami of C2 and C3, whereas for the trapezius, they are derived from C3 and C4.
Incorrect. The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and the platysma, not the SCM or trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): [Table 12.7] Sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive. ... [Page 1680 (Book Page)] The spinal root ... enters the deep surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which it supplies, and then crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to supply the trapezius muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 45-year-old female presents to the clinic three weeks after a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. She complains of difficulty brushing her hair and a 'heavy' feeling in her right shoulder. On examination, there is noticeable sagging of the right shoulder and the patient is unable to shrug her right shoulder against resistance. However, she can still rotate her head to the left side with normal strength. Where is the most likely location of the nerve lesion?
options: At the origin of the spinal accessory nerve in the medulla oblongata
Deep to the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
At the level of the C3 and C4 spinal nerve roots
At the jugular foramen
Within the posterior triangle, distal to the sternocleidomastoid
correctOption: Within the posterior triangle, distal to the sternocleidomastoid
optionExplanations: A lesion at the origin in the central nervous system would paralyze all muscles supplied by that nerve (both SCM and trapezius) and would typically be associated with other brainstem signs, which is inconsistent with a localized biopsy-related injury.
A lesion deep to the SCM would paralyze the SCM itself, making rotation of the head to the opposite side difficult or weak, which is not the case here.
The C3 and C4 roots provide proprioception but not the primary motor drive for shrugging (which is CN XI). A lesion here would not cause the profound motor paralysis described.

A lesion at the jugular foramen would paralyze both the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius, as well as potentially affecting the glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves. The patient can still rotate her head, meaning the SCM is intact.

The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) enters the SCM, supplies it, and then emerges from its posterior border to cross the posterior triangle to reach the trapezius. A lesion in the posterior triangle (common during biopsies) spares the SCM but paralyzes the trapezius, causing shoulder drop and shrugging weakness.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): [Accessory Nerve Injury] The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position... The trapezius muscle is paralyzed... the shoulder will drop... The patient will experience difficulty in elevating the arm above the head... asking the patient to rotate the head to one side... causing the sternocleidomastoid of the opposite side to come into action.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: In the physiological regulation of shoulder movement, the trapezius muscle must work in coordination with other muscles to allow the arm to be raised above the head. What is the specific mechanical role of the trapezius in this process?
options: It depresses the clavicle to prevent it from hitting the first rib
The upper and lower fibers act together to rotate the scapula, directing the glenoid cavity upward
It acts as a primary flexor of the humerus at the glenohumeral joint
It stabilizes the humerus within the glenoid fossa via its lower fibers
It retracts the scapula to provide a stable base for the pectoralis major
correctOption: The upper and lower fibers act together to rotate the scapula, directing the glenoid cavity upward
optionExplanations: The trapezius elevates the clavicle (via its upper fibers) rather than depressing it; the subclavius muscle is the one that depresses the clavicle.

For overhead reach, the scapula must rotate so the glenoid cavity faces upward. This is achieved by the upper fibers pulling the acromion up and the lower fibers pulling the medial spine down, acting as a force couple.
The primary flexors of the humerus are the anterior deltoid and pectoralis major. The trapezius moves the scapula and clavicle, not the humerus directly.
Stabilizing the humerus in the glenoid fossa is the primary job of the rotator cuff muscles (SITS), not the superficial trapezius.
While the middle fibers retract the scapula, this stabilization is for general back strength and posture, not the specific 'loop' required for upward rotation and abduction above 90 degrees.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5 Neck Muscles] Trapezius... Action: ...upper and lower fibers together rotate the scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A first-year medical student is asked to identify the superior attachment of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which of the following anatomical landmarks is the correct insertion site?
options: The mastoid process of the temporal bone
The styloid process of the temporal bone
The coronoid process of the mandible
The zygomatic arch
The mental spines of the mandible
correctOption: The mastoid process of the temporal bone
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid muscle originates from the manubrium and clavicle and inserts superiorly on the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the superior nuchal line.
The styloid process provides attachment for the styloid muscles (stylohyoid, styloglossus, stylopharyngeus) and the stylohyoid ligament, not the sternocleidomastoid.
The coronoid process is an attachment site for the muscles of mastication, specifically the temporalis muscle, not the sternocleidomastoid.
The zygomatic arch provides the origin for the masseter muscle and attachment for the temporal fascia, but the sternocleidomastoid attaches posterior to this on the mastoid process.
The mental spines (genial tubercles) on the medial surface of the mandible give origin to the genioglossus and geniohyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1623 (Book Page): [When the sternocleidomastoid muscle contracts, it appears as an oblique band crossing the side of the neck from the sternoclavicular joint to the mastoid process of the skull.]

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Proprioceptive vs Motor innervation of neck muscles
statement: A clinician is evaluating the proprioceptive pathways of the neck muscles. When comparing the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius, which of the following describes the correct origin of proprioceptive fibers for these muscles?
options: Sternocleidomastoid from C3–C4; Trapezius from C4–C5.
Both receive proprioception from the Accessory nerve (CN XI).
Sternocleidomastoid from C1–C2; Trapezius from C2–C3.
Both receive proprioception from the facial nerve via the cervical branch.
Sternocleidomastoid from C2–C3; Trapezius from C3–C4.
correctOption: Sternocleidomastoid from C2–C3; Trapezius from C3–C4.
optionExplanations: C5 is primarily part of the brachial plexus and does not supply proprioception to these specific muscles in the standard cervical plexus layout.
The accessory nerve provides motor innervation; proprioception is provided by the cervical plexus rami.
C1 does not typically provide cutaneous or proprioceptive branches in this manner; C2 and C3 are specific to the SCM.
The facial nerve provides motor supply to the platysma, but it is not the source of proprioception for the SCM or trapezius.
According to the cervical plexus distribution, C2 and C3 provide proprioceptive fibers to the sternocleidomastoid, while C3 and C4 provide them to the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Anatomical Localization of Accessory Nerve Lesion
statement: A 55-year-old male undergoes a radical neck dissection for laryngeal carcinoma. Post-operatively, he is unable to shrug his left shoulder, and physical examination shows a significant 'dropping' of the shoulder on the affected side. However, he is still able to rotate his head to the right against resistance. Where is the most likely site of the nerve lesion?
options: Anterior rami of cervical nerves C3 and C4
Spinal part of the accessory nerve at the jugular foramen
Spinal part of the accessory nerve within the posterior triangle
Vagus nerve just below the inferior sensory ganglion
Hypoglossal nerve in the carotid triangle
correctOption: Spinal part of the accessory nerve within the posterior triangle
optionExplanations: C3 and C4 provide proprioception to the trapezius. Their loss would not cause a complete motor paralysis or a dramatic shoulder drop, which is a motor nerve deficit.
A lesion at the jugular foramen would paralyze both the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius. Since the patient can still rotate his head (SCM function), the lesion must be more distal.

The accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid first, then enters the posterior triangle to reach the trapezius. A lesion in the posterior triangle spares the SCM but paralyzes the trapezius, causing shoulder drop.
The vagus nerve does not supply the trapezius or SCM; its injury would present with vocal cord palsy or swallowing difficulties rather than shoulder issues.
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles. Damage would result in tongue deviation, not the inability to shrug the shoulder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position. It can be injured at operation... The trapezius muscle is paralyzed, the muscle will show wasting, and the shoulder will drop.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient is asked to perform an action that requires the upper fibers of the trapezius to work in isolation. Which movement most accurately tests this specific portion of the muscle?
options: Flexing the head forward against resistance
Depressing the scapula downward
Retracting the scapulae toward the midline
Shrugging the shoulders
Rotating the face toward the same side
correctOption: Shrugging the shoulders
optionExplanations: Head flexion is an action of the bilateral sternocleidomastoids, not the trapezius.
Depression of the scapula is the function of the lower fibers of the trapezius.
This is primarily the action of the middle fibers of the trapezius and the rhomboids.
Elevation of the scapula (shrugging) is the specific functional test for the upper fibers of the trapezius.
This is not a function of the trapezius; unilateral SCM rotates the face to the opposite side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Trapezius Action: Upper fibers elevate scapula; middle fibers adduct scapula; lower fibers depress scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A student is tracing the origins of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. The sternal head of this muscle originates from which specific part of the manubrium sterni?
options: Superior border.
Lateral border.
Anterior surface.
Posterior surface.
Jugular notch.
correctOption: Anterior surface.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The superior border of the manubrium contains the jugular notch and the clavicular notches, but the muscle origin is specified on the anterior surface.
Incorrect. The lateral borders of the manubrium articulate with the first and second ribs; they are not the origin site for the SCM.
Correct. The sternal head of the sternocleidomastoid originates from the anterior surface of the manubrium sterni.
Incorrect. The posterior surface of the manubrium gives origin to the sternohyoid and sternothyroid muscles, not the sternocleidomastoid.
Incorrect. The jugular (suprasternal) notch is a midline depression on the superior border, not the origin of the muscle head itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Sternocleidomastoid ... Origin: Sternal head: manubrium sterni (anterior surface); clavicular head: medial third of clavicle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A medical student is asked to differentiate the sensory innervation of the two largest muscles of the neck to determine their role in proprioception. Which of the following correctly contrasts the proprioceptive nerve supply for the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) and the trapezius?
options: SCM is supplied by the transverse cervical nerve; Trapezius is supplied by the great auricular nerve
SCM is supplied by C1; Trapezius is supplied by C2
SCM is supplied by C3 and C4; Trapezius is supplied by C1 and C2
SCM is supplied by C2 and C3; Trapezius is supplied by C3 and C4
SCM is supplied by the facial nerve; Trapezius is supplied by the trigeminal nerve
correctOption: SCM is supplied by C2 and C3; Trapezius is supplied by C3 and C4
optionExplanations: The transverse cervical and great auricular nerves are cutaneous (sensory to skin) branches of the cervical plexus, not the muscular branches carrying proprioceptive fibers to the muscles themselves.
The C1 nerve has no cutaneous branch and primarily joins the hypoglossal nerve; it is not the primary proprioceptive supply for either the SCM or the trapezius.
This option reverses the levels; C3 and C4 supply the trapezius, and C1/C2 are not the standard proprioceptive duo for these large muscles.
According to the cervical plexus distribution, the sternocleidomastoid receives proprioceptive fibers from the C2 and C3 ventral rami, while the trapezius is supplied by C3 and C4.
The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression (mimetic muscles), and the trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication; neither provides proprioception to these neck muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Spasmodic Torticollis and Accessory Nerve Management
statement: A 30-year-old patient presents with chronic, involuntary contractions of the neck muscles, resulting in the head being pulled toward the shoulder and the face rotated upward to the opposite side. If conservative management fails, which surgical intervention is traditionally considered for severe cases of this condition?
options: Catheterization of the internal jugular vein through the supraclavicular approach.
Suture of the platysma muscle to reduce skin tension.
Ligature of the facial artery at the margin of the mandible.
Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve.
Compression of the third part of the subclavian artery against the first rib.
correctOption: Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is a procedure for central venous access and is unrelated to the treatment of torticollis or muscle spasms in the neck region.
Incorrect. While suturing the platysma is important for neck incisions to prevent scars, it does not treat the underlying muscular spasm of torticollis.
Incorrect. The facial artery supplies the face and submandibular gland; ligating it has no effect on neck muscle spasms.

Correct. Spasmodic torticollis involves chronic contractions of the SCM and trapezius. Since both are supplied by the spinal accessory nerve, sectioning this nerve is a surgical option to alleviate severe, recalcitrant spasms.
Incorrect. This is a technique to control hemorrhage in the upper limb, not a treatment for muscular dystonia or spasms.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): Spasmodic torticollis, which results from repeated chronic contractions of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, is usually psychogenic in origin. Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve may be necessary in severe cases.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The trapezius muscle is a large, triangular sheet covering the posterior aspect of the neck and thorax. Which of the following describes its insertion?
options: The mastoid process and the superior nuchal line.
The lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula.
The coracoid process of the scapula.
The floor of the bicipital groove of the humerus.
The medial third of the clavicle and the manubrium sterni.
correctOption: The lateral third of the clavicle, acromion, and spine of the scapula.
optionExplanations: The mastoid process and superior nuchal line are the insertion sites for the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not the trapezius.
The trapezius inserts onto the pectoral girdle, specifically the lateral third of the clavicle and the acromion/spine of the scapula, allowing it to move the shoulder.
The coracoid process is the insertion for the pectoralis minor and the origin for the short head of the biceps and coracobrachialis; it does not receive the trapezius.
The floor of the bicipital groove is the insertion for the latissimus dorsi muscle, which is located in the back but deeper and more inferior.
The medial third of the clavicle and the manubrium serve as the origins for the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5 Neck Muscles... Trapezius... Insertion: Lateral third of clavicle, acromion, spine of scapula.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient is unable to shrug their shoulders during a physical exam. Which of the following muscles is most likely paralyzed, and which specific part of the muscle is responsible for this action?
options: Trapezius; lower fibers.
Platysma; cervical branch.
Sternocleidomastoid; clavicular head.
Omohyoid; inferior belly.
Trapezius; upper fibers.
correctOption: Trapezius; upper fibers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The lower fibers of the trapezius depress the scapula, which is the opposite of shrugging.
Incorrect. The platysma is a muscle of facial expression that tenses the skin of the neck and can depress the mandible, but it does not shrug the shoulders.
Incorrect. The sternocleidomastoid acts on the head and neck (tilting/rotation/flexion), not on the elevation of the scapula.
Incorrect. The omohyoid is an infrahyoid strap muscle that depresses the hyoid bone and larynx; it does not shrug the shoulders.
Correct. Shrugging the shoulders is the clinical test for the upper fibers of the trapezius muscle, which elevate the scapula.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Trapezius ... Action: Upper fibers: elevate scapula. ... [Page 1681 (Book Page)] Then, the patient is asked to shrug the shoulders, causing the trapezius muscles to come into action.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: In the complex neurovascular organization of the neck, which spinal nerves provide the proprioceptive (sensory) fibers to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles respectively?
options: C1, C2 and C2, C3
C2, C3 and C3, C4
C1 only for both
C3, C4 and C4, C5
C5, C6 and C6, C7
correctOption: C2, C3 and C3, C4
optionExplanations: C1 does not have a cutaneous branch and its motor fibers typically join the hypoglossal nerve; it is not the primary proprioceptive source for the SCM.
The cervical plexus provides sensory/proprioceptive branches: C2 and C3 for the sternocleidomastoid, and C3 and C4 for the trapezius. This is distinct from their motor supply via CN XI.
C1 fibers do not provide significant proprioceptive innervation to these muscles; they mostly supply the geniohyoid and thyrohyoid via the hypoglossal nerve.
C4 and C5 are more involved in the phrenic nerve and the brachial plexus; they are too low to be the primary proprioceptive supply for the SCM.
C5 through C7 are the roots of the brachial plexus and do not supply proprioception to these superficial neck and back muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 1-month-old infant presents with a 'tumor-like' mass on the left side of the neck. The infant's head is persistently flexed and tilted to the left, while the chin is pointed toward the right shoulder. What is the anatomical explanation for this clinical presentation?
options: Congenital absence of the accessory nerve.
Enlargement of the deep cervical lymph nodes.
Cervical rib compressing the brachial plexus.
Fibrosis and shortening of the sternocleidomastoid following a birth hematoma.
Spasmodic contraction of the trapezius muscle.
correctOption: Fibrosis and shortening of the sternocleidomastoid following a birth hematoma.
optionExplanations: Absence of the accessory nerve would cause flaccid paralysis and wasting, not the contracture seen in torticollis.
Lymph node enlargement (adenitis) can cause pain but rarely causes the classic fixed postural deformity of torticollis.
A cervical rib causes neurovascular symptoms in the upper limb (Thoracic Outlet Syndrome) but not neck contracture in a neonate.
Congenital torticollis involves a hematoma in the SCM that turns into fibrous tissue, shortening the muscle and pulling the mastoid toward the sternum (tilting the head) and rotating the face away.
Spasmodic torticollis is usually psychogenic and occurs in adults, not infants with a localized mass.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Most cases of congenital torticollis are a result of excessive stretching of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a difficult labor. Hemorrhage occurs into the muscle... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 19-year-old medical student is asked to demonstrate the nerve supply of the sternocleidomastoid muscle during a viva voce. Which of the following accurately describes the motor innervation of this muscle?
options: The transverse cervical nerve
The phrenic nerve
The cervical branch of the facial nerve
The spinal part of the accessory nerve
The ansa cervicalis (C1–C3 roots)
correctOption: The spinal part of the accessory nerve
optionExplanations: The transverse cervical nerve is a cutaneous (sensory) branch of the cervical plexus that supplies the skin of the neck.
The phrenic nerve is responsible for the motor and sensory supply of the diaphragm; it is not involved in the innervation of the muscles of the neck like the sternocleidomastoid.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) is responsible for the motor supply of the platysma muscle, not the sternocleidomastoid.
The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the primary motor fibers to the sternocleidomastoid muscle after exiting the skull through the jugular foramen.
The ansa cervicalis is a loop of the cervical plexus that provides motor innervation to the infrahyoid (strap) muscles, not the sternocleidomastoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): The spinal root runs downward and laterally and enters the deep surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which it supplies, and then crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to supply the trapezius muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: To clinically evaluate the integrity of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle, a physician asks a patient to rotate their head against resistance. Which observation confirms the strength of the right sternocleidomastoid?
options: The patient successfully turns their face to the right.
The patient tilts their head toward the left shoulder.
The patient successfully turns their face to the left.
The patient protrudes their tongue in the midline.
The patient shrugs their right shoulder upward.
correctOption: The patient successfully turns their face to the left.
optionExplanations: Rotating the face to the right would test the left sternocleidomastoid muscle, as the muscle pulls the mastoid process toward the sternum on the same side, causing the face to turn opposite.
Tilting the head to the left shoulder would involve the left lateral flexors, not a test for the right SCM's rotation strength.
The right sternocleidomastoid muscle, when acting alone, pulls the right mastoid process anteriorly and inferiorly, which rotates the head so the face looks toward the left.
Tongue protrusion is a test for the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not the accessory nerve or SCM.
Shrugging the shoulder is a test for the trapezius muscle, also supplied by CN XI, but it does not evaluate the SCM.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): Clinical examination of this nerve involves asking the patient to rotate the head to one side against resistance, causing the sternocleidomastoid of the opposite side to come into action.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: In the physiological maintenance of head posture, the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles participate in a multi-step regulatory loop. When the body is in the upright position, what is the specific bilateral action of the sternocleidomastoid muscles regarding the atlanto-occipital joint?
options: Extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
Lateral tilt of the head toward the shoulder
Flexion of the head to the chest
Protrusion of the mandible against the hyoid
Rotation of the head to the ipsilateral side
correctOption: Extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
optionExplanations: Due to their insertion on the mastoid process (posterior to the transverse axis of the atlanto-occipital joint), the SCMs acting together assist in extending the head, which is crucial for balancing the skull on the vertebral column.
Lateral tilt (lateral flexion) occurs when only one sternocleidomastoid contracts (unilateral action), tilting the ear toward the shoulder on the same side.

Bilateral contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscles flexes the cervical part of the vertebral column (pulling the neck forward), but its effect at the atlanto-occipital joint specifically is extension of the head.
Mandibular protrusion is a function of the muscles of mastication (primarily lateral pterygoid) and is not influenced by the sternocleidomastoid muscles.
Rotation of the face occurs unilaterally, and it is directed to the opposite (contralateral) side, not the same side as the contracting muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): Table 12.5 Sternocleidomastoid ... Action: Acting together, flex neck, extend head; one muscle: rotates head to opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The sternocleidomastoid muscle serves as a critical landmark for dividing the neck into major regions. Which anatomical area is bounded by the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, the anterior border of the trapezius, and the middle third of the clavicle?
options: The muscular triangle
The anterior triangle
The posterior triangle
The submandibular triangle
The carotid triangle
correctOption: The posterior triangle
optionExplanations: The muscular triangle is bounded by the midline, the SCM, and the superior belly of the omohyoid.
The anterior triangle is bounded by the SCM anterior border, the midline, and the mandible.
The posterior triangle is defined by the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, the anterior margin of the trapezius, and the clavicle inferiorly.
The submandibular triangle is bounded by the mandible and the two bellies of the digastric muscle.
The carotid triangle is a subdivision of the anterior triangle, bounded by the SCM, omohyoid, and digastric muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1626 (Book Page): Posterior Triangle... The boundaries are the sternocleidomastoid muscle, the trapezius muscle, and the clavicle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Proprioceptive Nerve Supply of the Trapezius
statement: A first-year medical student is asked to identify the specific nerves responsible for proprioception within the trapezius muscle during a gross anatomy dissection. Which of the following cervical spinal nerve branches fulfill this role?
options: C2 and C3
C7 and T1
C3 and C4
C1 and C2
C5 and C6
correctOption: C3 and C4
optionExplanations: C2 and C3 provide proprioceptive fibers specifically to the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not the trapezius.

C7, C8, and T1 contribute to the middle and lower trunks of the brachial plexus, supplying muscles of the upper limb, not the trapezius proprioception loop in the neck region. Control of the trapezius is more superiorly located in the cervical plexus (C3-C4).Abbreviated spinal nerves like C7-T1 are far too low for this muscle's cervical supply provided (C3,4).

The trapezius muscle receives its motor supply from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), while its proprioceptive (sensory) information regarding muscle position and tension is carried by the anterior rami of C3 and C4.
C1 and C2 do not provide proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius; C1 primarily contributes to the ansa cervicalis and nerves to the geniohyoid and thyrohyoid via the hypoglossal nerve.
C5 and C6 are the primary roots for the upper trunk of the brachial plexus and are not involved in the proprioceptive supply of the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Anatomy and Clinical Presentation of Congenital Torticollis
statement: A newborn is brought to the clinic because the parents noticed the infant's head is tilted to the right and the chin is turned toward the left shoulder. A small, firm mass is palpable within the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. If this condition results in permanent muscle shortening, what is the most likely pathological diagnosis?
options: Congenital torticollis
Cervical rib syndrome
Spasmodic torticollis
Accessory nerve palsy
Mylohyoid muscle hypertrophy
correctOption: Congenital torticollis
optionExplanations: Congenital torticollis involves a fibrous contraction of the SCM, often following birth trauma, leading to the head being tilted toward the affected side and the face rotated to the opposite side.
Cervical rib syndrome involves compression of the brachial plexus or subclavian artery, causing upper limb symptoms, not neck muscular tilting.
Spasmodic torticollis occurs in adults and is usually psychogenic or neurological in origin (chronic contractions), rather than a fibrous mass in a newborn.
Accessory nerve palsy would cause muscle wasting and a 'shoulder drop' due to trapezius failure, rather than the characteristic tilted head/rotated face of torticollis.
The mylohyoid is a muscle of the floor of the mouth; its hypertrophy would not cause a lateral tilt of the head or a mass in the neck side.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Congenital Torticollis... Later, this becomes invaded by fibrous tissue, which contracts and shortens the muscle. The mastoid process is thus pulled down toward the sternoclavicular joint of the same side, the cervical spine is flexed, and the face looks upward to the opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Motor Innervation of the Lateral and Posterior Neck Muscles
statement: Which nerve provides the primary motor innervation to both the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles?
options: Phrenic nerve
Spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Ansa cervicalis
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
correctOption: Spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI)
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm and is found on the surface of the scalenus anterior, not supplying the SCM.
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is the unique cranial nerve that provides motor supply to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
The facial nerve (CN VII) innervates the muscles of facial expression and the platysma, but not the sternocleidomastoid or trapezius.
The ansa cervicalis (C1-C3) supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles, such as the sternohyoid and omohyoid, but does not provide motor supply to the SCM.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies all intrinsic and most extrinsic muscles of the tongue, excluding the palatoglossus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): The spinal root runs downward and laterally and enters the deep surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, which it supplies, and then crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to supply the trapezius muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which of the following describes the correct superior attachment of the Sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: The coronoid process of the mandible
The spine of the scapula and the acromion process
The external occipital protuberance and the medial third of the superior nuchal line
The transverse processes of the C1 to C4 cervical vertebrae
The mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line
correctOption: The mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line
optionExplanations: The coronoid process of the mandible is the insertion site for the temporalis muscle (a muscle of mastication), which is located in the temporal fossa.
The spine of the scapula and acromion process are insertion sites for the trapezius muscle fibers, which allow it to manipulate the shoulder girdle.
The external occipital protuberance and medial part of the superior nuchal line are origin sites for the trapezius, not the sternocleidomastoid.
The transverse processes of C1-C4 are the origin sites for the levator scapulae and other deep neck muscles, not the sternocleidomastoid.

The sternocleidomastoid originates from the manubrium and clavicle and inserts superiorly onto the mastoid process of the temporal bone and the lateral portion of the superior nuchal line of the occipital bone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Sternocleidomastoid... Insertion: Mastoid process of temporal bone and lateral part of superior nuchal line.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 60-year-old male is undergoing an evaluation for neck mobility. When asked to perform a maneuver involving the bilateral contraction of the sternocleidomastoid muscles, the physician notes the specific resulting movement of the head and neck. Which of the following accurately describes the mechanical effect of bilateral SCM contraction?
options: Lateral rotation of the scapula to allow abduction of the arm
Elevation of the scapula and retraction of the shoulder girdle
Depression of the mandible and opening of the oral cavity
Flexion of the cervical part of the vertebral column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
Rotation of the chin toward the shoulder and lateral tilting of the head
correctOption: Flexion of the cervical part of the vertebral column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
optionExplanations: Lateral rotation of the scapula is a function of the trapezius (lower fibers) and serratus anterior, which helps the glenoid cavity face upward for arm abduction.
Scapular elevation and retraction are the functions of the trapezius, levator scapulae, and rhomboids, not the sternocleidomastoid.
Mandible depression is performed by the digastric, mylohyoid, and geniohyoid muscles. The SCM has no role in jaw opening.

Bilateral SCM contraction is unique; it pulls the head forward (flexing the cervical vertebrae) while simultaneously tilting the head back (extending the head at the atlanto-occipital joint) due to the muscle's insertion behind the joint's axis.
Rotation of the chin and lateral tilting are the results of unilateral (one-sided) contraction of the SCM, not bilateral action.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): [Table 12.5] Sternocleidomastoid... Action: Two muscles acting together flex the cervical part of the vertebral column and extend the head at the atlanto-occipital joint.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A patient presents following a deep laceration to the lateral side of the neck. On examination, the patient exhibits a drooping shoulder, an inability to elevate the arm above the head (after abduction to 90 degrees), and wasting of the muscle that forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle. The patient can still rotate their head with full strength. Where is the most likely site of the nerve injury?
options: Within the posterior triangle of the neck
Foramen magnum
The anterior triangle of the neck
Deep to the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid
Jugular foramen
correctOption: Within the posterior triangle of the neck
optionExplanations: Because the accessory nerve supplies the SCM first and then crosses the posterior triangle to reach the trapezius, an injury in the triangle only paralyzes the trapezius, sparing head rotation.
Foramen magnum injury would affect the spinal roots of CN XI before they even join the cranial part, resulting in complete paralysis of both muscles.
The accessory nerve is not typically at risk for isolated trapezius injury in the anterior triangle; it enters the SCM from its deep surface near the carotid triangle.
Nerve injury deep to the SCM would likely damage the fibers before they supply the muscle, affecting both muscles.
Injury at the jugular foramen would paralyze both the SCM and the trapezius, meaning head rotation would also be weak.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position. It can be injured at operation or from penetrating wounds. The trapezius muscle is paralyzed... the shoulder will drop.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which set of spinal nerves provides the proprioceptive innervation for the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscles, respectively?
options: SCM: C2 and C3; Trapezius: C3 and C4
Both muscles are supplied purely by CN XI for both motor and proprioceptive functions.
SCM: C5 and C6; Trapezius: C1 and C2
SCM: C1 and C2; Trapezius: C2 and C3
SCM: C3 and C4; Trapezius: C5 and C6
correctOption: SCM: C2 and C3; Trapezius: C3 and C4
optionExplanations: While the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the motor power, the sensory (proprioceptive) fibers are derived from the cervical plexus: C2 and C3 for the sternocleidomastoid, and C3 and C4 for the trapezius.
CN XI is purely motor in its function for these muscles; the sensory component must be provided by the spinal nerves of the cervical plexus.
C5 and C6 are too low in the plexus for these muscles; C1/C2 are too high for the trapezius.
C1 does not have a cutaneous branch and its muscular fibers typically join the hypoglossal nerve; it is not the standard proprioceptive supply for SCM.
C5 and C6 are part of the brachial plexus and supply the upper limb muscles (like the deltoid), not the trapezius proprioception.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): Table 12.7... Sternocleidomastoid: C2 and 3 (proprioceptive)... Trapezius: C3 and 4 (proprioceptive).

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: The sternocleidomastoid muscle is an essential landmark in the neck. During neck extension, which critical neurovascular structure is anatomically protected by sliding posteriorly beneath this muscle?
options: The phrenic nerve.
The carotid sheath and its large vessels.
The submental artery.
The anterior jugular vein.
The external jugular vein.
correctOption: The carotid sheath and its large vessels.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While the phrenic nerve is deep to the SCM's posterior border, the text specifically identifies the carotid sheath as the structure that slides posteriorly for protection during extension.

Correct. The sternocleidomastoid acts as a thick protective band. During extension, the carotid sheath (containing the carotid arteries and internal jugular vein) moves posteriorly under the muscle, protecting these vital structures from superficial trauma.
Incorrect. The submental artery is a branch of the facial artery and lies near the chin, not protected by the sliding of the SCM in the mid-neck.
Incorrect. The anterior jugular veins lie in the superficial fascia of the anterior midline, not under the SCM during extension.
Incorrect. The external jugular vein lies superficial to the sternocleidomastoid and is therefore not protected by it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1624 (Book Page): Extension of the cervical part of the vertebral column and extension of the head at the atlanto-occipital joint cause the carotid sheath with its contained large blood vessels to slide posteriorly beneath the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Accessory Nerve Lesion in Posterior Triangle
statement: A 45-year-old male undergoes a deep lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. Post-operatively, he complains of difficulty elevating his right arm above 90 degrees and a 'heavy' feeling in the shoulder. On examination, the right shoulder is lower than the left, and there is wasting of the muscle that forms the posterior boundary of the triangle. Which nerve and muscle are most likely involved?
options: Spinal accessory nerve and Trapezius
Phrenic nerve and Scalenus anterior
Long thoracic nerve and Serratus anterior
Axillary nerve and Deltoid
Suprascapular nerve and Supraspinatus
correctOption: Spinal accessory nerve and Trapezius
optionExplanations: The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is superficial in the posterior triangle. Its damage leads to trapezius paralysis, characterized by a drooping shoulder and inability to rotate the scapula for full arm abduction.
Injury to the phrenic nerve would cause diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory issues, not shoulder drop or muscle wasting in the posterior triangle.

While serratus anterior palsy (long thoracic nerve) causes difficulty in arm elevation, it typically presents with 'winging' of the scapula, and the nerve is not the primary superficial structure of the posterior triangle.
The axillary nerve is located in the axilla/shoulder region, not the posterior triangle of the neck, and its injury would primarily affect the deltoid and teres minor.

The suprascapular nerve supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus; while its injury affects the initiation of abduction, it does not cause the visible drop of the shoulder girdle seen in trapezius paralysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position. It can be injured at operation... The trapezius muscle is paralyzed, the muscle will show wasting, and the shoulder will drop. The patient will experience difficulty in elevating the arm above the head.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: A 28-year-old patient presents with recurring, involuntary, and painful contractions of both the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, causing the head to twist significantly. The physician suspects a psychogenic origin. How does this condition differ clinically from the congenital form of torticollis?
options: It involves primary muscle agenesis rather than spasm
It is characterized by chronic repeated contractions rather than fixed fibrotic shortening
It is treated exclusively by massaging the carotid sinus
It results in a 'pond' fracture of the mastoid process
It specifically spares the spinal accessory nerve
correctOption: It is characterized by chronic repeated contractions rather than fixed fibrotic shortening
optionExplanations: Agenesis refers to the failure of an organ to develop; torticollis involves either muscular spasm (spasmodic) or fibrotic shortening (congenital).

Spasmodic torticollis involves active, chronic muscular contractions and is often psychogenic. In contrast, congenital torticollis is a static condition caused by the replacement of muscle fibers with non-contractile fibrous tissue following birth trauma.
Carotid sinus massage is used to evaluate baroreceptor hypersensitivity or certain arrhythmias; it is not a treatment for muscular torticollis.
A 'pond' fracture is a type of skull fracture in children and is unrelated to the muscular pathology of torticollis.
Both conditions involve the muscles supplied by the spinal accessory nerve; in severe spasmodic cases, the nerve may even be surgically sectioned to provide relief.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): Spasmodic torticollis, which results from repeated chronic contractions of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, is usually psychogenic in origin. Section of the spinal part of the accessory nerve may be necessary in severe cases.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: Which specific nerve roots provide the proprioceptive (sensory) fibers for the trapezius muscle, distinct from its primary motor supply?
options: C3 and C4
C1 and C2
C5 and C6
C2 and C3
T1 and T2
correctOption: C3 and C4
optionExplanations: While the accessory nerve provides motor innervation, the C3 and C4 spinal nerves from the cervical plexus provide sensory/proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius.
C1 fibers primarily travel with the hypoglossal nerve and contribute to the ansa cervicalis and nerves to the thyrohyoid.
C5 and C6 are roots of the brachial plexus and primarily supply muscles of the upper limb and shoulder girdle (like the deltoid).
C2 and C3 provide the proprioceptive fibers for the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not the trapezius.
T1 and T2 are thoracic nerves; T1 is part of the brachial plexus and supplies the small muscles of the hand, but they do not supply the trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): [The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.]

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
statement: During a physical examination, a patient is asked to contract only their right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Which mechanical movement pattern would confirm the isolated action of this muscle?
options: The head tilts toward the right and the face rotates toward the left.
The head is pulled directly forward, resulting in neck flexion.
The head is pulled directly backward, resulting in neck extension.
The chin is retracted toward the midline without lateral rotation.
The head tilts toward the left and the face rotates toward the right.
correctOption: The head tilts toward the right and the face rotates toward the left.
optionExplanations: Contraction of a single sternocleidomastoid muscle pulls the mastoid process of the temporal bone toward the sternum, which tilts the head toward the ipsilateral shoulder while simultaneously rotating the neck so the chin/face points toward the contralateral side.
Direct neck flexion is the result of both (bilateral) sternocleidomastoid muscles contracting together, not the action of an isolated single muscle.

Neck extension is generally produced by postvertebral muscles; while the sternocleidomastoid can assist in head extension at the atlanto-occipital joint, isolated unilateral contraction produces rotation.
Retraction of the chin without rotation does not involve the unilateral pull of the sternocleidomastoid on the mastoid process, which is offset from the midline axis of rotation.
Rotation toward the same side and tilting toward the opposite side is the reverse of the anatomical action produced by the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1615 (Book Page): One muscle: tilts head toward shoulder of same side and rotates head so that face looks toward opposite side.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Accessory Nerve Vulnerability in the Posterior Triangle
statement: A 48-year-old woman undergoes a lymph node biopsy in the posterior triangle of the neck. Postoperatively, she complains of a 'heavy' feeling in her right shoulder and difficulty combing her hair. Physical exam reveals a drooping right shoulder and an inability to shrug against resistance. No sensory loss is noted. Which anatomical structure was most likely damaged?
options: The upper trunk of the brachial plexus
The transverse cervical artery
The spinal part of the accessory nerve
The supraclavicular nerves
The dorsal scapular nerve
correctOption: The spinal part of the accessory nerve
optionExplanations: Upper trunk (Erb's palsy) injury would cause sensory loss and 'waiter's tip' position (adduction/internal rotation), which does not match the isolated trapezius paralysis described.
The transverse cervical artery is a blood vessel; its ligation might cause ischemia but not immediate focal paralysis of shrugging.
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) is superficial in the posterior triangle. Damage here paralyzes the trapezius, leading to shoulder drop and inability to shrug or elevate the arm above the head.
The supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) provide sensation to the shoulder skin; their damage would cause anesthesia, not the motor deficit described (inability to shrug).
The dorsal scapular nerve supplies the levator scapulae and rhomboids; while its damage affects the scapula, it would not cause a complete inability to shrug as the trapezius is the primary elevator.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): The accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle of the neck in a relatively superficial position... The trapezius muscle is paralyzed, the muscle will show wasting, and the shoulder will drop.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Clinical Testing of Trapezius vs. Sternocleidomastoid
statement: A clinician is evaluating a patient for a suspected lesion of the spinal accessory nerve. To specifically differentiate the function of the trapezius from that of the sternocleidomastoid, which clinical maneuver should be performed?
options: Asking the patient to rotate the head to the opposite side against resistance.
Asking the patient to clench their teeth firmly to visualize muscle sheets.
Asking the patient to shrug their shoulders against downward pressure.
Asking the patient to whistle to check for lip sphincter strength.
Asking the patient to protrude the tongue and check for midline deviation.
correctOption: Asking the patient to shrug their shoulders against downward pressure.
optionExplanations: Rotating the head to the opposite side against resistance tests the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not the trapezius.
Clencing the teeth allows for the visualization of the platysma and masseter muscles but does not test the accessory nerve or the trapezius.

Shrugging the shoulders is the primary action of the upper fibers of the trapezius muscle; failure to do so against resistance indicates a lesion in the nerve supply (CN XI) to the trapezius specifically.
Whistling involves the orbicularis oris and buccinator muscles, which are innervated by the facial nerve (CN VII).
Protrusion of the tongue tests the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), not the accessory nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1681 (Book Page): Then, the patient is asked to shrug the shoulders, causing the trapezius muscles to come into action.

category: Describe the attachments, actions and nerve supply of sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
coreConcept: Mechanical Action of SCM in Torticollis
statement: A newborn is diagnosed with congenital torticollis following a breech delivery. The physician explains that the infant's head is tilted toward the right shoulder with the chin pointing toward the left. Which of the following mechanical descriptions of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle best accounts for this pathological posture?
options: Fibrosis of the right SCM resulting in rotation of the face toward the right
Paralysis of the left SCM causing the head to fall toward the right side
Hypoplasia of the left clavicular head of the SCM leading to right-sided tilt
