The lower premolars drain to the submandibular nodes, not directly to the specialized jugulodigastric node of the deep chain.
The jugulodigastric node is the 'tonsillar node' of the deep cervical chain, frequently enlarged and tender in cases of tonsillitis.

Submental nodes
Occipital nodes
Parotid nodes

statement: Contrast the drainage areas of the retropharyngeal lymph nodes with those of the paratracheal lymph nodes in the neck's deep regional system.

Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Occipital lymph nodes
Submandibular lymph nodes
Deep cervical lymph nodes

Parotid lymph nodes are incorrect because they drain the lateral scalp, eyelids, and external auditory meatus, rather than the oral cavity proper.
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes are incorrect as they are positioned behind the pharynx and primarily receive lymph from the nasopharynx and auditory tube.
Submandibular lymph nodes are incorrect because they primarily drain the sides of the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, the nose, cheek, and upper lip, rather than the isolated tip.
Occipital lymph nodes are incorrect because they are located at the back of the skull and serve the posterior scalp region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submental nodes: Located in the submental triangle just below the chin, they drain lymph from the tip of the tongue, the floor of the anterior part of the mouth, the incisor teeth, the center part of the lower lip, and the skin over the chin.

category: Name the superficial and deep cervical lymph nodes and give their location and drainage areas
coreConcept: Regional Lymphatic Drainage of the Oral Floor and Lip
statement: A clinical examiner asks a student to identify the specific group of lymph nodes that receives primary drainage from the tip of the tongue, the central part of the lower lip, and the skin over the chin. Which of the following is the correct anatomical group?
options: Mastoid nodes
Occipital nodes
Parotid nodes
Submental nodes
Submandibular nodes
correctOption: Submental nodes
optionExplanations: Mastoid nodes, also known as retroauricular nodes, are located behind the ear and drain the auricle and the scalp above the ear.
Occipital nodes are situated at the back of the skull and primarily drain the posterior aspect of the scalp.
Parotid nodes are located on or within the parotid gland and receive drainage from the lateral scalp, eyelids, and external auditory meatus.

The submental nodes are specifically located in the submental triangle and are the primary filters for the midline structures of the lower face, including the tip of the tongue and the central lower lip.

Submandibular nodes drain the sides of the tongue (anterior two-thirds), the nose, cheek, upper lip, and lateral parts of the lower lip, rather than the central lower lip or the very tip of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Submental nodes: Located in the submental triangle just below the chin, they drain lymph from the tip of the tongue, the floor of the anterior part of the mouth, the incisor teeth, the center part of the lower lip, and the skin over the chin.

category: Name the superficial and deep cervical lymph nodes and give their location and drainage areas
coreConcept: Hierarchical Lymphatic Drainage of the Cheek
statement: The lymphatic drainage of the face is organized such that lymph from certain regional nodes must pass through intermediary groups before reaching the deep terminal chain. Lymph originating in the buccal (facial) nodes, located over the buccinator muscle, typically drains into which secondary group?
options: Parotid nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Mastoid nodes
Occipital nodes
Submandibular nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: Parotid nodes receive drainage from the lateral face and eyelids but are not the primary destination for the buccal nodes located on the buccinator muscle.
Retropharyngeal nodes drain deep structures like the nasopharynx; they are located posterior to the oral cavity and do not receive superficial facial lymph.
Mastoid nodes are situated behind the ear and drain the posterior scalp; they are not part of the pathway for lymph from the anterior cheek or buccal region.
Occipital nodes are at the back of the head and receive drainage from the posterior scalp; they have no anatomical connection to the facial or buccal drainage systems.
The buccal nodes act as small relay stations on the face; lymph from these nodes moves inferiorly and posteriorly to join the larger submandibular group at the margin of the jaw.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Buccal (facial) nodes: One or two nodes lie in the cheek over the buccinator muscle. They drain lymph that ultimately passes into the submandibular nodes.

category: Name the superficial and deep cervical lymph nodes and give their location and drainage areas
coreConcept: Sequential Lymphatic Drainage of the Face
statement: Lymphatic fluid from the cheek region may pass through one or two small nodes located over the buccinator muscle. Into which larger regional group does the lymph from these 'buccal nodes' ultimately pass?
options: Retropharyngeal nodes
Occipital nodes
Submandibular nodes
Mastoid nodes
Submental nodes
correctOption: Submandibular nodes
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal nodes are deep nodes for the nasopharynx and are not involved in the superficial drainage of the cheek.
Occipital nodes are located on the posterior aspect of the skull, far from the facial drainage route.
The buccal nodes act as intercalated or intermediate stations for the cheek's lymph, which then flows following the facial vessels into the submandibular nodes.
Mastoid nodes are located behind the auricle and do not participate in the anterior facial lymphatic pathway.
Submental nodes drain the midline of the chin and lower lip; they do not receive lymph from the buccal region over the buccinator.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Buccal (facial) nodes: One or two nodes lie in the cheek over the buccinator muscle. They drain lymph that ultimately passes into the submandibular nodes.

category: Name the superficial and deep cervical lymph nodes and give their location and drainage areas
statement: Which specific group of lymph nodes is located behind the ear over the mastoid process?
options: Buccal nodes
Submental nodes
Occipital nodes
Parotid nodes
Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes
correctOption: Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes
optionExplanations: Buccal nodes are facial nodes located in the cheek area over the buccinator muscle.
Submental nodes are located in the midline of the neck below the chin.
Occipital nodes are located on the back of the skull, not behind the ear.
Parotid nodes are located on or within the parotid gland, anterior to the mastoid process.
The mastoid (also called retroauricular) nodes are situated directly over the mastoid process of the temporal bone, posterior to the auricle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1655 (Book Page): Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes: Located behind the ear over the mastoid process, they receive lymph from the scalp above the ear, the auricle, and the external auditory meatus.

category: Name the superficial and deep cervical lymph nodes and give their location and drainage areas
statement: Which group of regional lymph nodes is specifically situated behind the pharynx and in front of the prevertebral fascia, receiving lymph from the auditory tube?
options: Mastoid nodes
Laryngeal nodes
Retropharyngeal nodes
Tracheal nodes
Anterior cervical nodes
correctOption: Retropharyngeal nodes
optionExplanations: Mastoid nodes are superficial nodes behind the ear; while they drain the external auditory meatus, they do not drain the internal auditory tube.
Laryngeal nodes are located in front of the larynx and receive lymph from the larynx itself, not the auditory tube.
Retropharyngeal nodes occupy the retropharyngeal space and are the primary site of drainage for the nasopharynx and the auditory tube (eustachian tube).
Tracheal nodes are located alongside the trachea and receive lymph from neighboring structures like the thyroid, not the auditory tube.
Anterior cervical nodes lie along the anterior jugular veins and drain the skin of the front of the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1656 (Book Page): Retropharyngeal nodes: These lie behind the pharynx and in front of the vertebral column. They receive lymph from the nasopharynx, the auditory tube, and the vertebral column.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A 50-year-old female presents with persistent pain localized to the mediastinal parietal pleura and the pericardium following a thoracic surgery. Which nerve, originating from the cervical plexus, mediates this internal sensory transmission?
options: Vagus nerve
Phrenic nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Transverse cervical nerve
Greater occipital nerve
correctOption: Phrenic nerve
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve (CN X) provides parasympathetic and sensory fibers to the thoracic viscera, but the specific parietal pleura and pericardium sensation described is primarily phrenic.

The phrenic nerve, while primarily known as the motor nerve to the diaphragm, also carries sensory fibers from the mediastinal pleura, fibrous pericardium, and the central part of the diaphragmatic pleura/peritoneum.
The ansa cervicalis is a motor loop supplying the infrahyoid strap muscles and has no sensory function for thoracic membranes.
The transverse cervical nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the anterior and lateral skin of the neck; it does not enter the thoracic cavity.
The greater occipital nerve is the posterior ramus of C2 and supplies the back of the scalp; it has no thoracic distribution.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): It also carries sensory branches from the pericardium, the mediastinal parietal pleura, and the pleura and peritoneum covering the upper and lower surfaces of the central part of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves. In which specific anatomical plane is this plexus located relative to the deep cervical fascia?
options: Anterior to the carotid sheath within the visceral space
Superficial to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Deep to the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
Within the substance of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Between the investing and pretracheal layers
correctOption: Deep to the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath, but it is posterior, not anterior, and it is not in the visceral space of the neck center.
Incorrect. The cutaneous branches eventually pierce the fascia to reach the superficial layer, but the plexus itself is deep.
Correct. The cervical plexus loops lie in front of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles, but are situated posterior to (deep to) the prevertebral fascia.
Incorrect. The plexus is related to the internal jugular vein and the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, but it is not located within the muscle fibers.
Incorrect. This space usually contains strap muscles and viscera, not the primary roots/loops of the cervical plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles... The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Nerve point of the neck anatomical landmark
statement: The 'nerve point of the neck' (punctum nervosum) is a critical diagnostic and surgical landmark. Which criteria define this specific location in the cervical region?
options: The posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at approximately its midpoint.
The level of the thyroid notch in the anterior triangle of the neck.
The junction of the superior and inferior bellies of the omohyoid muscle.
The site where the accessory nerve (CN XI) enters the trapezius muscle.
The midpoint of the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
correctOption: The posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at approximately its midpoint.
optionExplanations: The nerve point of the neck is defined as the midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. At this point, the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (Lesser Occipital, Great Auricular, Transverse Cervical, and Supraclavicular) emerge and diverge.
The nerve point is located in the posterior triangle/posterior border region, whereas the thyroid notch is a midline structure in the anterior neck/anterior triangle.
The omohyoid muscle is a landmark in the neck triangles but does not define the nerve point for the emergence of these cutaneous nerves.

While the accessory nerve also emerges from the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (usually slightly above the nerve point), it is a motor nerve and not part of the 'nerve point' cutaneous cluster described.
The cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge from the posterior border, not the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which of the following describes the correct distribution of the lateral branch of the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4)?
options: Hooks around the accessory nerve to supply the scalp.
Crosses the middle of the clavicle to supply the chest wall.
Supplies the skin as far as the median plane of the chest.
Supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.
Supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle.
correctOption: Supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle.
optionExplanations: This description refers to the lesser occipital nerve, not the supraclavicular nerves.
The intermediate supraclavicular nerve (C3, 4) crosses the middle of the clavicle to supply the skin of the chest wall.
The medial supraclavicular nerve (C3, 4) is the one that crosses the medial end of the clavicle to supply the skin near the median plane.
The skin over the angle of the mandible is supplied by the great auricular nerve.
The lateral branch of the supraclavicular nerve group specifically targets the lateral shoulder, upper deltoid, and posterior shoulder down to the scapular spine.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The lateral supraclavicular nerve crosses the lateral end of the clavicle and supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle; this nerve also supplies the posterior aspect of the shoulder as far down as the spine of the scapula.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Unilateral phrenic nerve palsy leads to a characteristic shift in respiratory mechanics. In a patient with a right-sided phrenic nerve lesion, which of the following describes the most accurate physiological loop during inspiration?
options: The right dome of the diaphragm is pushed upward into the thorax as abdominal pressure increases.
The right lung remains at functional residual capacity while the left lung collapses.
The right dome of the diaphragm descends lower than the left due to unopposed gravity.
The intercostal muscles on the right side relax to prevent mediastinal shift.
The right lung expands more than the left to compensate for the loss of diaphragmatic movement.
correctOption: The right dome of the diaphragm is pushed upward into the thorax as abdominal pressure increases.
optionExplanations: Normally, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward during inspiration. In phrenic palsy, the muscle is flaccid. When the other respiratory muscles contract to increase thoracic volume, the intra-abdominal pressure increases relative to the thoracic pressure, pushing the flaccid right dome upward (paradoxical movement).
The right lung does not stay at FRC; it is compressed by the elevated diaphragm and may collapse. The left lung remains functional unless other pathology exists.
Without motor tone, the diaphragm cannot resist abdominal pressure; it does not descend, it ascends.
The intercostal muscles usually work harder to compensate, rather than relaxing.
The right lung expands *less* because the space it would normally occupy is taken up by the elevated diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Formation and Distribution of the Ansa Cervicalis
statement: The formation of the ansa cervicalis involves a complex hitchhiking mechanism. Which of the following correctly describes the contribution of the first cervical nerve (C1) to this structure?
options: C1 fibers join the vagus nerve and descend to the thorax to form the cardiac plexus.
C1 fibers form the superior root of the ansa cervicalis after exiting the jugular foramen.
C1 fibers provide sensory innervation to the dura mater of the posterior cranial fossa.
C1 fibers hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve and leave as the descending branch.
C1 fibers unite directly with the C4 root to form the phrenic nerve.
correctOption: C1 fibers hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve and leave as the descending branch.
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve is the source of parasympathetic fibers; C1 is a spinal nerve that does not provide fibers to the cardiac plexus.
While C1 forms the superior root, it does so by hitchhiking on the hypoglossal nerve, and it does not exit the jugular foramen (it originates from the C1 spinal segment).
A meningeal branch of C1/C2 does supply dura, but this is not related to the formation of the ansa cervicalis loop.
C1 fibers join the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) for a short distance before branching off as the superior root (descending branch) of the ansa cervicalis.
The phrenic nerve is formed by C3, C4, and C5; C1 does not contribute to its formation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve. Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A surgeon is performing a dissection and identifies a cutaneous nerve hooking around the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) as it ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid. Which nerve is this?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
Phrenic nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
correctOption: Lesser occipital nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve (C2) has a characteristic course where it hooks around the spinal accessory nerve before ascending to the scalp.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) ascends across the sternocleidomastoid muscle but does not hook around the accessory nerve.
The phrenic nerve is a motor nerve that runs deep to the prevertebral fascia on the scalenus anterior and is not a cutaneous branch crossing the accessory nerve.
Supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) descend from the nerve point toward the clavicle, not ascending toward the scalp.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2, 3) emerges behind the sternocleidomastoid and passes forward across it, rather than ascending along its posterior border.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1613 (Book Page): The lesser occipital nerve (C2) hooks around the accessory nerve and ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle...

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Sensory Distribution of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: The phrenic nerve, a major branch of the cervical plexus, provides sensory innervation to several serous membranes. Which of the following is NOT typically supplied by the phrenic nerve?
options: Costal parietal pleura
Pleura of the upper surface of the central diaphragm
Mediastinal parietal pleura
Peritoneum of the central part of the diaphragm
Pericardium
correctOption: Costal parietal pleura
optionExplanations: The costal parietal pleura is supplied by the intercostal nerves, not the phrenic nerve. This is an important diagnostic distinction when evaluating the location of chest pain.
The diaphragmatic pleura covering the central part of the upper surface of the diaphragm is indeed innervated by the sensory branches of the phrenic nerve.
Sensory fibers for the mediastinal parietal pleura are carried by the phrenic nerve, which is why mediastinal irritation can cause referred shoulder pain.
The peritoneum covering the inferior surface of the central part of the diaphragm is supplied by the phrenic nerve, allowing for pain referral from subphrenic abscesses.
The phrenic nerve provides the primary sensory innervation to the fibrous pericardium and the parietal layer of the serous pericardium.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): It also carries sensory branches from the pericardium, the mediastinal parietal pleura, and the pleura and peritoneum covering the upper and lower surfaces of the central part of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Referred pain mechanism via Phrenic and Supraclavicular nerves
statement: A patient with acute gallbladder inflammation complains of significant pain referred to the tip of the right shoulder. Which pathophysiological mechanism involving the cervical plexus best explains this referred pain pattern?
options: Reflex spasm of the trapezius muscle mediated by the dorsal rami of C3 and C4.
Irritation of the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) at the diaphragm, with sensory impulses entering the spinal cord segments shared by the supraclavicular nerves.
Compression of the accessory nerve (CN XI) by the inflamed gallbladder via the sympathetic chain.
Direct involvement of the lesser occipital nerve (C2) through the prevertebral fascial space.
Irritation of the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) leading to direct cutaneous hyperesthesia.
correctOption: Irritation of the phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) at the diaphragm, with sensory impulses entering the spinal cord segments shared by the supraclavicular nerves.
optionExplanations: While the trapezius receives proprioception from C3-C4, the referred pain in gallbladder disease is a sensory phenomenon in the skin (supraclavicular dermatome), not primarily a muscular spasm.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the peritoneum covering the diaphragm. When irritated by gallbladder disease, the sensory signals enter the C3-C4 spinal segments. Since the supraclavicular nerves also arise from C3-C4, the brain interprets the visceral pain as coming from the shoulder skin.
The accessory nerve is a cranial nerve (CN XI) and does not mediate pain from the subdiaphragmatic viscera.

The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and is not involved in the C3-C4-C5 pathway of the diaphragm or shoulder tip pain helpfully explained by the phrenic nerve relationship. This nerve is too high and unrelated to the diaphragmatic segments.
The supraclavicular nerves are the site where the pain is felt (the dermatome), but they are not the source of the initial irritation; the irritation begins at the phrenic nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Topographical Anatomy of the Cervical Plexus
statement: The cervical plexus, which supplies the skin and muscles of the head and neck, is primarily situated in which anatomical location relative to the prevertebral muscles?
options: Between the investing layer of deep cervical fascia and the platysma muscle.
Posterior to the trunks of the brachial plexus and lateral to the vertebral artery.
Behind the scalenus anterior muscle and within the substance of the carotid sheath.
Deep to the prevertebral muscles and superficial to the cervical vertebrae.
In front of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles, covered by the prevertebral fascia.
correctOption: In front of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles, covered by the prevertebral fascia.
optionExplanations: This describe the location of the superficial fascia and platysma, which is far more superficial than the neural plexus.
The cervical plexus is superior and medial to the trunks of the brachial plexus, not posterior.
While the plexus is related to the carotid sheath, it is not located behind the scalenus anterior; that is the location of the brachial plexus and subclavian artery.
The plexus lies in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius, which are part of the prevertebral/lateral muscle group, not deep to them.
The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C1-C4 and is specifically located on the surface of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius, just deep to the prevertebral fascia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles (see Fig. 12.54). The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Nerve Point of the Neck Location
statement: The 'Nerve Point of the Neck' is a critical surface landmark for administering local anesthesia. Where is this point anatomically situated?
options: At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at its midpoint
Directly over the carotid tubercle of C6
At the junction of the upper and middle thirds of the trapezius muscle
At the angle of the mandible
Just above the sternoclavicular joint
correctOption: At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at its midpoint
optionExplanations: Correct. The midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid is where the four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular) exit the deep fascia to become superficial.
Incorrect. This is the landmark for the stellate ganglion block or palpating the carotid pulse, not the 'nerve point' for cutaneous blockade.
Incorrect. This does not correspond to the emergence of the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus.
Incorrect. The great auricular nerve travels toward this area, but it originates from the nerve point located further down the SCM.
Incorrect. This area is more related to the root of the neck and the emergence of the supraclavicular nerves specifically, but not the whole plexus point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient undergoes a surgical procedure in the posterior triangle of the neck. Postoperatively, the patient retains the ability to shrug their shoulders (motor function), but shows significant impairment in proprioceptive feedback from the trapezius muscle. Which specific nerve fibers were likely damaged?
options: Phrenic nerve
Cervical plexus branches C3 and C4
Cervical plexus branches C1 and C2
Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
Dorsal rami of C5 and C6
correctOption: Cervical plexus branches C3 and C4
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is primarily motor to the diaphragm and sensory to the pleura/pericardium.
Proprioception for the trapezius is provided by sensory fibers from the C3 and C4 anterior rami via the cervical plexus. Shrugging (motor) is handled by CN XI.
C1 and C2 contribute to the ansa cervicalis and lesser occipital nerves; they do not provide proprioception to the trapezius.
The spinal accessory nerve is the primary motor supply to the trapezius; its damage would cause motor paralysis, which is not present here.
Dorsal rami supply the intrinsic back muscles, not the trapezius proprioception.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Ansa Cervicalis Formation and C1 Integration
statement: Which of the following describes the multi-step pathway by which C1 fibers contribute to the motor innervation of the infrahyoid muscles via the ansa cervicalis?
options: C1 fibers emerge from the spinal cord and pass through the carotid canal to the ansa cervicalis.
C1 fibers join the vagus nerve and descend to the thyroid cartilage.
C1 fibers join the hypoglossal nerve and leave it as the descending branch to join the descending cervical nerve.
C1 fibers form the inferior root of the ansa cervicalis independently of other cranial nerves.
C1 fibers directly enter the ansa cervicalis loop from the prevertebral muscles.
correctOption: C1 fibers join the hypoglossal nerve and leave it as the descending branch to join the descending cervical nerve.
optionExplanations: The carotid canal transmits the internal carotid artery and sympathetic plexuses, not somatic fibers of C1.
The vagus nerve (CN X) does not carry C1 motor fibers for the infrahyoid muscles; it carries the cranial root of the accessory nerve for pharyngeal and laryngeal innervation.

This is the classic description of the superior root (descendens hypoglossi). C1 fibers travel briefly with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) before descending as a distinct branch to meet the C2/C3 fibers.
C1 fibers form the superior root, not the inferior root. The inferior root is formed by the descending cervical nerve, which consists of fibers from C2 and C3.
C1 fibers do not enter the ansa cervicalis directly from prevertebral muscles; they must first 'hitchhike' with a cranial nerve (the hypoglossal) before forming the superior root.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): A branch from C1 joins the hypoglossal nerve. Some of these C1 fibers later leave the hypoglossal as the descending branch, which unites with the descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3), to form the ansa cervicalis.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Anatomic Variations of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: In approximately one-third of the population, an 'accessory phrenic nerve' is present. This nerve typically originates from the fifth cervical nerve (C5) and follows which specific anatomical pathway before joining the main phrenic nerve trunk?
options: It is incorporated into the nerve to the subclavius muscle.
It travels within the sheath of the internal jugular vein.
It descends through the interscalene triangle behind the subclavian artery.
It pierces the scalenus medius muscle to reach the thoracic inlet.
It joins the descending branch of the hypoglossal nerve (C1).
correctOption: It is incorporated into the nerve to the subclavius muscle.
optionExplanations: The accessory phrenic nerve, often derived from C5, frequently hitch-hikes with the nerve to the subclavius before merging with the main phrenic trunk, usually within the thorax.
The phrenic nerve and its accessories are associated with the prevertebral fascia and the scalenus anterior muscle, not the carotid sheath containing the internal jugular vein.
The main phrenic nerve passes in front of the subclavian artery, and the accessory phrenic typically follows a similar anterior path rather than entering the interscalene triangle.
The phrenic nerve and its accessories typically lie on or in front of the scalenus anterior muscle, whereas the roots of the brachial plexus pass between the scalenus anterior and medius.
The descending branch of C1 joins C2 and C3 to form the ansa cervicalis, which is separate from the phrenic nerve's diaphragmatic supply.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve . The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Neuroanatomical Basis of Referred Pain (Phrenic to Supraclavicular)
statement: A patient with chronic gallbladder inflammation reports a sharp, localized pain in the right shoulder region. Which neural pathway explains this referred pain phenomenon involving the cervical plexus?
options: Pain signals travel through the sympathetic trunk to the superior cervical ganglion.
Irritation of the diaphragm's peritoneum travels via the phrenic nerve and is perceived in the supraclavicular nerve distribution.
The lesser occipital nerve communicates with the glossopharyngeal nerve in the pharynx.
Afferents from the gallbladder travel via the vagus nerve and synapse with the great auricular nerve.
The transverse cervical nerve shares a common root with the nerve to the subclavius.
correctOption: Irritation of the diaphragm's peritoneum travels via the phrenic nerve and is perceived in the supraclavicular nerve distribution.
optionExplanations: While the sympathetic trunk is involved in visceral pain, referred pain to the shoulder specifically involves the overlap of somatic spinal segments in the cervical plexus.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) and the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) share common spinal segments (C3 and C4). Irritation of phrenic sensory fibers in the diaphragm is misperceived by the brain as coming from the supraclavicular skin.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the scalp and auricle; it does not share the C3-C4 segments required for shoulder-referred pain from the diaphragm.
The vagus nerve does not provide the sensory fibers for the supraclavicular region; referred pain to the shoulder is typically phrenic-mediated.
The nerve to the subclavius is part of the brachial plexus and is not the primary mediator for gallbladder-related referred pain.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) have medial, intermediate, and lateral branches that supply the skin over the shoulder region. These nerves are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Fascial and Vascular Relations of the Cervical Plexus
statement: When identifying the cervical plexus during a surgical approach, what is its primary anatomical relationship with the deep cervical fascia and the internal jugular vein?
options: It lies deep to the prevertebral fascia, related to the vein within the carotid sheath.
It is located within the visceral space, anterior to the vein.
It lies deep to the prevertebral layer of deep fascia, medial to the vein.
It lies superficial to the investing layer of deep fascia, lateral to the vein.
It is embedded within the pretracheal fascia, posterior to the vein.
correctOption: It lies deep to the prevertebral fascia, related to the vein within the carotid sheath.
optionExplanations: The plexus is situated behind (deep to) the prevertebral layer of the deep cervical fascia and maintains a close relationship with the internal jugular vein, which is a component of the carotid sheath.
The visceral space contains the trachea, esophagus, and thyroid; it does not contain the cervical plexus.
While it is deep to the prevertebral fascia, the text specifies it is related to the vein within the carotid sheath, rather than strictly being 'medial' to it as a defining location.
The cutaneous branches become superficial to the investing fascia, but the plexus itself (the loops) is deeply placed.
The pretracheal fascia surrounds the thyroid, parathyroid, and infrahyoid muscles; it does not house the cervical plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The supraclavicular nerves are categorized into three distinct branches based on their terminal distribution. Which of the following areas is specifically supplied by the lateral supraclavicular nerve branch?
options: The skin over the shoulder and upper half of the deltoid
The skin over the angle of the mandible
The skin of the medial surface of the auricle
The skin as far as the median plane of the sternum
The skin over the parotid gland
correctOption: The skin over the shoulder and upper half of the deltoid
optionExplanations: The lateral (posterior) supraclavicular nerve crosses the lateral end of the clavicle to provide sensory innervation to the shoulder and the skin over the upper half of the deltoid muscle.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, not the supraclavicular nerves.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) and the great auricular nerve supply the skin of the auricle, not the supraclavicular branches.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin as far as the median plane/sternum, not the lateral branch.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) is specifically responsible for the skin over the parotid gland and angle of the jaw.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The lateral supraclavicular nerve crosses the lateral end of the clavicle and supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle; this nerve also supplies the posterior aspect of the shoulder as far down as the spine of the scapula.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The cervical plexus provides both motor and proprioceptive branches. What is the functional significance of the branches originating from the C3 and C4 rami that enter the trapezius muscle?
options: They carry parasympathetic fibers for sweat glands over the shoulder
They are purely proprioceptive fibers for the muscle
They provide sensory innervation to the skin overlying the trapezius
They provide the primary motor drive for shrugging the shoulders
They control the autonomic tone of the vessels within the muscle
correctOption: They are purely proprioceptive fibers for the muscle
optionExplanations: Parasympathetic fibers are not carried by the cervical plexus; autonomic fibers to the skin are sympathetic and derived from the cervical sympathetic trunk.
While the spinal accessory nerve provides motor innervation, the C3 and C4 rami of the cervical plexus provide the essential proprioceptive feedback for the trapezius muscle.
Cutaneous innervation over the trapezius on the back of the neck is supplied by the posterior rami of cervical nerves, not the C3/C4 proprioceptive branches to the muscle itself.
The primary motor drive for the trapezius is provided by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), not the cervical plexus.
Autonomic tone of blood vessels is regulated by sympathetic postganglionic fibers from the cervical sympathetic ganglia, not the somatic muscular branches of the plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: In the 'nerve point of the neck' (Erb's point), which is commonly used as a site for local anesthetic injection to block the cervical plexus, where exactly is this point located?
options: Deep to the pretracheal fascia in the carotid triangle
At the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, near its insertion
Between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the clavicle
Immediately superior to the transverse process of the atlas
At the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about its midpoint
correctOption: At the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about its midpoint
optionExplanations: The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and infrahyoid muscles, while the cervical plexus is related to the prevertebral fascia.
The anterior border of the SCM is where the carotid sheath and ansa cervicalis are found, not the cutaneous nerve point.
The gap between the heads of the SCM is used for internal jugular vein catheterization (lesser supraclavicular fossa).
The transverse process of the atlas is much higher than the midpoint of the sternocleidomastoid.

The nerve point of the neck (punctum nervosum) is located at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, approximately halfway between its origin and insertion. Here, the four main cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient suffers a penetrating wound to the neck resulting in a complete lesion of the right phrenic nerve. Which of the following clinical findings is most likely on radiographic evaluation?
options: Deviation of the trachea toward the right side.
Hyperexpansion of the lower lobe of the right lung.
Anesthesia over the skin of the right shoulder and deltoid.
Contraction and descent of the right half of the diaphragm during inspiration.
Elevation of the right half of the diaphragm due to positive abdominal pressure.
correctOption: Elevation of the right half of the diaphragm due to positive abdominal pressure.
optionExplanations: Tracheal deviation is more common with tension pneumothorax or massive lung collapse, but it is not a direct consequence of an isolated phrenic nerve injury.
The upward displacement of the diaphragm typically leads to collapse (atelectasis) of the lower lobe of the lung on that side, not hyperexpansion.
Shoulder anesthesia would result from a lesion of the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4), not the phrenic nerve itself (which is primarily motor and visceral sensory).
A paralyzed diaphragm cannot contract or descend; it would move passively upward rather than downward during inspiration.
When the phrenic nerve is severed, the corresponding hemi-diaphragm loses motor tone, relaxes, and is forced upward (paradoxical movement) by intra-abdominal pressure.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Penetrating wounds in the neck can injure the phrenic nerve. If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with acute cholecystitis and complains of sharp pain referred to the tip of the right shoulder. Which physiological mechanism best explains this referred pain pattern via the cervical plexus?
options: Hypoglossal nerve irritation (CN XII) shared with C1 fibers
Vagus nerve irritation (CN X) shared with Great Auricular nerve (C2-C3)
Accessory nerve irritation (CN XI) shared with Lesser Occipital nerve (C2)
Sympathetic chain irritation shared with Transverse Cervical nerve (C2-C3)
Phrenic nerve irritation (C3-C5) shared with Supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4)
correctOption: Phrenic nerve irritation (C3-C5) shared with Supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4)
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This pathway (C1 fibers in XII) is involved in the ansa cervicalis and thyrohyoid innervation, not cutaneous referral from the diaphragm.
Incorrect. The vagus nerve does not share the same spinal root territory (C3-C4) with the great auricular nerve for shoulder referral.
Incorrect. The accessory nerve is motor (CN XI); it does not provide the cutaneous referral described for visceral pain.
Incorrect. The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior neck, not the shoulder tip, and the sympathetic chain follows different pathways.

Correct. The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) innervates the diaphragm/peritoneum. Gallbladder inflammation irritates the phrenic nerve, and because the supraclavicular nerves also originate from C3 and C4, the brain interprets the signal as coming from the shoulder skin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves [supraclavicular] are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which specific neural components participate in the formation of the cervical plexus?
options: Anterior rami of C1 to C4
Anterior rami of C5 to T1
Posterior rami of C5 to C8
Posterior rami of C1 to C4
Anterior rami of C1 to C5
correctOption: Anterior rami of C1 to C4
optionExplanations: The cervical plexus is formed by the union of the anterior rami of the first four cervical spinal nerves (C1-C4), which form loops in front of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles.
The anterior rami of C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus, which is responsible for the motor and sensory innervation of the upper limb, not the cervical region.
The posterior rami of the lower cervical nerves supply the deep muscles of the back and do not contribute to the formation of any major named plexus like the cervical or brachial plexus.
The posterior rami of cervical nerves supply the skin on the back of the neck and the intrinsic muscles of the back; they do not form the cervical plexus, which is an anterior rami structure.

While the phrenic nerve (a branch of the plexus) often receives a contribution from C5, the standard anatomical definition of the cervical plexus itself is restricted to the first four cervical rami (C1-C4).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus specifically innervates the skin over the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle?
options: Great auricular nerve
Greater occipital nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
correctOption: Lesser occipital nerve
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve supplies the angle of the mandible and the skin over the parotid gland, as well as both surfaces of the auricle, but not the occipital scalp.
The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2. The cervical plexus is formed by anterior rami, making this a different anatomical system.
The lesser occipital nerve is a C2 branch of the cervical plexus. It tracks along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid to reach the scalp behind the ear and the medial side of the auricle.
The supraclavicular nerves descend toward the chest and shoulder; they do not ascend to the scalp or the auricle.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible to the sternum, not the scalp or auricle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1613 (Book Page): The lesser occipital nerve (C2) hooks around the accessory nerve and ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply the skin over the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: When classifying the supraclavicular nerves, which are branches of the cervical plexus (C3 and C4), how are they divided according to their anatomical distribution?
options: Ascending, descending, and transverse
Superior, inferior, and deep
Medial, intermediate, and lateral
Anterior, middle, and posterior
Superficial, middle, and profound
correctOption: Medial, intermediate, and lateral
optionExplanations: While they descend, they are not named ascending or transverse; the transverse cervical nerve is a separate branch of the plexus.
These terms describe depths or vertical levels, whereas supraclavicular nerves spread horizontally across the shoulder.
The supraclavicular nerves are categorized into medial, intermediate, and lateral branches based on the part of the clavicle and shoulder they cross.
Anterior, middle, and posterior are standard terms for other structures (like scalene muscles), but not for supraclavicular nerves.
These are not standard anatomical classifications for these nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) emerge from beneath the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle and descend across the side of the neck. ... The medial supraclavicular nerve ... The intermediate supraclavicular nerve ... The lateral supraclavicular nerve...

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: While the spinal accessory nerve provides the primary motor supply to the trapezius, the cervical plexus contributes to the same muscle through which functional modality?
options: Primary motor efferents via the ansa cervicalis.
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers via C3-C4.
Proprioceptive fibers via C3 and C4.
Sympathetic vasoconstriction via C1-C2.
General somatic sensation via the lesser occipital nerve.
correctOption: Proprioceptive fibers via C3 and C4.
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis specifically supplies the infrahyoid (strap) muscles, not the trapezius.
There are no parasympathetic fibers in the cervical plexus; parasympathetics in the head/neck are carried by CN III, VII, IX, and X.
Though CN XI is motor, the sensory/proprioceptive feedback (sensing muscle position and tension) for the trapezius is provided by the C3 and C4 spinal nerves of the cervical plexus.
Sympathetic fibers to muscles generally travel via the sympathetic chain and perivascular plexuses, not primarily as identified branches of C1-C2 of the cervical plexus.
The lesser occipital nerve provides cutaneous sensation to the scalp, not proprioception to the trapezius muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: During its descent in the neck, the phrenic nerve is held in a constant anatomical relationship to the scalenus anterior muscle. Which statement accurately describes this relationship?
options: It descends within the substance of the muscle fibers to reach the first rib.
It is bound to the anterior surface of the muscle by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
It lies lateral to the muscle and medial to the trunks of the brachial plexus.
It crosses the muscle horizontally, passing superficial to the internal jugular vein.
It runs vertically downward behind the muscle, separated from the pleura by the medius muscle.
correctOption: It is bound to the anterior surface of the muscle by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
optionExplanations: The nerve remains on the surface of the muscle; it does not pierce or travel within the muscle substance.
The phrenic nerve descends vertically across the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle and is securely bound to it by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
The phrenic nerve is medial to the emerging roots and trunks of the brachial plexus, not lateral.
The phrenic nerve runs vertically, not horizontally. Furthermore, it lies deep to the internal jugular vein, which is within the more superficial carotid sheath.
The phrenic nerve runs in front of the scalenus anterior, not behind it. The structures behind the muscle include the pleura and the subclavian artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia bind the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the muscle

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which of the following explains why a patient with acute gallbladder inflammation may perceive pain in the right shoulder region?
options: The vagus nerve transmits visceral pain that is localized to the dermatome of the accessory nerve
The cystic duct and the shoulder joint share common sympathetic fibers from the stellate ganglion
Direct compression of the brachial plexus by the distended liver
The gallbladder is directly innervated by the supraclavicular nerves
Irritation of the diaphragm's peritoneum is transmitted via the phrenic nerve to the C3-C4 spinal levels
correctOption: Irritation of the diaphragm's peritoneum is transmitted via the phrenic nerve to the C3-C4 spinal levels
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve does not project to the C3-C4 dermatomes; somatic referred pain to the shoulder is a classic example of phrenic nerve referral, not vagal.
Sympathetic fibers from the stellate ganglion are involved in cardiovascular and sudomotor regulation; they are not the primary pathway for the referred somatic pain seen in phrenic nerve irritation.
The liver does not distend significantly enough to compress the brachial plexus in the neck, which is located superior to the first rib.
The supraclavicular nerves are somatic nerves of the cervical plexus and do not provide visceral innervation to the gallbladder.

The phrenic nerve provides sensory fibers to the peritoneum covering the diaphragm. Irritation here (as in gallbladder disease) sends impulses to spinal segments C3 and C4, which also receive sensory input from the supraclavicular nerves supplying the shoulder skin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves [supraclavicular] are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Basic Formation and Location of the Cervical Plexus
statement: A first-year medical student is asked to identify the neural structure formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical spinal nerves. Which of the following describes the correct constitution and structural organization of this network?
options: It is formed by the anterior rami of C1 to C4 and forms loops in front of the levator scapulae.
It is formed by the posterior rami and lies within the vertebral canal.
It consists of roots, trunks, and divisions located primarily in the axilla.
It is formed by the cranial nerves IX, X, and XI in the carotid triangle.
It is formed by the anterior rami of C5 to T1 and passes through the interscalene triangle.
correctOption: It is formed by the anterior rami of C1 to C4 and forms loops in front of the levator scapulae.
optionExplanations: The cervical plexus is indeed formed by the anterior rami of C1, C2, C3, and C4, organized as loops situated on the prevertebral muscles (levator scapulae and scalenus medius).
The cervical plexus is formed by anterior (ventral) rami, not posterior rami; posterior rami supply the intrinsic back muscles and skin of the posterior trunk/neck.
Roots, trunks, and divisions are structural components of the brachial plexus; the cervical plexus does not follow this specific nomenclature of trunks and cords.
While the cervical plexus is related to these cranial nerves in the neck, it is a spinal nerve plexus and does not involve the cranial nerves in its primary formation.
The rami of C5 to T1 constitute the brachial plexus, which is responsible for the innervation of the upper limb, not the cervical plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus. The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Cutaneous Nerve Distribution of the Neck
statement: A patient presents with a localized sensory loss over the skin of the angle of the mandible. Which cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus is most likely compromised?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Greater occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve (C2) primarily supplies the back of the scalp and the upper part of the auricle, not the angle of the mandible.
The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2 and supplies the back of the scalp; it is not a branch of the cervical plexus, which is formed by anterior rami.
The great auricular nerve (C2 and C3) ascends across the sternocleidomastoid to provide sensation to the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland area, and the auricle.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2 and C3) passes forward across the sternocleidomastoid to supply the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum.
The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and C4) descend to supply the skin over the shoulder, the lateral neck, and the upper chest down to the level of the second rib.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: While the accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the primary motor supply to the trapezius muscle, the cervical plexus contributes specific fibers to this muscle. What is the functional modality of these cervical plexus fibers (C3 and C4)?
options: Nociceptive fibers for deep muscular pain
Proprioceptive fibers for muscle position sense
Postganglionic sympathetic fibers for vasomotor control
General somatic efferent fibers for branchiomeric contraction
Secretomotor fibers for overlying sebaceous glands
correctOption: Proprioceptive fibers for muscle position sense
optionExplanations: While nociceptive fibers are present, the text specifically identifies the contribution of the C3 and C4 rami to the trapezius and SCM as proprioceptive in nature.

The fibers from the C3 and C4 rami of the cervical plexus are specifically described as carrying proprioceptive information, providing sensory feedback about the muscle's state to the central nervous system.
Sympathetic fibers reach the muscle via vascular plexuses from the sympathetic trunk, not directly as named muscular branches of the plexus.
The motor (efferent) supply to the trapezius is provided by the spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI), while the cervical plexus contribution is non-motor.
Secretomotor fibers are parasympathetic and are not distributed to skeletal muscle via the cervical plexus; sebaceous glands in the skin are supplied by the sympathetic system.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient presents with a unilateral phrenic nerve injury following a deep penetrating neck wound. Pathophysiologically, what is the primary mechanism leading to the characteristic elevation of the diaphragm on the affected side?
options: Negative intrathoracic pressure causing active suction of the abdominal contents
Relaxation of the muscle and subsequent displacement by positive abdominal pressure
Active contraction of the intercostal muscles during inspiration
Sympathetic overactivity causing tonic contraction of the unaffected crus
Fibrosis of the pleura pulling the central tendon superiorly
correctOption: Relaxation of the muscle and subsequent displacement by positive abdominal pressure
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While negative intrathoracic pressure exists, the primary force mentioned in clinical anatomy is the upward push from abdominal pressure.
Correct. In phrenic nerve paralysis, the muscle loses its motor tone and relaxes; the relatively higher pressure within the abdominal cavity then pushes the dome upward into the thorax.
Incorrect. Intercostal muscle contraction expands the thorax but does not cause the specific elevation of the paralyzed diaphragm.
Incorrect. The unaffected side behaves normally; there is no specific 'sympathetic overactivity' mechanism involved in the positional shift of the paralyzed side.
Incorrect. While chronic conditions might lead to fibrosis, the immediate anatomical result of nerve injury is due to pressure differentials and muscle relaxation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which fascial layer of the neck is specifically responsible for covering the cervical plexus loops as they lie in front of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles?
options: Pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia
Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Carotid sheath
Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
Superficial fascia
correctOption: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
optionExplanations: The pretracheal layer encloses the thyroid gland and infrahyoid muscles in the anterior neck and is not related to the cervical plexus in the posterior triangle.
The investing layer encircles the whole neck and splits to enclose the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, but it is superficial to the plexus.

The carotid sheath lies anterior to the cervical plexus; while the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the sheath, the sheath itself does not form the immediate floor/covering of the plexus loops.
The cervical plexus loops are situated deep to the prevertebral fascia, which covers the prevertebral muscles (levator scapulae, scalenus medius) and the plexus itself.
The superficial fascia contains the platysma and cutaneous nerves after they have pierced the deep fascia, but it does not cover the plexus loops directly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A 52-year-old male presents with acute cholecystitis. He complains of sharp pain not only in the right hypochondrium but also referred to the tip of his right shoulder. Which anatomical pathway best explains this referred pain pattern?
options: Right sympathetic trunk and the lesser occipital nerve (C2)
Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) and the dorsal scapular nerve (C5)
Vagus nerve (CN X) and the transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3)
Intercostal nerves (T7-T11) and the greater occipital nerve (C2)
Sensory fibers of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) and cutaneous supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4)
correctOption: Sensory fibers of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) and cutaneous supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4)
optionExplanations: The sympathetic trunk carries visceral pain, but the referred somatic pain is mediated via common spinal cord segments shared with the supraclavicular nerves.
The spinal accessory nerve is motor to the trapezius; it does not mediate cutaneous referred sensation from the diaphragm.
The vagus nerve provides visceral sensation but does not typically refer pain to the C3-C4 dermatomes in this manner.
Intercostal nerves supply the body wall; the greater occipital nerve supplies the scalp. Neither is involved in gallbladder-to-shoulder referral.

The phrenic nerve (C3-5) provides sensory innervation to the peritoneum covering the diaphragm. Irritation from the gallbladder is carried by the phrenic nerve to the spinal cord segments C3-C4, which also receive sensory input from the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) supplying the shoulder skin.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Cervical Plexus
statement: During a superficial neck block for a minor procedure, the anesthetic is injected at the 'nerve point of the neck.' Where is this landmark accurately located?
options: Level with the thyroid notch, deep to the carotid sheath.
At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, approximately at its midpoint.
Just above the clavicle at the junction of its medial and middle thirds.
At the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, level with the hyoid bone.
At the apex of the posterior triangle, level with the mastoid process.
correctOption: At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, approximately at its midpoint.
optionExplanations: The thyroid notch is much more medial, and the nerve point is superficial, not deep to the carotid sheath.

The nerve point of the neck (Erb's point) is the location where the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (Lesser occipital, Great auricular, Transverse cervical, and Supraclavicular) emerge.
This describes the area where the supraclavicular nerves descend, but not the common emergence point.
The anterior border of the SCM is a landmark for the carotid triangle, not the cutaneous nerve point.
The apex of the posterior triangle contains the occipital artery and the spinal accessory nerve, but the nerve point is at the midpoint of the muscle belly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there (see Fig. 12.48).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The transverse cervical nerve, arising from the C2 and C3 rami of the cervical plexus, supplies the skin of which anatomical region?
options: The skin of the shoulder and the upper part of the chest.
The anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible to the sternum.
The vertex of the scalp and the upper neck.
The area over the parotid gland and the earlobe.
The skin of the chin and the mental region.
correctOption: The anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible to the sternum.
optionExplanations: The shoulder and upper chest are supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4).

The transverse cervical nerve (also called transverse cutaneous) emerges from the nerve point, crosses the sternocleidomastoid, and provides sensation to the majority of the anterior and lateral neck.
The vertex of the scalp is supplied by the greater occipital nerve (posterior ramus) and the supraorbital nerve (trigeminal), not the transverse cervical.
The parotid and earlobe regions are primarily the territory of the great auricular nerve.
The skin of the chin is supplied by the mental nerve from CN V3 and the submental rami, not the transverse cervical nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3)... supply the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, from the body of the mandible to the sternum.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: At which specific landmark do the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus typically emerge collectively from behind the sternocleidomastoid muscle?
options: The apex of the posterior triangle
The nerve point of the neck
The supraclavicular fossa
The upper third of the posterior border
The junction of the lower and middle thirds
correctOption: The nerve point of the neck
optionExplanations: The apex of the posterior triangle is where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line, which is superior to the emergence of the cervical plexus branches.

The nerve point (Erb's point) is located at the midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, serving as the exit for the lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular nerves.

The supraclavicular fossa contains the supraclavicular nerves as they descend, but it is not the point where all cutaneous branches of the plexus first emerge collectively from the deep fascia of the neck.
The upper third of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid is the site where the accessory nerve (CN XI) enters the muscle, but it is not the exit point for the cutaneous plexus branches.
The junction of the lower and middle thirds is too inferior; the cervical plexus branches emerge more superiorly at the midpoint of the muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: In the neck, the phrenic nerve follows a rigorous topographical course. Which anatomical structure is responsible for binding the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle?
options: Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
The axillary sheath
Pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia
The carotid sheath
Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
correctOption: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The investing layer is more superficial, splitting to enclose the SCM and trapezius.

Incorrect. The axillary sheath is a lateral/inferior extension of the prevertebral fascia enclosing the brachial plexus and subclavian artery, but the phrenic nerve is already medially placed on the scalenus anterior.
Incorrect. The pretracheal layer surrounds the thyroid, parathyroid, and larynx/trachea.
Incorrect. The phrenic nerve lies posterior to the carotid sheath, separated by the prevertebral fascia.
Correct. The prevertebral fascia covers the scalene muscles and specifically tethers the phrenic nerve to the scalenus anterior as it descends.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia bind the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the muscle

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Referred Pain Mechanism via Phrenic and Supraclavicular Nerves
statement: A patient with acute cholecystitis (gallbladder inflammation) complains of referred pain to the tip of the right shoulder. Which neuro-anatomical pathway best explains this phenomenon?
options: Sympathetic crossover from the superior cervical ganglion to the brachial plexus
Irritation of the lesser occipital nerve (C2) communicating with the greater occipital nerve
Irritation of the transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3) communicating with the phrenic nerve
Irritation of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) sharing roots with the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4)
Phrenic nerve irritation referred through the great auricular nerve (C2-C3)
correctOption: Irritation of the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) sharing roots with the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4)
optionExplanations: Sympathetic fibers are involved in visceral pain, but the classic somatic referral to the shoulder tip is mediated via the spinal cord segments shared by the phrenic and supraclavicular nerves.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the lateral scalp and auricle; it does not share segments with the nerves supplying the diaphragm or the gallbladder's peritoneal covering.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior neck skin and does not extend to the shoulder region or share sufficient segmental overlap for gallbladder referral.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) supplies the peritoneum covering the diaphragm. Irritation from the gallbladder (via the diaphragm) sends impulses to the spinal cord segments C3-C4, which also receive sensory input from the supraclavicular nerves supplying the shoulder skin.
The great auricular nerve supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland, a region far removed from the diaphragmatic and shoulder referral pathways of C3-C4.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves [supraclavicular] are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Basic Formation of the Cervical Plexus
statement: A first-year medical student is asked to identify the spinal nerves responsible for the formation of the cervical plexus. Which of the following correctly describes its components?
options: Posterior rami of C1 to C4.
Anterior rami of C5 to T1.
Anterior and posterior rami of C1 to C4.
Anterior rami of C1 to C8.
Anterior rami of C1 to C4.
correctOption: Anterior rami of C1 to C4.
optionExplanations: Posterior rami of spinal nerves supply the deep muscles and skin of the back; they do not form the cervical plexus.
Anterior rami of C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus, which supplies the upper limb.
The plexus is specifically a product of the anterior rami; posterior rami remain segmental and do not form a plexus in the neck.
C1 to C8 represents the entire cervical spinal nerve group, but only the upper four contribute to the cervical plexus.
The cervical plexus is exclusively formed by the anterior rami of the C1, C2, C3, and C4 spinal nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient presents with localized numbness in the skin overlying the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. Which nerve, derived from the C2 and C3 rami of the cervical plexus, is most likely affected?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Great auricular nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve supplies the lateral occipital region of the scalp and the medial auricle.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum.
The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and supplies the temple and part of the ear, but the angle of the jaw is a classic cervical plexus territory.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) ascends across the sternocleidomastoid to supply the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and both surfaces of the auricle.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the lower neck, upper chest, and shoulder regions.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Motor Distribution of the Ansa Cervicalis
statement: During a complex radical neck dissection for a laryngeal malignancy, a surgeon inadvertently sacrifices the C1 fibers as they leave the hypoglossal nerve and the descending cervical nerve (C2, C3). Which combination of muscles will lose their primary motor supply as a result of this specific lesion?
options: Stylopharyngeus and Cricothyroid
Digastric and Mylohyoid
Sternocleidomastoid and Trapezius
Thyrohyoid and Geniohyoid only
Omohyoid, Sternohyoid, and Sternothyroid
correctOption: Omohyoid, Sternohyoid, and Sternothyroid
optionExplanations: Stylopharyngeus is supplied by CN IX (glossopharyngeal), and Cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve (CN X).
Digastric (anterior belly) and Mylohyoid are supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (from the mandibular division of CN V).
SCM and Trapezius are primarily supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); the cervical plexus only provides proprioception.
While C1 does supply thyrohyoid and geniohyoid, these fibers leave the hypoglossal nerve independently of the ansa cervicalis loop. The question specifies the loss of the ansa cervicalis components.
The ansa cervicalis (formed by the superior C1 root and the inferior C2-C3 root) provides motor innervation to three of the four infrahyoid muscles: omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid.
