correctOption: Relaxation of the paralyzed muscle allowing positive abdominal pressure to push it upward.
optionExplanations: Lung collapse is a consequence of the diaphragm's elevation (atelectasis), not the primary cause of the movement itself.
Intercostal contraction creates negative thoracic pressure, which would actually tend to pull a flaccid diaphragm upward, but the primary force is the positive pressure from the abdomen.
While the mediastinum may shift, it is not the primary mechanism for the localized elevation of the paralyzed hemidiaphragm.
When the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is severed, the diaphragm loses all motor tone. The higher pressure within the abdominal cavity then forces the flaccid dome into the chest.
Abdominal muscle tone contributes to abdominal pressure, but it is the normal intra-abdominal pressure versus the negative intra-thoracic pressure that drives the elevation, not muscle spasticity.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply the skin over the lateral part of the occipital region?
options: Transverse cervical nerve
Great auricular nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Phrenic nerve
correctOption: Lesser occipital nerve
optionExplanations: The transverse cervical nerve crosses the SCM to supply the anterior neck skin.
The great auricular nerve supplies the angle of the mandible and the parotid area, not the occipital region.
The supraclavicular nerves descend toward the shoulder and chest, not up toward the occiput.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) follows the posterior border of the SCM upward to supply the lateral occipital scalp and the cranial surface of the auricle.
The phrenic nerve is a motor and sensory nerve for the diaphragm and serous membranes; it has no cutaneous distribution on the scalp.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Topographical Formation of the Cervical Plexus
statement: The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of specific spinal nerves, which communicate through loops. Based on its topographical anatomy, where do these loops primarily reside in relation to the deep prevertebral musculature?
options: Embedded within the substance of the longus capitis muscle.
Superficial to the investing layer of the deep cervical fascia.
Between the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle.
Directly posterior to the belly of the scalenus anterior muscle.
In front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles.
correctOption: In front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles.
optionExplanations: While the longus capitis is a prevertebral muscle, the cervical plexus is more laterally placed relative to the midline-oriented longus capitis and longus colli.
The cervical plexus is a deep structure; it is covered by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia, not superficial to the investing layer, which is the most superficial deep fascia.
The digastric muscle bellies define the submandibular and carotid triangles, which contain terminal neurovascular structures but not the primary formation loops of the cervical plexus.
The phrenic nerve, a branch of the plexus, runs anterior to the scalenus anterior, but the main plexus loops are situated further posterior on the levator scapulae and scalenus medius.

The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C1-C4. These rami unite to form loops that are specifically situated anterior to the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles, serving as a landmark for the deep cervical region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles (see Fig. 12.54).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Phrenic Nerve Lesion and Diaphragmatic Paralysis
statement: A surgeon inadvertently transects the phrenic nerve during a deep surgical procedure in the root of the neck. Which of the following best describes the immediate pathophysiological consequence for the ipsilateral diaphragm?
options: The diaphragm descends passively due to the negative intrathoracic pressure created by the contralateral side.
The diaphragm maintains its position but loses its rhythmic ability to respond to autonomic respiratory signals.
The diaphragm undergoes tonic contraction, causing permanent flattening and basal lung compression.
The diaphragm undergoes compensatory hypertrophy to assist the accessory muscles of respiration.
The diaphragm relaxes and is pushed superiorly into the thorax by positive abdominal pressure.
correctOption: The diaphragm relaxes and is pushed superiorly into the thorax by positive abdominal pressure.
optionExplanations: Negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration would actually tend to pull a paralyzed diaphragm further upward (paradoxical movement), rather than causing it to descend.
Loss of motor supply does not just stop rhythmic signals; it results in a total loss of muscle tone and subsequent displacement.
Tonic contraction would imply persistent nerve stimulation or a different pathology; a transection results in flaccid paralysis and loss of tone.
Muscle tissue that loses its nerve supply undergoes denervation atrophy, not hypertrophy.

When the phrenic nerve is injured, the affected half of the diaphragm loses its motor supply, becomes flaccid, and is pushed cranially by the relatively higher pressure within the abdominal cavity compared to the thorax.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Distribution of the Great Auricular Nerve
statement: A patient presents with complete loss of sensation specifically over the skin of the angle of the mandible and the lower half of the auricle. A localized lesion in the cervical plexus is suspected. Which nerve is most likely affected?
options: Great auricular nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) is the specific branch of the cervical plexus that supplies the skin over the parotid gland, the angle of the mandible, and the auricle.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and the upper part of the medial auricle, not the angle of the mandible.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin over the medial end of the clavicle and the chest wall down to the second rib.
The zygomaticofacial nerve is a branch of the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2) and supplies the skin over the prominence of the cheek.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2, C3) supplies the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum, but not specifically the angle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Muscular Branches of the Cervical Plexus
statement: The cervical plexus provides numerous muscular branches. To which of the following muscles does the plexus provide direct somatic motor innervation as part of the 'deep' muscular branches?
options: Palatoglossus muscle
Stylohyoid muscle
Anterior belly of the digastric
Mylohyoid muscle
Prevertebral muscles
correctOption: Prevertebral muscles
optionExplanations: The palatoglossus muscle is supplied by the pharyngeal plexus via the vagus nerve (CN X).
The stylohyoid muscle is supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII), not the cervical plexus.
The anterior belly of the digastric is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid (CN V3).
The mylohyoid muscle is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3).
The cervical plexus provides motor nerves to the deep prevertebral muscles (like longus capitis and longus colli), as well as levator scapulae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Muscular Branches (Neck) Nerve branches supply the prevertebral muscles, sternocleidomastoid, levator scapulae, and trapezius.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Phrenic Nerve Course and Fascial Relations
statement: The phrenic nerve's course in the neck is a critical surgical landmark. It descends vertically across the anterior surface of which muscle, being bound to it by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia?
options: Sternocleidomastoid
Scalenus medius
Omohyoid
Scalenus anterior
Levator scapulae
correctOption: Scalenus anterior
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid is superficial to the phrenic nerve; they are separated by the carotid sheath and the prevertebral fascia.
The phrenic nerve lies anterior to the scalenus medius, but it specifically descends across the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior.
The omohyoid (superior belly) is a strap muscle that crosses the carotid sheath; the phrenic nerve is much deeper, located on the prevertebral muscle layer.
The phrenic nerve is classically found descending on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle, held in place by the prevertebral fascia, and passes behind the internal jugular vein.
The levator scapulae is located posterior to the cervical plexus; the plexus loops form in front of it, but the phrenic nerve descends further medially on the scalenus anterior.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle (see Fig. 12.54) and enters the thorax by passing in front of the subclavian artery.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient undergoes a biopsy of a skin lesion located precisely over the angle of the mandible. Which specific branch of the cervical plexus must be anesthetized to ensure a painless procedure in this localized area?
options: Transverse cervical nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The transverse cervical nerve (C2-C3) supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum.
Incorrect. Supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) supply the skin of the shoulder and upper chest.
Incorrect. The zygomaticofacial nerve is a branch of the Maxillary (V2) nerve, supplying the cheek prominence, not the angle of the mandible.
Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and the auricle, not the angle of the mandible.
Correct. The great auricular nerve (C2-C3) specifically provides sensory innervation to the skin overlying the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Beyond providing motor innervation to the infrahyoid muscles, the cervical plexus contributes to the sensation of body position. Which rami specifically provide proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius muscle?
options: C4 and C5
C1 only
C3 and C4
C1 and C2
C2 and C3
correctOption: C3 and C4
optionExplanations: Incorrect. C5 is generally the root for the phrenic and the beginning of the brachial plexus, not the primary proprioceptive supply for trapezius.
Incorrect. C1 does not contribute to the trapezius muscle; it supplies the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid via CN XII.
Correct. While the Spinal Accessory nerve (CN XI) provides motor supply to the trapezius, the C3 and C4 rami of the cervical plexus carry the proprioceptive (sensory) fibers from the muscle.
Incorrect. C1 fibers are largely motor and travel with the hypoglossal nerve; C2 contributes to SCM proprioception.
Incorrect. C2 and C3 provide proprioception specifically for the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: A 35-year-old male sustains a deep penetrating wound to the lower neck just lateral to the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Physical examination shows respiratory distress. Chest X-ray reveals the right dome of the diaphragm is significantly elevated. Which anatomical relationship best explains the vulnerability of the phrenic nerve in this specific cervical location?
options: It loops around the subclavian artery before entering the thorax
It passes through the interscalene triangle with the brachial plexus
It descends posterior to the scalenus medius muscle
It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle
It is protected within the carotid sheath medial to the vagus nerve
correctOption: It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle
optionExplanations: The recurrent laryngeal nerve loops around the subclavian artery (on the right), but the phrenic nerve passes in front of it to enter the thorax.
The phrenic nerve passes in front of the scalenus anterior, whereas the brachial plexus and subclavian artery pass behind it through the interscalene triangle.
The phrenic nerve is anterior to the scalenus anterior, not posterior to the scalenus medius; the latter relationship would place it in the posterior triangle floor.
The phrenic nerve's position on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior, covered only by the prevertebral fascia, makes it highly vulnerable to injuries just lateral to the SCM.
The phrenic nerve is lateral to the carotid sheath, separated from its contents by the prevertebral fascia and the scalenus anterior muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle (see Fig. 12.54) and enters the thorax by passing in front of the subclavian artery.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A clinician plans to perform a superficial cervical plexus block for regional anesthesia. To target the common exit point of the cutaneous branches, where should the anesthetic be injected?
options: At the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle near the angle of the mandible
Deep to the pretracheal fascia in the midline of the neck
Immediately superior to the midpoint of the clavicle
At the midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Between the heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at the suprasternal notch
correctOption: At the midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
optionExplanations: The anterior border of the SCM is where the carotid sheath and its contents are located; the cutaneous nerves of the plexus emerge posteriorly.
The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and trachea. This area does not contain the exit point for the cervical plexus cutaneous branches.
The supraclavicular nerves pass this area as they descend, but the other branches (lesser occipital, etc.) would be missed by an injection this low.

The 'nerve point' (Erb's point) is the midpoint of the posterior border of the SCM, where the four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular) radiate.
This location (the lesser supraclavicular fossa) is used for internal jugular vein access and contains the phrenic nerve deep to the SCM, but it is not the superficial nerve point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Proprioceptive Distribution of the Cervical Plexus
statement: The cervical plexus provides proprioceptive fibers to which of the following muscles of the neck and back?
options: Omohyoid and Thyrohyoid
Scalenus Anterior and Scalenus Medius
Sternocleidomastoid and Trapezius
Sternohyoid and Sternothyroid
Longus Capitis and Longus Colli
correctOption: Sternocleidomastoid and Trapezius
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The omohyoid is supplied by the ansa cervicalis and the thyrohyoid by C1 fibers via CN XII, neither of which are primarily proprioceptive branches to the trapezius.
Incorrect. The scalene muscles receive direct segmental motor supply from the cervical and brachial plexus roots, not proprioceptive branches from the main plexus loops.

Correct. While the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the motor supply to the SCM and Trapezius, the cervical plexus (C2-C4) provides the necessary proprioceptive (sensory) feedback from these muscles.
Incorrect. The sternohyoid and sternothyroid are supplied by motor fibers from the ansa cervicalis for muscle contraction.
Incorrect. The prevertebral muscles (Longus capitis and colli) receive direct motor branches from the plexus, not specifically proprioceptive branches described for the large strap muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: In about one third of individuals, an 'accessory phrenic nerve' is present. From which cervical nerve is this accessory structure usually derived and what is its typical course?
options: C3, passing superficial to the platysma
C1, following the hypoglossal nerve
C2, following the lesser occipital nerve
C5, incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius
C4, descending within the carotid sheath
correctOption: C5, incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius
optionExplanations: C3 is a primary root of the phrenic nerve, not the 'accessory' root (which refers to the extra C5 contribution).
C1 fibers join the hypoglossal nerve but contribute to the ansa cervicalis, not the phrenic nerve.
C2 contributes to the lesser occipital and great auricular nerves, but is not the primary source of an accessory phrenic root.
The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly arises from C5. It often 'hitchhikes' with the nerve to the subclavius before joining the main phrenic nerve (C3–C4) in the thorax.
The phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5) descends on the scalenus anterior, not within the carotid sheath.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve. The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which specific branch of the cervical plexus is responsible for the cutaneous innervation of the skin over the posterior aspect of the shoulder as far down as the spine of the scapula?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Lateral supraclavicular nerve
Great auricular nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Lateral supraclavicular nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve (C2) ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid to supply the scalp and medial auricle, not the shoulder.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2, 3) passes forward across the sternocleidomastoid to supply the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck.
The lateral supraclavicular nerve (C3, 4) specifically descends to cover the shoulder region, including the upper deltoid and the posterior shoulder down to the scapular spine.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland, extending to the auricle.
The medial supraclavicular nerve (C3, 4) crosses the medial end of the clavicle to supply the skin of the chest as far as the median plane.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The lateral supraclavicular nerve crosses the lateral end of the clavicle and supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle; this nerve also supplies the posterior aspect of the shoulder as far down as the spine of the scapula.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Functional Modality of Cervical Plexus Muscular Branches
statement: In the neurological evaluation of the neck, a clinician must distinguish between the functional modalities of the cervical plexus. Which of the following correctly describes the nature of the nerve fibers supplied by the cervical plexus to the trapezius and sternocleidomastoid muscles?
options: General visceral efferent fibers from the cranial root
Somatic motor fibers for voluntary contraction
Branchial motor fibers from the cervical outflow
Proprioceptive fibers from C2, C3, and C4
Postganglionic sympathetic fibers for muscle tone
correctOption: Proprioceptive fibers from C2, C3, and C4
optionExplanations: General visceral efferents are autonomic; these muscles are skeletal and are supplied by somatic or branchial motor nerves (CN XI).
Somatic motor fibers for voluntary contraction are provided by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); the cervical plexus contribution is specifically sensory/proprioceptive.
Branchial motor fibers are carried by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), which provides the actual motor supply to these muscles, not the cervical plexus.
The cervical plexus provides sensory (proprioceptive) information from these muscles (C2-C3 for SCM; C3-C4 for trapezius), while the motor supply is via CN XI.
Sympathetic fibers are present in the neck for vascular supply, but the specific branches from C2-C4 to these muscles are primarily for proprioception.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient undergoing thoracic surgery still exhibits partial diaphragmatic movement despite a confirmed total lesion of the main phrenic nerve trunk in the neck. What anatomical variation provides the most likely explanation for this clinical finding?
options: An accessory phrenic nerve arising from the fifth cervical nerve.
Presence of a second phrenic nerve arising from C1 and C2.
Cross-innervation from the contralateral vagus nerve.
Supply from the intercostal nerves to the central tendon.
Direct motor branches from the ansa cervicalis.
correctOption: An accessory phrenic nerve arising from the fifth cervical nerve.
optionExplanations: An accessory phrenic nerve often arises from C5 (via the nerve to subclavius). If the main trunk (C3-C4) is injured in the neck, the accessory fibers joining lower in the thorax can preserve some function.
The phrenic nerve is composed of C3, C4, and C5. There is no standard or common variant involving C1 and C2 supplying the diaphragm.
The vagus nerve is purely autonomic (parasympathetic) and sensory in the thorax; it does not provide somatic motor supply to the skeletal muscle of the diaphragm.
Intercostal nerves provide sensory innervation to the peripheral part of the diaphragm but do not provide motor innervation to the muscle or central tendon.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid (strap) muscles of the neck; it has no anatomical pathway or distribution to the diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve. The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient presents with sharp pain over the skin of the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle. If this pain is referred from an irritation of the diaphragmatic pleura, which specific branches of the cervical plexus are involved in the sensory delivery of this referred sensation?
options: Supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4)
Transverse cervical nerves (C2 and 3)
Great auricular nerve (C2 and 3)
Lesser occipital nerve (C2)
Descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3)
correctOption: Supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4)
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) and the supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) share common spinal segments. Irritation of the diaphragm (sensory via phrenic) is perceived by the brain as coming from the C3-C4 dermatomes on the shoulder.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, not the shoulder region.
The great auricular nerve supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid region.
The lesser occipital nerve supplies the back of the scalp and the auricle, which is unrelated to diaphragmatic referred pain.
The descending cervical nerve is a motor component that forms part of the ansa cervicalis to supply infrahyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) have medial, intermediate, and lateral branches that supply the skin over the shoulder region. These nerves are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Deep Anatomical Relations of the Cervical Plexus
statement: During a deep dissection of the neck, a surgeon identifies a nerve plexus lying deep to the internal jugular vein and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia. What is the precise topographical relationship of this plexus to the underlying musculature?
options: It lies superficial to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
It is situated posterior to the trapezius muscle within the suboccipital triangle.
It sits directly on the surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
It is located medial to the longus colli muscle in the visceral space.
It is located in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles.
correctOption: It is located in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles.
optionExplanations: The plexus is located deep to the prevertebral fascia, not superficial to the investing fascia; cutaneous branches must pierce the investing fascia to reach the skin.
The cervical plexus is an anterior structure relative to the vertebral column and is not found in the suboccipital triangle, which contains the posterior ramus of C1.
The plexus is deep to the sternocleidomastoid; only its cutaneous branches emerge at the posterior border of the muscle.
The plexus is a somatic structure located in the prevertebral region, whereas the longus colli is more medial and the visceral space contains the trachea and esophagus.
Anatomically, the loops of the cervical plexus are specifically positioned on the anterior surface of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles (see Fig. 12.54). The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: About one third of the population possesses an 'accessory phrenic nerve.' Which spinal nerve root provides this contribution and what is its typical course?
options: C1; joining the hypoglossal nerve
T1; ascending from the first intercostal nerve
C2; traveling with the lesser occipital nerve
C5; incorporated into the nerve to the subclavius
C6; hitchhiking with the transverse cervical artery
correctOption: C5; incorporated into the nerve to the subclavius
optionExplanations: C1 provides motor fibers to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid via the hypoglossal nerve, but it is not involved in diaphragmatic innervation.
T1 is the first thoracic nerve and contributes to the brachial plexus; it does not provide an accessory phrenic component to the diaphragm.
C2 contributes to the cervical plexus and cutaneous nerves like the great auricular, but it is not the source of the accessory phrenic nerve.
The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly arises from the C5 nerve root. It often joins the nerve to the subclavius before eventually merging with the phrenic nerve proper in the thoracic cavity.
C6 is part of the brachial plexus and does not typically form an accessory phrenic nerve that would join the main C3-C5 phrenic trunk.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve. The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which specific branch of the cervical plexus is responsible for providing the motor fibers to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid muscles?
options: Descending cervical nerve (C2 and 3)
C1 fibers hitchhiking with the hypoglossal nerve
Transverse cervical nerve (C2 and 3)
Nerve to the stylopharyngeus
Supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4)
correctOption: C1 fibers hitchhiking with the hypoglossal nerve
optionExplanations: The descending cervical nerve (C2, C3) joins the ansa cervicalis to supply the omohyoid, sternohyoid, and sternothyroid, but not the thyrohyoid.
The thyrohyoid and geniohyoid are unique in that they are supplied by C1 fibers that hitchhike on the hypoglossal nerve and branch off directly, rather than via the ansa loop.
The transverse cervical nerve is a cutaneous sensory nerve and does not provide motor fibers to muscles.
The nerve to the stylopharyngeus is a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), not the cervical plexus.
The supraclavicular nerves are entirely sensory and supply the skin of the shoulder and chest.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Other C1 fibers within the hypoglossal nerve leave it as the nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Fascial Relations of the Cervical Plexus
statement: A physician is evaluating the deep anatomical relations of the cervical plexus. Which structure binds the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle?
options: The carotid sheath.
The investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
The axillary sheath.
The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
The pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia.
correctOption: The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
optionExplanations: The carotid sheath contains the carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve. While the cervical plexus is related to the sheath, the fascia within the sheath does not bind the phrenic nerve to the scalenus anterior.
The investing layer encircles the entire neck and encloses the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, but it is too superficial to bind nerves to the deep prevertebral muscles.
The axillary sheath is a lateral extension of the prevertebral fascia that surrounds the brachial plexus and subclavian artery into the axilla; it does not bind the phrenic nerve in the neck.

The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles, including the scalenus anterior. It serves as a structural anchor, binding the phrenic nerve (a critical branch of the cervical plexus) in place as it descends toward the thorax.
The pretracheal layer is located in the anterior neck, surrounding the thyroid gland, trachea, and esophagus; it does not extend to the lateral scalene muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia bind the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the muscle (scalenus anterior).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A 48-year-old male presents with right-sided diaphragmatic paralysis following a traumatic penetrating injury to the mid-cervical region. During inspiration, the affected side of the diaphragm is observed to rise. What is the anatomical and physiological basis for this lesion?
options: Injury to the ansa cervicalis resulting in loss of infrahyoid muscle stabilization
Paralysis of the scalene muscles leading to inability to elevate the first rib
Damage to the spinal accessory nerve leading to compensatory thoracic breathing
Sectioning of the recurrent laryngeal nerve causing airway obstruction and secondary elevation
Sectioning of the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) causing the diaphragm to be pushed up by positive abdominal pressure
correctOption: Sectioning of the phrenic nerve (C3–C5) causing the diaphragm to be pushed up by positive abdominal pressure
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles. While they help stabilize the hyoid, their paralysis does not cause diaphragmatic paradoxical movement.
Scalene muscles are accessory muscles of respiration, but their loss would not cause the diaphragm to rise during inspiration; they primarily act on the ribs.
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the SCM and trapezius. Paralysis leads to shoulder drop and weak head rotation, not diaphragmatic elevation.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies laryngeal muscles. Injury causes hoarseness or stridor but does not affect diaphragmatic mechanics.

The phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. Unilateral injury results in paradoxical movement where the paralyzed muscle is pushed cranially by intra-abdominal pressure during inspiration instead of contracting caudally.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): Each phrenic nerve supplies the corresponding half of the diaphragm... If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient presents with a loss of sensation specifically over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. Which branch of the cervical plexus is most likely involved?
options: Transverse cervical nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Great auricular nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The transverse cervical nerve (C2, C3) supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum.
Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the skin of the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle, not the mandible.
Incorrect. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), not the cervical plexus, and it supplies the temple and external meatus area.
Correct. The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) is the specific branch of the cervical plexus that ascends to provide sensation to the skin overlying the parotid gland and the mandibular angle.
Incorrect. Supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4) supply the skin of the lower neck, shoulder, and upper chest down to the second rib.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1613 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) ascends across the sternocleidomastoid muscle and divides into branches that supply the skin over the angle of the mandible, on the parotid gland, and on both surfaces of the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Proprioceptive Distribution of the Cervical Plexus
statement: During a surgical dissection of the posterior triangle, the spinal accessory nerve is identified. It provides motor supply to the trapezius. Which spinal nerve rami from the cervical plexus provide the corresponding proprioceptive fibers for this muscle?
options: C2 and C3
C5 and T1
C1 and C2
C3 and C4
C4 and C5
correctOption: C3 and C4
optionExplanations: Incorrect. C2 and C3 provide proprioception for the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Incorrect. These are primarily brachial plexus roots for the upper limb muscles.
Incorrect. C1 has no cutaneous branch and usually contributes to motor fibers via the ansa cervicalis.
Correct. According to the cervical plexus distribution, C3 and C4 provide the sensory (proprioceptive) component for the trapezius, while CN XI is motor.
Incorrect. C5 is primarily involved in the phrenic nerve and the brachial plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient suffers a penetrating wound to the neck, resulting in complete transection of one phrenic nerve. What is the most significant clinical finding expected in this lesion?
options: Paradoxical movement of the vocal folds during inspiration
Loss of sensation over the angle of the jaw
Relaxation of the ipsilateral diaphragm and its elevation by abdominal pressure
Paralysis of the strap muscles with hyoid instability
Wasting of the trapezius and drooping of the shoulder
correctOption: Relaxation of the ipsilateral diaphragm and its elevation by abdominal pressure
optionExplanations: Vocal fold movements are controlled by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (CN X), whereas the phrenic nerve controls the diaphragm.
The skin over the angle of the jaw is supplied by the great auricular nerve, a cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus, not the phrenic nerve.
The phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. Transection leads to paralysis; the affected side is then pushed upward into the thorax by intra-abdominal pressure during respiration.
The strap muscles (infrahyoid) are supplied by the ansa cervicalis, not the phrenic nerve.
Trapezius wasting occurs with lesions to the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) or its proprioceptive cervical rami (C3, 4), not the phrenic nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient presents with numbness specifically localized to the skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland. Which branch of the cervical plexus has likely been affected?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
Zygomaticofacial nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve supplies the scalp behind the ear, not the facial skin over the mandible or the parotid region.

The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) is the specific branch of the cervical plexus that supplies the skin over the angle of the jaw and the parotid gland; this is a classic 'exception' area often tested.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin of the lower neck and upper chest near the sternum, far inferior to the mandible.
The zygomaticofacial nerve is a branch of the Maxillary division of the Trigeminal nerve (CN V2), not a branch of the cervical plexus.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior neck skin below the mandible, but not the skin directly over the angle of the mandible or the parotid gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1613 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) ascends across the sternocleidomastoid muscle and divides into branches that supply the skin over the angle of the mandible, on the parotid gland, and on both surfaces of the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: While assessing the motor and sensory functions of the neck, a neurologist notes that certain branches of the cervical plexus provide proprioception to specific muscles. Which cervical nerve segments provide this modality to the Sternocleidomastoid?
options: C1 only
C2 and C3
C3 and C4
C1 and C2
C4 and C5
correctOption: C2 and C3
optionExplanations: C1 does not have a cutaneous or proprioceptive branch in the cervical plexus; its fibers are exclusively motor (efferent).

Branches from the anterior rami of C2 and C3 carry proprioceptive (sensory) information from the sternocleidomastoid muscle to the CNS. This is distinct from the motor supply, which is provided by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
C3 and C4 provide proprioceptive fibers to the trapezius muscle, not the sternocleidomastoid. Correctly distinguishing these segmental levels is vital for clinical neuro-localization.
C1 fibers primarily provide motor innervation to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid via the hypoglossal nerve and do not contribute to the proprioception of the sternocleidomastoid.
C5 is primarily involved with the phrenic nerve and the upper trunk of the brachial plexus; it does not provide proprioceptive fibers for the muscles of the cervical plexus's standard distribution.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient suffers a deep penetrating injury to the posterior triangle of the neck. Radiographic evaluation shows a paralyzed right hemidiaphragm that is pushed superiorly into the thorax. Which anatomical fact explains this specific upward displacement of the paralyzed muscle?
options: Negative intrathoracic pressure pulling the muscle up
Elastic recoil of the pulmonary visceral pleura
Positive abdominal pressure pushing the relaxed muscle up
Active contraction of the intercostal muscles
Compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral hemidiaphragm
correctOption: Positive abdominal pressure pushing the relaxed muscle up
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Although intrathoracic pressure is negative, the primary driving force for the massive upward shift in paralysis is the higher pressure in the abdominal cavity.
Incorrect. Elastic recoil affects lung collapse but is not the primary mechanism for diaphragmatic displacement in a phrenic lesion.
Correct. When the phrenic nerve is severed, the muscle loses its tone. The positive pressure within the abdominal cavity then forces the flaccid hemidiaphragm upward into the thoracic cavity.
Incorrect. While intercostals assist in breathing, they do not directly push the diaphragm into the thorax.
Incorrect. Contralateral hypertrophy does not explain the mechanical displacement of the injured side's muscle fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Referred Pain and Cervical Plexus Convergence
statement: A 55-year-old female with a known history of cholelithiasis presents with sharp pain in her right shoulder. Based on the neuroanatomy of the cervical plexus, which nerves facilitate the final cutaneous perception of this referred pain?
options: Supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4)
Phrenic nerves (C3, 4, and 5)
Intercostobrachial nerves (T2)
Greater occipital nerves (C2)
Transverse cervical nerves (C2 and 3)
correctOption: Supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4)
optionExplanations: Correct. Irritation of the diaphragm (innervated by the phrenic nerve, C3-C5) sends signals to the spinal cord segments C3 and C4. These same segments provide cutaneous innervation to the shoulder via the supraclavicular nerves, leading the brain to perceive the pain in the shoulder.

Incorrect. The phrenic nerve is the afferent pathway carrying the irritation from the gallbladder/diaphragm to the cord, but it is not the nerve that provides the cutaneous perception 'on' the shoulder.
Incorrect. The intercostobrachial nerve provides sensation to the axilla and medial arm; it is involved in referred pain from cardiac ischemia (T1-T4), not gallbladder disease (C3-C5).
Incorrect. The greater occipital nerve supplies the back of the scalp; it is not involved in shoulder sensation or diaphragmatic referred pain.
Incorrect. The transverse cervical nerves supply the anterior neck; they do not typically receive referred pain from the diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves [supraclavicular] are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A surgeon is using the 'nerve point of the neck' (Erb's point) as a landmark for a cervical plexus block. Where is this point anatomically located?
options: Between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid just above the clavicle.
At the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the hyoid bone.
At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, at about its midpoint.
Deep to the carotid sheath at the level of the cricoid cartilage.
At the junction of the middle and lateral thirds of the clavicle.
correctOption: At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, at about its midpoint.
optionExplanations: The space between the sternal and clavicular heads is the lesser supraclavicular fossa, used for internal jugular vein catheterization, not for blocking cutaneous nerves.
The anterior border of the SCM is a landmark for the carotid pulse and the internal jugular vein, but the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge posteriorly.
The nerve point is the site where the four cutaneous branches (Lesser Occipital, Great Auricular, Transverse Cervical, and Supraclavicular) radiate from the posterior border of the SCM.
The cervical plexus is deep to the SCM and prevertebral fascia, but the 'nerve point' refers to the superficial emergence of its branches, not its deep origin.
This location is more relevant for the third part of the subclavian artery or the trunks of the brachial plexus, not the nerve point of the cervical plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle...

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: In approximately one-third of the population, an accessory phrenic nerve is present. From which cervical nerve is this accessory component typically derived before it joins the main phrenic nerve trunk?
options: C4
C3
C6
C5
C2
correctOption: C5
optionExplanations: C4 is the primary contributor to the main phrenic nerve and is not the origin of the accessory phrenic nerve that hitchhikes with the nerve to subclavius.
C3 is a major constituent of the main phrenic nerve but is not typically described as the source of a separate accessory phrenic branch.
C6 contributes to the brachial plexus and does not participate in the formation of the phrenic or accessory phrenic nerve.
The accessory phrenic nerve is usually a branch from C5, often travelling via the nerve to the subclavius before joining the phrenic nerve in the thorax.
The C2 nerve contributes to the superior part of the cervical plexus and cutaneous branches but does not form an accessory phrenic nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Functional Modalities of Cervical Plexus Muscular Branches
statement: A neurologist evaluates a patient with a suspected lesion of the cervical plexus. While the patient can move their head normally, they show a deficit in proprioceptive feedback from the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. Which specific branches are likely involved?
options: Proprioceptive branches from C2, C3, and C4.
The phrenic nerve (C3-C5).
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI).
The transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves.
Nerve to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid (C1).
correctOption: Proprioceptive branches from C2, C3, and C4.
optionExplanations: The cervical plexus provides specific proprioceptive fibers: C2 and C3 for the sternocleidomastoid, and C3 and C4 for the trapezius.
The phrenic nerve is the primary motor nerve for the diaphragm and carries sensation from serous membranes, but not proprioception for neck muscles.
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the motor supply to these muscles, but the sensory (proprioceptive) supply is derived from the cervical plexus.
The transverse cervical and supraclavicular nerves are purely cutaneous (sensory to skin) and do not provide proprioceptive fibers to muscles.
The nerves to the thyrohyoid and geniohyoid are motor nerves carrying C1 fibers via the hypoglossal nerve, not proprioceptive fibers for the SCM or trapezius.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Nerve branches supply the prevertebral muscles, sternocleidomastoid, levator scapulae, and trapezius. The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Regarding the cutaneous distribution of the cervical plexus, which of the following nerves provides sensation to the skin of the anterior and lateral neck from the body of the mandible down to the sternum?
options: Intermediate supraclavicular nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Great auricular nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
correctOption: Transverse cervical nerve
optionExplanations: The intermediate supraclavicular nerve crosses the middle of the clavicle to supply the chest wall skin, not the neck proper.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies skin over the medial end of the clavicle and the chest wall down to the second rib.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2, 3) emerges from the nerve point and crosses the sternocleidomastoid to supply the skin of the anterior and lateral parts of the neck.
The great auricular nerve supplies the angle of the jaw and parotid region, which is superior to the main distribution of the transverse cervical nerve.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) ascends to supply the scalp behind the auricle and the auricle itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The transverse cervical nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the front of the neck.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A surgeon is performing a deep neck dissection and identifies a nerve running vertically downward across the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle, deep to the prevertebral fascia. During the procedure, the nerve is accidentally transected. Despite the injury, the ipsilateral diaphragm maintains partial mobility. Which anatomical variation explains this findings?
options: Innervation from the ansa cervicalis
The presence of a recurrent laryngeal nerve loop
Bilateral crossover of phrenic fibers at the thoracic inlet
Collateral supply from the supraclavicular nerves
The presence of an accessory phrenic nerve from C5
correctOption: The presence of an accessory phrenic nerve from C5
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles and is not involved in diaphragmatic motor control.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the larynx and does not provide any innervation to the diaphragm.

The phrenic nerve is strictly unilateral; the text states 'Each phrenic nerve supplies the corresponding half of the diaphragm.' No bilateral crossover exists to restore function after unilateral injury.
Supraclavicular nerves are cutaneous branches and have no motor fibers for the diaphragm.

An accessory phrenic nerve (often derived from C5) may bypass the cervical part of the main phrenic nerve (C3, 4) by traveling with the nerve to the subclavius, potentially preserving partial diaphragmatic function if the main trunk is injured in the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve . The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the specific neural origin of the cervical plexus during a gross anatomy dissection. Which of the following best describes the formation of this plexus?
options: Communication between the roots of the hypoglossal and vagus nerves
Anterior rami of the C5 to T1 spinal nerves
Posterior rami of the upper four cervical nerves
Sympathetic trunk ganglia from C1 to C4
Anterior rami of the upper four cervical nerves
correctOption: Anterior rami of the upper four cervical nerves
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While C1 fibers hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve, the plexus itself is formed by spinal rami, not cranial nerve communications.
Incorrect. This describes the roots of the brachial plexus, which supplies the upper limb.
Incorrect. The posterior rami of cervical nerves supply the skin of the back of the neck and the postvertebral muscles; they do not form the cervical plexus.
Incorrect. These are components of the autonomic nervous system, specifically the superior cervical ganglion, not the somatic cervical plexus.
Correct. The cervical plexus is a network formed specifically by the anterior (ventral) rami of the first through fourth cervical spinal nerves (C1-C4).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy: Nerve Point of the Neck
statement: Where is the clinical 'nerve point of the neck' located, where cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge to distribute to the skin?
options: At the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at its superior third.
Directly over the carotid tubercle of the C6 vertebra.
Deep to the pretracheal fascia in the midline.
Between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid at about its midpoint.
correctOption: At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid at about its midpoint.
optionExplanations: The anterior border of the SCM is associated with the carotid sheath and the anterior triangle; it is not the exit point for the superficial cervical plexus nerves.
The carotid tubercle (Chassaignac tubercle) is used for stellate ganglion blocks, but the nerve point of the neck is located higher and more posteriorly on the SCM muscle.
The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid and trachea; the cervical plexus is more lateral and posterior, located in the posterior triangle area.
The space between the sternal and clavicular heads of the SCM is the site for internal jugular vein catheterization (the lesser supraclavicular fossa), not the nerve point.
This is a critical landmark for administering cervical plexus blocks. The four cutaneous nerves (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular) radiate from this point.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The phrenic nerve is typically formed by the C3, C4, and C5 rami. In approximately one-third of the population, an accessory phrenic nerve exists. From which specific nerve does this accessory contribution usually arise before joining the main trunk in the thorax?
options: Nerve to the thyrohyoid
Descending cervical nerve
Ansa cervicalis inferior root
Nerve to the subclavius
Nerve to the geniohyoid
correctOption: Nerve to the subclavius
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The nerve to the thyrohyoid is composed of C1 fibers hitchhiking with the hypoglossal nerve.
Incorrect. The descending cervical nerve is simply another name for the inferior root (C2,3) of the ansa cervicalis.
Incorrect. The inferior root of the ansa cervicalis is formed by C2 and C3.
Correct. The C5 contribution to the phrenic nerve is often aberrant and travels with the nerve to the subclavius (from the brachial plexus) before eventually joining the phrenic trunk.
Incorrect. The nerve to the geniohyoid is composed of C1 fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve. The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Topographical Relations of the Cervical Plexus
statement: Regarding the topographical relationships of the cervical plexus, which fascial layer and vascular structure are most immediately related to its anterior surface?
options: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia and the internal jugular vein.
Investing layer of deep cervical fascia and the external jugular vein.
Cribriform plate and the ophthalmic vein.
Buccopharyngeal fascia and the retromandibular vein.
Pretracheal fascia and the common carotid artery.
correctOption: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia and the internal jugular vein.
optionExplanations: The cervical plexus is sandwiched between the prevertebral muscles posteriorly and the prevertebral fascia anteriorly. The internal jugular vein (within the carotid sheath) sits just anterior to this fascia.
The investing layer is the most superficial deep fascia; the cervical plexus is much deeper, located in the prevertebral region.
The cribriform plate is in the skull (ethmoid bone), and the ophthalmic vein is in the orbit. These are far removed from the neck's cervical plexus.
The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the pharynx; the retromandibular vein is within the parotid gland. Neither is an immediate relation to the cervical plexus.
The pretracheal fascia is in the anterior neck; the cervical plexus is located on the surface of the prevertebral muscles (levator scapulae and scalenus medius).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A surgeon is performing a radical neck dissection and must identify the nerves supplying the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle. Which branch of the cervical plexus must be preserved to maintain sensation in this specific region?
options: Intermediate supraclavicular nerve.
Medial supraclavicular nerve.
Great auricular nerve.
Transverse cervical nerve.
Lateral supraclavicular nerve.
correctOption: Lateral supraclavicular nerve.
optionExplanations: The intermediate supraclavicular nerve primarily supplies the skin of the chest wall over the pectoralis major and the middle of the clavicle.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin near the median plane and the sternoclavicular joint area.
The great auricular nerve supplies the skin around the ear and the angle of the jaw, which is far superior to the deltoid muscle.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the skin of the anterior and lateral neck, not the shoulder or deltoid region.
The lateral (or posterior) supraclavicular nerve specifically targets the lateral aspect of the shoulder and the skin overlying the superior half of the deltoid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The lateral supraclavicular nerve crosses the lateral end of the clavicle and supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle; this nerve also supplies the posterior aspect of the shoulder.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Clinical Lesion of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: A 28-year-old female presents to the emergency department after a deep laceration to the root of the neck just above the right clavicle. Radiography reveals that the right dome of the diaphragm is significantly elevated compared to the left. If the phrenic nerve was severed, what other physiological finding would most likely be observed in this patient?
options: Paralysis of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles
Loss of taste sensation on the posterior third of the tongue
Complete loss of sensation over the lateral part of the occipital region
Deviation of the tongue toward the side of the lesion upon protrusion
Ipsilateral lung collapse of the lower lobe due to diaphragmatic relaxation
correctOption: Ipsilateral lung collapse of the lower lobe due to diaphragmatic relaxation
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are primarily supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), though they receive proprioceptive fibers from the cervical plexus (C2-C4).
Taste sensation on the posterior third of the tongue is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which is not part of the cervical plexus.
Loss of sensation in the lateral occipital region would indicate a lesion of the lesser occipital nerve, not the phrenic nerve.
Deviation of the tongue indicates a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII); although C1 fibers hitchhike with CN XII, the deviation itself is caused by intrinsic/extrinsic tongue muscle paralysis.
The phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. Severing it causes the ipsilateral hemi-diaphragm to relax and rise into the thorax, which can lead to collapse of the lower lung lobe.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure. Consequently, the lower lobe of the lung on that side may collapse.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Regarding the topographical anatomy of the cervical plexus, what is its primary relationship to the contents of the carotid sheath?
options: It is embedded within the vagus nerve trunk
It is located within the sheath, lateral to the common carotid artery
It is located posterior to the sheath and related to the internal jugular vein
It is located anterior to the sheath, crossing the internal jugular vein
It lies medial to the sheath, between the carotid and the pharynx
correctOption: It is located posterior to the sheath and related to the internal jugular vein
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve is a distinct cranial nerve (CN X) that descends within the carotid sheath and does not contain the cervical plexus.
The plexus is prevertebral, located behind the prevertebral fascia, not inside the carotid sheath alongside the artery.
The cervical plexus is situated behind the prevertebral fascia and is topographically related to the internal jugular vein, which lies within the carotid sheath immediately in front of it.
The ansa cervicalis is often anterior to the sheath, but the cervical plexus proper (loops) is posterior to it.
The medial relationship to the sheath is occupied by the pharynx and larynx, whereas the plexus is located in the prevertebral position laterally and posteriorly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia covers the plexus in front, and the plexus is related to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Cutaneous Distribution of the Transverse Cervical Nerve
statement: Which of the following nerves of the cervical plexus is responsible for providing cutaneous sensation to the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the body of the mandible down to the sternum?
options: Supraclavicular nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Transverse cervical nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
correctOption: Transverse cervical nerve
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The supraclavicular nerves (C3,4) supply the lower neck, shoulder, and chest wall down to the second rib.
Incorrect. The ansa cervicalis is a motor loop supplying the infrahyoid muscles, not a cutaneous nerve.
Correct. The transverse cervical (or transverse cutaneous) nerve (C2,3) supplies the majority of the anterior and lateral neck skin.
Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the lateral occipital region and medial auricle.
Incorrect. The great auricular nerve (C2,3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and the auricle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3) emerges from behind the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It passes forward across that muscle and divides into branches that supply the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, from the body of the mandible to the sternum.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: An anatomy professor highlights a clinical variation where an additional nerve root from C5 joins the phrenic nerve within the thoracic cavity rather than in the neck. What is the most likely origin of this 'accessory phrenic nerve'?
options: Suprascapular nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Long thoracic nerve
Nerve to the subclavius
Nerve to the medial pterygoid
correctOption: Nerve to the subclavius
optionExplanations: The suprascapular nerve (C5-C6) supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid muscles and is formed by C1-C3; it does not contribute to the phrenic nerve.
The long thoracic nerve (C5-C7) supplies the serratus anterior and does not typically join the phrenic nerve.
The accessory phrenic nerve most commonly arises from the nerve to the subclavius (a branch of the brachial plexus roots C5-C6) and joins the main phrenic nerve in the thorax.
The nerve to the medial pterygoid is a branch of the mandibular nerve (CN V3).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve. The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Functional Modalities of Cervical Plexus Muscular Branches
statement: While the Spinal Accessory nerve (CN XI) provides the primary motor supply to the Trapezius and Sternocleidomastoid, the cervical plexus contributes branches to these muscles. What is the functional modality of these specific cervical plexus branches?
options: Somatic motor fibers for the initiation of muscle contraction.
Special visceral afferent fibers for taste perception in the neck.
Sympathetic vasomotor fibers to the intramuscular arterioles.
Proprioceptive fibers to sense muscle position and tension.
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the overlying skin.
correctOption: Proprioceptive fibers to sense muscle position and tension.
optionExplanations: Somatic motor fibers to these muscles are primarily carried by the Spinal Accessory nerve (CN XI), although some minor motor contribution to the Trapezius is debated, the source identifies them as proprioceptive.
Special visceral afferents (SVA) are associated with taste and smell (CN I, VII, IX, X) and are never found in spinal nerves like the cervical plexus.
Sympathetic fibers reach the muscles via the cervical sympathetic trunk and plexuses around arteries, not via the primary muscular branches of the cervical plexus.
The cervical plexus (C2-C3 for SCM and C3-C4 for Trapezius) provides the proprioceptive (sensory) feedback necessary for coordinating head and neck movements.
Parasympathetic fibers are not carried by the cervical plexus; they are restricted to certain cranial nerves and sacral spinal nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which branch of the supraclavicular nerves is specifically responsible for supplying the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle?
options: Medial supraclavicular nerve
Posterior supraclavicular nerve
Intermediate supraclavicular nerve
Lateral supraclavicular nerve
Anterior supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Lateral supraclavicular nerve
optionExplanations: The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin as far as the median plane near the medial end of the clavicle.
There is no nerve formally named 'posterior supraclavicular nerve' in the cervical plexus; the three branches are medial, intermediate, and lateral.
The intermediate supraclavicular nerve crosses the middle of the clavicle to supply the skin of the chest wall.
The lateral supraclavicular nerve is the specific branch that innervates the skin over the shoulder and the proximal part of the deltoid muscle.
There is no nerve formally named 'anterior supraclavicular nerve' in the cervical plexus classification.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The lateral supraclavicular nerve crosses the lateral end of the clavicle and supplies the skin over the shoulder and the upper half of the deltoid muscle

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A 32-year-old male sustains a deep penetrating knife wound to the lower neck. Radiographs subsequently show his right diaphragm is elevated and moves superiorly during inspiration (paradoxical movement). Which branch of the cervical plexus was most likely severed?
options: Accessory nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Descending branch of C1
Phrenic nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Phrenic nerve
optionExplanations: The accessory nerve (CN XI) is a cranial nerve that supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius; injury would cause shoulder drop and head rotation weakness.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the strap (infrahyoid) muscles; its injury would affect hyoid/laryngeal movements but not the diaphragm.
The descending branch of C1 (superior root of ansa) supplies only infrahyoid muscles and the geniohyoid/thyrohyoid; it does not contribute to diaphragmatic motor function.

The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is the only motor supply to the diaphragm. Severing it results in paralysis where the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax (elevation) and moves paradoxically during inspiration due to changes in intrathoracic/abdominal pressure.
The supraclavicular nerve is purely sensory to the skin over the shoulder and upper chest; injury would only result in localized anesthesia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve is of considerable clinical importance because it is the sole nerve supply to the muscle of the diaphragm... the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: When distinguishing between the cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus, which nerve is correctly matched with its specific cutaneous distribution?
options: Lesser occipital nerve: Skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland
Greater occipital nerve: Lateral part of the occipital region and medial auricle
Transverse cervical nerve: Back of the scalp and the auricle
Great auricular nerve: Skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from mandible to sternum
Supraclavicular nerves: Skin over the shoulder and upper half of the deltoid
correctOption: Supraclavicular nerves: Skin over the shoulder and upper half of the deltoid
optionExplanations: The skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland is supplied by the great auricular nerve, not the lesser occipital nerve.

The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2 and is not part of the cervical plexus; the lateral occipital/medial auricle is supplied by the lesser occipital nerve (cervical plexus).
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the neck skin; the back of the scalp and auricle are supplied by the lesser occipital nerve.
The great auricular nerve supplies the angle of the mandible and the auricle; the anterior and lateral neck is supplied by the transverse cervical nerve.
The supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4) divide into three branches (medial, intermediate, lateral) to supply the chest wall and the shoulder skin down to the deltoid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) have medial, intermediate, and lateral branches that supply the skin over the shoulder region.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The loops of the cervical plexus, formed by the union of the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves, are anatomically situated immediately anterior to which of the following muscles?
options: Sternocleidomastoid and Trapezius
Digastric and Mylohyoid
Levator scapulae and Scalenus medius
Longus capitis and Platysma
Scalenus anterior and Omohyoid
correctOption: Levator scapulae and Scalenus medius
optionExplanations: The sternocleidomastoid covers the plexus superficially; the trapezius is posterior and lateral to the plexus area.
The digastric and mylohyoid are suprahyoid muscles located in the submandibular and submental regions, far from the plexus loops on the posterior triangle floor.
The cervical plexus is formed as a series of loops that rest upon the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles, deep to the prevertebral fascia.
The longus capitis is a prevertebral muscle more medially located, and the platysma is a superficial muscle of facial expression located in the superficial fascia.
The phrenic nerve runs in front of the scalenus anterior, but the main loops of the plexus are situated on the scalenus medius and levator scapulae.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A 28-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a stabbing incident involving a deep laceration at the root of the neck. Radiographic imaging shows the left hemidiaphragm is significantly elevated. Which physiological mechanism explains this finding following a lesion to a cervical plexus branch?
options: Adhesion of the diaphragmatic pleura to the lung apex.
Negative intra-abdominal pressure pulling the diaphragm into the thoracic cavity.
Paralyzed muscle relaxation and upward displacement by positive abdominal pressure.
Active contraction of the diaphragm during expiration due to nerve irritation.
Compensatory hypertrophy of the contralateral hemidiaphragm pushing the mediastinum.
correctOption: Paralyzed muscle relaxation and upward displacement by positive abdominal pressure.
optionExplanations: Elevation in this context is a result of nerve-induced paralysis and mechanical pressure differentials, not pleural adhesions.
Intra-abdominal pressure is typically positive relative to the intrathoracic pressure. It is this positive pressure that forces the paralyzed diaphragm upward.
The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. When it is severed, the muscle loses tone and the higher pressure in the abdomen pushes the relaxed dome into the thoracic cavity.
Nerve irritation usually causes spasms, but a complete lesion results in flaccid paralysis. Elevation is a passive process, not an active contraction.
