While the other side may attempt to compensate, it does not push the paralyzed side; the elevation of the paralyzed side is due to the loss of its own structural integrity and motor resistance.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure. Consequently, the lower lobe of the lung on that side may collapse.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Surgical Complication of Cervical Nerve Damage
statement: A 38-year-old female undergoes a superficial biopsy of an enlarged lymph node at the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Post-operatively, she complains of numbness on the lateral aspect of her auricle and the skin overlying the parotid gland. Which nerve was most likely damaged during the procedure?
options: Great auricular nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Facial nerve (Cervical branch)
Auriculotemporal nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) is the largest cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus. Its proximity to the midpoint of the SCM's posterior border makes it vulnerable during biopsies, leading to numbness of the ear and parotid region.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the skin of the lower neck and shoulder; they do not ascend to the level of the auricle or parotid gland.
The cervical branch of the facial nerve is a motor nerve supplying the platysma muscle; damage would cause motor dysfunction rather than sensory loss over the parotid/auricle.

The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular nerve (V3) and supplies the skin in front of the ear; it does not originate from the cervical plexus and is not located at the posterior border of the SCM.
The lesser occipital nerve supplies the back of the scalp and the medial surface of the auricle, but not the lateral skin over the parotid gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible... and the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which specific spinal nerve rami are responsible for the anatomical formation of the cervical plexus?
options: Posterior rami of C1 to C5
Posterior rami of C1 to C4
Anterior rami of C1 to C5
Anterior rami of C1 to C4
Anterior and posterior rami of C2 to C4
correctOption: Anterior rami of C1 to C4
optionExplanations: The posterior rami of C1 to C5 do not form plexuses for the head and neck; they remain segmental to supply the deep back muscles and overlying skin.
Posterior rami of cervical nerves supply the skin of the back of the neck and scalp but do not form the cervical plexus, which is a network derived from anterior rami.
The C5 nerve primarily contributes to the brachial plexus, although it does provide a small contribution to the phrenic nerve; however, it is not part of the core cervical plexus formation.
The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical spinal nerves (C1-C4), which join by connecting branches to form loops in front of the prevertebral muscles.
The cervical plexus is exclusively formed by anterior rami, and it must include the C1 nerve, which provides motor fibers to the ansa cervicalis and geniohyoid/thyrohyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Following a deep penetrating wound to the mid-neck, a patient develops unilateral diaphragmatic paralysis. What is the physiological mechanism leading to the characteristic radiographic finding in this condition?
options: Atmospheric air entering the pleural space pushes the diaphragm into the abdominal cavity.
Active contraction of the intercostal muscles forces the paralyzed diaphragm inferiorly.
The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pulled down by negative intrathoracic pressure.
The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax by positive abdominal pressure.
The phrenic nerve triggers a counter-reflex that tenses the contralateral hemidiaphragm.
correctOption: The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax by positive abdominal pressure.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes a tension pneumothorax, where air pressure pushes the mediastinum and diaphragm away from the site of injury, which is not the standard mechanism for simple phrenic nerve palsy.
Incorrect. The intercostal muscles are used for rib cage expansion; they do not act directly to force the diaphragm inferiorly.
Incorrect. Negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration would normally pull a healthy diaphragm up if it were flaccid, but the primary force is the positive pressure from the abdomen.

Correct. When the phrenic nerve is severed, the muscle of the hemidiaphragm loses its tone and relaxes; the relatively higher pressure in the abdominal cavity then displaces the flaccid muscle upward into the chest.
Incorrect. There is no counter-regulatory reflex that tenses the opposite side; the contralateral side continues to function normally under its own phrenic nerve control.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Dermatomal Distribution of Cervical Cutaneous Nerves
statement: A patient presents with altered sensation over the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, extending from the body of the mandible down to the sternum. Which specific cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus is most likely involved?
options: Great auricular nerve (C2 and 3).
Lesser occipital nerve (C2).
Supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4).
Greater occipital nerve (C2).
Transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3).
correctOption: Transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3).
optionExplanations: The great auricular nerve supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland area, and the auricle, but not the lower anterior neck down to the sternum.
The lesser occipital nerve supplies the lateral part of the occipital region (back of the scalp) and the medial surface of the auricle, not the front of the neck.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the lower neck, shoulder, and upper chest wall down to the level of the second rib, but they do not supply the upper neck near the mandible.
The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2 and supplies the back of the scalp up to the vertex; it is not a branch of the cervical plexus (which is anterior rami).
The transverse cutaneous nerve (C2-3) specifically provides sensory innervation to the skin of the anterior and lateral neck, bridging the gap between the mandible and the manubrium.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3) emerges from behind the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It passes forward across that muscle and divides into branches that supply the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, from the body of the mandible to the sternum.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: In the muscular distribution of the cervical plexus, which of the following nerve branches are specifically identified as providing proprioceptive rather than primary motor function?
options: Branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4)
Nerve to the geniohyoid (C1)
Branches to the levator scapulae (C3, 4)
Ansa cervicalis to the omohyoid
Phrenic nerve to the diaphragm (C3, 4, 5)
correctOption: Branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4)
optionExplanations: While the motor supply to the SCM and trapezius comes from the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), the cervical plexus (C2, 3 for SCM and C3, 4 for trapezius) provides the necessary proprioceptive sensory fibers.
The nerve to the geniohyoid consists of C1 motor fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve to provide motor supply to that muscle.
Branches to the levator scapulae provide motor innervation for muscle contraction, not just proprioception.
The ansa cervicalis provides the primary motor innervation to the infrahyoid muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid).
The phrenic nerve is the primary motor supply to the diaphragm and also carries significant somatic sensory fibers, but it is not classified as a primarily 'proprioceptive' branch in this context.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Cutaneous Distribution of the Transverse Cervical Nerve
statement: A patient presents with a deep laceration across the anterior surface of the neck, just above the sternum. Which branch of the cervical plexus is most likely damaged if the patient has lost sensation in the skin between the mandible and the sternum?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Great auricular nerve
Lateral supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Transverse cervical nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve supplies the back of the scalp and the auricle, not the anterior neck.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin over the medial clavicle and chest as far as the median plane, but not the anterior neck skin up to the mandible.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2,3) crosses the SCM to supply the skin of the anterior triangle and the lateral neck from the mandible to the sternum.
The great auricular nerve supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and the parotid gland, but not the lower anterior neck down to the sternum.
The lateral supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin over the shoulder and deltoid, well lateral to the anterior neck midline.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The transverse cervical nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the front of the neck.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The cervical plexus is formed by a network of loops. Which specific rami of the spinal nerves constitute the formation of this plexus?
options: Anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8, and T1
Anterior rami of C3, C4, C5, and C6
Posterior rami of C1, C2, C3, and C4
Posterior rami of C2, C3, C4, and C5
Anterior rami of C1, C2, C3, and C4
correctOption: Anterior rami of C1, C2, C3, and C4
optionExplanations: The anterior rami of C5 to T1 form the brachial plexus, which is responsible for the innervation of the upper limb.
This range overlaps with the brachial plexus (C5, C6) and excludes the higher roots (C1, C2) essential for the cervical plexus.
The posterior rami of the cervical nerves supply the deep muscles of the back and the skin of the back of the neck/scalp; they do not form the cervical plexus.
The posterior rami of these nerves contribute to the greater occipital nerve and others, but are not the constituent rami of the cervical plexus loops.
The cervical plexus is exclusively formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical spinal nerves (C1-C4).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Clinical Presentation of Phrenic Nerve Lesions
statement: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with a deep penetrating stab wound to the lower neck, just lateral to the sternocleidomastoid and anterior to the scalenus anterior muscle. Physical examination reveals shortness of breath, and an X-ray shows an abnormally elevated right hemidiaphragm. Damage to which nerve from the cervical plexus is the most likely cause?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Phrenic nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Supraclavicular nerve
Brachial plexus roots
correctOption: Phrenic nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve is a purely cutaneous branch supplying the scalp and would not cause respiratory symptoms or diaphragmatic elevation.
The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is the sole motor supply to the diaphragm. Its injury causes paralysis and subsequent elevation of the hemidiaphragm due to positive abdominal pressure.
The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid), which are not involved in diaphragmatic movement.
Supraclavicular nerves supply the skin over the shoulder and chest wall; their injury would result in localized anesthesia, not motor paralysis of the diaphragm.

The brachial plexus roots are located between the scalenus anterior and medius; while they could be injured, the specific presentation of an elevated diaphragm points to the phrenic nerve, which lies anterior to the scalenus anterior.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve arises in the neck from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus. It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle... each phrenic nerve supplies the corresponding half of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Structural Formation of the Cervical Plexus
statement: Which of the following describes the fundamental structural formation of the cervical plexus?
options: Anastomosis between the cranial nerve XII and the C1-C3 spinal nerves.
Union of the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves (C1-C4).
Union of the posterior rami of the first four cervical nerves (C1-C4).
Anastomosis between the anterior rami of C1 to C5 nerves.
Formation of a plexus by the anterior rami of C5 to T1 nerves.
correctOption: Union of the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves (C1-C4).
optionExplanations: While C1 fibers do hitchhike with the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), the formation of the plexus itself is independent of the cranial nerves, resulting from the interweaving of spinal nerve anterior rami.

The cervical plexus is formed specifically by the anterior rami of the C1, C2, C3, and C4 spinal nerves. These rami interconnect to form three loops that lie deep to the internal jugular vein and the sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Posterior rami of the cervical nerves supply the skin and muscles of the back of the neck and scalp; they do not participate in the formation of the cervical plexus, which is an anterior rami structure.
The cervical plexus only involves the first four cervical nerves. C5 is primarily involved in the formation of the phrenic nerve and the brachial plexus.
The anterior rami of C5 through T1 form the brachial plexus, which is responsible for the innervation of the upper limb, not the cervical plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus. The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops...

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Accessory Phrenic Nerve
statement: During a radical neck dissection, a surgeon identifies an 'accessory phrenic nerve' in the patient. According to the standard anatomical variation described for the cervical plexus, what is the most likely origin and pathway for this nerve?
options: It arises from C2 and C3 and descends along the internal jugular vein.
It arises from C4 and passes through the interscalene triangle to the apex of the lung.
It arises from the C5 root, travels with the nerve to the subclavius, and joins the phrenic nerve in the thorax.
It arises from C1 and joins the hypoglossal nerve in the carotid triangle.
It arises from the sympathetic trunk and provides autonomic fibers to the diaphragm.
correctOption: It arises from the C5 root, travels with the nerve to the subclavius, and joins the phrenic nerve in the thorax.
optionExplanations: C2 and C3 form the descending cervical nerve (inferior root of ansa), but not the accessory phrenic nerve.
The main phrenic nerve already receives a major contribution from C4; the 'accessory' refers to the extra C5 contribution taking a different path via the subclavius nerve.

An accessory phrenic nerve occurs in about one-third of individuals. It typically represents a contribution from the C5 root that is initially incorporated into the nerve to the subclavius before eventually joining the main phrenic nerve trunk within the thorax.
The C1 fibers that join the hypoglossal nerve are related to the ansa cervicalis and muscles like the thyrohyoid, not the accessory phrenic nerve.

The phrenic nerve (main or accessory) is a somatic nerve providing motor supply to the diaphragm; it is not a branch of the sympathetic trunk, although it may carry some sympathetic fibers for blood vessels.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: In the structural organization of the cervical plexus, the primary loops formed by the anterior rami of C1 to C4 are situated immediately anterior to which specific prevertebral structures?
options: Sympathetic trunk and carotid sheath
Levator scapulae and scalenus medius
Scalenus anterior and phrenic nerve
Thyroid gland and esophagus
Longus capitis and longus colli
correctOption: Levator scapulae and scalenus medius
optionExplanations: The sympathetic trunk and carotid sheath lie anterior to the prevertebral fascia; the cervical plexus lies deep to the prevertebral fascia and posterior to these vascular/autonomic structures.

The cervical plexus is formed as the anterior rami of C1-C4 emerge and loop directly in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles, covered by the prevertebral fascia.
The scalenus anterior is located anterior to the brachial plexus and medial to the cervical plexus; the phrenic nerve actually descends on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior.
The thyroid gland and esophagus are midline visceral structures and are separated from the cervical plexus by the prevertebral fascia and the carotid sheath.
The longus capitis and longus colli are prevertebral muscles located more medially and anteriorly than the levator scapulae/scalenus medius complex where the plexus loops form.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: During the administration of a cervical plexus block, the clinician identifies a common point of emergence for the four cutaneous branches. This area, known as the 'nerve point of the neck', is located at which precise landmark?
options: The junction of the upper third and lower two-thirds of the trapezius.
The anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid at the level of the hyoid bone.
Directly superior to the midpoint of the clavicle in the omoclavicular triangle.
The apex of the posterior triangle where the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius meet.
The midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
correctOption: The midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
optionExplanations: The trapezius forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle, but the cutaneous nerves emerge from the SCM (the anterior boundary).
The cutaneous branches emerge from the *posterior* border of the SCM to enter the posterior triangle; the anterior border is related to the carotid sheath.
The supraclavicular nerves do descend toward the clavicle, but they emerge higher up at the midpoint of the SCM, not just above the clavicle.
The apex of the posterior triangle is where the occipital artery and the greater occipital nerve are found, but the nerve point for the plexus branches is midway down the SCM.

The 'nerve point' or Erb's point is where the lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular nerves emerge from behind the SCM. It is found at the midpoint of the SCM's posterior border.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck ) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there (see Fig. 12.48).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Cutaneous Distribution of the Cervical Plexus
statement: A patient sustains a laceration at the angle of the mandible. On examination, they have lost sensation in the skin overlying the parotid gland and the lower half of the auricle. Which specific branch of the cervical plexus has most likely been damaged?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Auriculotemporal nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Great auricular nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve supplies the scalp behind the ear and the upper part of the medial surface of the auricle, not the angle of the jaw.
The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3), not the cervical plexus, and supplies the upper auricle and temple.
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the anterior and lateral skin of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the skin of the lower neck and shoulder region down to the level of the second rib.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) provides sensory innervation to the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and both surfaces of the lower auricle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Regarding the anatomical relations of the phrenic nerve as it descends from the cervical plexus, which structure is it specifically bound to by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia?
options: The posterior surface of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
The internal jugular vein
The carotid artery
The anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle
The trunks of the brachial plexus
correctOption: The anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The nerve is deep to the SCM and the carotid sheath; it is not bound to the SCM's posterior surface.
Incorrect. The internal jugular vein is located anterior to the phrenic nerve but is contained within the carotid sheath, not the prevertebral fascia on the scalenus anterior.
Incorrect. The carotid artery is medially located within the carotid sheath and does not share the same immediate fascial binding as the phrenic nerve.

Correct. The phrenic nerve is a critical landmark that descends vertically across the scalenus anterior, held in place by the prevertebral fascia, separating it from the more superficial structures of the carotid sheath.
Incorrect. The roots of the brachial plexus emerge between the scalenus anterior and medius, whereas the phrenic nerve specifically lies on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia bind the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the muscle [scalenus anterior].

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: During a superficial cervical plexus block for carotid endarterectomy, the anesthetic solution spreads deeper than intended. Which side effect is most likely to occur due to involvement of a major muscular branch of the plexus?
options: Loss of sensation in the pharynx
Paralysis of the vocal cords
Drooping of the upper eyelid
Deviation of the tongue to the affected side
Hemi-diaphragmatic paralysis
correctOption: Hemi-diaphragmatic paralysis
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Pharyngeal sensation is primarily provided by the glossopharyngeal (CN IX) and vagus (CN X) nerves.
Incorrect. Vocal cord paralysis is caused by damage to the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which is a branch of the vagus nerve, not the cervical plexus.
Incorrect. Ptosis is part of Horner syndrome, caused by interruption of the sympathetic trunk, or oculomotor nerve palsy.
Incorrect. Tongue deviation is caused by a lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which is distinct from the cervical plexus, though C1 fibers briefly travel with it.

Correct. The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is a major muscular branch of the cervical plexus; if the anesthetic spreads to the scalenus anterior surface, it can cause transient ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve arises in the neck from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus. It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Segmental Origin of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: In the structural organization of the cervical plexus, the phrenic nerve is identified as the solitary motor supply to the diaphragm. From which specific combination of anterior rami does this nerve typically derive its fibers?
options: C2, C3, and C4
C4, C5, and C6
C3, C4, and C5
C1, C2, and C3
C5, C6, and C7
correctOption: C3, C4, and C5
optionExplanations: While C3 and C4 contribute, the phrenic nerve requires the C5 root (the 'keep the diaphragm alive' mnemonic refers to C3-4-5).
Segments C5 and C6 are primarily involved in the brachial plexus (upper trunk), although C5 contributes to the phrenic.
The phrenic nerve classically arises from the anterior rami of C3, C4, and C5, with C4 being the major contributor in most individuals.
The segments C1-C3 contribute to the ansa cervicalis and muscles like the thyrohyoid, but not to the phrenic nerve.
The C5-C7 rami form the long thoracic nerve and contribute to the brachial plexus, but are not the primary origin of the phrenic nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve arises in the neck from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Cutaneous Distribution of the Cervical Plexus
statement: A neurologist is distinguishing between sensory deficits on the neck. If a patient has lost sensation specifically over the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle, which branch of the cervical plexus is most likely lesioned?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Great auricular nerve
Greater occipital nerve
correctOption: Lesser occipital nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve (C2) specifically targets the lateral occipital area and the medial (cranial) surface of the ear.
Supraclavicular nerves (C3, 4) supply the lower neck, the skin over the shoulder, and the chest wall down to the second rib.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2, 3) provides sensation to the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible to the sternum.
The great auricular nerve (C2, 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the parotid gland, and both surfaces of the auricle, but not the lateral occipital region.
The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2, not the cervical plexus, and it supplies the back of the scalp as far as the vertex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1613 (Book Page): The lesser occipital nerve (C2) hooks around the accessory nerve and ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply the skin over the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Mechanism of Referred Pain via Phrenic Nerve
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with acute right upper quadrant pain that is referred to her right shoulder. Anatomically, this referred pain is mediated by the phrenic nerve and travels to the spinal cord segments that also contribute to which specific cutaneous nerves of the cervical plexus?
options: Transverse cervical nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Greater occipital nerve
Great auricular nerve
Supraclavicular nerves
correctOption: Supraclavicular nerves
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The transverse cervical nerve (C2,3) supplies the anterior neck skin.
Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve arises from C2 and supplies the back of the scalp/auricle.
Incorrect. The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2 and is not part of the cervical plexus cutaneous branches (anterior rami).
Incorrect. The great auricular nerve (C2,3) supplies the angle of the mandible, which is not the typical site for gallbladder-referred shoulder pain.

Correct. Gallbladder disease irritates the diaphragm (phrenic nerve, C3-5). The sensory input enters the C3-4 cord segments, where it is misinterpreted as coming from the supraclavicular nerves (C3-4) covering the shoulder.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) have medial, intermediate, and lateral branches that supply the skin over the shoulder region. These nerves are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Differential cutaneous distribution of the cervical plexus
statement: When performing a clinical sensory evaluation of the neck, a physician must contrast the distribution of the Great Auricular nerve with the Transverse Cervical nerve. Which statement accurately describes their diagnostic boundaries?
options: The Great Auricular originates from C1, while the Transverse Cervical originates from C4.
The Great Auricular supplies the back of the scalp, while the Transverse Cervical supplies the auricle.
The Great Auricular is purely motor, whereas the Transverse Cervical is purely sensory.
The Great Auricular supplies the shoulder, while the Transverse Cervical supplies the parotid region.
The Great Auricular supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, whereas the Transverse Cervical supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck.
correctOption: The Great Auricular supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, whereas the Transverse Cervical supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck.
optionExplanations: Both nerves typically arise from the anterior rami of C2 and C3. C1 has no cutaneous branch.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp, not the Great Auricular, which focuses on the parotid and mandibular angle region.
Both the Great Auricular and Transverse Cervical nerves are classified as cutaneous (sensory) branches of the cervical plexus; they are not motor nerves.
The supraclavicular nerves (C3,4) supply the shoulder, not the Great Auricular.

The Great Auricular nerve (C2,3) provides sensation to the skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland, whereas the Transverse Cervical (C2,3) supplies the anterior and lateral neck from the mandible to the sternum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible. The transverse cervical nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the front of the neck.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Phrenic Nerve Origin and Pathological Implications
statement: A 45-year-old male undergoes an ultrasound-guided nerve block for a procedure in the posterior triangle. Following the injection of local anesthetic deep to the prevertebral fascia, the patient develops ipsilateral diaphragmatic paralysis. Which anatomical relationship explains this specific complication regarding the cervical plexus formation?
options: The phrenic nerve enters the thorax by passing behind the subclavian artery.
The phrenic nerve supplies the central part of the diaphragm via the thoracic duct.
The phrenic nerve arises from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus.
The phrenic nerve descends across the posterior surface of the scalenus medius.
The phrenic nerve arises from the posterior rami of C3, C4, and C5.
correctOption: The phrenic nerve arises from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus.
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve passes in front of (not behind) the subclavian artery as it enters the thoracic inlet.
The phrenic nerve is a somatic nerve and has no functional or anatomical relationship to the thoracic duct's lymphatic drainage.
The phrenic nerve's roots (C3, C4, C5) are part of the cervical plexus (C1-C4 plus C5 contribution); a deep block in the neck can easily involve these roots, leading to diaphragmatic palsy.
The phrenic nerve runs vertically downward across the anterior surface (not posterior) of the scalenus anterior muscle.
The phrenic nerve arises from the anterior rami (not posterior rami) of C3, C4, and C5.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve arises in the neck from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus. It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle (see Fig. 12.54) and enters the thorax by passing in front of the subclavian artery.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Surgical Relations of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: The phrenic nerve (C3, 4, 5) is a vital muscular branch of the cervical plexus. During surgical exploration of the root of the neck, what specific anatomical relationship allows for its identification and stabilization against the scalenus anterior muscle?
options: It is situated within the carotid sheath alongside the internal jugular vein.
It emerges from the interscalene triangle between the scalenus anterior and medius.
It descends medially to the vertebral artery within the prevertebral space.
It is bound to the muscle's anterior surface by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
It passes posterior to the second part of the subclavian artery for protection.
correctOption: It is bound to the muscle's anterior surface by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve is not a content of the carotid sheath; the sheath contains the carotid arteries, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve.

The phrenic nerve runs on the surface of the scalenus anterior, whereas the roots of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass through the interscalene triangle (between anterior and medius).
The phrenic nerve is lateral to the vertebral artery; the sympathetic trunk is the structure found more medially in that prevertebral area.

In the root of the neck, the phrenic nerve is held firmly against the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle by the prevertebral fascia. This 'binding' is a critical surgical landmark for nerve identification.
The phrenic nerve actually passes anterior to the subclavian artery, specifically the first part on the left and after the brachiocephalic on the right, as it enters the thorax.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia bind the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the muscle (see Fig. 12.54).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Muscular Distribution of the Cervical Plexus
statement: While the cervical plexus is primarily known for cutaneous and motor distribution, it also supplies the 'prevertebral muscles'. Which of the following muscles receives innervation directly from branches of the cervical plexus?
options: Sternocleidomastoid
Mylohyoid
Buccinator
Longus capitis
Masseter
correctOption: Longus capitis
optionExplanations: The SCM's motor supply is the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI); the cervical plexus only provides proprioceptive fibers to it.
The mylohyoid is supplied by the nerve to mylohyoid, a branch of the inferior alveolar nerve (V3).
The buccinator is a muscle of facial expression supplied by the buccal branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).
The prevertebral muscles, including the longus capitis, longus colli, and rectus capitis anterior/lateralis, are supplied by direct muscular branches from the cervical plexus.
The masseter is a muscle of mastication supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Muscular Branches (Neck)... Nerve branches supply the prevertebral muscles, sternocleidomastoid, levator scapulae, and trapezius.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Differential Diagnosis of Cutaneous Nerve Lesions
statement: A patient presents with isolated sensory loss on the skin of the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, extending from the body of the mandible down to the sternum. Sensation over the shoulder and the angle of the mandible is intact. Which specific nerve of the cervical plexus is likely lesioned?
options: Lateral supraclavicular nerve
Great auricular nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Medial supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Transverse cervical nerve
optionExplanations: The lateral supraclavicular nerve supplies the shoulder skin; its preservation indicates this branch is unaffected.
The great auricular nerve supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland, which is intact in this patient.
The transverse cervical (cutaneous) nerve (C2-C3) specifically innervates the anterior and lateral neck from the mandible to the sternum. Its isolated loss matches the patient's symptoms.
The lesser occipital nerve supplies the lateral occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle, which is not the area of loss described.
The medial supraclavicular nerve supplies the skin of the lower neck and chest as far as the median plane, but the primary supply for the broad anterior/lateral neck is the transverse cervical nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3) emerges from behind the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It passes forward across that muscle and divides into branches that supply the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, from the body of the mandible to the sternum.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Beyond motor supply to the diaphragm, the phrenic nerve (C3-C5) provides essential sensory innervation to several structures. Which of the following is included in its sensory distribution?
options: Muscles of the soft palate
Skin over the parotid gland
Mucous membrane of the laryngopharynx
Skin of the medial surface of the auricle
Parietal pleura and pericardium
correctOption: Parietal pleura and pericardium
optionExplanations: The muscles of the soft palate are primarily supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X/XI), except for the tensor veli palatini (CN V3).
The skin over the parotid gland is supplied by the great auricular nerve.
The laryngopharynx is supplied by the internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve.
The skin of the medial surface of the auricle is supplied by the lesser occipital and great auricular nerves.
The phrenic nerve is not just motor; it carries sensory fibers from the central tendon of the diaphragm, the mediastinal pleura, the fibrous pericardium, and the parietal peritoneum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): It also carries sensory branches from the pericardium, the mediastinal parietal pleura, and the pleura and peritoneum covering the upper and lower surfaces of the central part of the diaphragm.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Cervical Plexus (Erb's Point)
statement: A clinical instructor demonstrates the 'nerve point of the neck' to a group of medical students. At which specific anatomical landmark do the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge to reach their respective areas of distribution?
options: The junction of the medial and lateral thirds of the clavicle.
The anterior border of the trapezius muscle at the level of the cricoid cartilage.
The posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at approximately its midpoint.
The superior border of the omohyoid muscle in the muscular triangle.
The apex of the posterior triangle near the mastoid process.
correctOption: The posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at approximately its midpoint.
optionExplanations: The junction of the clavicle thirds is where supraclavicular nerves descend toward the chest, but it is not the common emergence point for all four cutaneous branches.
The anterior border of the trapezius forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle, but the cutaneous nerves of the cervical plexus do not emerge from this margin.

The 'nerve point' or Erb's point is located at the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, where the lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular nerves diverge.
The superior border of the omohyoid muscle is a landmark for dividing the anterior triangle, not the exit point for the cutaneous cervical plexus branches.
The apex of the posterior triangle is where the SCM and trapezius meet at the superior nuchal line, far superior to the nerve point of the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there (see Fig. 12.48).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: During a surgical exploration of the root of the neck, the phrenic nerve is identified. Which fascial layer is responsible for binding this nerve to the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle?
options: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
Investing layer of deep cervical fascia
Buccopharyngeal fascia
Carotid sheath
Pretracheal layer of deep cervical fascia
correctOption: Prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia
optionExplanations: The prevertebral fascia covers the prevertebral muscles and the scalenes; it specifically tethers the phrenic nerve to the scalenus anterior as it descends toward the thorax.
The investing layer splits to enclose the SCM and trapezius but does not reach deep enough to bind the phrenic nerve to the scalenus anterior.
The buccopharyngeal fascia covers the pharynx and is unrelated to the scalenus anterior muscle surface.
The carotid sheath contains the carotid arteries, IJV, and vagus nerve; while it is anterior to the phrenic nerve, it does not bind it to the muscle.
The pretracheal layer surrounds the thyroid, parathyroid, and infrahyoid muscles; it is anterior to the scalene muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1625 (Book Page): The transverse cervical and suprascapular arteries and the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia bind the phrenic nerve to the anterior surface of the muscle (scalenus anterior).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Pain Referral via the Cervical Plexus
statement: A patient with gallbladder disease describes a sharp pain felt over the tip of the right shoulder. Which branch of the cervical plexus is the primary mediator of this referred pain due to its shared segmental origin with the phrenic nerve?
options: Phrenic nerve (motor fibers)
Transverse cervical nerve
Great auricular nerve
Supraclavicular nerves
Lesser occipital nerve
correctOption: Supraclavicular nerves
optionExplanations: While the phrenic nerve carries the original sensory impulse from the diaphragm, the 'felt' pain is referred to the cutaneous territory of the supraclavicular nerves, not the phrenic nerve's motor distribution.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2, C3) supplies the skin over the front of the neck and would not be the site for referred pain from the shoulder (C3-C4 area).
The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and parotid gland, which is superior to the shoulder region.

The supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4) supply the skin over the shoulder. Because the phrenic nerve (sensory to the diaphragm) also carries C3-C4 fibers, the CNS misinterprets diaphragmatic irritation as coming from the shoulder dermatome.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and auricle; it does not share the C3-C4 segmental levels required for shoulder pain referral from the diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves (supraclavicular) are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Topographical Anatomy of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: A 24-year-old male sustains a deep penetrating wound to the mid-neck. Physical examination reveals that his diaphragm is elevated on the side of the injury and his lung on that side is partially collapsed. If the injury occurred specifically where the phrenic nerve crosses a landmark muscle, which muscle is most likely involved?
options: Omohyoid
Scalenus anterior
Sternocleidomastoid
Scalenus medius
Levator scapulae
correctOption: Scalenus anterior
optionExplanations: The omohyoid is a strap muscle that crosses the posterior triangle and covers the lower portion of the phrenic nerve, but it is not the primary muscular landmark the nerve descends upon.
The phrenic nerve is a critical branch of the cervical plexus (C3, 4, 5) that descends vertically on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle before entering the thorax.
While the phrenic nerve is deep to the SCM, the specific muscle it 'runs vertically downward across the front of' as a defining landmark is the scalenus anterior.
The cervical plexus loops lie in front of the scalenus medius, but the phrenic nerve specifically descends on the surface of the scalenus anterior.
The cervical plexus loops are related to the levator scapulae, but the phrenic nerve's iconic descending path is on the scalenus anterior.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): [The phrenic nerve] runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle (see Fig. 12.54) and enters the thorax by passing in front of the subclavian artery.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of Cervical Plexus Loops
statement: The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves. These rami join by connecting branches to form loops that lie in front of which anatomical structures?
options: Longus capitis and Longus colli
Thyroid gland and Trachea
Levator scapulae and Scalenus medius
Scalenus anterior and Omohyoid
Sternocleidomastoid and Trapezius
correctOption: Levator scapulae and Scalenus medius
optionExplanations: The longus capitis and longus colli are prevertebral muscles located medial to the plexus, not directly behind its formation loops.
The thyroid gland and trachea are visceral structures in the anterior midline of the neck, completely separated from the prevertebral location of the plexus.
The loops of the cervical plexus are situated deep in the neck, specifically lying anterior to the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius.
The scalenus anterior is medial to the plexus, and the omohyoid is a strap muscle situated more superficially and anteriorly.
The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are superficial to the plexus, which is located in the prevertebral region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles (see Fig. 12.54).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Segmental distribution of the Lesser Occipital nerve
statement: A patient presents with isolated numbness strictly over the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle. Following a traumatic neck injury. Based on the distribution of the cervical plexus, which specific nerve has been compromised?
options: Great auricular nerve.
Greater occipital nerve.
Lesser occipital nerve.
Transverse cervical nerve.
Supraclavicular nerve.
correctOption: Lesser occipital nerve.
optionExplanations: The Great Auricular nerve (C2,3) supplies the angle of the mandible, parotid area, and both surfaces of the lower auricle, but not the lateral occipital scalp.

The Greater Occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2. While it supplies the scalp, the question asks about the cervical plexus (which is formed by anterior rami) and specifically mentions the medial surface of the auricle (supplied by the Lesser Occipital).

The Lesser Occipital nerve (C2) is specifically responsible for the cutaneous supply of the lateral occipital region and the medial (cranial) surface of the auricle. It typically 'hooks' around the accessory nerve.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2,3) supplies the skin over the anterior and lateral neck, not the scalp.
The supraclavicular nerves (C3,4) supply the skin over the shoulder and upper chest, far below the occipital region.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1613 (Book Page): The lesser occipital nerve (C2) hooks around the accessory nerve and ascends along the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle to supply the skin over the lateral part of the occipital region and the medial surface of the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Topographical Relations of the Cervical Plexus
statement: The cervical plexus is formed by the anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves. Regarding its topographical relations, where do the loops of this plexus specifically lie before providing their motor and sensory branches?
options: Medial to the common carotid artery within the visceral space.
Within the substance of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Superficial to the investing layer of deep cervical fascia.
In front of the origins of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles.
Between the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle.
correctOption: In front of the origins of the levator scapulae and scalenus medius muscles.
optionExplanations: The plexus is lateral to the carotid sheath structures, although it is related to the internal jugular vein within the sheath's vicinity posteriorly.
While the SCM covers the plexus, the plexus itself lies on the prevertebral muscles (levator scapulae and scalenus medius), not within the SCM muscle fibers.
The plexus is deep to the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia, not superficial to the investing layer.
The anterior rami of C1-C4 form loops that are positioned anterior to the levator scapulae and scalenus medius, covered by the prevertebral fascia.
The digastric muscle is located in the submandibular and carotid triangles, superior to the primary formation and location of the cervical plexus loops.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The rami join by connecting branches, which form loops that lie in front of the origins of the levator scapulae and the scalenus medius muscles (see Fig. 12.54).

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Lesser Occipital Nerve
statement: A patient complains of a lack of sensation on the skin covering the medial surface of the auricle and the posterior part of the scalp on one side. Which nerve, originating from the C2 segment of the cervical plexus, is most likely affected?
options: Lesser occipital nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Greater occipital nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Great auricular nerve
correctOption: Lesser occipital nerve
optionExplanations: The lesser occipital nerve is derived from C2, ascends along the posterior border of the SCM, and supplies the lateral occipital scalp and the medial/cranial surface of the auricle.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the shoulder and chest skin, far inferior to the scalp and ear.
The greater occipital nerve is a branch of the posterior ramus of C2, not the cervical plexus (which is formed from anterior rami).
The transverse cervical nerve supplies the skin of the anterior neck, not the scalp or auricle.
The great auricular nerve (C2,3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible and both surfaces of the auricle, but specifically targets the lower auricle and parotid area.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: While the cervical plexus is primarily known for its cutaneous and somatic motor branches, it also provides specific fibers to the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles. What is the functional modality of these specific plexus branches?
options: General visceral afferent
Special visceral efferent
Somatic motor for contraction
Parasympathetic secretomotor
Proprioceptive sensation
correctOption: Proprioceptive sensation
optionExplanations: General visceral afferent fibers transmit sensory information from internal organs (viscera), whereas these branches transmit proprioceptive data from skeletal muscles.

Special visceral efferent (SVE) fibers supply muscles derived from pharyngeal arches (like the SCM and Trapezius); however, the SVE component travels in the accessory nerve, not the cervical plexus loops.
The main somatic motor innervation for the contraction of the SCM and Trapezius is provided by the spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI), not the cervical plexus.
Parasympathetic secretomotor fibers are carried by cranial nerves (III, VII, IX, X), not by the somatic branches of the cervical plexus.

The cervical plexus (C2, 3 for SCM and C3, 4 for Trapezius) provides the essential proprioceptive (positional sense) information for these muscles, complementing the motor supply from the accessory nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A thoracic surgeon notices that after a radical procedure, a patient still retains partial diaphragmatic function despite a confirmed complete transection of the phrenic nerve in the mid-neck. Which anatomical variation likely explains this finding?
options: Presence of an accessory phrenic nerve from C5
Innervation from the intercostal nerves
Cross-innervation from the contralateral phrenic nerve
Direct innervation from the sympathetic trunk
Vagus nerve contribution to the diaphragm
correctOption: Presence of an accessory phrenic nerve from C5
optionExplanations: Correct. An accessory phrenic nerve (found in ~33% of people) often arises from C5 and travels with the nerve to the subclavius. If it joins the main phrenic nerve distal to the site of injury, some motor function is preserved.
Incorrect. The intercostal nerves supply only the peripheral sensory margins of the diaphragm, not its motor function.
Incorrect. Each phrenic nerve strictly supplies only its corresponding half of the diaphragm with no functional crossing.
Incorrect. The sympathetic trunk is autonomic and does not provide skeletal motor innervation to the diaphragm.
Incorrect. The vagus nerve does not provide motor innervation to the diaphragm.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): About one third of persons have an accessory phrenic nerve . The root from the fifth cervical nerve may be incorporated in the nerve to the subclavius and may join the main phrenic nerve trunk in the thorax.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Regarding the cutaneous distribution of the cervical plexus, which nerve supplies the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible down to the sternum?
options: Supraclavicular nerve
Great auricular nerve
Phrenic nerve
Transverse cervical nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
correctOption: Transverse cervical nerve
optionExplanations: The supraclavicular nerves supply the lower neck, upper chest, and shoulder areas.
The great auricular nerve supplies the skin of the ear and the angle of the jaw.
The phrenic nerve is a deep muscular/sensory nerve and does not provide cutaneous innervation to the surface of the neck.
The transverse cervical (or transverse cutaneous) nerve (C2, C3) is the primary sensory nerve for the majority of the skin of the anterior and lateral neck.
The lesser occipital nerve supplies the scalp behind the ear.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1614 (Book Page): The transverse cutaneous nerve (C2 and 3) emerges from behind the middle of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It passes forward across that muscle and divides into branches that supply the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck, from the body of the mandible to the sternum.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Which specific branch of the cervical plexus serves as the sole motor supply to the diaphragm?
options: Phrenic nerve
Ansa cervicalis
Nerve to the subclavius
Transverse cervical nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
correctOption: Phrenic nerve
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve, arising from C3, C4, and C5, is the exclusive motor nerve for the diaphragm, the primary muscle of respiration.
The ansa cervicalis provides motor supply only to the infrahyoid muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, and omohyoid).
The nerve to the subclavius is a branch of the brachial plexus and supplies the small subclavius muscle, though it may occasionally carry accessory phrenic fibers.
The transverse cervical nerve is a cutaneous branch providing sensation to the neck skin.
The supraclavicular nerves are purely sensory (cutaneous) branches of the cervical plexus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1690 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve is the only motor nerve supply to the diaphragm.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Cutaneous Distribution of Cervical Plexus Branches
statement: A patient suffers from localized loss of sensation over the skin at the angle of the mandible and the lower portion of the auricle following a parotidectomy. Which nerve from the cervical plexus was most likely compromised during the surgical dissection?
options: Transverse cervical nerve
Phrenic nerve
Lesser occipital nerve
Supraclavicular nerve
Great auricular nerve
correctOption: Great auricular nerve
optionExplanations: The transverse cervical nerve supplies the skin on the anterior and lateral surfaces of the neck from the mandible to the sternum, but not the angle or auricle specifically.
The phrenic nerve is a motor nerve for the diaphragm and provides no cutaneous sensation to the face or neck.
The lesser occipital nerve primarily supplies the back of the scalp and the medial/superior surface of the auricle, not the angle of the mandible.
The supraclavicular nerves supply the skin over the shoulder and chest wall, far below the mandible.
The great auricular nerve (C2, C3) ascends across the SCM and supplies the skin over the parotid gland and the angle of the mandible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The great auricular nerve (C2 and 3) supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible. ... The lesser occipital nerve (C2) supplies the back of the scalp and the auricle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: A patient undergoing an elective neck procedure requires a regional block at the 'nerve point of the neck.' At which specific anatomical location should the clinician inject the local anesthetic to target the emergence of the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus?
options: The interval between the anterior and middle scalene muscles at the first rib
The apex of the posterior triangle just inferior to the mastoid process
The superior border of the thyroid cartilage in the carotid triangle
The posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at about its midpoint
The anterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at its superior third
correctOption: The posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at about its midpoint
optionExplanations: The interval between the anterior and middle scalene (interscalene triangle) is where the roots of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery emerge, not the cutaneous cervical plexus.

The apex of the posterior triangle contains the accessory nerve and occipital artery but is superior to the common emergence point of the cutaneous cervical nerves at the midpoint of the muscle's border.
The superior border of the thyroid cartilage marks the bifurcation of the common carotid artery, unrelated to the superficial cutaneous nerves.

The posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle at its midpoint (Erb's point) is the anatomical landmark where the four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular) emerge from the deep fascia.
The anterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid is where the carotid pulse is palpated and does not serve as the exit point for the superficial cervical nerves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck ) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Proprioceptive vs Motor innervation of SCM and Trapezius
statement: A 45-year-old patient undergoes a deep neck dissection for a metastatic tumor. During the procedure, the surgeon preserves the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) but unavoidably transects the branches from the C3 and C4 spinal nerves that enter the trapezius muscle. What is the most significant clinical deficit expected from this specific cervical plexus lesion?
options: Numbness over the skin of the shoulder and upper deltoid.
Complete paralysis and wasting of the trapezius muscle.
Paralysis of the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Loss of proprioceptive sensation from the trapezius muscle.
Inability to shrug the shoulders due to loss of motor supply.
correctOption: Loss of proprioceptive sensation from the trapezius muscle.
optionExplanations: Cutaneous numbness over the shoulder would involve the supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4 cutaneous branches), not the deep muscular proprioceptive branches.
The motor supply to the trapezius is provided by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI). Since it was preserved, complete paralysis and wasting will not occur.
The sternocleidomastoid is supplied by C2, C3 proprioceptive branches and CN XI motor fibers; it would not be paralyzed by a C3/C4 lesion specifically targeting the trapezius branches.

In humans, the branches from the cervical plexus (C2, C3 to the SCM and C3, C4 to the trapezius) are generally considered to be purely proprioceptive (carrying sensory info about muscle position), while the motor supply is via CN XI. Transecting them leads to loss of proprioception.
Shrugging is a motor function of the trapezius, which is primarily innervated by the preserved spinal accessory nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The cervical plexus branches to the sternocleidomastoid (C2, 3) and trapezius (C3, 4) are proprioceptive.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: To perform a regional anesthesia block for a minor surgery on the side of the neck, a clinician injects a local anesthetic at the 'nerve point of the neck.' Which combination of cervical plexus nerves is primarily targeted by this procedure to achieve comprehensive cutaneous anesthesia?
options: Hypoglossal, accessory, and branches to the levator scapulae
Internal laryngeal, recurrent laryngeal, and cardiac branches
Lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular
Phrenic, nerve to subclavius, and ansa cervicalis
Greater occipital, third occipital, and dorsal rami of C2-C4
correctOption: Lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal and accessory nerves are cranial nerves (XII and XI) and are not cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus.
The laryngeal and cardiac nerves are branches of the vagus (CN X) and supply deeper visceral structures, not the skin of the neck.
These four nerves are the primary cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus that emerge at the posterior border of the SCM; blocking them provides anesthesia to the neck skin.
The phrenic nerve and ansa cervicalis are deep motor nerves; blocking them at the nerve point is not the primary goal for cutaneous anesthesia.
The greater occipital and third occipital nerves are derived from posterior (dorsal) rami, whereas the cervical plexus is formed by anterior rami.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): Four cutaneous nerves (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular) branch off the cervical plexus and supply the skin over the lower head and the front and sides of the neck (see Fig. 12.20). These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck)...

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: Following a traumatic penetrating injury to the neck, a patient suffers from paralysis of the right half of the diaphragm. Which pathophysiological change occurs because the phrenic nerve is the sole motor supply to this muscle?
options: The paralyzed half of the diaphragm remains fixed in a state of chronic contraction.
The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pulled down by negative intrathoracic pressure.
The accessory phrenic nerve from the sixth cervical nerve prevents any upward movement.
The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax by positive abdominal pressure.
The diaphragm undergoes hypertrophic compensation, expanding into the mediastinum.
correctOption: The paralyzed half of the diaphragm is pushed up into the thorax by positive abdominal pressure.
optionExplanations: Paralysis leads to relaxation and flaccidity, not chronic contraction (which would require constant neural input).
While there is negative pressure in the thorax, the positive pressure from the abdomen is the active force pushing the relaxed muscle upward.
Accessory phrenic nerves usually involve C5 (Page 1690), but they are not present in everyone and typically join the main trunk, which would also be severed in a complete lesion.

Because the phrenic nerve is the only motor supply, its lesion causes the muscle to go flaccid. The resting positive pressure within the abdominal cavity then forces the dome of the diaphragm upward into the thoracic cavity.
Muscle paralysis leads to atrophy over time, not hypertrophy; there is no compensatory expansion into the mediastinum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): If that occurs, the paralyzed half of the diaphragm relaxes and is pushed up into the thorax by the positive abdominal pressure. Consequently, the lower lobe of the lung on that side may collapse.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: The Nerve Point of the Neck
statement: In clinical practice, the 'nerve point of the neck' is a landmark where cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus emerge. Where is this point located?
options: Between the two heads of the sternocleidomastoid muscle
At the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, near the angle of the jaw
At the apex of the posterior triangle, near the mastoid process
Immediately superior to the sternoclavicular joint
At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, at about its midpoint
correctOption: At the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid, at about its midpoint
optionExplanations: The space between the sternal and clavicular heads of the SCM is the lesser supraclavicular fossa, used for internal jugular vein catheterization.
The anterior border of the SCM is a landmark for the carotid pulse and the internal jugular vein, but not the exit of the cervical plexus cutaneous branches.
The apex of the posterior triangle is where the occipital artery and greater occipital nerve emerge; the cervical plexus branches emerge lower at the midpoint of the SCM.
The area superior to the sternoclavicular joint is the root of the neck, containing the subclavian vessels and the insertion of the SCM, not the nerve point.

The midpoint of the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid is the 'nerve point,' where the four cutaneous branches (lesser occipital, great auricular, transverse cervical, and supraclavicular) radiate outward.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Topographic Anatomy of the Phrenic Nerve
statement: A 55-year-old patient undergoing a lower neck dissection for a deep tumor requires the identification of the phrenic nerve to avoid respiratory complications. Which anatomical relationship is most reliable for locating this nerve in the neck?
options: It passes posterior to the subclavian artery at the thoracic inlet.
It lies immediately medial to the internal jugular vein within the carotid sheath.
It runs vertically downward across the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle.
It descends through the gap between the scalenus anterior and scalenus medius muscles.
It is found hitch-hiking with the spinal accessory nerve across the posterior triangle.
correctOption: It runs vertically downward across the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle.
optionExplanations: The phrenic nerve passes anterior to the subclavian artery as it leaves the neck and enters the thorax.
The vagus nerve is found within the carotid sheath, whereas the phrenic nerve is located deep to the prevertebral fascia, external to the sheath.
The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) is found descending on the anterior surface of the scalenus anterior muscle, held in place by the prevertebral layer of deep cervical fascia.
The roots of the brachial plexus and the subclavian artery pass between the scalenus anterior and medius, not the phrenic nerve.
The spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) crosses the posterior triangle to reach the trapezius, but it does not carry phrenic fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): The phrenic nerve arises in the neck from the third, fourth, and fifth cervical nerves of the cervical plexus. It runs vertically downward across the front of the scalenus anterior muscle

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
statement: The cervical plexus is formed by the union of which specific spinal nerve components?
options: Posterior rami of C1 to C4
Anterior rami of C2 to C4
Anterior rami of C1 to C5
Posterior rami of C2 to C5
Anterior rami of C1 to C4
correctOption: Anterior rami of C1 to C4
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The cervical plexus is formed by anterior rami, which provide motor and sensory innervation to the neck and diaphragm, whereas posterior rami generally supply the intrinsic back muscles and skin of the back.
Incorrect. The first cervical nerve (C1) is a vital component of the plexus, specifically contributing to the loops that provide motor fibers to the infrahyoid muscles.
Incorrect. While C5 contributes to the phrenic nerve (a major branch of the plexus), it is primarily considered a root of the brachial plexus rather than a constituent of the cervical plexus proper.
Incorrect. Posterior rami do not form plexuses like the cervical or brachial plexuses; they remain segmental in their distribution to the posterior neck and trunk.
Correct. Anatomically, the cervical plexus arises from the anterior rami of the C1, C2, C3, and C4 spinal nerves, forming a series of loops deep to the internal jugular vein.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1687 (Book Page): The anterior rami of the first four cervical nerves form the cervical plexus.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: The Nerve Point of the Neck
statement: A patient is brought to the emergency department with a deep laceration at the midpoint of the posterior border of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Clinical examination reveals anesthesia over the angle of the mandible, the skin of the anterior neck, and the lateral occipital scalp. Which anatomical landmark was most likely involved in this injury?
options: The jugular foramen
The carotid sinus
The pharyngeal raphe
The nerve point of the neck
The interscalene triangle
correctOption: The nerve point of the neck
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The jugular foramen is at the base of the skull, far superior to the midpoint of the sternocleidomastoid.
Incorrect. The carotid sinus is located at the bifurcation of the common carotid artery, deep and anterior to the SCM.
Incorrect. The pharyngeal raphe is a midline posterior structure of the pharynx, not related to the cutaneous nerves at the SCM border.

Correct. The 'nerve point of the neck' (Erb's point) is where the four cutaneous branches of the cervical plexus (Lesser occipital, Great auricular, Transverse cervical, Supraclavicular) emerge to become superficial.
Incorrect. The interscalene triangle contains the brachial plexus and subclavian artery, located deeper and lower in the neck root.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves emerge at a common point (the nerve point of the neck) at the posterior margin of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, at about the midpoint of the muscle, and distribute from there

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
coreConcept: Referred Pain Mechanics in Cervical Plexus
statement: A 52-year-old male with chronic cholecystitis experiences sharp pain in his right shoulder region. This phenomenon of referred pain is anatomically explained by the common spinal cord segments shared by the phrenic nerve and which cutaneous branch of the cervical plexus?
options: Auriculotemporal nerve.
Supraclavicular nerves.
Great auricular nerve.
Lesser occipital nerve.
Transverse cervical nerve.
correctOption: Supraclavicular nerves.
optionExplanations: The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3) and is not part of the cervical plexus or the C3-C4 dermatomes.

Inflammation of the gallbladder can irritate the diaphragmatic peritoneum, which is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3-5). The sensory input enters the spinal cord at the same levels as the supraclavicular nerves (C3-4), causing the brain to perceive pain in the shoulder.
The great auricular nerve (C2-3) primarily supplies the ear and angle of the jaw; while it shares C3, it is not the primary site for shoulder referred pain.
The lesser occipital nerve (C2) does not share the C3-C4 roots required for the classic phrenic-to-shoulder referred pain pathway.
The transverse cervical nerve (C2-3) supplies the anterior neck; referred pain from the diaphragm specifically targets the shoulder and clavicular region via the supraclaviculars.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1689 (Book Page): These nerves are important clinically, because pain may be referred along them from the phrenic nerve (e.g., in gallbladder disease). ... The supraclavicular nerves (C3 and 4) have medial, intermediate, and lateral branches that supply the skin over the shoulder region.

category: Describe the location, formation, branches, distribution and lesions of cervical plexus
