options: Contraction of the middle constrictor and depression of the hyoid
Contraction of the stylopharyngeus and opening of the glottis
Relaxation of the cricopharyngeus and elevation of the larynx
Contraction of the inferior constrictor and retroflexion of the epiglottis
Contraction of the superior constrictor and elevation of the soft palate
correctOption: Contraction of the superior constrictor and elevation of the soft palate
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor propels the bolus through the oropharynx, but it does not contribute to the nasopharyngeal seal.
The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx; the glottis must be closed, not open, to protect the airway.
While these actions occur during swallowing, they facilitate the passage into the esophagus and the protection of the airway, respectively, not the nasopharynx.
The inferior constrictor propels the bolus into the esophagus; epiglottic retroflexion protects the larynx, not the nasopharynx.
The pharyngeal isthmus is closed by the elevation of the soft palate meeting the posterior pharyngeal wall (Passavant's ridge), which is pulled forward by the superior constrictor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The nasal part of the pharynx is now shut off from the oral part of the pharynx by the elevation of the soft palate, the pulling forward of the posterior wall of the pharynx by the upper fibers of the superior constrictor muscle...

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Structures traversing pharyngeal gaps: Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve
statement: A 52-year-old female undergoes a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goiter. Post-operatively, she complains of significant hoarseness. An endoscopic exam reveals a paralyzed vocal fold. This nerve injury occurred in the anatomical gap between which of the following structures?
options: The inferior constrictor muscle and the esophagus
The middle and inferior constrictor muscles
The base of the skull and the superior constrictor muscle
The thyrohyoid membrane and the thyroid cartilage
The superior and middle constrictor muscles
correctOption: The inferior constrictor muscle and the esophagus
optionExplanations: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (the source of vocal fold motor supply) ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove and enters the larynx by passing deep to the lower border of the inferior constrictor muscle at its junction with the esophagus.
This gap (Gap 3) transmits the internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal artery.
This gap (Gap 1) contains the auditory tube and levator veli palatini, not the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
This area relates to the internal laryngeal nerve piercing the thyrohyoid membrane, which provides sensory supply above the vocal folds, not motor supply to the folds.
This gap (Gap 2) transmits the stylopharyngeus muscle and the glossopharyngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1789 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends the neck and becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve when it passes the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and enters the larynx.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: In the physiological coordination of deglutition, which component of the pharyngeal constrictor mechanism must relax to allow the bolus to enter the esophagus?
options: Ceratopharyngeus
Cricopharyngeus
Chondropharyngeus
Thyropharyngeus
Pterygopharyngeus
correctOption: Cricopharyngeus
optionExplanations: Ceratopharyngeus is a division of the middle constrictor (attaching to greater cornu) and is propulsive.
The cricopharyngeus acts as the upper esophageal sphincter; its relaxation is essential for the bolus to move from the pharynx into the esophagus.
Chondropharyngeus is a division of the middle constrictor (attaching to lesser cornu) and is propulsive.
The thyropharyngeus is the propulsive (upper) part of the inferior constrictor and contracts to push the bolus.
Pterygopharyngeus is a part of the superior constrictor involved in closing the nasopharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): Finally, the lower part of the pharyngeal wall (the cricopharyngeus muscle) relaxes, and the bolus enters the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Functional and Structural Contrast of the Inferior Constrictor Parts
statement: When contrasting the components of the inferior constrictor muscle, which anatomical feature distinguishes the cricopharyngeus from the thyropharyngeus?
options: The cricopharyngeus originates from the thyroid cartilage oblique line
The cricopharyngeus has horizontal fibers, while the thyropharyngeus has oblique fibers
The thyropharyngeus is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, while the cricopharyngeus is not
The cricopharyngeus is propulsive, while the thyropharyngeus is sphincteric
The thyropharyngeus forms the Killian dehiscence internally
correctOption: The cricopharyngeus has horizontal fibers, while the thyropharyngeus has oblique fibers
optionExplanations: The thyropharyngeus originates from the thyroid cartilage; the cricopharyngeus originates from the cricoid cartilage.
The thyropharyngeus has fibers that run obliquely, whereas the cricopharyngeus has fibers that pass horizontally, acting as a functional sphincter.
Both parts are typically considered to receive supply via the pharyngeal plexus and external laryngeal/recurrent laryngeal branches; this is not the primary distinguishing structural feature.
This is reversed; the thyropharyngeus (the upper part) is propulsive, while the cricopharyngeus (the lower part) is sphincteric.
The Killian dehiscence is a potential gap between these two parts, not a structure formed internally by the thyropharyngeus alone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): The fibers of the cricopharyngeus pass horizontally around the lowest and narrowest part of the pharynx and act as a sphincter. Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The superior constrictor muscle is distinct because of its multiple anterior points of attachment. Which of the following is an attachment site for the uppermost fibers of this muscle?
options: Oblique line of the mandible
Pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe
Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
Stylohyoid ligament
Internal surface of the thyroid lamina
correctOption: Pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor attaches to the mylohyoid line of the mandible, not the oblique line (which is on the external surface).
The superior constrictor originates from the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, and the adjacent mylohyoid line of the mandible.
The greater cornu of the hyoid is the origin for the middle constrictor muscle, not the superior.
The stylohyoid ligament provides origin for the middle constrictor muscle.
The internal surface of the thyroid lamina provides the attachment for the vocal ligaments and the thyroepiglottic ligament, not the superior constrictor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe) : Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: While performing a cranial nerve examination on a patient with suspected bulbar palsy, a physician notes a lack of contraction in most pharyngeal muscles. Which of the following correctly identifies the neural contrast between the constrictor muscles and the stylopharyngeus?
options: All pharyngeal muscles are supplied by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve.
The inferior constrictor is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve; others by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
Constrictors are supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve; stylopharyngeus by the vagus nerve.
Both groups are supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) exclusively.
Constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X); stylopharyngeus by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
correctOption: Constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X); stylopharyngeus by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
optionExplanations: The trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and the tensor veli palatini, but it does not provide motor innervation to the pharyngeal constrictors.
While the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies laryngeal muscles, the primary motor supply to the constrictors is the pharyngeal plexus, though the inferior constrictor receives additional branches.
This is incorrect; the glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the stylopharyngeus, while the vagus (via the pharyngeal plexus) supplies the constrictors.
While CN XI (cranial part) contributes fibers to the pharyngeal plexus, it does not supply the stylopharyngeus, which is derived from the third pharyngeal arch.

The pharyngeal plexus, primarily formed by the vagus nerve (carrying CN XI fibers), supplies the superior, middle, and inferior constrictors. The stylopharyngeus is unique as it is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1679 (Book Page): [Pharyngeal branch contains nerve fibers from the cranial part of the accessory nerve. This branch joins the pharyngeal plexus and supplies all the muscles of the pharynx (except the stylopharyngeus)] and Page 1676 (Book Page): [Nerve to the stylopharyngeus muscle. This is the sole muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.]

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: When viewing the pharynx from its posterior aspect, which statement best describes the structural relationship and overlap of the constrictor muscles?
options: The superior constrictor overlaps the middle constrictor from the outside
The inferior constrictor is the only one that does not overlap another muscle
Each lower constrictor overlaps the one above it on its external surface
The muscles are separated by distinct gaps with no overlap
The middle constrictor is situated internal to the superior constrictor
correctOption: Each lower constrictor overlaps the one above it on its external surface
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor is the most internal; the middle constrictor actually overlaps the superior constrictor from the outside.
The inferior constrictor overlaps the middle constrictor, thus it does indeed participate in the overlapping arrangement.
In a 'nested' arrangement, the middle constrictor overlaps the superior, and the inferior constrictor overlaps the middle constrictor on their external aspects.
There is significant overlap between the muscles, although gaps exist laterally for the passage of neurovascular structures.
The middle constrictor is external (outside) to the superior constrictor, not internal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles overlap each other so that the middle constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the superior constrictor and the inferior constrictor lies outside the lower part of the middle constrictor.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Auditory Tube Mechanics and Pharyngeal Relations
statement: The physiological regulation of middle ear pressure depends on the active opening of the pharyngotympanic tube. Which pharyngeal muscle relationship is essential for this function?
options: The inferior constrictor relaxing to allow air into the esophagus
The superior constrictor fibers meeting at the pharyngeal raphe
The middle constrictor attaching to the stylohyoid ligament
The salpingopharyngeus pulling the torus tubarius inferiorly
The levator veli palatini and tensor veli palatini passing superior to the superior constrictor
correctOption: The levator veli palatini and tensor veli palatini passing superior to the superior constrictor
optionExplanations: The inferior constrictor (cricopharyngeus) prevents air from entering the esophagus, but is unrelated to the middle ear.
The pharyngeal raphe provides a posterior attachment for all constrictors but does not facilitate the opening of the auditory tube.
The middle constrictor is involved in bolus propulsion and has no role in auditory tube mechanics.
Salpingopharyngeus assists in elevating the pharynx during swallowing but tensor/levator veli palatini are the primary openers of the tube.
The auditory tube and the palatal muscles (Levator and Tensor veli palatini) traverse the gap above the superior constrictor; their contraction opens the tube during swallowing.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1709 (Book Page): Contractions of the tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini muscles cause the collapsed mucous membrane to separate from the cartilage wall and open the auditory tube... Page 1750 (Book Page): As the tube descends, it passes over the upper border of the superior constrictor muscle.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During the involuntary phase of swallowing, which muscle contracts to elevate the pharyngeal wall and widen the pharynx to receive the bolus?
options: Superior constrictor
Thyrohyoid
Mylohyoid
Cricopharyngeus
Salpingopharyngeus
correctOption: Salpingopharyngeus
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor acts to propel the bolus downward via circular contraction, not by elevating the pharyngeal wall to receive it.
The thyrohyoid elevates the larynx toward the hyoid bone, but it is classified as an infrahyoid muscle rather than a pharyngeal wall muscle.
The mylohyoid is a suprahyoid muscle that elevates the floor of the mouth and hyoid, but it is not a muscle of the pharyngeal wall itself.
The cricopharyngeus acts as a sphincter that must relax, not contract, to allow the bolus to enter the esophagus.
The salpingopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle that, along with the stylopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus, elevates the pharynx during swallowing.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): The larynx and the laryngeal part of the pharynx are pulled upward by the contraction of the stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, thyrohyoid, and palatopharyngeus muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which structure is found passing below the lower border of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
options: Stylopharyngeus muscle
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Superior laryngeal artery
correctOption: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The stylopharyngeus muscle also passes through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the superior and middle constrictors.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve (and the inferior laryngeal artery) pass below the inferior border of the cricopharyngeus (inferior constrictor) to enter the larynx.
The internal laryngeal nerve passes between the middle and inferior constrictors, not below the inferior constrictor.
The superior laryngeal artery accompanies the internal laryngeal nerve through the gap between middle and inferior constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends the neck and becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve when it passes the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and enters the larynx. [Context: This corresponds to passing below the inferior constrictor muscle.]

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 70-year-old male complains of progressive dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food. Barium swallow reveals a diverticulum in the posterior pharyngeal wall. Anatomically, this protrusion occurs through Killian’s dehiscence. Between which two muscular components is this potential gap located?
options: Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor
Salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus
Superior and middle constrictors
Stylopharyngeus and middle constrictor
Cricopharyngeus and the first ring of the trachea
correctOption: Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor
optionExplanations: Killian's dehiscence is a weak area between the thyropharyngeus (oblique fibers) and cricopharyngeus (horizontal fibers) of the inferior constrictor.
These are longitudinal muscles of the internal layer of the pharynx and do not define the gaps in the outer constrictor layer.
The gap between superior and middle constrictors conveys the stylopharyngeus muscle, not a diverticulum.
The stylopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle and its relationship with the middle constrictor does not form Killian's dehiscence.
The cricopharyngeus is continuous with the esophagus; the gap between it and the trachea is not a site for pharyngeal pouches.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient is evaluated for a condition where air is abnormally entering the esophagus during respiration. In a healthy individual, which specific component of the pharyngeal constrictor mechanism is responsible for preventing the entry of air into the esophagus?
options: The middle constrictor at the hyoid bone
The cricopharyngeus muscle
The superior constrictor at the pharyngeal tubercle
The longitudinal fibers of the salpingopharyngeus
The palatopharyngeus muscle
correctOption: The cricopharyngeus muscle
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor is primarily involved in the propulsive phase of deglutition and does not serve as a valve or sphincter.
The cricopharyngeus is the sphincteric, horizontal part of the inferior constrictor that remains tonically contracted to prevent air entry into the esophagus and reflux of gastric contents.
The superior constrictor aids in sealing the nasopharynx during swallowing but has no role in preventing air from entering the esophagus.
The salpingopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle that assists in elevating the pharynx during swallowing but does not act as an esophageal sphincter.
The palatopharyngeus pulls the pharyngeal wall upward during swallowing; it does not regulate the opening or closing of the esophageal inlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1754 (Book Page): [The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle. ... It is believed that the function of the cricopharyngeus is to prevent the entry of air into the esophagus.]

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Innervation Mechanism of the Pharyngeal Constrictors
statement: A patient presents with significant dysphagia following a brainstem injury affecting the pharyngeal plexus. Pathophysiologically, the motor fibers supplying the pharyngeal constrictors are primarily derived from which source?
options: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) following a long curving course
The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2)
The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) via the vagus nerve
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) originating in the medulla
The external laryngeal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
correctOption: The cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) via the vagus nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is entirely motor but specifically supplies the muscles of the tongue, not the pharynx.
The maxillary nerve (V2) provides sensory innervation to the nasopharynx but has no motor supply to the pharyngeal wall.

The pharyngeal constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, specifically receiving motor fibers from the cranial root of the accessory nerve (CN XI) that join and travel with the vagus nerve (CN X).
CN IX provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx and motor supply only to the stylopharyngeus, not the constrictors.

The external laryngeal nerve supplies only the cricothyroid muscle of the larynx and the inferior constrictor (specifically the cricopharyngeus), but it is not the primary source for the entire constrictor group.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1680 (Book Page): The cranial root joins the vagus nerve and is distributed in its branches to the muscles of the soft palate and pharynx (via the pharyngeal plexus) and to the muscles of the larynx (except the cricothyroid muscle).

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which of the following describes a specific bony and ligamentous origin for the fibers of the superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx?
options: The greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone
The pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe
The posterior border of the cricoid cartilage
The oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage
The lower part of the stylohyoid ligament
correctOption: The pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe
optionExplanations: The cornua of the hyoid bone serve as the origin for the middle constrictor muscle.
The superior constrictor originates from a continuous line including the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe (which connects it to the buccinator), and the mylohyoid line of the mandible.
The cricoid cartilage provides attachment for the cricopharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is the origin for the thyropharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor, not the superior constrictor.
The stylohyoid ligament provides attachment for the middle pharyngeal constrictor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): [Table 12.11] Superior constrictor: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, posterior end of mylohyoid line of mandible.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Glossopharyngeal Nerve in the Pharyngeal Gap
statement: During a surgical procedure on the lateral neck, a surgeon must identify structures passing between the superior and middle constrictor muscles. Damage to the nerve in this gap would most likely result in which clinical deficit?
options: Reduced lacrimation in the ipsilateral eye
Loss of taste to the anterior two thirds of the tongue
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle
Loss of general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue
Inability to adduct the vocal folds
correctOption: Loss of general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue
optionExplanations: Lacrimation is controlled by the facial nerve (CN VII) via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion, not CN IX in this gap.
Taste to the anterior two thirds is carried by the chorda tympani (CN VII), not the glossopharyngeal nerve in the pharyngeal gap.
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle results from injury to the external laryngeal nerve, which does not pass through this specific gap.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors; it provides both taste and general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue.
Adduction of vocal folds is managed by the lateral cricoarytenoid and transverse arytenoid muscles, supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): [Glossopharyngeal nerve] Lingual branch carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue... Page 1756 (Book Page): Middle constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the superior constrictor... Gap 2: Stylopharyngeus and CN IX.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: In the physiological regulation of the upper digestive tract, the lower portion of the inferior constrictor muscle functions differently from the rest of the pharyngeal musculature. What is the primary functional role of the cricopharyngeus muscle?
options: To act as a sphincter preventing air from entering the esophagus
To tense the soft palate against the posterior pharyngeal wall
To shorten the pharynx to receive the bolus
To dilate the pharyngotympanic tube
To elevate the larynx during the first stage of swallowing
correctOption: To act as a sphincter preventing air from entering the esophagus
optionExplanations: The cricopharyngeus is the sphincteric component of the inferior constrictor that remains contracted at rest to prevent aerophagia.
Tensing the soft palate is the function of the tensor veli palatini muscle.
Shortening of the pharynx is the role of the longitudinal pharyngeal muscles, not the circular constrictors.
Dilation of the auditory tube is performed by the tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini, not by the constrictors.
Elevation of the larynx is primarily performed by the longitudinal muscles (stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus) and suprahyoid muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1754 (Book Page): It is believed that the function of the cricopharyngeus is to prevent the entry of air into the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with halitosis and regurgitation of undigested food. A barium swallow reveals a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker’s diverticulum). This herniation typically occurs at Killian’s dehiscence, which is found between which two components of the pharyngeal musculature?
options: Superior constrictor and the skull base
Superior and middle constrictors
Palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus
Middle and inferior constrictors
Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
correctOption: Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
optionExplanations: The gap between the superior constrictor and the skull base is covered by the pharyngobasilar fascia and contains the auditory tube; it is not the site of Zenker’s diverticulum.
Gaps between the superior and middle constrictors are usually well-supported and do not result in pulsion diverticula.
Palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles located internally to the constrictors; they do not form the boundaries of this dehiscence.
While a gap exists between the middle and inferior constrictors (thyrohyoid membrane), it is not the site of Zenker’s diverticulum.
The inferior constrictor has two parts: the thyropharyngeus (propulsive) and the cricopharyngeus (sphincteric). Killian's dehiscence is the weak area between these two where the mucosa can herniate.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The three pharyngeal constrictor muscles all converge posteriorly to insert into a common structure. What is this structure and where does it attach superiorly?
options: Stylomandibular ligament; attaches to the styloid process
Pterygomandibular raphe; attaches to the pterygoid hamulus
Median thyrohyoid ligament; attaches to the hyoid bone
Pharyngeal raphe; attaches to the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
Prevertebral fascia; attaches to the basilar part of the pons
correctOption: Pharyngeal raphe; attaches to the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
optionExplanations: The stylomandibular ligament is a lateral ligament of the TMJ/neck and does not serve as the insertion for pharyngeal muscles.
The pterygomandibular raphe is a lateral structure that serves as an origin for the superior constrictor, not a posterior midline insertion for all three.
The thyrohyoid ligament connects the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone anteriorly; it is not the posterior insertion of the constrictors.
The pharyngeal raphe is the posterior midline insertion point for all three constrictors; it is anchored superiorly to the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone.
Prevertebral fascia lies posterior to the pharynx (retropharyngeal space) but is not the insertion site for the constrictor muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): [The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone...].

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: While the motor nerve supply to most of the pharynx is provided by the pharyngeal plexus via the cranial root of the accessory nerve, which muscle is the distinct exception to this rule?
options: Salpingopharyngeus
Stylopharyngeus
Inferior constrictor
Middle constrictor
Superior constrictor
correctOption: Stylopharyngeus
optionExplanations: The salpingopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle of the pharynx, but it is also innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X).
The stylopharyngeus is the only muscle of the pharynx (and the only muscle derived from the 3rd pharyngeal arch) innervated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
The inferior constrictor is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus, specifically its pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches.
The middle constrictor is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X with fibers from CN XI).
The superior constrictor is innervated by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X with fibers from CN XI).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Table 12.11: Stylopharyngeus – Nerve supply: Glossopharyngeal nerve. ... Superior, Middle, and Inferior Constrictors – Nerve supply: Pharyngeal plexus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Functional Coordination of Pharyngeal Constrictors in Swallowing
statement: During the second stage of deglutition (swallowing), a bolus moves through the oropharynx. Which of the following describes a correct structural event involving the pharyngeal constrictors and the associated anatomy to protect the airway?
options: The superior constrictor relaxes to allow the soft palate to descend
The inferior constrictor fibers contract upward to push the bolus into the nasopharynx
The larynx is pulled upward by the stylopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus as the constrictors contract sequentially
The cricopharyngeus remains firmly contracted to prevent the bolus from entering the esophagus too quickly
The middle constrictor contracts while the stylopharyngeus lowers the larynx
correctOption: The larynx is pulled upward by the stylopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus as the constrictors contract sequentially
optionExplanations: The soft palate is actually elevated, and the posterior pharyngeal wall is pulled forward by the superior constrictor to shut off the nasopharynx.
The inferior constrictor contracts to move food downward; moving food into the nasopharynx would be a failure of the swallowing mechanism (regurgitation).
Deglutition requires laryngeal elevation to meet the epiglottis, while the constrictors contract in a superior-to-inferior wave to propel the bolus.
The cricopharyngeus must relax, not contract, to allow the bolus to pass from the pharynx into the esophagus.
The stylopharyngeus elevates the larynx, it does not lower it, to help close the laryngeal inlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): The larynx and the laryngeal part of the pharynx are pulled upward by the contraction of the stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, thyrohyoid, and palatopharyngeus muscles. ... The bolus moves downward ... as the result of the successive contraction of the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Structures in the Sinus of Morgagni
statement: In a patient with chronic middle ear effusions, a surgeon considers the anatomical relationship of the auditory tube. Which structure enters the pharynx by passing through the gap above the superior constrictor muscle?
options: Superior laryngeal nerve
Stylopharyngeus muscle
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Levator veli palatini muscle
correctOption: Levator veli palatini muscle
optionExplanations: The superior laryngeal nerve is a branch of the vagus that descends lateral to the pharynx and does not enter through this superior gap.
The stylopharyngeus muscle enters the pharynx between the superior and middle constrictors, not above the superior constrictor.
The glossopharyngeal nerve enters the pharynx through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors.
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane between the middle and inferior constrictors.
The levator veli palatini muscle and the auditory tube pass together through the gap between the superior border of the superior constrictor and the base of the skull.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1709 (Book Page): Contractions of the tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini muscles cause the collapsed mucous membrane to separate from the cartilage wall and open the auditory tube. Page 1750 (Book Page): As the tube descends, it passes over the upper border of the superior constrictor muscle.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which muscle is specifically identified as the portion of the inferior constrictor that arises from the cricoid cartilage?
options: Thyropharyngeus
Salpingopharyngeus
Palatopharyngeus
Cricopharyngeus
Stylopharyngeus
correctOption: Cricopharyngeus
optionExplanations: The thyropharyngeus is the upper part of the inferior constrictor arising from the thyroid cartilage.
The salpingopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle originating from the auditory tube, not the cricoid cartilage.
The palatopharyngeus is a longitudinal pharyngeal muscle, not a part of the inferior constrictor.
The cricopharyngeus is the sphincteric lower portion of the inferior constrictor arising from the cricoid cartilage.
The stylopharyngeus is an extrinsic pharyngeal muscle arising from the styloid process of the temporal bone.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A specific area of potential muscular weakness exists on the posterior pharyngeal wall due to the divergent fiber orientations of the inferior constrictor. Between which two muscular components is this clinical landmark situated?
options: Middle constrictor and stylopharyngeus
Superior and middle constrictors
Palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus
Cricopharyngeus and trachealis
Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
correctOption: Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
optionExplanations: The stylopharyngeus muscle passes through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors, not within the inferior constrictor's components.

The gap between the superior and middle constrictors transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve and stylopharyngeus muscle, but is not known as a major site for pulsion diverticula like Killian's dehiscence.
Palatopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles of the internal pharyngeal layer, not part of the external constrictor arrangement defining Killian's dehiscence.
The trachealis is smooth muscle on the posterior trachea; the cricopharyngeus is the lower limit of the pharynx. They do not form the specific dehiscence described.
The inferior constrictor is divided into the thyropharyngeus (oblique fibers) and cricopharyngeus (horizontal fibers). The area between them is Killian's dehiscence, a site prone to herniation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 75-year-old male presents with chronic halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, and a 'gurgling' sound in the neck while swallowing. A barium swallow reveals a posterior midline pouch. The physician explains that the 'cricopharyngeus' muscle failed to relax, increasing intrapharyngeal pressure. Which statement accurately describes this muscle's attachment?
options: It originates from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
It originates from the styloid process of the temporal bone.
It originates from the pterygomandibular raphe.
It originates from the greater cornu of the hyoid bone.
It originates from the cricoid cartilage and acts as a sphincter.
correctOption: It originates from the cricoid cartilage and acts as a sphincter.
optionExplanations: The thyropharyngeus (the upper part of the inferior constrictor) originates from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage, but not the cricopharyngeus part.
The stylopharyngeus muscle originates from the styloid process; it is a longitudinal muscle, not a constrictor or sphincter.
The superior constrictor originates from the pterygomandibular raphe, which links it to the buccinator muscle of the cheek.
The middle constrictor, not the inferior or its cricopharyngeus part, originates from the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone.
The cricopharyngeus is the horizontal, lower component of the inferior constrictor that arises from the cricoid cartilage; its failure to relax during deglutition leads to Zenker's diverticulum.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The pharyngeal constrictor muscles are essential for the involuntary phase of deglutition. Which cranial nerve provides the primary motor innervation for these muscles via the pharyngeal plexus?
options: Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Trigeminal nerve (CN V)
Vagus nerve (CN X)
Facial nerve (CN VII)
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
correctOption: Vagus nerve (CN X)
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve provides motor supply to the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, but not to the pharyngeal wall.
The trigeminal nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and the tensor veli palatini, but not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The vagus nerve (specifically its pharyngeal branch carrying fibers from the cranial root of the accessory nerve) is the primary motor supply to the superior, middle, and inferior constrictors.
The facial nerve supplies the muscles of facial expression and the posterior belly of the digastric, but not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides motor supply only to the stylopharyngeus; for the constrictors, it provides sensory innervation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1679 (Book Page): Pharyngeal branch contains nerve fibers from the cranial part of the accessory nerve . This branch joins the pharyngeal plexus and supplies all the muscles of the pharynx (except the stylopharyngeus) and of the soft palate (except the tensor veli palatini).

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Attachments of the Middle Pharyngeal Constrictor
statement: A student is asked to identify the origin of the middle pharyngeal constrictor. Which of the following describes its attachment correctly?
options: The pterygomandibular ligament and the mylohyoid line
The lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and the cricoid cartilage
The medial pterygoid plate and the pterygoid hamulus
The pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
correctOption: The lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The pterygomandibular ligament and mylohyoid line provide attachment for the superior constrictor, not the middle constrictor.
The middle constrictor specifically originates from the lower end of the stylohyoid ligament and both the greater and lesser cornua (horns) of the hyoid bone.
The thyroid and cricoid cartilages serve as the origin points for the inferior constrictor muscle.
The medial pterygoid plate and pterygoid hamulus are part of the origin for the superior pharyngeal constrictor.
The pharyngeal tubercle is an insertion/anchor point for the pharyngeal raphe, not an origin for the middle constrictor muscle fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Table 12.11: Middle constrictor... Origin: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and lesser and greater cornua of hyoid bone.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During a physical examination, the clinician observes that the patient's soft palate fails to elevate symmetrically, and the gag reflex is diminished. However, the stylopharyngeus muscle remains functional. Which of the following describes the unique anatomical or neurological feature of the stylopharyngeus in contrast to the pharyngeal constrictors?
options: It is the only muscle responsible for opening the auditory tube.
It is the only pharyngeal muscle that does not insert into the pharyngeal raphe.
It is the only pharyngeal muscle derived from the second pharyngeal arch.
It is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
It is the only muscle that traverses the gap above the superior constrictor.
correctOption: It is the only pharyngeal muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve.
optionExplanations: The tensor veli palatini and levator veli palatini are primarily responsible for opening the auditory tube, not the stylopharyngeus.

The stylopharyngeus inserts into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall, whereas constrictors insert into the raphe, but this is not its most clinically unique feature compared to its nerve supply.
The stylopharyngeus is derived from the third pharyngeal arch, while the muscles of facial expression are derived from the second arch.
The stylopharyngeus is the exception in pharyngeal innervation; while others are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN X), it is supplied by CN IX.
The stylopharyngeus passes through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors (Gap 2), not the gap above the superior constrictor (Gap 1).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Nerve to the stylopharyngeus muscle. This is the sole muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve... The pharyngeal branch [of vagus] supplies all the muscles of the pharynx (except the stylopharyngeus)

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: As the auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube descends to enter the nasopharynx, it traverses which anatomical relationship relative to the pharyngeal muscles?
options: It emerges below the lower border of the inferior constrictor.
It runs deep to the cricopharyngeus muscle.
It passes over the upper border of the superior constrictor.
It pierces the fibers of the middle constrictor.
It passes between the middle and inferior constrictors.
correctOption: It passes over the upper border of the superior constrictor.
optionExplanations: The recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal vessels are the structures located below the lower border of the inferior constrictor.
The cricopharyngeus is the lowest part of the pharynx; the auditory tube is located much higher in the nasopharyngeal region.
The auditory tube, along with the levator veli palatini muscle and ascending pharyngeal artery, enters the pharynx by passing over the superior border of the superior constrictor muscle.
No major structures pierce the middle constrictor fibers; the stylopharyngeus and CN IX pass above it.
The gap between the middle and inferior constrictors transmits the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels, not the auditory tube.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1709 (Book Page): As the tube [auditory tube] descends, it passes over the upper border of the superior constrictor muscle.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle is functionally divided into two distinct components. Which of these parts is specifically responsible for acting as a sphincter at the lower end of the pharynx to prevent the entry of air into the esophagus?
options: Chondropharyngeus muscle
Cricopharyngeus muscle
Ceratopharyngeus muscle
Thyropharyngeus muscle
Hyopharyngeus muscle
correctOption: Cricopharyngeus muscle
optionExplanations: The 'chondropharyngeus' is a sub-division of the middle constrictor (attaching to the lesser cornu); it is not part of the inferior constrictor or the lower sphincter.
The cricopharyngeus is the horizontal, lower part of the inferior constrictor that remains tonically contracted to act as the upper esophageal sphincter, relaxing only during swallowing.
The 'ceratopharyngeus' is the part of the middle constrictor that attaches to the greater cornu of the hyoid bone, not the sphincteric part of the inferior constrictor.
The thyropharyngeus is the upper part of the inferior constrictor arising from the thyroid cartilage; its fibers are oblique and serve a propulsive rather than a sphincteric function.
The 'hyopharyngeus' is an older term sometimes used to describe the middle constrictor based on its hyoid attachment; it does not act as the pharyngoesophageal sphincter.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle. The fibers of the cricopharyngeus pass horizontally around the lowest and narrowest part of the pharynx and act as a sphincter.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 72-year-old male presents with chronic halitosis, regurgitation of undigested food, and a 'gurgling' sound in the neck during swallowing. Radiographic studies confirm a posterior herniation of the mucosa. This condition most likely involves a structural weakness in which specific anatomical area?
options: The thyrohyoid membrane at the site of internal laryngeal nerve penetration
The oropharyngeal isthmus at the palatoglossal arch
The pteryomaxillary fissure superior to the buccinator
The gap between the superior and middle constrictor muscles
The Killian dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
correctOption: The Killian dehiscence between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
optionExplanations: While the thyrohyoid membrane is a site of neurovascular entry, herniations here are rare compared to the classic posterior pharyngeal pouch at the Killian dehiscence.
The oropharyngeal isthmus is an anterior opening between the mouth and pharynx, not a site of posterior wall structural failure.
The pteryomaxillary fissure is a lateral skull feature and is not related to the posterior pharyngeal mucosal herniation seen in this clinical presentation.
The gap between the superior and middle constrictors transmits the stylopharyngeus muscle but is not the typical site for a Zenker's diverticulum.

The Killian dehiscence is a potential site of weakness on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the two parts of the inferior constrictor. Failure of the cricopharyngeus to relax increases pressure, forcing the mucosa out to form a pouch.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: How are the three pharyngeal constrictor muscles structurally arranged in relation to one another to form the pharyngeal wall?
options: They overlap such that the superior is internal to the middle, and the middle is internal to the inferior.
They overlap like shingles on a roof, with the inferior being the most internal.
They are placed side-by-side with no overlap.
The middle constrictor is the only one that completely encircles the pharynx.
They are separated by thick sheets of prevertebral fascia.
correctOption: They overlap such that the superior is internal to the middle, and the middle is internal to the inferior.
optionExplanations: The constrictors have a 'telescoping' or 'stacked cup' arrangement where the inferior constrictor is the most superficial/external, and the superior is the most deep/internal at the points of overlap.
This is incorrect because the 'shingle' arrangement is such that the lower muscle is external to the one above it, not internal.
The constrictors do not sit side-by-side; they overlap significantly to ensure a continuous muscular wall during the propulsive phase of swallowing.
All three constrictors are incomplete anteriorly (where they attach to bones/ligaments) and overlap each other; the middle is not unique in its encircling nature.
The constrictors are covered by buccopharyngeal fascia externally and are separated from the prevertebral fascia by the retropharyngeal space, not by fascia between the muscles themselves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles overlap each other so that the middle constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the superior constrictor and the inferior constrictor lies outside the lower part of the middle constrictor.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the structures passing through the 'Sinus of Morgagni', the gap located between the superior border of the superior pharyngeal constrictor and the base of the skull. Which structures should they name?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels
Stylopharyngeus and glossopharyngeal nerve
Salpingopharyngeus muscle and palatine tonsil
Auditory tube and levator veli palatini muscle
Recurrent laryngeal nerve and esophagus
correctOption: Auditory tube and levator veli palatini muscle
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels pass through the thyrohyoid membrane between the middle and inferior constrictors.
The stylopharyngeus and glossopharyngeal nerve pass through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors.
The salpingopharyngeus muscle is an internal longitudinal muscle of the pharynx; the palatine tonsil is located in the oropharynx between the pillars.
The gap above the superior constrictor (Sinus of Morgagni) is where the auditory (pharyngotympanic) tube and the levator veli palatini muscle enter the pharynx to reach the soft palate.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve and esophagus are located at the very bottom of the pharyngeal column, inferior to the cricopharyngeus muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): Table 12.11 [Superior constrictor]... Auditory tube, levator veli palatini, and ascending pharyngeal artery pass through the gap between the superior constrictor and the skull.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The pharyngeal constrictors contract in a coordinated sequence to propel a food bolus. Which mechanism describes the transition from the voluntary to the involuntary phase of deglutition?
options: Squeezing of the bolus into the pharynx by the palatoglossus
Elevation of the soft palate by the superior constrictor
Relaxation of the stylopharyngeus to lower the larynx
Adduction of the vocal folds by the cricothyroid muscle
Contraction of the cricopharyngeus to open the esophageal inlet
correctOption: Squeezing of the bolus into the pharynx by the palatoglossus
optionExplanations: Deglutition begins voluntarily with the tongue and palate. Once the palatoglossus squeezes the bolus into the pharynx, the involuntary contraction of the constrictors begins.
The soft palate is elevated by the levator veli palatini; while the superior constrictor pulls the posterior wall forward, it does not elevate the palate itself.
The stylopharyngeus contracts to elevate the larynx during swallowing, it does not relax to lower it until the phase is complete.
The cricothyroid muscle tenses the vocal folds but does not adduct them; adduction is primarily by the lateral cricoarytenoid muscles.
The cricopharyngeus must relax, not contract, to allow the bolus to enter the esophagus; this occurs at the end of the pharyngeal phase.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The palatoglossus muscles then squeeze the bolus backward into the pharynx. From this point onward, the process of swallowing becomes an involuntary act.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The inferior pharyngeal constrictor is unique in its dual-part composition. What is the functional significance of the cricopharyngeus portion during the physiological process of swallowing?
options: It acts as a sphincter to prevent air entry into the esophagus.
It tenses the vocal folds via the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
It elevates the larynx to meet the epiglottis.
It initiates the voluntary phase of deglutition.
It shortens the pharyngeal wall to facilitate bolus passage.
correctOption: It acts as a sphincter to prevent air entry into the esophagus.
optionExplanations: The cricopharyngeus acts as the upper esophageal sphincter, maintaining tonic contraction to prevent air from entering the esophagus during respiration.
The cricopharyngeus is a constrictor muscle; tensing the vocal folds is a function of intrinsic laryngeal muscles like the cricothyroid muscle.
Elevation of the larynx is primarily performed by longitudinal muscles like stylopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus, not the horizontal cricopharyngeus.
The voluntary phase is managed by the tongue (styloglossus/palatoglossus); the cricopharyngeus is involved in the involuntary phase.
Shortening of the pharyngeal wall is the role of the longitudinal muscles (salpingopharyngeus, palatopharyngeus, stylopharyngeus).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle. The fibers of the cricopharyngeus pass horizontally around the lowest and narrowest part of the pharynx and act as a sphincter... it is believed that the function of the cricopharyngeus is to prevent the entry of air into the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 72-year-old male presents with chronic dysphagia, halitosis, and a midline neck swelling that 'gurgles' during palpation. Based on the anatomy of the pharyngeal constrictors, what is the most likely pathophysiological site for this presentation?
options: Within the thyropharyngeus fibers of the inferior constrictor
In the gap between the middle and inferior constrictors
Deep to the pteryomandibular ligament
Above the superior constrictor near the auditory tube
Between the horizontal and oblique fibers of the inferior constrictor
correctOption: Between the horizontal and oblique fibers of the inferior constrictor
optionExplanations: The diverticulum does not occur through the thyropharyngeus itself, but rather at the site where its fibers meet the cricopharyngeus.
The gap between middle and inferior constrictors transmits the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery; it is not a common site for pharyngeal pouches.
The pterygomandibular ligament provides the anterior origin for the superior constrictor; hernias do not occur deep to this structure in the manner described.
The gap above the superior constrictor contains the levator veli palatini and auditory tube; hernia here is extremely rare compared to Zenker's diverticulum.

The clinical vignette describes Zenker’s diverticulum, which occurs at Killian's dehiscence—the weak zone between the thyropharyngeus (oblique) and cricopharyngeus (horizontal) fibers of the inferior constrictor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1754 (Book Page): A dimple marks this area in the lining mucous membrane... Should the cricopharyngeus fail to relax during swallowing, the internal pharyngeal pressure may rise and force the mucosa and submucosa of the dimple posteriorly, to produce a diverticulum.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Into which anatomical structure do all three pairs of pharyngeal constrictor muscles eventually insert?
options: The buccinator muscle
The median pharyngeal raphe
The prevertebral fascia
The body of the hyoid bone
The thyroid cartilage lamina
correctOption: The median pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The buccinator is connected to the superior constrictor via the pterygomandibular raphe, which is an origin point.
The pharyngeal raphe is a midline fibrous band extending from the pharyngeal tubercle to the esophagus where the constrictors of both sides meet.
The prevertebral fascia lies posterior to the pharynx, separated from it by the retropharyngeal space.
The hyoid bone is an origin for the middle constrictor, not an insertion for all three.
The thyroid cartilage is an origin for the inferior constrictor, not a common insertion.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe).

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The superior pharyngeal constrictor has a multi-focal origin anteriorly. Which of the following structures serves as a common attachment for both the superior constrictor muscle posteriorly and the buccinator muscle anteriorly?
options: Mylohyoid line of the mandible
Lateral pterygoid plate
Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)
Pharyngeal tubercle
Styloid process
correctOption: Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)
optionExplanations: While the superior constrictor attaches to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line, the mylohyoid line itself is primarily for the mylohyoid muscle; the buccinator attaches to the alveolar margins.
The superior constrictor attaches to the pterygoid hamulus (medial plate), but the lateral pterygoid plate is the site of origin for the pterygoid muscles of mastication.
The pterygomandibular raphe is a fibrous thickening of the buccopharyngeal fascia that serves as a bridge between the buccinator (anteriorly) and the superior pharyngeal constrictor (posteriorly).
The pharyngeal tubercle is the posterior midline insertion point (via the raphe) for the constrictors, not an anterior origin point shared with the buccinator.
The styloid process is the origin for the stylopharyngeus and styloglossus muscles, and provides the superior attachment for the stylohyoid ligament, but not the buccinator.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe): Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Structures in the Fourth Pharyngeal Gap
statement: Which neurovascular pair traverses the gap between the inferior constrictor muscle and the esophagus to enter the larynx from below?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery
Glossopharyngeal nerve and ascending pharyngeal artery
Recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal artery
Vagus nerve and common carotid artery
External laryngeal nerve and superior thyroid artery
correctOption: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal artery
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery traverse the gap between the middle and inferior constrictors, not the fourth gap.
The glossopharyngeal nerve enters the pharynx between the superior and middle constrictors.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve (becoming the inferior laryngeal nerve) and the inferior laryngeal artery enter the larynx by passing deep to the lower border of the inferior constrictor.
The vagus nerve and common carotid artery remain within the carotid sheath lateral to the pharyngeal constrictors.
The external laryngeal nerve travels on the superficial surface of the inferior constrictor, not below it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1789 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends the neck and becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve when it passes the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and enters the larynx. Page 1812 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve... is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient undergoes a neurological assessment following a brainstem stroke affecting the nucleus ambiguus. The physician observes that during the involuntary phase of swallowing, the bolus fails to move from the oropharynx into the esophagus despite normal tongue movements. This failure is most directly attributed to the paralysis of which sequence of muscles?
options: Tensor veli palatini and masseter
Superior, middle, and inferior constrictors
Digastric, stylohyoid, and mylohyoid
Genioglossus and hyoglossus
Orbicularis oris and buccinator
correctOption: Superior, middle, and inferior constrictors
optionExplanations: The tensor veli palatini tenses the soft palate, and the masseter is a muscle of mastication; neither provides the propulsive force in the pharynx.

The involuntary stage of swallowing requires a coordinated wave of contraction (peristalsis) involving the successive firing of the superior, middle, and then inferior constrictor muscles to drive the bolus downward.
These are suprahyoid muscles involved in elevating the hyoid bone and larynx; while important, they are not the primary propulsive circular muscles of the pharynx.
These are extrinsic tongue muscles responsible for the voluntary phase of deglutition (shaping and moving the bolus to the back of the mouth).
These are facial muscles involved in keeping the bolus within the oral cavity (the vestibule) but are not active in the pharyngeal phase of swallowing.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): [The bolus moves downward over the epiglottis, the closed entrance into the larynx, and reaches the lower part of the pharynx as the result of the successive contraction of the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles.]

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 68-year-old male presents with persistent dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food. A barium swallow reveals a posterior protrusion of the pharyngeal mucosa. This pathology most likely occurs through a potential weakness known as Killian's dehiscence. Between which two muscular components is this area located?
options: Middle constrictor and the thyrohyoid membrane
Cricopharyngeus and the circular esophagus
Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
Superior and middle constrictors
Superior constrictor and the buccinator
correctOption: Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
optionExplanations: This gap is traversed by the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery but is not termed Killian's dehiscence.
While the diverticulum hangs near the esophagus, the anatomical dehiscence itself is strictly within the parts of the inferior constrictor.
Killian's dehiscence is a weakness between the oblique fibers (thyropharyngeus) and horizontal fibers (cricopharyngeus) of the inferior constrictor; it is the site where Zenker's diverticulum forms.
The gap between superior and middle constrictors is a site for the stylopharyngeus muscle, not the typical location for pharyngeal pouches.
The superior constrictor and buccinator meet at the pterygomandibular raphe; this is not a site for mucosal herniation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A medical student is asked to identify the primary source of motor innervation for the pharyngeal constrictor muscles during a dissection. Which nerve provides the majority of these motor fibers via the pharyngeal plexus?
options: External laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Ansa cervicalis
Vagus nerve (CN X) carrying cranial accessory fibers
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
correctOption: Vagus nerve (CN X) carrying cranial accessory fibers
optionExplanations: The external laryngeal nerve only supplies the cricothyroid muscle and a portion of the inferior constrictor, but is not the primary plexus source.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is primarily sensory to the pharynx; its only motor contribution is to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
Ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid (strap) muscles of the neck, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The pharyngeal constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, with motor fibers originating from the cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) traveling with the vagus (CN X).
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue, with no motor contribution to the pharyngeal constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1679 (Book Page): Below the inferior ganglion, the cranial root of the accessory nerve joins the vagus nerve and distributes mainly in its pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Attachments of the Middle Pharyngeal Constrictor
statement: The middle pharyngeal constrictor is a fan-shaped muscle. Which of the following structures serves as its anterior point of attachment?
options: Cricoid cartilage
Mylohyoid line of the mandible
Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Pterygoid hamulus
Lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and hyoid bone
correctOption: Lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The cricoid cartilage is an attachment for the inferior constrictor (cricopharyngeus).
The mylohyoid line is an attachment for the superior constrictor and the mylohyoid muscle.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is an attachment for the thyropharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor.
The pterygoid hamulus is an attachment for the superior constrictor.
The middle constrictor originates from the hyoid bone (lesser and greater cornua) and the stylohyoid ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): [Table 12.11] Middle constrictor: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater cornua of the hyoid bone.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Gap between Middle and Inferior Constrictors
statement: During a surgical procedure on the neck, a surgeon inadvertently damages the nerve traversing the thyrohyoid membrane alongside the superior laryngeal artery. Which clinical deficit would most specifically relate to this anatomical gap between the middle and inferior constrictors?
options: Inability to abduct the vocal folds
Deviation of the uvula to the contralateral side
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle
Loss of the sensory limb of the cough reflex above the vocal folds
Loss of taste from the posterior third of the tongue
correctOption: Loss of the sensory limb of the cough reflex above the vocal folds
optionExplanations: Abduction of vocal folds is mediated by the posterior cricoarytenoid muscle, innervated by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, which enters the larynx below the inferior constrictor.
Uvular deviation is a sign of vagal motor trunk or pharyngeal plexus injury, affecting the levator veli palatini, not a localized sensory branch injury in the constrictor gap.
Cricothyroid paralysis is caused by damage to the external laryngeal nerve, which is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve but does not traverse this gap.
The internal laryngeal nerve traverses the gap between the middle and inferior constrictors. It is sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds; damage results in loss of the cough reflex.
Taste from the posterior third of the tongue is carried by the glossopharyngeal nerve, which traverses the gap between the superior and middle constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1755 (Book Page): Laryngopharynx (around the entrance into the larynx): Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve. [Note: This nerve passes through the gap between middle and inferior constrictors as per Figure 12.82].

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During the final phase of deglutition, what is the critical physiological role of the cricopharyngeus portion of the inferior constrictor muscle?
options: Elevation of the larynx to meet the epiglottic base
Dilation of the oropharyngeal isthmus for airway protection
Relaxation to allow the bolus to enter the esophagus
Closure of the rima glottidis via adduction of vocal processes
Contraction to shorten the pharyngeal wall and propel food
correctOption: Relaxation to allow the bolus to enter the esophagus
optionExplanations: Laryngeal elevation is performed by longitudinal muscles like the stylopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus, not the circular cricopharyngeus.
Dilation of the oropharyngeal isthmus involves the palatoglossus and is part of the oral phase, whereas the cricopharyngeus is part of the esophageal entry phase.
The cricopharyngeus acts as a tonic sphincter at the pharyngoesophageal junction; it must relax specifically to permit the food bolus to pass from the laryngopharynx into the esophagus.
Closure of the rima glottidis is an intrinsic laryngeal function involving the lateral cricoarytenoid and transverse arytenoid muscles, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
While the thyropharyngeus (upper part of the inferior constrictor) is propulsive, the cricopharyngeus is primarily sphincteric and must relax, not contract, for the bolus to pass.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Finally, the lower part of the pharyngeal wall (the cricopharyngeus muscle) relaxes, and the bolus enters the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 72-year-old male presents with chronic dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, and halitosis. A barium swallow reveals a posterior herniation of the pharyngeal mucosa. This pathology most likely occurs at a potential weakness known as Killian's dehiscence. Between which two muscular components is this area located?
options: The stylohyoid muscle and the posterior belly of the digastric
The thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor
The superior constrictor and the middle constrictor
The salpingopharyngeus and the palatopharyngeus muscles
The middle constrictor and the hyoid bone
correctOption: The thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor
optionExplanations: These are suprahyoid muscles and are not part of the posterior pharyngeal wall where Killian's dehiscence is located.
Correct. Killian's dehiscence is found between the oblique fibers (thyropharyngeus) and horizontal fibers (cricopharyngeus) of the inferior constrictor.
Gaps between constrictors (superior/middle) contain the stylopharyngeus but are not the primary site for Zenker's diverticulum.
These are longitudinal muscles of the pharynx and do not form the boundary of Killian's dehiscence.
This is a site of attachment for the middle constrictor (hyoid bone) but is not the site of the mucosal herniation described.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Into which structure do all three pharyngeal constrictor muscles insert posteriorly?
options: The pharyngeal raphe
The carotid sheath
The posterior longitudinal ligament
The prevertebral fascia
The bodies of the cervical vertebrae
correctOption: The pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal raphe is a midline fibrous cord on the posterior aspect of the pharynx that receives the insertion of all three pairs of constrictor muscles.
The carotid sheath is a lateral structure containing the neurovascular bundle of the neck and is not the posterior insertion point for these muscles.
The posterior longitudinal ligament is located inside the vertebral canal on the back of the vertebral bodies and has no connection to the pharyngeal wall.
The prevertebral fascia lies posterior to the pharynx and provides a surface over which the pharynx slides, but it is not an insertion point for the constrictors.
The constrictors do not attach to the cervical vertebrae; they are separated from them by the retropharyngeal space and prevertebral fascia.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle... down to the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which specific anatomical landmark serves as the anterior attachment for the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
options: Cricoid cartilage
Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Styloid process
Greater cornu of the hyoid bone
Pterygomandibular raphe
correctOption: Pterygomandibular raphe
optionExplanations: The cricoid cartilage serves as the origin for the cricopharyngeus part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is the origin for the thyropharyngeus part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.
The styloid process provides the origin for the stylopharyngeus, styloglossus, and stylohyoid muscles, but not the superior constrictor.
The greater cornu of the hyoid bone is the site of attachment for the middle pharyngeal constrictor, not the superior constrictor.
The pterygomandibular raphe is the primary anterior attachment for the superior constrictor, connecting it to the buccinator muscle.
