citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe) : Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Gap Between Superior and Middle Constrictors
statement: A patient suffers a deep penetrating injury to the upper neck. Clinical examination reveals a loss of general sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and a weakened gag reflex. The physician suspects damage to a nerve and a longitudinal muscle that enter the pharynx together through which specific gap?
options: Between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
Between the superior and middle constrictor muscles
Above the superior constrictor muscle
Below the inferior constrictor muscle
Between the middle and inferior constrictor muscles
correctOption: Between the superior and middle constrictor muscles
optionExplanations: This is the Killian dehiscence, a site of potential herniation, but it does not transmit the glossopharyngeal nerve or the stylopharyngeus.
The stylopharyngeus muscle and the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) enter the pharynx through the gap between the superior and middle constrictor muscles.
The gap above the superior constrictor transmits the auditory tube and levator veli palatini, but not the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The area below the inferior constrictor transmits the recurrent laryngeal nerve into the larynx, which is not associated with the gag reflex or posterior tongue sensation.
The gap between the middle and inferior constrictors is occupied by the internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1638 (Book Page): The stylopharyngeus muscle, the glossopharyngeal nerve... pass between the external and internal carotid arteries [and enter the pharynx]. Page 1756 (Book Page): The muscles in the wall of the pharynx are the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles... and the stylopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Nerve Relationships at the Inferior Constrictor
statement: During a thyroidectomy, a surgeon must be cautious while ligating the inferior thyroid artery due to its close relationship with a nerve that passes deep to the lower border of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. What is this nerve?
options: Superior laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The superior laryngeal nerve is the parent trunk of the internal and external laryngeal nerves and is located superiorly in the carotid triangle.
The external laryngeal nerve is related to the superior thyroid artery and the cricothyroid muscle.
The glossopharyngeal nerve is located much higher in the neck, near the superior and middle constrictors.
The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory and enters the pharynx well above the inferior constrictor via the thyrohyoid membrane.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve is closely related to the inferior thyroid artery and enters the larynx/pharynx region at the lower border of the inferior constrictor (cricopharyngeus).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends the neck and becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve when it passes the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and enters the larynx.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 60-year-old patient presents with a 'pharyngeal pouch' (Zenker's diverticulum). This condition arises because of a lack of coordination between the propulsive thyropharyngeus and the sphincteric cricopharyngeus. Regarding the cricopharyngeus, what is its unique anatomical feature compared to the other constrictors?
options: It originates from the thyroid cartilage oblique line
It is the only constrictor with longitudinal fibers
It is the only constrictor that does not insert into the pharyngeal raphe
It is the only constrictor supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve
It acts as a physiological sphincter and has horizontal fibers
correctOption: It acts as a physiological sphincter and has horizontal fibers
optionExplanations: The cricopharyngeus originates from the cricoid cartilage; the thyropharyngeus originates from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
All pharyngeal constrictors are essentially circular/oblique muscles; the longitudinal muscles are the stylopharyngeus, salpingopharyngeus, and palatopharyngeus.
While its fibers are horizontal and continuous, the text describes the constrictors collectively inserting into the raphe, though cricopharyngeus is specialized as a sphincter.
All constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus (CN XI via CN X); only stylopharyngeus is supplied by CN IX.

The cricopharyngeus is the lower part of the inferior constrictor; its fibers are horizontal (unlike the oblique thyropharyngeus) and it maintains a tonic contraction to act as the upper esophageal sphincter.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page): The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle. The fibers of the cricopharyngeus pass horizontally around the lowest and narrowest part of the pharynx and act as a sphincter.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Where do the three pharyngeal constrictor muscles primarily insert to form a unified muscular wall posteriorly?
options: The lateral margins of the esophagus
The posterior midline pharyngeal raphe
The stylohyoid ligament
The pterygomandibular raphe
The pharyngeal tubercle on the occipital bone
correctOption: The posterior midline pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The pharynx is continuous with the esophagus inferiorly, but the constrictors do not insert onto the lateral esophageal walls; they transition into its muscular layers.
The pharyngeal raphe is the central fibrous band where fibers from the superior, middle, and inferior constrictors meet posteriorly to complete the pharyngeal tube.
The stylohyoid ligament serves as an origin point for the middle constrictor, not an insertion point.
The pterygomandibular raphe is an origin point for the superior constrictor and buccinator, not the primary posterior insertion of all three constrictors.
The pharyngeal tubercle is the superior anchoring point for the pharyngeal raphe, but the muscles insert into the raphe itself rather than directly onto the bone across the entire posterior wall.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band ( pharyngeal raphe ) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone of the skull down to the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which specific anatomical structure provides the anterior attachment for the superior pharyngeal constrictor and also gives origin to the buccinator muscle?
options: The medial pterygoid plate
The pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)
The pharyngeal tubercle
The lesser cornu of the hyoid bone
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
correctOption: The pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor attaches to the hamulus of the medial pterygoid plate, but the pterygomandibular raphe is the shared structure with the buccinator.
The pterygomandibular raphe is a fibrous band extending from the pterygoid hamulus to the mylohyoid line, serving as a shared anterior origin for the superior constrictor and the buccinator.
The pharyngeal tubercle is a posterior insertion site on the skull base for the superior constrictor fibers, not an anterior origin shared with the buccinator.
The lesser cornu of the hyoid bone is an attachment site for the middle constrictor, not the superior constrictor.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is an origin for the thyropharyngeus (part of the inferior constrictor) and insertion for the sternothyroid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe) : Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which of the following describes the multi-step physiological interaction of the constrictor muscles during the involuntary phase of swallowing?
options: Elevation of the superior constrictor by the stylopharyngeus muscle.
Simultaneous contraction of all three constrictors to increase pressure.
Successive contraction of the superior, then middle, then inferior constrictors to propel the bolus.
Contraction of the cricopharyngeus followed by relaxation of the superior constrictor.
Relaxation of the pharyngeal raphe to allow pharyngeal expansion.
correctOption: Successive contraction of the superior, then middle, then inferior constrictors to propel the bolus.
optionExplanations: The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharyngeal wall as a whole, but it does not specifically elevate just the superior constrictor in a multi-step loop described this way.
Contraction is not simultaneous; it is a coordinated, sequential wave of peristalsis.
The involuntary phase involves a wave of contraction starting from the superior constrictor, moving to the middle, and finally the inferior constrictor to drive the bolus toward the esophagus.
The superior constrictor contracts first to move the bolus from the oropharynx; the cricopharyngeus is the last to relax to allow entry into the esophagus.
The pharyngeal raphe is a fixed fibrous insertion and does not 'relax' to expand the pharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): The bolus moves downward... reaches the lower part of the pharynx as the result of the successive contraction of the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient is undergoing surgery to remove a foreign body from the pharynx. The surgeon notes that the fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle differ from the rest of the inferior constrictor. What is the primary functional role of the cricopharyngeus during the resting state?
options: To act as a sphincter preventing air entry into the esophagus
To relax and allow the passage of the bolus into the stomach
To constrict the oropharyngeal isthmus
To propel the bolus into the esophagus via peristalsis
To elevate the larynx during speech
correctOption: To act as a sphincter preventing air entry into the esophagus
optionExplanations: The cricopharyngeus remains tonically contracted at rest to prevent air from being swallowed into the esophagus during respiration.
While it must relax during swallowing to allow food passage, its 'primary functional role' during the resting state is sphincteric contraction.
The oropharyngeal isthmus is constricted by the palatoglossal muscles, not the cricopharyngeus which is much lower in the pharynx.
The thyropharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor is propulsive, but the cricopharyngeus is sphincteric.
Laryngeal elevation is primarily performed by longitudinal muscles like the stylopharyngeus and thyrohyoid, not the cricopharyngeus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1757 (Book Page)-1758: The lower part of the inferior constrictor, which arises from the cricoid cartilage, is called the cricopharyngeus muscle... it acts as a sphincter. It is believed that the function of the cricopharyngeus is to prevent the entry of air into the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 72-year-old male presents with long-standing dysphagia and the regurgitation of undigested food. Barium swallow reveals a diverticulum projecting through a weakened area on the posterior pharyngeal wall. This weakness occurs between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus. What is the most likely pathophysiological cause?
options: Premature relaxation of the middle pharyngeal constrictor
Inability of the stylopharyngeus to elevate the larynx
Failure of the superior constrictor to pull the pharyngeal wall forward
Failure of the cricopharyngeus to relax during the process of swallowing
Congenital absence of the median pharyngeal raphe
correctOption: Failure of the cricopharyngeus to relax during the process of swallowing
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor is involved in propelling the bolus; its premature relaxation would not cause the localized high pressure needed for a diverticulum.
The stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx; its dysfunction leads to poor clearing of the bolus but not specifically a posterior diverticulum through Killian's gap.
The superior constrictor aids in closing the nasopharynx; its failure does not typically lead to diverticulum formation in the lower pharynx.
If the cricopharyngeus (the lower part of the inferior constrictor) fails to relax, intrapharyngeal pressure rises during swallowing, forcing the mucosa through Killian's Dehiscence.
While the raphe is the insertion for constrictors, its absence is not the clinical mechanism described for pharyngeal pouches.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1754 (Book Page): Should the cricopharyngeus fail to relax during swallowing, the internal pharyngeal pressure may rise and force the mucosa and submucosa of the dimple posteriorly, to produce a diverticulum.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The pharyngeal constrictor muscles are primarily innervated by the pharyngeal plexus. This plexus receives its motor fibers most significantly from which of the following cranial nerve components?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII)
Cranial root of the Accessory nerve (CN XI) via the Vagus
Mandibular division of the Trigeminal nerve (V3)
Spinal root of the Accessory nerve (CN XI)
correctOption: Cranial root of the Accessory nerve (CN XI) via the Vagus
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve is primarily sensory to the pharynx and motor only to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
The hypoglossal nerve is the motor supply for the muscles of the tongue, excluding the palatoglossus.
The pharyngeal constrictors are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus, specifically by fibers from the cranial accessory nerve that travel within the vagus nerve.
The mandibular nerve supplies the muscles of mastication and the tensor veli palatini, but not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The spinal root of the accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, not the pharyngeal muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1679 (Book Page): The cranial root of the accessory nerve joins the vagus nerve and distributes mainly in its pharyngeal and recurrent laryngeal branches.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which specific bony and ligamentous structures serve as the anterior attachments for the middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
options: Lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone
Pterygoid hamulus and pterygomandibular raphe
Styloid process and the pharyngeal tubercle
Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage and cricoid cartilage
Medial pterygoid plate and the mandible
correctOption: Lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor is unique in its hyoid bone attachment, specifically the greater and lesser cornua and the stylohyoid ligament.
These are the origins of the superior constrictor muscle.
The styloid process is an origin for the stylopharyngeus; the pharyngeal tubercle is a posterior insertion/base point, not an anterior origin.
These are the origins of the inferior constrictor muscle.
The medial pterygoid plate and mandible are associated with the superior constrictor, not the middle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Table 12.11: Middle constrictor – Origin: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater cornua of the hyoid bone.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During the involuntary phase of deglutition, the nasopharynx is sealed from the oropharynx. Which mechanism involves the pharyngeal constrictors in this process?
options: Depression of the hyoid bone by the middle constrictor muscle
Elevation of the soft palate and pulling forward of the posterior pharyngeal wall by the superior constrictor
Approximation of the aryepiglottic folds by the inferior constrictor
Contraction of the cricopharyngeus to prevent air entry
Relaxation of the middle constrictor to accommodate the bolus
correctOption: Elevation of the soft palate and pulling forward of the posterior pharyngeal wall by the superior constrictor
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor originates from the hyoid bone but its role is propulsive, not depressing the bone to seal the airway.
Sealing the nasopharynx requires the elevation of the soft palate and the simultaneous contraction of the superior constrictor to pull the posterior pharyngeal wall forward.
Closing the laryngeal inlet involves intrinsic laryngeal muscles, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The cricopharyngeus prevents air from entering the esophagus during breathing, but it is not involved in nasopharyngeal closure.
The middle and inferior constrictors contract successively to propel the bolus, they do not relax to seal the nasopharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The nasal part of the pharynx is now shut off from the oral part of the pharynx by the elevation of the soft palate, the pulling forward of the posterior wall of the pharynx by the upper fibers of the superior constrictor muscle...

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient undergoes a procedure where a foreign body is removed from the piriform fossa. To avoid neurovascular injury during the maneuver, the clinician must remember that the internal laryngeal nerve passes into the larynx in the interval between which muscles?
options: Cricopharyngeus and Esophagus
Thyrohyoid and Sternothyroid
Stylopharyngeus and Salpingopharyngeus
Superior and Middle constrictors
Middle and Inferior constrictors
correctOption: Middle and Inferior constrictors
optionExplanations: The gap below the cricopharyngeus contains the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
Thyrohyoid and sternothyroid are infrahyoid strap muscles superficial to the pharynx.
Stylopharyngeus and salpingopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles located internally to the constrictor layer.
The gap between the superior and middle constrictors contains the stylopharyngeus and CN IX.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the piriform fossa and enters the larynx by passing through the gap between the middle and inferior constrictor muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1781 (Book Page): The superior laryngeal vessels and the internal laryngeal nerve pierce the [thyrohyoid] membrane on each side... [Page 1756 (Book Page)] The three constrictor muscles overlap each other so that the middle constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the superior constrictor and the inferior constrictor lies outside the lower part of the middle constrictor.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 34-year-old male presents with persistent dysphagia. During an endoscopic examination, a small mucosal protrusion is noted in the 'Killian dehiscence' area of the posterior pharynx. This potential anatomical weakness is located between which two specific muscle components?
options: Stylopharyngeus and superior constrictor muscles
Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor
Superior and middle constrictor muscles
Middle and inferior constrictor muscles
Salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus muscles
correctOption: Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor
optionExplanations: The stylopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle that enters the pharyngeal wall between the superior and middle constrictors; it does not contribute to the inferior posterior wall anatomy associated with this dehiscence.

Killian’s dehiscence is a triangular area of relative weakness in the posterior wall of the pharynx, specifically located between the oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus and the horizontal fibers of the cricopharyngeus (both parts of the inferior constrictor). Increased intrapharyngeal pressure can lead to the formation of a Zenker’s diverticulum here.
The gap between the superior and middle constrictors transmits the glossopharyngeal nerve and the stylopharyngeus muscle; it is not the site of Killian’s dehiscence.
The gap between the middle and inferior constrictors is traversed by the internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal vessels, rather than serving as the site for this specific diverticulum.
The salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles of the pharynx that elevate it during swallowing; they do not form the boundaries of the posterior pharyngeal dehiscence.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which of the following describes the correct functional and anatomical arrangement of the pharyngeal constrictor muscles regarding their posterior insertions?
options: They overlap such that the superior is outermost
The inferior constrictor is covered posteriorly by the middle constrictor
They all insert into a median fibrous band termed the pharyngeal raphe
They attach to the transverse processes of cervical vertebrae
They insert independently into the prevertebral fascia
correctOption: They all insert into a median fibrous band termed the pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The overlapping pattern is 'bottom-over-top': the inferior constrictor is the most superficial (outermost) at its overlap with the middle, and the middle is outermost at its overlap with the superior.
Anatomically, the inferior constrictor lies on the outside (superficial to) the lower part of the middle constrictor, not vice versa.
All three pairs of pharyngeal constrictors meet in the midline posteriorly at a common fibrous insertion called the pharyngeal raphe, which hangs from the pharyngeal tubercle of the skull.
The pharynx is separated from the cervical vertebrae by the retropharyngeal space; the muscles do not attach to the vertebral processes.
The pharyngeal constrictors are separated from the prevertebral fascia by the retropharyngeal space; they do not insert into it.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone of the skull down to the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The superior pharyngeal constrictor shares a continuous point of attachment with which muscle of the face, facilitating coordinated movement during swallowing and chewing?
options: Orbicularis oris via the labial frenulum
Medial pterygoid via the lateral pterygoid plate
Masseter via the zygomatic arch
Temporalis via the coronoid process
Buccinator via the pterygomandibular raphe
correctOption: Buccinator via the pterygomandibular raphe
optionExplanations: The orbicularis oris is the sphincter of the mouth; while it blends with buccinator fibers, it does not directly attach to the pharyngeal constrictors.
The medial pterygoid muscle originates from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and inserts on the mandible; it does not share the raphe with the superior constrictor.
The masseter is a muscle of mastication that attaches to the zygomatic arch and the mandible; it has no direct attachment to the pharyngeal constrictors.
The temporalis is a large muscle of mastication inserting on the coronoid process of the mandible, unrelated to the pharyngeal wall attachments.
The pterygomandibular raphe (or ligament) acts as a bridge; the buccinator muscle attaches to its anterior border, and the superior pharyngeal constrictor attaches to its posterior border.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): Table 12.11 [Superior constrictor]... Origin: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, alveolar process of mandible... Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe): Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: While the primary innervation of the pharyngeal constrictors is via the pharyngeal plexus, the inferior constrictor receives additional motor supply. Which nerve provides this supplementary innervation to the inferior constrictor?
options: External laryngeal nerve
Greater petrosal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
correctOption: External laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The inferior constrictor (specifically the thyropharyngeus part) is partially supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, which also supplies the cricothyroid muscle.
The greater petrosal nerve is a branch of the facial nerve providing parasympathetic secretomotor fibers to the lacrimal gland, not motor supply to pharynx muscles.
The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds and does not provide motor supply to constrictors.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides motor supply only to the stylopharyngeus muscle among the pharyngeal muscles.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) supplies the intrinsic and extrinsic muscles of the tongue, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Table 12.11: Inferior constrictor... Nerve Supply: Pharyngeal plexus and external laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient undergoes a deep neck dissection. The surgeon identifies a muscle originating from the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone. If this muscle is damaged, which functional deficit is most likely?
options: Weakness in the middle phase of the pharyngeal pump
Loss of taste from the anterior tongue
Paralysis of the tensor tympani
Inability to tense the vocal folds
Failure of the upper esophageal sphincter to close
correctOption: Weakness in the middle phase of the pharyngeal pump
optionExplanations: The description identifies the middle constrictor. Its damage would weaken the sequential peristaltic-like contraction (pharyngeal pump) needed to move the bolus through the oropharynx.
Taste from the anterior tongue is carried by the chorda tympani; it has no relation to the pharyngeal constrictor muscles.
The tensor tympani is an ear muscle supplied by the mandibular nerve and has no origin on the hyoid bone or stylohyoid ligament.
Tensing the vocal folds is the function of the cricothyroid muscle, which is not attached to the stylohyoid ligament.
The upper esophageal sphincter is primarily the cricopharyngeus, which is part of the inferior constrictor, not the middle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): [The middle constrictor muscle... Arises from the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and from the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone... It inserts into the pharyngeal raphe].

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a pharyngeal pouch (Zenker's diverticulum). This condition typically results from a failure of the cricopharyngeus muscle to relax, leading to increased pressure in which specific anatomical area?
options: The piriform fossa
The vallecula
The pharyngeal recess
The oropharyngeal isthmus
Killian's dehiscence
correctOption: Killian's dehiscence
optionExplanations: The piriform fossa is a lateral mucosal depression on either side of the laryngeal inlet, not the site of the posterior midline weakness involved in diverticula.
The vallecula is a depression between the epiglottis and the tongue, unrelated to the lower pharyngeal constrictor junctions.
The pharyngeal recess is located in the nasopharynx behind the tubal elevation, whereas pharyngeal pouches occur in the laryngopharynx.
The oropharyngeal isthmus is the opening between the mouth and the pharynx, far superior to the site of pharyngeal pouch formation.
Killian's dehiscence is a weak area between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus parts of the inferior constrictor; high pressure here forces the mucosa through the muscle to form a pouch.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The pharyngeal wall is characterized by an overlapping arrangement of the constrictor muscles. Which of the following correctly describes this structural relationship?
options: The middle constrictor lies on the outside of the inferior constrictor.
All three muscles meet at a single edge without overlapping.
The inferior constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the middle constrictor.
The superior constrictor lies on the outside of the thyropharyngeus.
The superior constrictor lies on the outside of the middle constrictor.
correctOption: The inferior constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the middle constrictor.
optionExplanations: The middle constrictor is overlapped by the inferior constrictor, meaning the inferior constrictor is the more superficial (outer) muscle in that region.
The muscles show significant overlap, which provides structural integrity to the pharyngeal wall during the high pressures of swallowing.
The pharyngeal constrictors overlap like flower pots; the middle overlaps the superior, and the inferior overlaps the middle from the outside.
The thyropharyngeus is a part of the inferior constrictor, which is the outermost muscle, while the superior constrictor is the innermost.
The superior constrictor is the innermost layer; the middle constrictor actually overlaps its lower portion externally.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles overlap each other so that the middle constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the superior constrictor and the inferior constrictor lies outside the lower part of the middle constrictor.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle takes part of its origin from which landmark on the mandible?
options: The posterior end of the mylohyoid line
The mental spine
The angle of the mandible
The condyloid process
The coronoid process
correctOption: The posterior end of the mylohyoid line
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor attaches to the pterygomandibular raphe, which is itself anchored to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line on the mandible.
The mental spines (genial tubercles) provide origin for the genioglossus and geniohyoid muscles, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The angle of the mandible is the site for the attachment of the masseter (laterally) and medial pterygoid (medially).
The condyloid process (head and neck) of the mandible articulates at the TMJ and provides attachment for the lateral pterygoid muscle.
The coronoid process is the insertion site for the temporalis muscle, not an origin for the pharyngeal constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe) : Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which specific anatomical structure is identified as traversing the gap between the middle and inferior constrictor muscles of the pharynx?
options: Ascending pharyngeal artery
Stylopharyngeus muscle
Internal laryngeal nerve
Levator veli palatini muscle
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The ascending pharyngeal artery is found above the superior constrictor or on the outer pharyngeal wall, not in the gap between the middle and inferior.
The stylopharyngeus muscle traverses the gap between the superior and middle constrictors.
The internal laryngeal nerve (along with the superior laryngeal vessels) traverses the gap between the middle and inferior constrictors to enter the larynx.
The levator veli palatini muscle passes above the superior constrictor muscle.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes into the larynx beneath the lower border of the inferior constrictor (cricopharyngeus).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1781 (Book Page): The superior laryngeal vessels and the internal laryngeal nerve pierce the membrane on each side. [Note: This membrane is the thyrohyoid membrane which occupies the space where the middle and inferior constrictors meet].

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During a complicated neck dissection, a patient suffers an injury to the nerve located in the interval between the superior and middle pharyngeal constrictors. What clinical finding would most likely be observed post-operatively?
options: Deviation of the tongue to the side of the lesion on protrusion
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle and inability to tense vocal cords
Loss of sensation in the laryngeal vestibule above the vocal folds
Inability to elevate the soft palate during speech
Loss of taste and general sensation on the posterior third of the tongue
correctOption: Loss of taste and general sensation on the posterior third of the tongue
optionExplanations: Tongue deviation is a sign of Hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) injury, which follows a different course in the submandibular region.
The cricothyroid is supplied by the external laryngeal nerve, which does not pass between the superior and middle constrictors.
Laryngeal sensation above the vocal folds is provided by the internal laryngeal nerve, which passes between the middle and inferior constrictors.
Soft palate elevation is primarily the function of the levator veli palatini (CN X via pharyngeal plexus), not the glossopharyngeal nerve.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) passes between the superior and middle constrictors. Injury would cause loss of taste and general sensation on the posterior third of the tongue and loss of the gag reflex.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1676 (Book Page): Glossopharyngeal Nerve (CN IX)... leaves the skull by passing through the jugular foramen... descends through the upper part of the neck to the back of the tongue. Page 1730 (Book Page): Posterior third: Glossopharyngeal nerve (general sensation and taste). [Gap context]: CN IX travels through the gap between superior and middle constrictors.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 65-year-old male presents with chronic halitosis, dysphagia, and the regurgitation of undigested food while bending over. A barium swallow reveals a posterior protrusion of the mucosa at the level of the C6 vertebra, between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus. What is the name of this anatomically weak area?
options: Vallecula
Piriform fossa
Oropharyngeal isthmus
Pharyngeal recess
Killian dehiscence
correctOption: Killian dehiscence
optionExplanations: The vallecula is a depression between the epiglottis and the posterior third of the tongue, involved in the initial stages of swallowing.
The piriform fossa is a depression in the laryngopharynx on either side of the laryngeal inlet, often where foreign bodies lodge, but not the site of diverticulum formation.
The oropharyngeal isthmus is the opening between the oral cavity and the pharynx, bounded by the palatoglossal arches.
The pharyngeal recess is a depression in the nasopharyngeal wall behind the tubal elevation, unrelated to inferior constrictor weakness.
Killian's dehiscence is the specific weak point in the inferior constrictor where the oblique fibers of thyropharyngeus meet the horizontal fibers of cricopharyngeus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During a barium swallow study, the radiologist observes the bolus passing from the oropharynx to the esophagus. Which of the following describes the correct sequence and anatomical arrangement of the pharyngeal constrictor overlaps?
options: Superior overlaps Middle; Middle overlaps Inferior
Middle overlaps both Superior and Inferior
The muscles are arranged edge-to-edge with no overlap
Inferior overlaps Middle; Middle overlaps Superior
Superior overlaps both Middle and Inferior
correctOption: Inferior overlaps Middle; Middle overlaps Superior
optionExplanations: This is incorrect; the sequence of overlap is from inferior to superior on the external surface (like stacked cups).
The middle constrictor only overlaps the superior; it is itself overlapped by the inferior constrictor.
The muscles are not edge-to-edge; they overlap to ensure the pharyngeal wall is continuous and strong during the high pressures of swallowing.
Anatomically, each lower constrictor overlaps the one above it on its external surface. Thus, the middle constrictor is outside the superior, and the inferior is outside the middle.
The superior constrictor is the innermost of the three at its lower border.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles overlap each other so that the middle constrictor lies on the outside of the lower part of the superior constrictor and the inferior constrictor lies outside the lower part of the middle constrictor.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle is characterized by its fan-shaped fibers that converge posteriorly on the pharyngeal raphe. From which of the following structures does this muscle primarily originate?
options: Stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone
Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
Cricoid cartilage and its arch
Pterygomandibular raphe and pterygoid hamulus
correctOption: Stylohyoid ligament and the cornua of the hyoid bone
optionExplanations: The middle pharyngeal constrictor originates from the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and both the greater and lesser cornua (horns) of the hyoid bone.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is the origin for the thyropharyngeus part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor muscle.
The pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone is the superior attachment point for the pharyngeal raphe, which is an insertion site, not an origin for the middle constrictor.
The cricoid cartilage is the origin for the cricopharyngeus part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor, which acts as a sphincter at the esophagus.
The pterygomandibular raphe and pterygoid hamulus are the points of origin for the superior pharyngeal constrictor, which also takes origin from the mandible.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): Table 12.11 [Middle constrictor]... Origin: Lower part of stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater cornua of hyoid bone.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: What is the primary posterior insertion site and structural completion point for all three pairs of pharyngeal constrictor muscles?
options: Bodies of the cervical vertebrae
Styloid process
Pharyngeal tubercle and pharyngeal raphe
Prevertebral fascia
Epiglottis
correctOption: Pharyngeal tubercle and pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal constrictors do not attach to the vertebral bodies; the prevertebral muscles occupy that space.
The styloid process is an origin for the stylopharyngeus, not an insertion for the constrictors.
The pharyngeal raphe is the midline insertion for all constrictors, anchored superiorly to the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone.
The pharyngeal wall is separated from the prevertebral fascia by the retropharyngeal space; it does not insert into it.
The epiglottis is a laryngeal cartilage and is not an insertion point for the pharyngeal constrictor muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band ( pharyngeal raphe ) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone of the skull down to the esophagus

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Recurrent Laryngeal Nerve and Inferior Constrictor
statement: A 45-year-old female undergoes a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goiter. Post-operatively, she experiences hoarseness. This is most likely due to injury to a nerve that traverses the neck in which anatomical relationship to the pharyngeal constrictors?
options: It passes above the superior constrictor to enter the auditory tube
It ascends in the groove between the trachea and esophagus, passing beneath the inferior constrictor
It pierce the thyrohyoid membrane between the middle and inferior constrictors
It passes between the superior and middle constrictors alongside the stylopharyngeus
It loops around the greater cornu of the hyoid bone near the middle constrictor
correctOption: It ascends in the groove between the trachea and esophagus, passing beneath the inferior constrictor
optionExplanations: This describes the levator veli palatini and auditory tube relationship to the skull base, not a laryngeal nerve.

Hoarseness after thyroidectomy is often due to recurrent laryngeal nerve injury; this nerve ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove and passes into the larynx beneath the inferior border of the inferior constrictor.
This is the internal laryngeal nerve, which is sensory above the vocal cords; its injury does not cause the characteristic motor hoarseness (vocal cord paralysis).
This describes the glossopharyngeal nerve, which is not typically injured in thyroid surgery to cause hoarseness.
The hypoglossal nerve loops around vessels and enters the tongue; it is not the cause of hoarseness.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends the neck and becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve when it passes the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and enters the larynx... The terminal branches of the inferior thyroid artery on each side are related to the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During the involuntary stage of deglutition, a specific coordination between the soft palate and the pharyngeal walls occurs to seal the nasopharynx. Which pharyngeal muscle activity is essential for this process?
options: Contraction of the stylopharyngeus to shorten the pharyngeal raphe
Elevation of the larynx by the inferior constrictor muscle
Relaxation of the middle constrictor to accommodate the bolus
Pulling forward of the posterior pharyngeal wall by the upper fibers of the superior constrictor
Contraction of the cricopharyngeus to widen the esophageal inlet
correctOption: Pulling forward of the posterior pharyngeal wall by the upper fibers of the superior constrictor
optionExplanations: While the stylopharyngeus elevates the pharynx, it does not participate in the specific seal of the nasopharynx against the soft palate.
The inferior constrictor does not elevate the larynx; it propels the bolus and acts as a sphincter.
The middle constrictor contracts, not relaxes, in a successive manner to propel the bolus downward.
To seal the nasopharynx, the soft palate is elevated and the superior constrictor pulls the posterior pharyngeal wall forward to meet it.
The cricopharyngeus must relax, not contract, to allow the bolus to enter the esophagus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The nasal part of the pharynx is now shut off from the oral part of the pharynx by the elevation of the soft palate, the pulling forward of the posterior wall of the pharynx by the upper fibers of the superior constrictor muscle

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Gap between Middle and Inferior Constrictors
statement: In the anatomical arrangement of the pharynx, the gap between the middle and inferior constrictor muscles is a critical passage for neurovascular structures. Which structure pierces the thyrohyoid membrane in this gap to provide sensory innervation to the larynx above the vocal folds?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Superior laryngeal nerve (main trunk)
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve passes between the superior and middle constrictors to reach the tongue and pharyngeal wall, not through the thyrohyoid membrane.

The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, pierces the thyrohyoid membrane (the space between the middle and inferior constrictors) to provide sensation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx below the lower border of the inferior constrictor/cricopharyngeus, not through the thyrohyoid membrane.
The external laryngeal nerve is motor to the cricothyroid muscle and remains on the exterior of the larynx; it does not pierce the thyrohyoid membrane.
The superior laryngeal nerve is the parent trunk that divides into the internal and external branches; it is the specific internal branch that pierces the membrane.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1781 (Book Page): Thyrohyoid membrane: This connects the upper margin of the thyroid cartilage to the hyoid bone... The superior laryngeal vessels and the internal laryngeal nerve pierce the membrane on each side.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which of the following describes a correct anterior attachment for the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
options: Pterygoid hamulus
Lesser cornu of the hyoid bone
Stylohyoid ligament
Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
Cricoid cartilage
correctOption: Pterygoid hamulus
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor originates from the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, and the mylohyoid line of the mandible.
The lesser cornu of the hyoid bone is an attachment point for the middle constrictor.
The stylohyoid ligament is an origin for the middle constrictor.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is an origin for the inferior constrictor (specifically the thyropharyngeus).
The cricoid cartilage is an attachment point for the inferior constrictor (specifically the cricopharyngeus).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Table 12.11: Superior constrictor – Origin: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, posterior end of mylohyoid line of mandible.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Differential Anatomy of Pharyngeal Wall Swellings
statement: A 58-year-old patient presents with a fever and a significant midline bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall. A clinician must distinguish between a retropharyngeal abscess and an abscess from cervical tuberculous osteomyelitis. Which anatomical fact regarding the pharyngeal environment is most helpful?
options: A tuberculous abscess always ruptures into the pharyngeal cavity, unlike a retropharyngeal abscess.
The investing layer of deep cervical fascia is the primary barrier for retropharyngeal infections.
The retropharyngeal nodes are located within the substance of the superior constrictor muscle.
The retropharyngeal abscess lies behind the prevertebral fascia, while the tuberculous abscess is in the visceral space.
The tuberculous abscess is limited in front by the prevertebral fascia, forming a midline swelling behind the pharynx.
correctOption: The tuberculous abscess is limited in front by the prevertebral fascia, forming a midline swelling behind the pharynx.
optionExplanations: Retropharyngeal abscesses (from nodes) often rupture into the pharynx, while tuberculous ones tend to track laterally into the neck.
The prevertebral fascia, not the investing fascia, is the critical layer separating these two types of posterior pharyngeal swellings.
Retropharyngeal nodes are in the retropharyngeal space, between the constrictor's buccopharyngeal fascia and the prevertebral fascia.
The retropharyngeal abscess lies in the retropharyngeal space (in front of the prevertebral fascia), whereas the tuberculous abscess is behind it.
Tuberculous pus from the vertebrae is trapped behind the prevertebral fascia, creating a midline bulge against the pharyngeal constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1755 (Book Page): Pus arising from tuberculosis of the upper cervical vertebrae is limited in front by the prevertebral layer of deep fascia. A midline swelling is formed and bulges forward in the posterior wall of the pharynx.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The cricopharyngeus muscle is unique among the pharyngeal constrictors for its horizontal fiber orientation and continuous tone. What is the physiological purpose of its relaxation during deglutition?
options: To permit the bolus to enter the esophagus from the pharynx
To prevent the soft palate from reaching the posterior pharyngeal wall
To facilitate the elevation of the hyoid bone
To allow the laryngeal inlet to close more tightly
To allow air to fill the pharynx for vocalization
correctOption: To permit the bolus to enter the esophagus from the pharynx
optionExplanations: The cricopharyngeus must relax at the end of the pharyngeal phase to allow the food bolus to pass from the laryngopharynx into the esophagus.
The soft palate reaching the posterior wall (Passavant's ridge) is assisted by the superior constrictor, not related to cricopharyngeus relaxation.
Elevation of the hyoid bone is performed by the suprahyoid and longitudinal pharyngeal muscles, not by the relaxation of the cricopharyngeus.
Closing the laryngeal inlet is the function of the oblique arytenoid and aryepiglottic muscles, not the relaxation of the cricopharyngeus.
Vocalization requires air to pass through the larynx, not the esophagus; the cricopharyngeus actually prevents air from entering the esophagus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): Finally, the lower part of the pharyngeal wall (the cricopharyngeus muscle) relaxes, and the bolus enters the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The pharyngeal constrictor muscles are characterized by their overlapping structure and shared insertion. Where do the fibers of all three constrictors primarily terminate posteriorly?
options: The pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
The buccopharyngeal membrane
The prevertebral fascia
The body of the C6 vertebra
The pharyngeal raphe
correctOption: The pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone is the superior attachment point for the pharyngeal raphe, not the insertion site for all muscle fibers.
The buccopharyngeal membrane is an embryological structure that separates the stomodeum from the foregut and disappears early in development.
The prevertebral fascia lies posterior to the pharynx, separated by the retropharyngeal space; the muscles do not insert into it.
The C6 vertebra marks the level where the pharynx becomes continuous with the esophagus, but it is not a muscle insertion site.
The pharyngeal raphe is the common midline fibrous insertion for the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle... down to the esophagus

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Anatomical Attachments of the Superior Pharyngeal Constrictor
statement: A student is identifying the origin of the superior constrictor muscle during a cadaveric dissection. Which of the following anatomical structures serves as a primary site of attachment for this muscle?
options: The stylohyoid ligament and the greater cornu of the hyoid bone
The oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage
The cricoid cartilage and the cricotracheal ligament
The pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe
The pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone
correctOption: The pterygoid hamulus and the pterygomandibular raphe
optionExplanations: The stylohyoid ligament and hyoid bone are the characteristic origins for the middle constrictor muscle.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is the attachment site for the inferior constrictor, not the superior.
The cricoid cartilage serves as the origin for the cricopharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor muscle.
The superior constrictor originates from the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, and the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible.
The pharyngeal tubercle is the site where the pharyngeal raphe (the common insertion for all constrictors) is attached to the skull, not the origin of the superior constrictor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe): Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Structures in the Lower Pharyngeal Gap
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with a voice that is 'hoarse' following a thyroidectomy. The surgeon suspects injury to a nerve that traverses the gap below the inferior pharyngeal constrictor. Which nerve and its associated artery are found in this location?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve and ascending pharyngeal artery
Superior laryngeal nerve and superior thyroid artery
Recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal artery
External laryngeal nerve and superior thyroid artery
Internal laryngeal nerve and superior laryngeal artery
correctOption: Recurrent laryngeal nerve and inferior laryngeal artery
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve is much higher, entering between the superior and middle constrictors.
The superior laryngeal nerve divides into internal and external branches before reaching the constrictors; it is not a content of the lower gap.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve (and the inferior laryngeal artery) passes under the lower border of the inferior constrictor (specifically the cricopharyngeus) to enter the larynx.
The external laryngeal nerve is found on the external surface of the inferior constrictor, supplying the cricothyroid, but does not pass 'below' the muscle into the larynx with an artery.
The internal laryngeal nerve passes through the thyrohyoid membrane between the middle and inferior constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1789 (Book Page): The recurrent laryngeal nerve ascends the neck and becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve when it passes the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage and enters the larynx.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: While assessing a patient with a known lesion of the pharyngeal plexus, the examiner notes a failure of the upper esophageal sphincter to relax. This indicates dysfunction in the cricopharyngeus muscle. What is the specific neurological origin of the motor fibers supplying this muscle?
options: Cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) via the vagus nerve
Spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) via the cervical plexus
Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3)
Cervical sympathetic trunk
Main trunk of the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)
correctOption: Cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) via the vagus nerve
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal constrictors, including the cricopharyngeus, are supplied by the pharyngeal plexus. The motor component of this plexus is derived from the cranial part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) which joins the vagus nerve (CN X).
The spinal part of the accessory nerve (CN XI) supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The mandibular nerve (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication and the tensor veli palatini, but not the pharyngeal constrictor muscles.
The sympathetic trunk provides vasomotor fibers to the pharyngeal wall but does not provide the primary motor supply for the constrictor muscles.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory fibers to the pharyngeal plexus and motor fibers *only* to the stylopharyngeus muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1679 (Book Page): Pharyngeal branch contains nerve fibers from the cranial part of the accessory nerve. This branch joins the pharyngeal plexus and supplies all the muscles of the pharynx (except the stylopharyngeus)... Page 1756 (Book Page): Table 12.11 [All Constrictors]... Nerve supply: Pharyngeal plexus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: During the final, involuntary phase of deglutition, a coordinated wave of contraction occurs in the constrictor muscles. Toward which midline structure do all three pairs of pharyngeal constrictors converge and insert?
options: The pharyngeal tubercle of the sphenoid bone
The cervical vertebral bodies (C1-C6)
The posterior pharyngeal raphe
The prevertebral fascia
The thyroid lamina
correctOption: The posterior pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal tubercle is on the basilar part of the occipital bone, not the sphenoid bone.
The pharyngeal wall is separated from the vertebral bodies by the retropharyngeal space and prevertebral fascia; it does not insert into the bones.
Correct. The pharyngeal raphe is the common midline insertion point for the circular fibers of all three constrictor muscles.
The prevertebral fascia lies posterior to the pharynx; the constrictors are covered by buccopharyngeal fascia, but they insert into the raphe, not the prevertebral fascia.
The thyroid lamina is an origin for the inferior constrictor, not a common insertion point for all constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone...

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Anatomical Attachments of the Superior Pharyngeal Constrictor
statement: An anatomist is demonstrating the anterior attachments of the superior constrictor muscle of the pharynx. Which structure serves as the primary origin for the uppermost part of this muscle?
options: The lateral surface of the cricoid cartilage
The styloid process of the temporal bone
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
The lesser cornu of the hyoid bone
The pterygoid hamulus and pterygomandibular raphe
correctOption: The pterygoid hamulus and pterygomandibular raphe
optionExplanations: The lateral surface of the cricoid cartilage gives origin to the cricopharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor.
The styloid process gives origin to the stylopharyngeus muscle, which is a longitudinal muscle of the pharynx, not a constrictor.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is a site of origin for the thyropharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor muscle.
The lesser cornu of the hyoid bone serves as an attachment point for the middle constrictor, not the superior constrictor.
The superior constrictor originates from the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, the mandible, and the side of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): Superior constrictor... Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, side of tongue, mandible

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Anatomy of the Pharyngeal Gaps and Cranial Nerve IX
statement: A 45-year-old patient presents with severe difficulty swallowing after a surgery involving the lateral wall of the oropharynx. Physical examination reveals a loss of the gag reflex on the affected side and loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue. The surgeon suspects a nerve was damaged in the gap between two constrictor muscles. Which gap and nerve are involved?
options: The gap above the superior constrictor; Lesser petrosal nerve
The gap between the superior and middle constrictors; Glossopharyngeal nerve
The gap between the middle and inferior constrictors; Internal laryngeal nerve
The Killian dehiscence; External laryngeal nerve
The gap below the inferior constrictor; Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: The gap between the superior and middle constrictors; Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The gap above the superior constrictor primarily transmits the auditory tube and levator veli palatini, not the nerve for taste on the tongue.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) and stylopharyngeus muscle pass through the gap between the superior and middle constrictors. Damage results in loss of gag reflex and taste/sensation to the posterior tongue.
The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane above the inferior constrictor; it provides sensation to the larynx, not taste to the tongue.
Killian's dehiscence is an area of potential weakness within the inferior constrictor; it does not house the glossopharyngeal nerve.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve passes below the inferior constrictor but supplies the larynx; its damage causes hoarseness, not taste loss.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1638 (Book Page): The stylopharyngeus muscle, the glossopharyngeal nerve, and the pharyngeal branch of the vagus pass between the external and internal carotid arteries. Page 1676 (Book Page): [The Glossopharyngeal nerve] carries general sensory and taste fibers from the mucous membrane of the posterior third of the tongue.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: Which anatomical landmark represents a potential site of weakness in the inferior pharyngeal constrictor due to the divergence of its muscular fibers?
options: Oropharyngeal isthmus
Torus tubarius
Pharyngeal recess
Killian dehiscence
Piriform fossa
correctOption: Killian dehiscence
optionExplanations: The oropharyngeal isthmus is the space between the palatoglossal arches marking the mouth-pharynx boundary.
The torus tubarius is the lymphoid-containing elevation of the auditory tube opening.
The pharyngeal recess is a mucosal depression behind the tubal elevation in the nasopharynx, not a muscular gap.
Killian dehiscence is a triangular gap between the thyropharyngeus (oblique fibers) and cricopharyngeus (horizontal fibers) of the inferior constrictor, making it a common site for herniation.
The piriform fossa is a mucosal recess lateral to the laryngeal inlet, not a gap within the constrictor muscle fibers themselves.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1758 (Book Page): The Killian dehiscence is the area on the posterior pharyngeal wall between the upper propulsive part of the inferior constrictor and the lower sphincteric part, the cricopharyngeus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The three pharyngeal constrictor muscles converge posteriorly to insert into which structure?
options: The median pharyngeal raphe
The pharyngeal tubercle on the sphenoid bone
The posterior border of the thyroid cartilage
The prevertebral muscles of the neck
The body of the sixth cervical vertebra
correctOption: The median pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The median pharyngeal raphe is the common fibrous insertion for the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles.
The pharyngeal raphe itself attaches to the pharyngeal tubercle, which is on the basilar part of the occipital bone, not the sphenoid.
The thyroid cartilage is a site of origin for the inferior constrictor, not the common posterior insertion.
The constrictors are separated from the prevertebral muscles by the retropharyngeal space and prevertebral fascia.
The pharynx ends at the level of C6, but the muscles do not insert into the vertebral body.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe)

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: What is the primary anterior attachment for the superior pharyngeal constrictor muscle?
options: The cricoid cartilage
The pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)
The greater cornu of the hyoid bone
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
The styloid process of the temporal bone
correctOption: The pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)
optionExplanations: The cricoid cartilage is the origin of the cricopharyngeus muscle, the lower part of the inferior constrictor.
Correct. The superior constrictor originates from the pterygomandibular raphe, which it shares with the buccinator muscle of the cheek.
The greater cornu of the hyoid bone is the primary origin for the middle pharyngeal constrictor.
The oblique line of the thyroid cartilage is the site of attachment for the thyropharyngeus part of the inferior constrictor.
The styloid process is the origin for the stylopharyngeus and styloglossus muscles, but not the superior constrictor.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe)... It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A 55-year-old patient presents with severe dysphagia following a brainstem stroke that damaged the nucleus ambiguus. On examination, the pharyngeal constrictors are paralyzed. Which specific motor deficiency would be most evident during the involuntary pharyngeal phase of swallowing?
options: Inability to depress the hyoid bone after swallowing
Inability to elevate the soft palate to seal the nasopharynx
Loss of sensation in the mucous membrane of the oropharynx
Failure to initiate the voluntary movement of the tongue
Loss of the sequential peristaltic-like contraction of the pharyngeal wall
correctOption: Loss of the sequential peristaltic-like contraction of the pharyngeal wall
optionExplanations: Depression of the hyoid bone is primarily the function of the infrahyoid (strap) muscles, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
While the soft palate is elevated during swallowing, this is the function of the levator veli palatini, not the constrictor muscles themselves.
Sensation in the oropharynx is mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve; the question focuses on the motor paralysis of the constrictors.
Tongue movement is the voluntary first stage of swallowing and is mediated by the hypoglossal nerve, not the pharyngeal constrictors.
The pharyngeal constrictors (superior, middle, and inferior) must contract in a specific temporal sequence to propel the food bolus downward through the pharynx into the esophagus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1759 (Book Page): The bolus moves downward over the epiglottis... and reaches the lower part of the pharynx as the result of the successive contraction of the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
coreConcept: Structures Between Middle and Inferior Constrictors
statement: The internal laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal artery reach the interior of the larynx by passing through the thyrohyoid membrane. This entry occurs at the gap between which two pharyngeal muscles?
options: Salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus
Middle and inferior constrictor
Superior and middle constrictor
Inferior constrictor and the esophagus
Thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus
correctOption: Middle and inferior constrictor
optionExplanations: Salpingopharyngeus and palatopharyngeus are longitudinal muscles of the internal pharyngeal wall, not the external constrictor layers defining this gap.

The thyrohyoid membrane spans the space between the hyoid bone (origin of the middle constrictor) and the thyroid cartilage (origin of the thyropharyngeus/inferior constrictor). Therefore, structures piercing it pass between these two muscles.
The stylopharyngeus and CN IX pass between the superior and middle constrictors.
The gap below the inferior constrictor and the esophagus transmits the recurrent laryngeal nerve, not the internal laryngeal nerve.
The area between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus is the Killian dehiscence and does not transmit these neurovascular structures.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1789 (Book Page): The internal laryngeal nerve penetrates the lateral aspect of the thyrohyoid membrane (in company with the superior laryngeal artery) and enters the larynx. Page 1781 (Book Page): Thyrohyoid membrane : This connects the upper margin of the thyroid cartilage [origin of inferior constrictor] to the hyoid bone [origin of middle constrictor].

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: The pharyngeal constrictor muscles are characterized by a circular arrangement of fibers that sequentially contract during deglutition. To which anatomical structure do all three of these muscles collectively insert posteriorly?
options: Prevertebral fascia
Pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
Stylohyoid ligament
Pharyngeal raphe
Pterygomandibular ligament
correctOption: Pharyngeal raphe
optionExplanations: The prevertebral fascia lies posterior to the pharynx, separating it from the prevertebral muscles, but it does not serve as an insertion site for the pharyngeal constrictor muscles themselves.

The pharyngeal tubercle is a small midline prominence on the undersurface of the basilar part of the occipital bone that serves as the superior attachment point for the pharyngeal raphe, but the muscles themselves insert into the raphe, not directly onto the bone across their entire posterior extent.

The stylohyoid ligament serves as a site of origin for the middle pharyngeal constrictor muscle, specifically connecting the styloid process to the hyoid bone, rather than an insertion point for all three.

The pharyngeal raphe is a posterior midline fibrous band that provides the common site of insertion for the superior, middle, and inferior constrictor muscles, allowing them to form a functional tube for bolus transport.

The pterygomandibular ligament (or raphe) is an origin point for the superior constrictor muscle anteriorly, connecting the hamulus to the mandible; it is not the posterior insertion site for all constrictors.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The three constrictor muscles extend around the pharyngeal wall and insert into a posterior midline fibrous band (pharyngeal raphe) that extends from the pharyngeal tubercle on the basilar part of the occipital bone of the skull down to the esophagus.

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: In a case of surgical reconstruction of the oral and pharyngeal regions, the surgeon identifies the pterygomandibular ligament (raphe). Which pharyngeal constrictor muscle takes its origin, in part, from this ligament?
options: Superior constrictor
Middle constrictor
Inferior constrictor
Cricopharyngeus
Stylopharyngeus
correctOption: Superior constrictor
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor originates from the pterygoid hamulus, the pterygomandibular raphe, the mylohyoid line of the mandible, and the side of the tongue.
The middle constrictor originates from the lower part of the stylohyoid ligament and the greater and lesser cornua of the hyoid bone.
The inferior constrictor (thyropharyngeal part) originates from the oblique line of the thyroid cartilage.
The cricopharyngeus is the lower part of the inferior constrictor and originates from the cricoid cartilage.
The stylopharyngeus is a longitudinal muscle that originates from the styloid process of the temporal bone, not the pterygomandibular raphe.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1628 (Book Page): [Pterygomandibular ligament (raphe): Connects the hamular process of the medial pterygoid plate to the posterior end of the mylohyoid line of the mandible. It gives attachment to the superior constrictor and the buccinator muscles]

category: Name the pharyngeal constrictor muscles defining their attachments, innervation and structure traversing the gaps between adjacent muscles
statement: A patient is evaluated for a disorder in the esophageal phase of deglutition. Physiologically, how does the cricopharyngeus portion of the inferior constrictor muscle uniquely facilitate the passage of a bolus into the esophagus?
options: By relaxing its tonic contraction to open the esophageal inlet
By rhythmic peristaltic contraction during the oral phase
By elevating the larynx to the level of the epiglottic base
By tensing the thyrohyoid membrane to increase pharyngeal pressure
By contracting to prevent the entry of air into the nasopharynx
correctOption: By relaxing its tonic contraction to open the esophageal inlet
