Expiration, followed by abduction of the arytenoid cartilages.
Relaxation of the oblique arytenoid muscles to widen the laryngeal inlet.
Closure of the vestibule by the vestibular folds while keeping the rima glottidis wide open.
Deep inspiration, followed by maximal abduction of the vocal folds and open rima glottidis.
correctOption: Deep inspiration, followed by adduction of the vocal folds and closure of the rima glottidis.
optionExplanations: The maneuver requires deep inspiration to fill the lungs, followed by forced expiration against adducted vocal folds (closed glottis). This increases intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure.
The maneuver requires closure of the airway (adduction), not abduction. Abduction occurs at the end of the maneuver to release air.
Widening the laryngeal inlet is the opposite of the sphincteric protection/closure required during high-pressure straining.
Both the vestibular folds and especially the vocal folds (rima glottidis) must close to trap the air effectively for the maneuver.
If the rima glottidis were open and folds abducted, the thoracic air would escape, failing to provide the internal pressure needed to stabilize the diaphragm for straining.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1788 (Book Page): In the Valsalva maneuver, forced expiration takes place against a closed glottis... After deep inspiration, the rima glottidis is closed. The muscles of the anterior abdominal wall now contract, and the upward movement of the diaphragm is prevented.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: In a patient experiencing acute respiratory distress, the physiological opening of the rima glottidis is essential. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is the sole abductor of the vocal folds responsible for this action?
options: Cricothyroid muscle
Thyroarytenoid muscle
Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle
Transverse arytenoid muscle
Lateral cricoarytenoid muscle
correctOption: Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle
optionExplanations: The cricothyroid muscle tenses and stretches the vocal folds by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward.
The thyroarytenoid muscle acts primarily to relax the vocal folds by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the thyroid cartilage.
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the vocal cords, making it the most important muscle for maintaining a patent airway during respiration.
The transverse arytenoid muscle closes the posterior part of the rima glottidis by approximating the arytenoid cartilages.
The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle is an adductor; it rotates the vocal process medially to close the airway.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1785 (Book Page): Abducting the vocal cords: Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: Clinical Anatomy of the External Laryngeal Nerve
statement: A 42-year-old female presents for a follow-up after a total thyroidectomy. She complains of a significant change in the quality of her singing voice, specifically an inability to reach high-pitched notes, though her quiet speaking voice remains clear. Laryngoscopy reveals that she cannot tense her vocal folds during phonation. Which nerve was most likely damaged during the ligation of the superior thyroid artery?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: External laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and pharynx; it does not supply laryngeal intrinsic muscles.
The external laryngeal nerve travels with the superior thyroid artery and supplies the cricothyroid muscle; this muscle tenses the vocal folds to produce high-pitched sounds.
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue and is not involved in tensing the vocal folds or laryngeal phonation.
The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory above the vocal folds; its damage would cause loss of the cough reflex but not an inability to tense the cords.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve damage usually causes significant hoarseness or breathiness because it supplies the abductors and adductors; it is typically found near the inferior thyroid artery.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Section of the external laryngeal nerve produces weakness of the voice because the cricothyroid muscle is paralyzed and the vocal fold cannot be tensed

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: In contrasting the anatomical features of the internal laryngeal cavity, which characteristic distinguishes the true vocal folds from the vestibular (false) vocal folds?
options: True vocal folds are fixed and do not move with respiration.
True vocal folds are pink and highly vascular, whereas vestibular folds are white.
The vestibular folds are the primary structures concerned with voice production.
True vocal folds are avascular and white, while vestibular folds are vascular and pink.
True vocal folds are covered with ciliated columnar epithelium exclusively.
correctOption: True vocal folds are avascular and white, while vestibular folds are vascular and pink.
optionExplanations: True vocal folds are highly mobile and essential for respiration and phonation, whereas vestibular folds are relatively fixed.
This is incorrect; the true vocal folds are notoriously white and avascular, whereas the false folds are pink.
The true vocal folds are the primary organs of phonation; the vestibular folds (false folds) do not typically participate in normal voice production.
True vocal folds lack a significant blood supply in their superficial layers, appearing white under laryngoscopy, while vestibular folds are vascular and appear pink.
While much of the larynx is ciliated, the vocal folds are covered with stratified squamous epithelium to withstand the mechanical stress of vibration during phonation.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1782 (Book Page): Vestibular Fold (False Vocal Fold): The vestibular fold is a fixed fold on each side of the larynx... it is vascular and pink in color. Vocal Fold (True Vocal Fold): The vocal fold is a mobile fold on each side of the larynx... it is avascular and white in color.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 52-year-old patient undergoes an extensive neck dissection for a malignant thyroid tumor. Post-operatively, the patient is found to have a paralyzed left vocal fold that remains fixed in a position midway between abduction and adduction. Which surgical complication best explains this finding?
options: Complete section of the external laryngeal nerve
Bilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Involvement of the superior laryngeal nerve only
Unilateral partial section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Section of the external laryngeal nerve would only paralyze the cricothyroid muscle, leading to voice weakness and inability to tense the cords, not a fixed midway position.
Bilateral complete section would result in both vocal folds being fixed in the midway position, leading to total loss of voice and significant respiratory distress.

In a unilateral complete section, the vocal fold assumes a 'cadaveric' or neutral position midway between abduction and adduction because all intrinsic muscles (except cricothyroid) are paralyzed on that side.
Isolated superior laryngeal nerve injury affects sensation (internal branch) and tension (external branch), but the recurrent laryngeal nerve governs the primary abduction/adduction positions.
Unilateral partial section typically results in the vocal fold assuming an adducted midline position due to the specific vulnerability of abductor fibers.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: During the physiological process of deep inspiration, the rima glottidis must widen to a diamond shape to facilitate maximum airflow. Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is the sole agent responsible for this abduction of the vocal folds?
options: Posterior cricoarytenoid
Cricothyroid
Thyroarytenoid
Transverse arytenoid
Lateral cricoarytenoid
correctOption: Posterior cricoarytenoid
optionExplanations: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally, essential for opening the airway during inspiration.
The cricothyroid muscle elongates and tenses the vocal folds by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward; it does not produce abduction.
The thyroarytenoid muscle primarily acts to relax and shorten the vocal cords, rather than abducting them.
The transverse arytenoid muscle draws the two arytenoid cartilages together, thereby adducting the posterior portion of the vocal folds.
The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle acts as an adductor by rotating the arytenoid cartilages medially, which closes the rima glottidis.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1785 (Book Page): Abducting the vocal cords: Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 52-year-old male presents to the emergency department after accidentally swallowing a sharp fish bone. He is gagging violently and points to the side of his throat. A laryngoscopy reveals the bone lodged in the piriform fossa. Which nerve is most at risk of irritation or injury by a foreign body in this specific location?
options: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Sympathetic trunk
Hypoglossal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The recurrent laryngeal nerve enters the larynx at the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage, far below the piriform fossa located near the laryngeal inlet.
The internal laryngeal nerve lies just beneath the mucous membrane of the piriform fossa; foreign bodies here irritate it, causing the characteristic violent gagging reflex.
The sympathetic trunk is located posterior to the carotid sheath and prevertebral fascia, separated from the laryngeal lumen by several layers of tissue and muscle.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) travels in the submandibular region and carotid triangle to reach the tongue muscles; it does not pass through the laryngeal recesses.
The external laryngeal nerve remains on the outer surface of the larynx to supply the cricothyroid muscle and is not exposed in the piriform fossa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1782 (Book Page): Piriform Fossa The piriform fossa is a recess on either side of the inlet... Page 1789 (Book Page): The internal laryngeal nerve penetrates the lateral aspect of the thyrohyoid membrane... and enters the larynx [near the fossa].

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: During a physiological assessment of a patient's vocal mechanics, which specific musculoskeletal action is primarily responsible for the maximal abduction of the vocal folds required for deep inspiration?
options: Contraction of the lateral cricoarytenoid muscles
Lateral rotation of the arytenoid cartilages by the posterior cricoarytenoid muscles
Forward tilting of the thyroid cartilage by the cricothyroid muscles
Contraction of the thyroarytenoid muscles
Adduction of the vocal processes by the transverse arytenoid muscles
correctOption: Contraction of the lateral cricoarytenoid muscles
optionExplanations: The lateral cricoarytenoid muscle is an adductor of the vocal folds, not an abductor.
The posterior cricoarytenoid muscles are the only muscles that abduct the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoid cartilages laterally.
The cricothyroid muscle tenses and stretches the vocal cords by tilting the thyroid cartilage, but it does not abduct them.
The thyroarytenoid muscle acts to relax and slacken the vocal folds, rather than abduct them.
The transverse arytenoid muscle approximates the cartilages to narrow the posterior rima glottidis (adduction).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1785 (Book Page): The rima glottidis opens by the contraction of the posterior cricoarytenoid, which rotates the arytenoid cartilage and abducts the vocal process.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A clinician is comparing the sensory and motor deficits associated with different laryngeal nerve injuries. Which anatomical contrast correctly distinguishes the internal laryngeal nerve from the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
options: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the cricothyroid membrane, whereas the recurrent laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides motor supply to the cricothyroid, whereas the recurrent laryngeal nerve is purely sensory.
The internal laryngeal nerve is a branch of the recurrent laryngeal nerve, whereas the external laryngeal nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve.
The internal laryngeal nerve carries sensation from the subglottic space, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the supraglottic mucosa.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensation above the vocal folds, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below them.
correctOption: The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensation above the vocal folds, while the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies sensation below them.
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery; the recurrent nerve enters the larynx at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.
The external laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle, not the internal laryngeal nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is mixed, providing motor supply to most intrinsic muscles.
Both the internal and external laryngeal nerves are branches of the superior laryngeal nerve. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is a separate branch of the vagus nerve (CN X).
This option is inverted; the internal laryngeal nerve supplies the supraglottic region (above the folds), and the recurrent (as the inferior laryngeal) supplies the subglottic region.
The internal laryngeal nerve is the primary sensory nerve for the laryngeal vestibule and mucosa down to the vocal folds, whereas the recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensation below the folds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Above the vocal folds: Internal laryngeal nerve. Below the level of the vocal cords: Inferior laryngeal nerve [terminal branch of recurrent].

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: During the physiological mechanism of forced expiration against a closed glottis (Valsalva maneuver), which intrinsic laryngeal muscle must contract to achieve the primary abduction of the vocal folds required to suddenly release intrathoracic pressure?
options: Transverse arytenoid
Thyroarytenoid
Cricothyroid
Posterior cricoarytenoid
Lateral cricoarytenoid
correctOption: Posterior cricoarytenoid
optionExplanations: The transverse arytenoid muscle approximates the two arytenoid cartilages to close the posterior part of the rima glottidis; it is an adductor.
The thyroarytenoid muscle acts to relax and shorten the vocal folds by pulling the arytenoid cartilages toward the thyroid cartilage.
The cricothyroid muscle tenses and elongates the vocal folds by tilting the thyroid cartilage forward; it does not abduct the folds.
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor of the vocal folds; it rotates the arytenoids laterally to open the rima glottidis for breathing and pressure release.
The lateral cricoarytenoid is an adductor of the vocal folds, functioning to close the rima glottidis, which is the opposite of abduction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1785 (Book Page): The rima glottidis opens by the contraction of the posterior cricoarytenoid, which rotates the arytenoid cartilage and abducts the vocal process.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 48-year-old female presents with persistent hoarseness following a subtotal thyroidectomy. Laryngoscopic examination reveals that the left vocal fold is stationary in a position midway between abduction and adduction (paramedian). What is the most likely neurological injury?
options: Unilateral partial section of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Damage to the left external laryngeal nerve only
Bilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerves
Unilateral complete section of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
Compression of the left internal laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Unilateral complete section of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Partial section often results in the fold assuming an adducted midline position because abductors are more sensitive or exposed than adductors.
The external laryngeal nerve supplies only the cricothyroid; its injury causes voice weakness and inability to tense the cords, but not a stationary paramedian fold.
Bilateral injury would involve both folds being stationary; this case specifies only the left fold is affected.

Complete unilateral section removes all intrinsic motor supply except to the cricothyroid. The fold assumes a 'cadaveric' or paramedian position (midway), though speech is often preserved as the healthy fold compensates.
The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory above the vocal folds; damage would cause loss of the cough reflex but not motor paralysis of the folds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction. It lies just laterally to the midline.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A clinician performing an indirect laryngoscopy compares the anatomical features of the vestibular folds and the vocal folds. Which of the following diagnostic contrasts is accurate regarding their appearance and function?
options: The vocal folds appear reddish because they are highly vascular.
The rima vestibuli is the narrowest part of the laryngeal cavity.
The vestibular folds move significantly during normal respiration.
The vocal folds are white and avascular, while the vestibular folds are pink and fixed.
The vestibular folds are white and avascular, serving as the primary source of sound.
correctOption: The vocal folds are white and avascular, while the vestibular folds are pink and fixed.
optionExplanations: Vocal folds are actually white and avascular under normal conditions; a reddish appearance would be pathological (e.g., laryngitis).
The rima glottidis (the space between the vocal folds), not the rima vestibuli, is the narrowest part of the adult laryngeal cavity.
Vestibular folds are 'fixed folds' and do not participate in the active abduction/adduction seen in vocal folds during the respiratory cycle or phonation.

Vocal folds are composed of the vocal ligament and vocalis muscle covered by stratified squamous epithelium, making them appear white and pearly due to low vascularity. Vestibular folds are vascularized mucous membrane folds that are relatively immobile.
Vestibular folds (false vocal cords) are pink and vascular; they do not produce sound but provide protection and lubrication via the saccule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1782 (Book Page)-1783: [Vestibular fold] is vascular and pink in color... [Vocal fold] is avascular and white in color.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: Which nerve provides the sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucous membrane located inferior to the level of the vocal folds?
options: Superior laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The superior laryngeal nerve is the parent nerve that divides into internal and external branches; it does not supply the subglottic region directly.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory supply to the pharynx and posterior tongue, not the internal larynx below the cords.
The external laryngeal nerve is primarily a motor nerve to the cricothyroid muscle.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve (via its terminal inferior laryngeal branch) provides sensory innervation to the mucous membrane below the vocal folds and motor supply to most intrinsic muscles.
The internal laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the larynx *above* the vocal folds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Sensory Nerves... Below the level of the vocal cords : Inferior laryngeal nerve [terminal branch of recurrent laryngeal nerve].

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: The 'safety muscle' of the larynx is essential for maintaining a patent airway. Which physiological loop describes its primary function?
options: Elevation of the larynx by the suprahyoid muscles to seal the inlet.
Narrowing of the rima glottidis by the transverse arytenoid during whispering.
Abduction of the vocal folds by the posterior cricoarytenoid during inspiration.
Adduction of the vocal processes by the lateral cricoarytenoid during swallowing.
Tension of the vocal cords by the cricothyroid during high-pitched phonation.
correctOption: Abduction of the vocal folds by the posterior cricoarytenoid during inspiration.
optionExplanations: Laryngeal elevation is a part of the swallowing loop to protect the airway from food, but it does not describe the specific intrinsic muscle responsible for cord abduction.
Narrowing the rima glottidis (adduction) is for sound production or airway protection, not for the loop of inspiration.

The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only muscle that abducts (opens) the vocal folds. It is called the 'safety muscle' because its contraction is the only way to open the rima glottidis for respiration.
Adduction closes the airway; while necessary for swallowing and speech, it is the opposite of the 'safety' function of keeping the airway open for breathing.
Tension of the cords is for pitch control, not for the primary safety of the airway patency during inspiration.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1785 (Book Page): Abducting the vocal cords : Posterior cricoarytenoid muscle... Page 1787 (Book Page): On deep inspiration, the vocal folds maximally abduct, and the triangular shape of the glottis becomes a diamond shape.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: Neurovascular Supply of the Laryngeal Mucosa
statement: During a neuro-anatomical evaluation, a physician tests the sensory integrity of the laryngeal mucosa. Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal cavity specifically above the level of the vocal folds?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Inferior laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensation to the oropharynx and posterior third of the tongue, but not the interior of the larynx.
The hypoglossal nerve is a purely motor nerve supplying the muscles of the tongue.
The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve from the vagus, is the primary sensory nerve for the laryngeal vestibule and middle region.
The inferior laryngeal nerve (terminal recurrent laryngeal) provides sensory supply to the mucosa below the vocal folds.
The external laryngeal nerve is primarily motor to the cricothyroid muscle and does not provide significant sensory supply to the internal mucosa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Sensory Nerves: Above the vocal folds: Internal laryngeal nerve

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 45-year-old female presents for a follow-up after a total thyroidectomy. She complains of hoarseness and a significant loss of vocal range, specifically an inability to reach high-pitched notes while singing in her choir. Laryngoscopy shows no paralysis of the vocal folds. Which nerve was most likely damaged during the ligation of the superior thyroid artery?
options: External laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Cervical sympathetic trunk
Hypoglossal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: External laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The external laryngeal nerve travels in close proximity to the superior thyroid artery and supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal folds to produce high-pitched sounds.
Injury to the internal laryngeal nerve would cause loss of sensation in the upper larynx and a loss of the cough reflex, but not loss of tension in the vocal folds.
Damage to the sympathetic trunk would result in Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis), which does not affect the pitch of the voice.
The hypoglossal nerve supplies the muscles of the tongue; its injury would cause tongue deviation and dysarthria, but not specific loss of vocal pitch control.
Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury would cause vocal fold paralysis (fixed in the paramedian position), which was explicitly ruled out by the laryngoscopy in this case.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Section of the external laryngeal nerve produces weakness of the voice because the cricothyroid muscle is paralyzed and the vocal fold cannot be tensed.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A patient is diagnosed with acute laryngeal edema. On examination, the swelling is severe above the level of the vocal folds but noticeably absent in the infraglottic cavity. Based on the anatomical features of the laryngeal mucosa, what explains this clinical presentation?
options: The mucosa is loosely attached above the folds but firmly attached to the vocal ligaments
The quadrangular membrane prevents fluid from descending into the ventricle
Lymphatic drainage is only present in the supraglottic region
The cricoid cartilage exerts external pressure that prevents mucosal swelling
The subglottic mucosa is supplied by the less permeable inferior laryngeal artery
correctOption: The mucosa is loosely attached above the folds but firmly attached to the vocal ligaments
optionExplanations: The loose attachment of the mucosa in the supraglottic area allows for significant edema, while its firm attachment to the vocal ligaments prevents fluid from crossing that boundary easily.
The quadrangular membrane actually forms the submucosal framework of the vestibule where the fluid accumulates.
Lymphatic drainage is present both above and below the vocal folds, draining into upper and lower deep cervical nodes respectively.
The cricoid cartilage is rigid and would cause fluid to swell inward toward the lumen, increasing obstruction, rather than preventing it.
While the inferior laryngeal artery supplies the lower half, vascular permeability differences are not the anatomical reason for the localized edema.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): The mucous membrane of the larynx is loosely attached to the underlying structures by submucous connective tissue. However, it is firmly attached to the vocal ligaments in the region of the vocal folds... The accumulation of tissue fluid causes the mucous membrane above the rima glottidis to swell and encroach on the airway.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 48-year-old female presents with a large multinodular goiter. Following a total thyroidectomy, she complains of significant hoarseness. Physical examination shows the right vocal fold is fixed in a position midway between abduction and adduction (paramedian). Which nerve was likely completely severed during the ligation of the inferior thyroid artery?
options: Right External laryngeal nerve
Right Superior laryngeal nerve
Right Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Right Internal laryngeal nerve
Right Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Right Recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Injury to the external laryngeal nerve paralyzes the cricothyroid muscle, leading to an inability to tense the vocal cord and a weak, husky voice, but the cord would still move.
The superior laryngeal nerve divides into internal and external branches; while its trunk is superior to the thyroid gland, its isolated injury is less common than its branches.

The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid. Complete section causes the vocal fold to sit in the paramedian position because both abductors and adductors are paralyzed.
The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds; its injury would lead to loss of the cough reflex but not vocal fold paralysis.
The glossopharyngeal nerve does not supply any intrinsic laryngeal muscles; it supplies the stylopharyngeus muscle and provides sensation to the posterior third of the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A medical student performing a direct laryngoscopy notes two pairs of folds. How can the true vocal folds be distinguished from the vestibular folds based on their anatomical features and appearance?
options: True vocal folds are superior to the laryngeal ventricle, while vestibular folds are inferior.
True vocal folds are avascular and white, while vestibular folds are vascular and pink.
True vocal folds are pink and highly vascular, whereas vestibular folds are white.
True vocal folds are fixed, while vestibular folds are highly mobile.
True vocal folds contain the vestibular ligament, while vestibular folds contain the vocal ligament.
correctOption: True vocal folds are avascular and white, while vestibular folds are vascular and pink.
optionExplanations: The vestibular folds are actually superior (the roof of the ventricle), and the vocal folds are inferior (the floor of the ventricle).
The true vocal folds' white color is a hallmark for identification during laryngoscopy, contrasting with the more fleshy pink appearance of the superior vestibular folds.
This is incorrect; the true vocal folds appear white due to their lack of direct superficial vasculature and their dense ligamentous structure.
This is the reverse of the true physiology; true vocal folds are the primary mobile structures for phonation, while vestibular folds are relatively fixed.
This reverses the internal anatomy; the vestibular fold contains the vestibular ligament, and the vocal fold contains the vocal ligament.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1782 (Book Page): Vestibular Fold (False Vocal Fold): The vestibular fold is a fixed fold on each side of the larynx... is vascular and pink in color. Vocal Fold (True Vocal Fold): The vocal fold is a mobile fold on each side of the larynx... is avascular and white in color.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: The sensory innervation of the laryngeal mucous membrane is partitioned by the vocal folds. Which nerve provides sensation to the region of the larynx located superior to the vocal folds?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is a purely motor nerve supplying the muscles of the tongue.
The external laryngeal nerve is primarily a motor nerve supplying the cricothyroid muscle and does not provide laryngeal mucosal sensation.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the larynx only below the level of the vocal folds.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensation to the oropharynx and posterior third of the tongue, not the internal larynx.
The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to supply sensation to the laryngeal vestibule above the vocal folds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Above the vocal folds: Internal laryngeal nerve

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 3-year-old child presents with sudden onset of severe dyspnea and inspiratory stridor. On examination, there is significant swelling of the mucous membrane above the rima glottidis. Based on laryngeal anatomy, why does this edema typically stop at the level of the vocal folds?
options: The vocal folds are composed of dense bone that prevents fluid passage.
The mucous membrane is replaced by skin at the vocal folds.
There is no lymphatic drainage below the vocal folds.
The rima glottidis is too narrow for fluid to pass through.
The mucous membrane is firmly attached to the vocal ligaments at the folds.
correctOption: The mucous membrane is firmly attached to the vocal ligaments at the folds.
optionExplanations: The vocal folds are composed of ligaments, muscles, and mucosa, not bone; the framework is cartilaginous.
The entire larynx is lined by mucous membrane (though the epithelium type changes); there is no skin inside the laryngeal cavity.
The larynx has a rich lymphatic drainage both above and below the vocal folds, which drains to the deep cervical nodes.
The rima glottidis is a space (airway); its width does not determine the mechanical attachment of the mucosal tissue layers.

Correct. Because the mucosa is loosely attached in the vestibule but tightly bound to the vocal ligaments, edema fluid accumulates above the folds but cannot easily pass them, causing supraglottic swelling.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): The mucous membrane of the larynx is loosely attached to the underlying structures by submucous connective tissue. However, it is firmly attached to the vocal ligaments in the region of the vocal folds.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A surgeon is performing a partial thyroidectomy and must be careful to avoid the nerve that supplies the cricothyroid muscle. This nerve is the:
options: Ansa cervicalis
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Inferior laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
correctOption: External laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The ansa cervicalis supplies the infrahyoid strap muscles (omohyoid, sternohyoid, sternothyroid) but not the intrinsic or cricothyroid laryngeal muscles.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except for the cricothyroid.
The inferior laryngeal nerve is the terminal continuation of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; it does not supply the cricothyroid.
The internal laryngeal nerve is the sensory branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and does not supply any muscles.
The external laryngeal nerve is the motor branch of the superior laryngeal nerve that specifically innervates the cricothyroid muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1789 (Book Page): The external laryngeal nerve ... supplies the cricothyroid muscle.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: Anatomical Landmarks of the Laryngeal Cavity
statement: A 35-year-old patient undergoes a diagnostic laryngoscopy. The physician notes a distinct difference in the appearance of the two sets of laryngeal folds. Which features accurately contrast the true vocal folds from the vestibular folds?
options: The rima glottidis is the space located between the opposite vestibular folds.
True vocal folds are pink and fixed, while vestibular folds are white and mobile.
Vestibular folds are involved in voice production, while true vocal folds are fixed and protective.
True vocal folds are avascular and white, while vestibular folds are vascular and pink.
True vocal folds are covered in ciliated columnar epithelium and are vascular.
correctOption: True vocal folds are avascular and white, while vestibular folds are vascular and pink.
optionExplanations: The rima glottidis is the aperture between the true vocal folds; the space between the vestibular folds is known as the rima vestibuli.
This is inverted; the true vocal folds are white and mobile for phonation, whereas the vestibular folds are pink, fixed, and lack intrinsic muscle for movement.
The opposite is true; the true vocal folds produce voice via vibration, while the vestibular folds (false cords) serve a protective and lubricating function.
The white appearance of the true vocal folds is due to their sparse blood supply and dense elastic tissue, which contrasts with the well-vascularized pink mucous membrane of the vestibular folds.
The true vocal folds are uniquely covered in stratified squamous epithelium to withstand the trauma of vibration, unlike the rest of the larynx which uses ciliated columnar cells.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1782 (Book Page)-1783: Vestibular Fold (False Vocal Fold)... is formed by mucous membrane covering the vestibular ligament and is vascular and pink in color. Vocal Fold (True Vocal Fold)... is formed by mucous membrane covering the vocal ligament and is avascular and white in color.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
coreConcept: Surgical Anatomy of the Piriform Fossa
statement: A 62-year-old male presents to the Emergency Department with intense pain and a persistent gagging sensation after swallowing a sharp fish bone. Physical examination and imaging reveal the object is lodged in the piriform fossa. Which nerve, providing sensory supply to this specific recess, is most at risk of irritation or damage during endoscopic removal?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is purely motor to the muscles of the tongue and has no sensory role in the pharyngeal recesses.
The external laryngeal nerve is a motor nerve to the cricothyroid muscle and does not provide sensory innervation to the piriform fossa.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensation to the oropharynx, but the laryngopharyngeal piriform fossa is specifically supplied by the vagus via the internal laryngeal nerve.
Correct. The internal laryngeal nerve provides the sensory supply to the supraglottic region, including the piriform fossa. Its irritation by a foreign body causes intense pain and the gag reflex.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensation to the laryngeal cavity below the vocal folds; it is not the primary sensory nerve of the piriform fossa.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1789 (Book Page): The internal laryngeal nerve is sensory to the mucous membrane of the piriform fossa and the larynx down as far as the vocal cords.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: The neurovascular supply to the larynx is segmented by the vocal folds. The superior laryngeal artery, which provides blood to the upper half of the larynx, is a direct branch of which vessel?
options: Inferior thyroid artery
Superior thyroid artery
Ascending pharyngeal artery
Maxillary artery
Internal carotid artery
correctOption: Maxillary artery
optionExplanations: The inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk) gives rise to the inferior laryngeal artery, supplying the lower half.
The superior laryngeal artery arises from the superior thyroid artery, which is a branch of the external carotid.
The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharyngeal walls but not the upper larynx directly.
The maxillary artery supplies deep facial structures and is not involved in laryngeal vascularization.
The internal carotid artery provides no branches in the neck.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Upper half of the larynx: Superior laryngeal branch of the superior thyroid artery.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 48-year-old female undergoes a total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goiter. Postoperatively, she presents with severe hoarseness. Laryngoscopy reveals that the right vocal fold is fixed in a position midway between abduction and adduction. Which nerve was most likely completely severed during the surgery?
options: Right Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Bilateral Recurrent laryngeal nerves
Right External laryngeal nerve
Right Internal laryngeal nerve
Right Superior laryngeal nerve trunk
correctOption: Right Recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Correct. Complete unilateral section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve paralyzes all intrinsic muscles except the cricothyroid, causing the fold to sit in a 'cadaveric' or midway position.
Incorrect. Bilateral injury would involve both folds and typically present with more severe airway compromise or loss of speech, rather than just a right-sided finding.
Incorrect. Section of the external laryngeal nerve paralyzes the cricothyroid muscle, leading to weakness of the voice/loss of pitch but not a midway fixation of the fold.
Incorrect. The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds; injury causes loss of the cough reflex but not motor paralysis of the folds.
Incorrect. Severing the trunk would involve both internal and external branches; the specific motor finding of a midway fold position is classically attributed to the recurrent nerve loss.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: An elite examiner is testing a student on laryngeal neuroanatomy. Which nerve provides the sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucous membrane situated superior to the vocal folds?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: Correct. The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, provides the sensory supply for the laryngeal vestibule and mucosa down to the vocal folds.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensation to the posterior third of the tongue and the oropharynx, but not the interior of the larynx.
The external laryngeal nerve is purely motor to the cricothyroid muscle and does not provide sensory innervation to the internal laryngeal mucosa.
The hypoglossal nerve is a purely motor nerve supplying the muscles of the tongue, excluding the palatoglossus.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation only to the mucous membrane below the level of the vocal folds.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Sensory Nerves Above the vocal folds : Internal laryngeal nerve

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: The sensory innervation of the laryngeal mucous membrane is divided into two distinct regions. Which nerve provides sensation to the region located inferior to the level of the vocal folds?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Inferior laryngeal nerve)
Pharyngeal branch of the vagus
correctOption: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (Inferior laryngeal nerve)
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensation to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue, not the internal cavity of the larynx.
The external laryngeal nerve is purely motor to the cricothyroid muscle and does not provide sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa.
The internal laryngeal nerve is the sensory supply for the laryngeal vestibule and the area strictly above the vocal folds.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve, which becomes the inferior laryngeal nerve as it enters the larynx, provides both motor supply to muscles and sensory supply to the mucosa below the cords.
The pharyngeal branch of the vagus supplies the muscles of the pharynx and soft palate but does not provide sensory fibers to the internal larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Sensory Nerves... Below the level of the vocal cords: Inferior laryngeal nerve

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A clinician is evaluating a patient with a suspected foreign body lodged in the laryngeal vestibule. If the patient has lost sensation specifically in the region above the vocal folds, which nerve is most likely compromised?
options: Internal laryngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The internal laryngeal nerve, a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve from the vagus, provides all sensory innervation to the larynx from the inlet down to the vocal folds.
The hypoglossal nerve (CN XII) is purely motor to the muscles of the tongue and does not provide sensory innervation to the larynx.
The external laryngeal nerve is primarily a motor nerve that supplies the cricothyroid muscle and has no significant sensory contribution to the laryngeal mucosa.
The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensation to the oropharynx and the posterior third of the tongue, but not the internal larynx.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa below the level of the vocal folds, not above them.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Above the vocal folds: Internal laryngeal nerve

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 45-year-old female presents with a weak, hoarse voice and an inability to hit high-pitched notes after a total thyroidectomy. Laryngoscopic exam reveals that her vocal folds can still abduct and adduct, but they fail to tense properly. During the surgery, the surgeon noted difficulty ligating the superior thyroid artery. Which nerve was most likely injured during this procedure?
options: Inferior laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Pharyngeal branch of the vagus
Internal laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
correctOption: External laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The inferior laryngeal nerve is the terminal part of the recurrent laryngeal nerve; its injury presents identically to a recurrent laryngeal nerve lesion.
The external laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle, which tenses the vocal folds. It is closely related to the superior thyroid artery and vulnerable during its ligation.
The pharyngeal branch of the vagus supplies the muscles of the pharynx and soft palate; injury would cause dysphagia or nasal regurgitation.
The internal laryngeal nerve is sensory; its injury would result in loss of the cough reflex above the vocal folds, not hoarseness or loss of pitch.
Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve would cause paralysis of the abductors/adductors, leading to a fixed vocal fold, not just a failure to tense.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): The superior thyroid artery on each side is related to the external laryngeal nerve, which supplies the cricothyroid muscle. Damage to the external laryngeal nerve results in an inability to tense the vocal folds and in hoarseness.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: An ENT surgeon is performing a procedure and must identify the neurovascular structures piercing the thyrohyoid membrane. Damage to the nerve that accompanies the superior laryngeal artery through this membrane would most likely result in which deficit?
options: Inability to abduct the vocal folds.
Loss of sensation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds.
Loss of sensation to the larynx below the vocal folds.
Loss of taste from the epiglottis.
Paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle.
correctOption: Loss of sensation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds.
optionExplanations: Abduction is controlled by the recurrent laryngeal nerve (specifically the inferior laryngeal nerve), which enters the larynx at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage.

The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery. It provides the sensory innervation to the laryngeal cavity from the inlet down to the level of the vocal folds.
Sensation below the vocal folds is provided by the recurrent (inferior) laryngeal nerve, not the internal laryngeal nerve.
While the internal laryngeal nerve carries some fibers from the epiglottic region, its primary clinical deficit upon damage is the loss of protective sensation/cough reflex in the upper larynx.
The external laryngeal nerve supplies the cricothyroid muscle, but it does not pierce the thyrohyoid membrane; it descends on the exterior of the larynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1781 (Book Page): The superior laryngeal vessels and the internal laryngeal nerve pierce the [thyrohyoid] membrane on each side.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 30-year-old patient presents with acute laryngeal edema. Clinical examination shows significant swelling of the mucosa in the laryngeal vestibule, but the swelling terminates abruptly at the level of the true vocal folds. What anatomical feature of the larynx explains this localized confinement of tissue fluid?
options: The lack of lymphatics in the vocal folds
The narrow diameter of the rima glottidis
The loose attachment of mucosa to the thyroid lamina
The presence of the cricoid cartilage as a complete ring
The firm attachment of the mucous membrane to the vocal ligaments
correctOption: The narrow diameter of the rima glottidis
optionExplanations: The vocal folds have limited lymphatics, but the mechanical barrier to fluid spread is the structural attachment.
The rima glottidis is the space between the folds; its width does not dictate the physical boundary of tissue fluid in the subepithelial space.
Loose attachment of mucosa superiorly allows swelling, but the question asks why it stops at the folds.
The cricoid cartilage determines the airway diameter but does not limit the spread of mucosal edema.
Mucosa is tightly bound to the vocal ligaments, preventing edema from tracking further inferiorly into the subglottic space.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): The accumulation of tissue fluid causes the mucous membrane above the rima glottidis to swell... however, it is firmly attached to the vocal ligaments in the region of the vocal folds.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A patient is undergoing a procedure that requires a local nerve block for the laryngeal vestibule. The clinician plans to target the nerve that pierces the thyrohyoid membrane. Which nerve provides sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa superior to the vocal folds?
options: Hypoglossal nerve
Internal laryngeal nerve
External laryngeal nerve
Recurrent laryngeal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Internal laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The hypoglossal nerve is a purely motor nerve supplying the muscles of the tongue; it has no sensory laryngeal function.
The internal laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal) pierces the thyrohyoid membrane and provides all sensory innervation to the larynx above the level of the vocal folds.
The external laryngeal nerve is motor to the cricothyroid muscle; it does not provide sensory innervation to the internal laryngeal mucosa.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve provides sensory innervation only to the laryngeal mucosa below the level of the vocal folds.
The glossopharyngeal nerve provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx and posterior tongue, but not the laryngeal vestibule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1791 (Book Page): Sensory Nerves... Above the vocal folds : Internal laryngeal nerve... it penetrates the lateral aspect of the thyrohyoid membrane (in company with the superior laryngeal artery) and enters the larynx.

category: Name the parts of larynx giving their extent, anatomical features, musculoskeletal framework and neurovascular supply
statement: A 45-year-old female undergoes a total thyroidectomy. Postoperatively, she presents with severe hoarseness. Laryngoscopy reveals that the left vocal fold is stationary in a position midway between abduction and adduction. Based on this clinical presentation, which nerve injury is most likely?
options: Unilateral section of the external laryngeal nerve
Unilateral section of the internal laryngeal nerve
Bilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerves
Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
Bilateral partial section of the recurrent laryngeal nerves
correctOption: Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve
optionExplanations: External laryngeal nerve injury causes paralysis of the cricothyroid muscle, leading to voice weakness but not a fixed midway position of the fold.
The internal laryngeal nerve is purely sensory; its injury causes loss of the cough reflex but does not affect vocal fold position.
Bilateral complete section would result in both cords being in the midway position, leading to total loss of speech.
Complete unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve damage paralyzes both abductors and adductors, causing the cord to rest in a neutral 'midway' position.
Bilateral partial section typically results in bilateral abductor paralysis and the drawing together of both folds in the midline.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1794 (Book Page): Unilateral complete section of the recurrent laryngeal nerve results in the vocal fold on the affected side assuming the position midway between abduction and adduction.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Palatine Tonsillar Recess
statement: An ENT specialist is identifying the boundaries of the tonsillar bed to localized a chronic infection. Which anatomical structure forms the anterior boundary of the recess containing the palatine tonsil?
options: Salpingopharyngeal fold
Tubal elevation
Superior constrictor muscle
Palatopharyngeal arch
Palatoglossal arch
correctOption: Palatoglossal arch
optionExplanations: The salpingopharyngeal fold is located in the nasopharynx, extending from the tubal elevation, and is not a boundary of the palatine tonsillar bed.
The tubal elevation (torus tubarius) is a feature of the nasopharyngeal wall surrounding the auditory tube, not the palatine tonsil bed.
The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (lateral boundary) of the tonsillar bed, not the anterior margin.
The palatopharyngeal arch forms the posterior boundary of the tonsillar recess, containing the palatopharyngeus muscle.
The palatoglossal arch, which contains the palatoglossus muscle, forms the anterior boundary of the tonsillar sinus or recess in the oropharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The palatine tonsils are two masses of lymphoid tissue, each located in the depression on the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Where is the pharyngeal tonsil specifically located within the pharyngeal wall?
options: In the submucosa of the lateral wall of the oropharynx
In the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
In the depression between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
On the posterior third of the tongue
Within the mucous membrane of the piriform fossa
correctOption: In the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
optionExplanations: This describes the location of the palatine tonsils, which are situated in the oropharynx, not the nasopharynx.
The pharyngeal tonsil is a midline collection of lymphoid tissue situated specifically in the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx.
This refers to the tonsillar sinus or bed, which houses the palatine tonsils.
This describes the location of the lingual tonsil, which occupies the pharyngeal part of the dorsal surface of the tongue.
The piriform fossa is a recess in the laryngopharynx and does not contain primary tonsillar tissue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1751 (Book Page): A collection of lymphoid tissue, the pharyngeal tonsil, sits in the submucosa of the roof.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Waldeyer’s ring refers to the circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue surrounding the openings of the digestive and respiratory systems. Which of the following components forms the inferior (lower) part of this ring?
options: Submandibular lymph nodes
Tubal tonsils
Pharyngeal tonsil
Lingual tonsil
Palatine tonsils
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: Submandibular lymph nodes are regional cervical nodes and are not part of the Waldeyer's ring of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue.
The tubal tonsils contribute to the lateral part of the ring, specifically near the auditory tube opening.
The pharyngeal tonsil forms the superior (upper) part of Waldeyer's ring.
The lingual tonsil, located on the posterior third of the tongue, constitutes the inferior or lower portion of the lymphoid ring.
The palatine tonsils form the lateral parts of the ring, located between the faucial pillars.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): The pharyngeal tonsil in the roof of the nasopharynx forms the upper part, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue forms the lower part.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Anatomy students are comparing the features of various tonsils. They note that one specific tonsil reaches its maximum size in early childhood and then significantly atrophies after puberty. Which tonsil exhibits this specific age-related physiological change?
options: Both the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils
Only the palatine tonsil
Only the pharyngeal tonsil
All tonsils except the pharyngeal tonsil
Only the lingual tonsil
correctOption: Both the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils
optionExplanations: Both the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils are maximal in childhood and undergo physiological atrophy following puberty as part of the general regression of lymphoid tissue.
The palatine tonsil does atrophy after puberty, but it is not the only one; the pharyngeal tonsil follows the same pattern.
The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) atrophies, but the palatine tonsils also diminish in size during the same period.
This is incorrect as the pharyngeal tonsil is one of the primary examples of this age-related change.
The lingual tonsil is also lymphoid but the text specifically highlights the childhood-to-puberty atrophy pattern for the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page)-1761: The [palatine] tonsil reaches its maximum size during early childhood, but after puberty, it diminishes considerably in size... Like the palatine tonsil, it [pharyngeal tonsil] is largest in early childhood and starts to atrophy after puberty.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of a Peritonsillar Abscess
statement: A 25-year-old male presents with high fever, severe throat pain, and 'hot potato' voice. Examination shows a peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy). According to the anatomical layers of the pharynx, where exactly is the pus collected in this condition?
options: In the loose connective tissue outside the tonsillar capsule
Within the substance of the tonsillar crypts
Lateral to the superior constrictor muscle in the masticatory space
Between the mucosa and the tonsillar tissue
In the retropharyngeal space behind the prevertebral fascia
correctOption: In the loose connective tissue outside the tonsillar capsule
optionExplanations: A peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy) occurs specifically in the loose areolar/connective tissue between the fibrous tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle.
Infection within the crypts is follicular tonsillitis, which precedes but is not the same as a peritonsillar abscess.
If infection passes lateral to the superior constrictor, it enters the parapharyngeal space, which is a more severe complication than a standard peritonsillar abscess.
An infection between the mucosa and tissue would be a superficial tonsillitis, not a peritonsillar abscess.
The retropharyngeal space is located behind the pharynx; a Quinsy is a lateral wall oropharyngeal infection.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is caused by spread of infection from the palatine tonsil to the loose connective tissue outside the capsule

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Which specific morphological feature distinguishes the posterior third of the tongue from the anterior two-thirds in the context of the lingual tonsil?
options: Presence of filiform papillae
Attachment to the hard palate
Irregular surface due to underlying lymph nodules
Absence of stratified squamous epithelium
Presence of the parotid duct opening
correctOption: Irregular surface due to underlying lymph nodules
optionExplanations: Filiform papillae are found on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, whereas the posterior third is devoid of papillae.
The tongue is not attached to the hard palate; it is related to the soft palate and pharynx posteriorly.
The posterior third of the tongue is characterized by an irregular, nodular surface which is formed by the masses of lymphoid tissue collectively called the lingual tonsil.
The entire tongue is covered by stratified squamous epithelium, though it varies in keratinization and specialized structures like papillae.
The parotid duct opens into the vestibule of the mouth opposite the upper second molar, not on the tongue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue is devoid of papillae but has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: In a patient with significant hypertrophy of the pharyngeal tonsils (adenoids), which physiological mechanism best explains the development of secondary middle ear effusion and recurrent otitis media?
options: Hypertrophy of the salpingopharyngeus muscle closing the pharyngeal recess
Mechanical obstruction or proximity of infected tissue to the torus tubarius
Paralysis of the tensor tympani muscle via the mandibular nerve
Direct compression of the internal carotid artery reducing middle ear perfusion
Invasion of the sigmoid sinus causing retrograde venous congestion
correctOption: Mechanical obstruction or proximity of infected tissue to the torus tubarius
optionExplanations: While the salpingopharyngeus muscle is related to the auditory tube opening, it is the lymphoid hypertrophy itself, not muscle hypertrophy, that causes the clinical symptoms.

The pharyngeal tonsils are located near the torus tubarius (the elevated ridge of the auditory tube). Hypertrophy can mechanically block the tube or lead to spread of infection/inflammation, preventing pressure equalization and drainage, leading to otitis media.
The tensor tympani is an internal ear muscle supplied by the mandibular nerve; its function is not directly altered by the presence of nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue.
While the internal carotid artery is lateral to the pharynx, adenoid hypertrophy does not typically compress it or affect middle ear perfusion in this manner.
The sigmoid sinus is related to the posterior wall of the mastoid antrum; adenoid hypertrophy occurs in the nasopharynx and does not directly involve this sinus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): The close relationship of the infected lymphoid tissue to the auditory tube may be the cause of deafness and recurrent otitis media.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Which cranial nerve provides the primary general sensory innervation to the palatine tonsil and its surrounding oropharyngeal mucosa?
options: Glossopharyngeal nerve
Hypoglossal nerve
Trigeminal nerve (Maxillary division)
Facial nerve (Chorda tympani)
Vagus nerve (Internal laryngeal branch)
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) is the sensory nerve for the oropharynx, including the palatine tonsil.
The hypoglossal nerve is the motor nerve to the tongue muscles and has no sensory role in the tonsils.
The maxillary nerve supplies the nasopharynx and hard/soft palate, but not the primary tonsillar bed.
The chorda tympani is responsible for taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue.
The internal laryngeal nerve supplies the laryngopharynx, specifically around the laryngeal inlet.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1755 (Book Page): [Oropharynx: Glossopharyngeal nerve]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A patient presents with acute tonsillitis. On examination, a specific lymph node located below and behind the angle of the mandible is found to be enlarged and tender. Which node is this?
options: Paratracheal lymph node
Jugulodigastric lymph node
Jugulo-omohyoid lymph node
Submental lymph node
Occipital lymph node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric lymph node
optionExplanations: Paratracheal nodes drain the thyroid and neighboring structures, not the oropharyngeal tonsils.
The jugulodigastric node, a member of the deep cervical chain, is the primary node for the palatine tonsils and is frequently enlarged in tonsillitis.
The jugulo-omohyoid node is associated with the tongue but is located lower in the neck than the jugulodigastric node.
Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue and the central lower lip, not the palatine tonsils.
Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Contrast the anatomical location and mucosal features of the pharyngeal tonsil with the lingual tonsil. Which of the following is a distinguishing characteristic of the lingual tonsil?
options: It is located in the roof of the nasopharynx.
It is related to the salpingopharyngeal fold.
It contains numerous tonsillar crypts on its free surface.
It is located on the posterior third of the tongue.
It often undergoes hypertrophy to become 'adenoids'.
correctOption: It is located on the posterior third of the tongue.
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal tonsil, not the lingual tonsil, is located in the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx.
The salpingopharyngeal fold is a feature of the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, related primarily to the pharyngeal tonsil and auditory tube opening.

The palatine tonsil is characterized by numerous small openings leading to tonsillar crypts; the lingual tonsil has an irregular surface but the term crypts is most associated with the palatine tonsils.
The lingual tonsil is specifically the collection of lymphoid nodules found in the posterior one-third (pharyngeal part) of the tongue, characterized by an irregular surface without papillae.
Hypertrophy of the pharyngeal tonsil, not the lingual tonsil, results in the clinical condition known as adenoids.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue is devoid of papillae but has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: During a postoperative evaluation of a patient who underwent a tonsillectomy, a significant hemorrhage occurs. The surgeon suspects the bleeding is coming from a vessel that descends from the soft palate within the loose areolar tissue of the tonsillar bed. Which vessel is the most likely culprit?
options: Ascending pharyngeal artery
Internal carotid artery
Tonsillar branch of the lingual artery
External palatine vein
Facial artery
correctOption: External palatine vein
optionExplanations: The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharynx but is not specifically noted for descending from the soft palate through the areolar tissue of the tonsillar bed.
The internal carotid artery is a deep lateral relation to the tonsil bed, but it is separated by the superior constrictor muscle and styloglossus; it is rarely injured in routine tonsillectomy.
The lingual artery provides branches to the tongue; while it may contribute to general pharyngeal supply, it is not the classic vessel described in the tonsillar bed areolar tissue.

The external palatine (paratonsillar) vein is a common source of hemorrhage after tonsillectomy because it lies in the loose areolar tissue lateral to the tonsillar capsule, descending from the soft palate.
The facial artery loops near the superior constrictor, but its tonsillar branch is an artery of supply, whereas the question specifies a vessel descending from the soft palate in areolar tissue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue, and the external palatine vein descends from the soft palate in this tissue to join the pharyngeal venous plexus.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: During an oral examination, the clinician asks the patient to say 'Ah' to visualize the palatine tonsils. Between which two anatomical landmarks are these tonsils specifically situated?
options: Torus tubarius and pharyngeal recess
Palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
Hard palate and the base of the uvula
Salpingopharyngeal and salpingopalatine folds
Median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds
correctOption: Palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
optionExplanations: The torus tubarius and pharyngeal recess are structures of the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.
The palatine tonsils reside in the 'tonsillar sinus' or recess, bounded anteriorly by the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar) and posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar).
The hard palate and uvula are components of the roof of the oral cavity and oropharynx but do not bound the tonsillar fossa laterally.
The salpingopharyngeal and salpingopalatine folds are features of the nasopharynx and are unrelated to the palatine tonsillar bed.
The glossoepiglottic folds are located between the tongue and the epiglottis, marking the vallecula, not the tonsillar bed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The palatine tonsils are two masses of lymphoid tissue, each located in the depression on the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Regarding the developmental physiology of pharyngeal lymphoid tissue, which statement accurately describes the changes in the palatine and pharyngeal tonsils as a person ages from childhood to adulthood?
options: They are replaced by adipose tissue during adolescence and reappear in old age.
They maintain a constant size relative to the pharyngeal lumen throughout life.
The pharyngeal tonsil grows continuously until age 40, while the palatine tonsil atrophies at age 5.
They are absent at birth and develop only after the age of 10.
They reach their maximum size in early childhood and gradually atrophy after puberty.
correctOption: They reach their maximum size in early childhood and gradually atrophy after puberty.
optionExplanations: Lymphoid tissue atrophies, but it does not cycle or reappear in old age.
Tonsils undergo significant size changes, being largest in children and smallest in adults.
The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) does not grow until age 40; it follows the general lymphoid pattern of atrophy after puberty.
Tonsils are present in early childhood and even in a rudimentary form at birth; they do not wait until age 10 to develop.
This is a key clinical fact: lymphoid tissue hypertrophy is normal in children, and natural involution (atrophy) occurs post-puberty.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The tonsil reaches its maximum size during early childhood, but after puberty, it diminishes considerably in size... Page 1761 (Book Page): Like the palatine tonsil, it [pharyngeal tonsil] is largest in early childhood and starts to atrophy after puberty.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Which sequence correctly describes the pathway for the arterial supply of the palatine tonsil starting from the external carotid artery?
options: External carotid -> Maxillary artery -> Descending palatine branch
External carotid -> Superior thyroid artery -> Superior laryngeal branch
External carotid -> Lingual artery -> Tonsillar branch
External carotid -> Facial artery -> Tonsillar branch
External carotid -> Ascending pharyngeal artery -> Tubal branch
correctOption: External carotid -> Facial artery -> Tonsillar branch
optionExplanations: The descending palatine artery supplies the palate, but the major supply to the tonsil itself is from the facial artery.
The superior thyroid artery supplies the larynx and thyroid gland, not the tonsils.
While the lingual artery supplies the tongue (lingual tonsil), it is not the primary source for the palatine tonsil.
The primary blood supply to the palatine tonsil is the tonsillar branch, which is a direct branch of the facial artery.
The ascending pharyngeal artery supplies the pharyngeal wall but is secondary to the facial artery's tonsillar branch.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): [The tonsillar branch of the facial artery.]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Waldeyer’s ring refers to a protective circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue at the entry of the aero-digestive tract. Which component forms the most superior (roof) portion of this ring?
options: Pharyngeal tonsil
Lingual tonsil
Palatine tonsil
Tubal tonsil
Submandibular nodes
correctOption: Pharyngeal tonsil
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal tonsil is situated in the submucosa of the nasopharyngeal roof, thereby constituting the superior-most element of the ring.
The lingual tonsil is located on the posterior third of the tongue and forms the inferior (lower) part of Waldeyer's ring.
The palatine tonsils are situated in the oropharyngeal lateral walls, forming the lateral components of the ring alongside the tubal tonsils.
The tubal tonsils are located around the openings of the auditory tubes and form the lateral portions of the ring, but not the superior roof.
