Palatine tonsil
Fungiform papillae
Filiform papillae
Lingual tonsil
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: Vallate papillae are located just anterior to the sulcus terminalis; they mark the boundary but are not part of the posterior third's nodular surface.
The palatine tonsils are located on the lateral walls of the oropharynx, not on the surface of the tongue itself.
Fungiform papillae are mushroom-shaped structures found on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, not the posterior third.
Filiform papillae are the most numerous papillae on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue; they are absent on the posterior third.
The lingual tonsil consists of numerous lymphoid nodules located in the submucosa of the posterior third (root) of the tongue, giving it an irregular surface.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue is devoid of papillae but has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: During a clinical examination of a patient with suspected acute tonsillitis, the physician palpates for the 'tonsillar' lymph node. Which specific node, located below and behind the angle of the mandible, is the primary terminal drainage site for the palatine tonsil?
options: Submental node
Mastoid node
Jugulodigastric node
Jugulo-omohyoid node
Submandibular node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue, the central lower lip, and the chin [Page 1655].
Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes drain the scalp above the ear, the auricle, and the external auditory meatus [Page 1655].
The jugulodigastric node is the largest of the upper deep cervical lymph nodes and is the principal node for the palatine tonsil, often becoming enlarged and tender in tonsillitis [Page 1756, 1760].
The jugulo-omohyoid node is a deep cervical node located lower in the neck, primarily associated with the lymphatic drainage of the tongue [Page 1756].
Submandibular nodes drain the front of the scalp, nose, cheek, lips, and anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but not the primary palatine tonsil mass [Page 1655].
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1756 (Book Page): The jugulodigastric node, which is located below and behind the angle of the jaw, is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil and the tongue.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 6-year-old child presents with chronic mouth breathing and snoring. Hypertrophy of the pharyngeal tonsil is suspected. By what mechanism does this hypertrophy primarily interfere with normal nasal respiration?
options: Blockage of the posterior nasal apertures (choanae)
Compression of the lingual frenulum
Adhesion of the palatoglossal folds
Obstruction of the oropharyngeal isthmus
Narrowing of the piriform fossae
correctOption: Blockage of the posterior nasal apertures (choanae)
optionExplanations: Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) is located in the roof of the nasopharynx; when enlarged, it physically obstructs the choanae (posterior nasal apertures), preventing air from passing from the nose to the pharynx.
The lingual frenulum is a midline fold under the tongue and has no relation to the nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue or nasal obstruction.
The palatoglossal folds are oropharyngeal structures; while they may be inflamed in tonsillitis, their 'adhesion' is not the mechanism for nasal obstruction in adenoiditis.
The oropharyngeal isthmus is the opening between the mouth and the pharynx; while relevant to swallowing, adenoids are located in the nasopharynx and block the upper airway, not the oral exit.
The piriform fossae are recesses in the laryngopharynx on either side of the laryngeal inlet; they are involved in swallowing and are too inferior to be affected by adenoids.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): Marked hypertrophy blocks the posterior nasal openings and causes the patient to snore loudly at night and to breathe through the open mouth.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Which of the following describes the anatomical feature known as the 'capsule' of the palatine tonsil?
options: It is a muscular layer formed by the styloglossus
It is a reflection of the pretracheal fascia
It is a continuation of the pharyngeal raphe
It is a fibrous layer on the lateral surface of the tonsil
It is an extension of the buccal fascia
correctOption: It is a fibrous layer on the lateral surface of the tonsil
optionExplanations: The styloglossus is a muscle that lies lateral to the superior constrictor; it does not form the tonsillar capsule.
The pretracheal fascia encloses the thyroid gland and trachea, not the tonsils.
The pharyngeal raphe is a midline posterior structure where the constrictor muscles insert; it does not form the capsule of the lateral palatine tonsil.
The tonsillar capsule is a specialized fibrous layer covering only the lateral surface of the tonsil, separating it from the superior constrictor muscle.
The buccal fascia (buccopharyngeal fascia) covers the outer surface of the pharyngeal muscles but is distinct from the internal tonsillar capsule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The tonsil is covered on its lateral surface by a fibrous tonsillar capsule.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Waldeyer's Ring represents a circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue at the gateway of the respiratory and digestive tracts. Which component of this ring is located on the posterior third of the tongue?
options: Submandibular nodules
Tubal tonsils
Palatine tonsils
Pharyngeal tonsils
Lingual tonsil
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: Submandibular nodules are lymph nodes located in the neck, not part of the specialized mucosal lymphoid ring (Waldeyer's).
Tubal tonsils are located near the opening of the auditory tube in the nasopharynx, forming the lateral portions of the ring.
The palatine tonsils are located on the lateral walls of the oropharynx between the faucial arches.
The pharyngeal tonsil is located in the roof of the nasopharynx.
The lingual tonsil consists of numerous lymphoid nodules on the pharyngeal (posterior) third of the tongue, completing the inferior aspect of Waldeyer's Ring.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The pharyngeal tonsil in the roof of the nasopharynx forms the upper part, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue forms the lower part.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Venous Relations of the Palatine Tonsil Capsule
statement: During a tonsillectomy, a surgeon identifies a significant venous vessel descending from the soft palate within the loose areolar tissue lateral to the tonsillar capsule. Damage to this vessel is a known cause of troublesome postoperative bleeding. Which vessel is this?
options: Anterior jugular vein
Superior thyroid vein
Retromandibular vein
Internal jugular vein
External palatine vein
correctOption: External palatine vein
optionExplanations: The anterior jugular vein is a superficial vein of the neck, running close to the midline in the superficial fascia, far removed from the internal tonsillar bed.
The superior thyroid vein drains the upper pole of the thyroid gland and the larynx, situated inferior to the oropharyngeal structures.
The retromandibular vein is formed within the parotid gland by the union of the superficial temporal and maxillary veins, lateral to the ramus of the mandible.
The internal jugular vein is located much deeper within the carotid sheath and is lateral to the superior constrictor muscle, not within the immediate areolar tissue of the tonsillar bed.

The external palatine (paratonsillar) vein is the specific vessel found in the loose areolar tissue between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle; it is a major source of hemorrhage post-tonsillectomy.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue, and the external palatine vein descends from the soft palate in this tissue to join the pharyngeal venous plexus.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 6-year-old boy presents with chronic mouth breathing, heavy snoring at night, and persistent hearing impairment. Hypertrophy of which tonsillar tissue is most likely obstructing the posterior nasal apertures and the openings of the auditory tubes?
options: Buccal tonsil
Lingual tonsil
Tubal tonsil
Nasopharyngeal tonsil
Palatine tonsil
correctOption: Nasopharyngeal tonsil
optionExplanations: Buccal nodes exist in the cheek but do not form a tonsillar mass capable of obstructing the nasopharyngeal airway.
The lingual tonsil is located on the posterior third of the tongue and its hypertrophy would not cause nasal obstruction or auditory tube blockage.
While tubal tonsils are near the auditory tube, the primary cause of massive nasal obstruction and snoring in children is the nasopharyngeal tonsil.
Hypertrophy of the pharyngeal (nasopharyngeal) tonsils, known as adenoids, directly blocks the choanae and can compress the auditory tube openings, leading to mouth breathing and middle ear issues.
Hypertrophy of the palatine tonsils primarily affects the oropharyngeal airway and swallowing, not the posterior nasal apertures (choanae).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): Marked hypertrophy blocks the posterior nasal openings and causes the patient to snore loudly at night and to breathe through the open mouth.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of the Palatine Tonsils
statement: During a routine oral examination of a 10-year-old child, a physician identifies the palatine tonsils. Between which two specific anatomical structures are these lymphoid masses located?
options: Salpingopharyngeal and salpingopalatine folds
Median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds
Torus tubarius and pharyngeal recess
Soft palate and the posterior wall of the nasopharynx
Palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
correctOption: Palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
optionExplanations: The salpingopharyngeal fold is a feature of the nasopharynx, extending from the tubal elevation, and is not a boundary for the oropharyngeal tonsils.
These folds are located at the base of the tongue, connecting it to the epiglottis, and define the boundaries of the valleculae, not the tonsillar fossa.
The torus tubarius and pharyngeal recess are structures of the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, located superior to the oropharyngeal isthmus.
This description corresponds to the location of the pharyngeal isthmus and the pharyngeal tonsil, not the palatine tonsils.
The palatine tonsil is situated in the tonsillar sinus (fossa), which is the space defined by the palatoglossal arch anteriorly and the palatopharyngeal arch posteriorly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1754 (Book Page): The palatine tonsil occupies the recess between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Waldeyer’s ring is a circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue at the entrance of the respiratory and digestive tracts. Which of the following correctly identifies its superior and inferior components?
options: Superior: Epiglottis; Inferior: Vocal folds
Superior: Palatine tonsils; Inferior: Tubal tonsils
Superior: Pharyngeal tonsil; Inferior: Lingual tonsil
Superior: Submandibular nodes; Inferior: Deep cervical nodes
Superior: Lingual tonsil; Inferior: Pharyngeal tonsil
correctOption: Superior: Pharyngeal tonsil; Inferior: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: The epiglottis and vocal folds are laryngeal structures and are not considered components of the lymphoid Waldeyer's ring.
Palatine tonsils form the lateral parts of the ring, not the superior part.
The pharyngeal tonsil (superiorly) and the lingual tonsil (inferiorly) complete the vertical extent of Waldeyer's ring.
Waldeyer's ring consists of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (tonsils), not the regional lymph nodes like submandibular or deep cervical nodes.
This reverses the correct anatomical positions; the pharyngeal tonsil is in the nasopharyngeal roof (high), and the lingual tonsil is on the tongue (low).
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page)-1761: The pharyngeal tonsil in the roof of the nasopharynx forms the upper part, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue forms the lower part.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Vascular Supply of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: The arterial supply to the palatine tonsil is multi-source, yet the primary supply is derived from a specific branch of the facial artery. Which branch must penetrate the superior constrictor muscle to reach the tonsillar tissue?
options: The tonsillar branch
The ascending pharyngeal artery
The dorsal lingual artery
The ascending palatine artery
The descending palatine artery
correctOption: The tonsillar branch
optionExplanations: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the main arterial supply; it is situated lateral to the superior constrictor and must reach the tonsil by passing through or around this muscle layer.
The ascending pharyngeal artery is a branch of the external carotid that supplies the pharyngeal wall, but it is not the primary vessel identified for the palatine tonsil.
Dorsal lingual arteries are branches of the lingual artery that primarily supply the posterior third of the tongue and lingual tonsils.
The ascending palatine artery provides accessory supply but is not the primary tonsillar branch mentioned as the main supply.
The descending palatine artery is a branch of the maxillary artery supplying the hard and soft palate, providing only minor collateral flow to the superior pole of the tonsil.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Blood Supply: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery. The veins pierce the superior constrictor muscle and join the external palatine, the pharyngeal, or the facial veins.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Sensory Innervation of the Oropharynx and Tonsils
statement: A patient with a deep-seated infection of the oropharynx presents with pain that is referred to the ear. Anatomically, this is explained by the sensory innervation of the palatine tonsil and its surrounding mucous membrane. Which nerve carries these sensations?
options: Vagus nerve (Recurrent laryngeal branch)
Facial nerve (Chorda tympani branch)
Trigeminal nerve (V3 division)
Hypoglossal nerve
Glossopharyngeal nerve
correctOption: Glossopharyngeal nerve
optionExplanations: The vagus nerve supplies the laryngopharynx and internal larynx, but its role in the oropharyngeal tonsillar sensation is minimal compared to CN IX.
The chorda tympani carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue but does not provide general sensation to the tonsils.
The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal nerve supplies general sensation to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, but not the oropharyngeal tonsillar region.
The hypoglossal nerve is a purely motor nerve supplying the muscles of the tongue.

The glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) provides sensory innervation to the oropharynx, including the tonsillar region. Because it also supplies the middle ear via the tympanic nerve, tonsillar pain is frequently referred to the ear.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1755 (Book Page): Oropharynx: Glossopharyngeal nerve.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 5-year-old child presents with chronic mouth breathing, loud snoring, and a 'nasal' quality to his voice. An endoscopic examination reveals a significant mass of hypertrophied lymphoid tissue. Anatomically, where is this specific collection of tissue primarily located?
options: Submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
Recess between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
Posterior one-third of the dorsum of the tongue
Lateral wall of the oropharynx inferior to the soft palate
Within the pharyngeal recess behind the tubal elevation
correctOption: Submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids when enlarged) is specifically located in the submucosa of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx.
This describes the tonsillar fossa, which houses the palatine tonsils, not the pharyngeal tonsils.
This is the location of the lingual tonsil, which is part of Waldeyer's ring but does not typically cause the described symptoms of nasopharyngeal obstruction.
The lateral wall of the oropharynx is where the palatine tonsils are situated, which would cause oropharyngeal rather than nasopharyngeal symptoms.
The pharyngeal recess (Rosenmüller's fossa) is a depression behind the tubal elevation but is not the primary site for the pharyngeal tonsil mass itself, although they are adjacent.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1751 (Book Page): A collection of lymphoid tissue, the pharyngeal tonsil, sits in the submucosa of the roof [of the nasopharynx].

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of Palatine vs. Lingual Tonsils
statement: When comparing the anatomical features of the tonsils, which characteristic is unique to the free medial surface of the palatine tonsils compared to the lingual tonsils?
options: Presence of numerous small openings leading into tonsillar crypts
Innervation primarily by the internal laryngeal nerve
Presence of a fibrous capsule
An irregular surface caused by simple lymph nodules
Absence of overlying mucous membrane
correctOption: Presence of numerous small openings leading into tonsillar crypts
optionExplanations: The palatine tonsil is characterized by deep invaginations of the surface epithelium called tonsillar crypts, which are prominent on its medial surface.
The palatine tonsil is primarily supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve and maxillary nerve branches, not the internal laryngeal nerve.
The fibrous capsule is a feature of the lateral surface of the palatine tonsil, not its free medial surface.
This describes the lingual tonsil, which has an irregular surface due to lymphoid nodules but lacks the organized crypt system of the palatine tonsil.
All tonsils in the pharynx are covered by mucous membrane; they are not exposed lymphoid tissue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Each tonsil is covered by mucous membrane, and its free medial surface projects into the pharynx. The surface is pitted by numerous small openings that lead into the tonsillar crypts.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Vascular Supply of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: While performing a tonsillectomy, a surgeon identifies the arterial supply to the palatine tonsil. Which artery is the source of the primary tonsillar branch that provides the main vascular supply to this organ?
options: Ascending pharyngeal artery
Maxillary artery
Internal carotid artery
Facial artery
Lingual artery
correctOption: Facial artery
optionExplanations: The ascending pharyngeal artery does supply the pharyngeal wall and sends branches to the tonsil, but it is not listed as the primary supply source [Page 1760].
The maxillary artery supplies the jaws, muscles of mastication, nose, and palate, but it is not the source of the primary tonsillar branch [Page 1639].
The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck and does not supply the tonsils [Page 1639-1640].
The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is identified as the primary arterial supply for the palatine tonsil [Page 1760].
The lingual artery supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth, but its contribution to the tonsil is secondary to the facial artery's tonsillar branch [Page 1638].
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Blood Supply The tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Which of the following lymphoid structures constitutes the inferior (lower) portion of the protective Waldeyer's ring?
options: Tubal tonsils
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes
Pharyngeal tonsils
Palatine tonsils
Lingual tonsil
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: Tubal tonsils form the lateral parts of the ring, specifically around the auditory tube openings.
Retropharyngeal lymph nodes are not part of Waldeyer's ring, which is composed of MALT (mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue) and not encapsulated nodes.
The pharyngeal tonsil (singular) forms the superior or upper part of the ring in the nasopharyngeal roof.
The palatine tonsils are paired structures forming the lateral parts of the ring within the oropharynx.
The lingual tonsil, located on the posterior third of the tongue, completes the ring inferiorly.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The pharyngeal tonsil in the roof of the nasopharynx forms the upper part, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue forms the lower part.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Clinical Relations of the Pharyngeal Tonsil
statement: A 6-year-old boy presents with recurring middle ear infections (otitis media) and impaired hearing. The physician explains that hypertrophy of a specific tonsil is obstructing the auditory tube. Which tonsil is most likely involved and where is its clinical relation to the auditory tube?
options: Pharyngeal tonsil; located in the roof of the nasopharynx near the tubal opening
Palatine tonsil; located in the nasopharynx
Palatine tonsil; located between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
Lingual tonsil; located on the posterior third of the tongue
Tubal tonsil; located in the oropharynx
correctOption: Pharyngeal tonsil; located in the roof of the nasopharynx near the tubal opening
optionExplanations: Hypertrophy of the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) in the nasopharynx can obstruct the nearby auditory tube opening, leading to middle ear dysfunction.
Palatine tonsils are located in the oropharynx, not the nasopharynx.
Palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx and their enlargement typically causes swallowing or airway issues, not primary auditory tube obstruction.
The lingual tonsil is on the tongue and is not anatomically situated to block the auditory tube.
While tubal tonsils exist, the text emphasizes the pharyngeal tonsil's role in otitis media, and tubal tonsils are not in the oropharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): The close relationship of the infected lymphoid tissue [pharyngeal tonsil] to the auditory tube may be the cause of deafness and recurrent otitis media.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A medical student is examining the oropharynx of a patient during a routine physical. They identify a mass of lymphoid tissue situated in a depression on the lateral wall. Between which specific anatomical structures is this lymphoid tissue located?
options: The torus tubarius and the salpingopharyngeal fold
The median and lateral glossoepiglottic folds
The salpingopharyngeal fold and the pharyngeal recess
The palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
The soft palate and the tubal elevation
correctOption: The palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
optionExplanations: These structures are located in the nasopharynx; the salpingopharyngeal fold extends downward from the torus tubarius but does not bound the palatine tonsil.
The glossoepiglottic folds are located in the region of the vallecula, which is between the posterior tongue and the epiglottis.
The salpingopharyngeal fold and pharyngeal recess are features of the nasopharynx, not the oropharynx where palatine tonsils are found.
The palatine tonsils are classically situated in the tonsillar sinus (fossa) between the palatoglossal arch anteriorly and the palatopharyngeal arch posteriorly.
The tubal elevation (torus tubarius) is located in the nasopharynx and surrounds the opening of the auditory tube.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The palatine tonsils are two masses of lymphoid tissue, each located in the depression on the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Surface Anatomy of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: Examination of the free medial surface of the palatine tonsil reveals several small, pitted openings. What are these anatomical features called?
options: Tonsillar papillae
Tonsillar sinuses
Tonsillar folds
Tonsillar crypts
Tonsillar capsules
correctOption: Tonsillar crypts
optionExplanations: Tonsils do not possess 'papillae'; papillae are found on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue [Page 1727].
The tonsillar sinus is the anatomical space/depression between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches where the tonsil resides [Page 1754].
While there are folds in the pharynx (like the salpingopharyngeal fold), the pits on the tonsil surface specifically lead to crypts, not folds [Page 1752, 1760].
The medial (free) surface of the palatine tonsil is characterized by numerous invaginations of the epithelium known as tonsillar crypts [Page 1760].
The tonsillar capsule is the fibrous layer covering the lateral surface of the tonsil, not the medial pitted surface [Page 1760].
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Its free medial surface projects into the pharynx. The surface is pitted by numerous small openings that lead into the tonsillar crypts.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Waldeyer's ring is a circular arrangement of lymphoid tissue at the entrance of the pharynx. Which component forms the lower (inferior) part of this ring?
options: Lingual tonsil
Palatine tonsils
Tubal tonsils
Submandibular nodes
Pharyngeal tonsil
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: The lingual tonsil, located on the posterior third of the tongue, completes the ring inferiorly.
The palatine tonsils form the lateral portions of the ring.
The tubal tonsils also contribute to the lateral aspects near the auditory tube openings.
Submandibular nodes are part of the lymphatic drainage system but are not components of the mucosal lymphoid ring itself.
The pharyngeal tonsil forms the superior (upper) part of the ring.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): [The pharyngeal tonsil in the roof of the nasopharynx forms the upper part, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue forms the lower part.]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 22-year-old male undergoes a tonsillectomy for chronic tonsillitis. Two hours postoperatively, he develops significant bleeding from the tonsillar bed. Anatomically, which vessel, descending from the soft palate in the loose areolar tissue lateral to the tonsillar capsule, is most likely responsible for this troublesome postoperative venous hemorrhage?
options: External palatine vein
Internal jugular vein
Ascending pharyngeal vein
Pharyngeal venous plexus
Facial vein
correctOption: External palatine vein
optionExplanations: The external palatine vein (paratonsillar vein) descends in the loose areolar tissue just lateral to the tonsillar capsule and is a common source of venous bleeding following the removal of the tonsil.
The internal jugular vein is separated from the tonsil by the superior constrictor, styloglossus, and carotid sheath; it is not in the immediate surgical field of a routine tonsillectomy.
The ascending pharyngeal vein is deeper and typically not the primary source of paratonsillar venous hemorrhage.
While the external palatine vein eventually joins the pharyngeal venous plexus, the specific vessel identified as the source in the bed is the external palatine vein.
The facial vein is a more superficial structure on the face and does not lie in the tonsillar bed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): After tonsillectomy, the external palatine vein, which lies lateral to the tonsil, may be the source of troublesome postoperative bleeding.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 19-year-old student presents with severe throat pain, high fever, and trismus (inability to open the mouth). Physical exam reveals the uvula is deviated to the right and the left peritonsillar area is bulging. If this is a peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy), what is the precise anatomical site of the pus collection?
options: In the sublingual space superior to the mylohyoid muscle
In the loose connective tissue between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor
In the retropharyngeal space behind the pharyngeal raphe
Between the mucous membrane and the medial surface of the tonsil
Within the parenchyma of the palatine tonsil
correctOption: In the loose connective tissue between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The sublingual space is in the floor of the mouth; while Ludwig's angina involves this space, Quinsy is localized to the oropharyngeal wall.
Correct. Quinsy occurs when infection spreads through the tonsillar capsule into the peritonsillar space (loose areolar tissue) between the capsule and the superior constrictor muscle.
Incorrect. The retropharyngeal space is posterior to the pharynx; infection here presents as a midline bulge in the posterior pharyngeal wall, not a peritonsillar bulge.
Incorrect. Pus on the surface or within crypts is characteristic of follicular tonsillitis, not a peritonsillar abscess.
Incorrect. An abscess within the tonsil itself is rare; the term 'peritonsillar' specifically refers to the space surrounding the tonsillar capsule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is caused by spread of infection from the palatine tonsil to the loose connective tissue outside the capsule (see Fig. 12.91).

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Features of the Palatine Tonsil Surface
statement: While using a laryngeal mirror to examine a patient's oropharynx, a physician observes the medial surface of the palatine tonsils. What characteristic anatomical feature is visible on this surface?
options: Small openings leading into tonsillar crypts
Smooth, non-pitted squamous epithelium
The stalk of the epiglottis
A thick, white, avascular membrane
Tubal elevations from the auditory tube
correctOption: Small openings leading into tonsillar crypts
optionExplanations: The medial surface of the palatine tonsil is pitted by 12–15 small openings called tonsillar crypts, which can often contain debris or 'tonsilloliths'.
The surface is specifically not smooth; it is irregular and pitted due to the crypts.
The stalk of the epiglottis is located inferiorly and anteriorly to the oropharynx, attached to the thyroid cartilage.
Avascular white membranes are characteristic of the 'true' vocal folds in the larynx, not the palatine tonsils.
The tubal elevation is a feature of the nasopharynx, not the palatine tonsil.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Each tonsil is covered by mucous membrane, and its free medial surface projects into the pharynx. The surface is pitted by numerous small openings that lead into the tonsillar crypts.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A patient presents with acute tonsillitis. The physician notes a specific enlarged and tender lymph node located just below and behind the angle of the mandible. This node is most representative of which group?
options: Submandibular nodes
Submental nodes
Jugulodigastric node
Mastoid nodes
Paratracheal nodes
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: Submandibular nodes drain the front of the scalp, nose, and lips, but the tonsil drains to the upper deep cervical group.
Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue and the center of the lower lip.
The jugulodigastric node, part of the upper deep cervical chain, is the primary node for tonsillar drainage and is located near the angle of the mandible.
Mastoid nodes receive lymph from the scalp above the ear and the external auditory meatus.
Paratracheal nodes lie alongside the trachea and primarily drain the thyroid and adjacent structures.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Tonsil Lymph Drainage: The upper deep cervical lymph nodes, just below and behind the angle of the mandible. [Page 1656 (Book Page)]: The jugulodigastric node... is mainly concerned with drainage of the tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Venous Drainage and Surgical Complications of Tonsillectomy
statement: During a tonsillectomy, a surgeon removes the palatine tonsil from its bed. After the removal, 'troublesome' venous bleeding is encountered from the loose areolar tissue layer separating the tonsillar capsule from the superior constrictor muscle. Which vessel is the most likely source of this hemorrhage?
options: External palatine vein
Superior thyroid vein
Facial vein
Lingual vein
Internal jugular vein
correctOption: External palatine vein
optionExplanations: The external palatine vein (paratonsillar vein) is clinically significant as it descends through the loose areolar tissue of the tonsillar bed; it is frequently the cause of postoperative bleeding.
The superior thyroid vein drains the upper part of the thyroid gland and larynx, located inferior to the oropharynx.
The facial vein is a larger vessel that eventually receives drainage but is not the specific vessel descending from the soft palate in the tonsillar bed areolar tissue.
The lingual vein drains the tongue and is situated in the floor of the mouth, not in the lateral wall of the oropharynx.
The internal jugular vein is located much deeper and lateral to the carotid sheath, not in the immediate areolar tissue of the tonsillar bed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): [The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue, and the external palatine vein descends from the soft palate in this tissue to join the pharyngeal venous plexus.]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 4-year-old child presents with chronic mouth breathing, snoring at night, and persistent nasal congestion. Clinical examination reveals excessive hypertrophy of lymphoid tissue in the roof of the nasopharynx. Which of the following describes the specific anatomical location of the affected tonsil?
options: Within the pharyngeal recess behind the tubal elevation
In the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
On the posterior third of the tongue behind the sulcus terminalis
Surrounding the opening of the auditory tube in the lateral wall
In the depression between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches
correctOption: In the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal recess is a depression behind the tubal elevation, but it is not the primary site of the pharyngeal tonsil itself.
The nasopharyngeal (pharyngeal) tonsil is specifically located in the submucosa of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx; when hypertrophied, it is referred to as adenoids.
This describes the location of the lingual tonsil, which occupies the pharyngeal part of the tongue and does not obstruct the posterior nasal apertures.
This describes the tubal tonsils, which are distinct collections of lymphoid tissue near the torus tubarius, though they contribute to Waldeyer's ring along with the pharyngeal tonsil.
This describes the location of the palatine tonsils, which are situated in the oropharynx, not the nasopharynx, and are typically associated with sore throats rather than nasal obstruction.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1751 (Book Page): A collection of lymphoid tissue, the pharyngeal tonsil, sits in the submucosa of the roof.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Vascular supply of the palatine tonsil
statement: Which specific arterial branch provides the primary vascular supply to the palatine tonsil?
options: Ascending palatine branch of the facial artery
Dorsal lingual branch of the lingual artery
Descending palatine artery
Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
Pharyngeal branch of the maxillary artery
correctOption: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
optionExplanations: The ascending palatine branch of the facial artery supplies the soft palate and pharyngeal wall but is not the primary supplier of the tonsillar tissue itself.
The dorsal lingual branches supply the posterior third of the tongue and the lingual tonsils, rather than the palatine tonsils.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Diagnostic Contrast: Adenoids vs. Palatine Tonsils
statement: How does the clinical presentation of hypertrophied nasopharyngeal tonsils contrast with palatine tonsillitis regarding respiratory mechanics?
options: Adenoids primarily cause difficulty in the oral phase of deglutition.
Nasopharyngeal tonsils obstruct the oropharyngeal isthmus during swallowing.
Hypertrophied adenoids cause mouth breathing by blocking the posterior nasal apertures.
Palatine tonsillitis primarily causes obstruction of the external nares.
Palatine tonsils prevent the elevation of the soft palate during speech.
correctOption: Hypertrophied adenoids cause mouth breathing by blocking the posterior nasal apertures.
optionExplanations: Adenoids affect the nasopharynx; the oral phase of swallowing is predominantly influenced by the tongue and palatine arches.
Obstruction of the oropharyngeal isthmus is a feature of massive palatine tonsil hypertrophy, not adenoids.
Because nasopharyngeal tonsils (adenoids) are located in the roof of the nasopharynx, their enlargement physically blocks the choanae, necessitating mouth breathing.
Palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx and do not affect the nasal apertures.
While palatine tonsils are near the soft palate, they do not typically prevent its elevation unless associated with severe peritonsillar edema.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): [Marked hypertrophy blocks the posterior nasal openings and causes the patient to snore loudly at night and to breathe through the open mouth.]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 22-year-old medical student is examining the dorsal surface of a cadaveric tongue. Posterior to the sulcus terminalis, the surface appears irregular but lacks the characteristic papillae found on the anterior two-thirds. This irregularity is primarily due to:
options: Tonsillar crypts
Fibrous capsule of the tongue
Vallate papillae
Filiform papillae
Lingual tonsil nodules
correctOption: Lingual tonsil nodules
optionExplanations: Tonsillar crypts are a feature of the palatine tonsil, while the lingual tonsil surface is described as irregular due to nodules.
The tongue is composed of muscle and a median septum; the surface irregularity is epithelial/lymphoid, not due to a fibrous capsule.
Vallate papillae are located along the sulcus terminalis but are not the cause of the irregular surface of the posterior third itself.
Filiform papillae are restricted to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and provide its abrasive texture.
The posterior third of the tongue contains no papillae; its irregular, nodular appearance is created by the underlying lymphoid follicles of the lingual tonsil.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): [The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue is devoid of papillae but has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 4-year-old boy presents with recurring middle ear infections (otitis media) and impaired hearing. Anatomical theory suggests that hypertrophied lymphoid tissue is obstructing the opening of the auditory tube. Which part of Waldeyer's ring is most likely involved in this mechanical obstruction?
options: Lingual tonsil
Adenoids
Palatine tonsil
Submental lymph nodes
Buccal nodes
correctOption: Adenoids
optionExplanations: The lingual tonsil is on the tongue and cannot reach or obstruct the auditory tube in the nasopharynx.

Adenoids (hypertrophied pharyngeal tonsils) are located near the nasopharyngeal opening of the auditory tube; their enlargement can block the tube, leading to negative middle ear pressure and infection.
The palatine tonsils are in the oropharynx; their hypertrophy causes airway obstruction at the level of the throat, not the auditory tube.
Submental lymph nodes are external and located under the chin, having no role in internal auditory tube obstruction.
Buccal nodes are located in the cheek and do not relate to the pharyngeal airway or auditory tube.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): The close relationship of the infected lymphoid tissue to the auditory tube may be the cause of deafness and recurrent otitis media. [Note: referring to pharyngeal tonsils/adenoids]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: Following a tonsillectomy, a patient is found to have an enlarged lymph node situated just below and behind the angle of the mandible. This node is classically the primary site for lymphatic drainage from the palatine tonsil. What is the name of this node?
options: Jugulodigastric node
Paratracheal node
Submental node
Occipital node
Mastoid node
correctOption: Jugulodigastric node
optionExplanations: The jugulodigastric node, an upper deep cervical node, is the primary node for tonsillar drainage; it is located where the posterior belly of the digastric muscle crosses the internal jugular vein.
Paratracheal nodes drain the trachea and the thyroid gland, located inferiorly in the neck.
Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue and the center of the lower lip, not the tonsils.
Occipital nodes drain the back of the scalp and are located on the posterior aspect of the skull.
Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes drain the scalp and the external ear canal.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Tonsil Lymph Drainage: The upper deep cervical lymph nodes, just below and behind the angle of the mandible. (Page 1656 (Book Page) confirms this is the jugulodigastric node).

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: Which anatomical structure defines the anterior boundary of the tonsillar sinus (the bed of the palatine tonsil)?
options: Palatopharyngeal arch
Superior constrictor muscle
Salpingopharyngeal fold
Styloglossus muscle
Palatoglosssal arch
correctOption: Palatoglosssal arch
optionExplanations: The palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar) forms the posterior boundary of the tonsillar sinus.
The superior constrictor muscle forms the floor (lateral wall) of the tonsillar bed, not the anterior boundary.
The salpingopharyngeal fold is located in the nasopharynx, superior to the palatine tonsil.
The styloglossus muscle is a lateral relation, found outside the pharyngeal wall/constrictor muscle.
The palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar) contains the palatoglossus muscle and forms the anterior boundary of the tonsillar sinus.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The palatine tonsils are two masses of lymphoid tissue, each located in the depression on the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: An elderly male smoker presents with a persistent feeling of a lump in his throat. On examination, the physician notes an irregular, 'cobblestone' appearance on the posterior one-third of the tongue, which is identified as the lingual tonsil. Which anatomical feature explains this irregular surface?
options: Ductal openings of the minor serous glands of von Ebner
Presence of underlying lymph nodules
Valleys of the large vallate papillae
Orifices of the sublingual ducts
Protrusion of the genioglossus muscle fibers
correctOption: Presence of underlying lymph nodules
optionExplanations: Von Ebner's glands are associated with vallate papillae on the oral part of the tongue, whereas the pharyngeal part is covered by the lingual tonsil.
The lingual tonsil consists of numerous lymphoid nodules embedded in the submucosa of the posterior 1/3 of the tongue, which lacks papillae but has an irregular surface due to these nodules.
Vallate papillae are located anterior to the sulcus terminalis and mark the boundary; they are not part of the posterior third's lingual tonsil surface.
Sublingual ducts open on the sublingual fold in the floor of the mouth, not the posterior third of the tongue.
Genioglossus forms the bulk of the tongue but is deep; the surface irregularity is purely mucosal/lymphoid.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue... has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 5-year-old patient is evaluated for recurrent middle ear infections (otitis media). Physical examination reveals enlarged adenoids. What anatomical structure is directly affected by this lymphoid hypertrophy, leading to impaired middle ear ventilation?
options: The piriform fossa
The opening of the auditory tube
The vestibule of the larynx
The vallecula
The sublingual fold
correctOption: The opening of the auditory tube
optionExplanations: The piriform fossa is in the laryngopharynx, far below the site of the adenoids and auditory tube.

Correct. The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) is located in the nasopharynx near the torus tubarius. Hypertrophy can mechanically compress or lead to infection of the auditory (Eustachian) tube, preventing pressure equalization and leading to otitis media.
The vestibule of the larynx is the area between the laryngeal inlet and the vestibular folds, unrelated to the nasopharynx.
The vallecula is a depression between the tongue and epiglottis in the oropharynx.
The sublingual fold is in the floor of the mouth, associated with the sublingual salivary gland.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1762 (Book Page): The close relationship of the infected lymphoid tissue to the auditory tube may be the cause of deafness and recurrent otitis media.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lymphatic Drainage of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: A patient presents with a severe infection of the right palatine tonsil. Which group of lymph nodes, located specifically below and behind the angle of the mandible, is expected to be enlarged and tender as the primary site of drainage?
options: Mastoid nodes
Jugulodigastric nodes
Submental nodes
Occipital nodes
Submandibular nodes
correctOption: Jugulodigastric nodes
optionExplanations: Mastoid (retroauricular) nodes receive lymph from the scalp and external auditory meatus, not from the oropharyngeal mucosa.
The jugulodigastric node, a member of the upper deep cervical group, is termed the 'tonsillar node' because it is the primary drainage site for the palatine tonsils.
Submental nodes drain the tip of the tongue, center of the lower lip, and chin; they do not receive primary drainage from the palatine tonsils.
Occipital nodes drain the posterior scalp and are unrelated to the lymphatic pathways of the pharynx or oral cavity.
Submandibular nodes drain the nose, cheeks, and anterior tongue; they may be involved in facial infections but the tonsil drains to a specific deep cervical node.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): The deep cervical lymph node situated below and behind the angle of the mandible, which drains lymph from this organ, is usually enlarged and tender.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: The Waldeyer’s ring of lymphoid tissue serves as a protective barrier at the entrance of the respiratory and digestive tracts. Which of the following correctly identifies the lower (inferior) component of this ring?
options: Pharyngeal tonsil
Tubal tonsils
Palatine tonsils
Palatoglossal arch
Lingual tonsil
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: The pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) is located in the roof of the nasopharynx and constitutes the superior (upper) part of Waldeyer's ring.
The tubal tonsils are located laterally around the auditory tube openings and form part of the lateral boundaries of the ring along with the palatine tonsils.
The palatine tonsils are located on the lateral walls of the oropharynx and form the lateral components of the ring.
The palatoglossal arch is a fold of mucous membrane covering a muscle; while it forms the boundary for the palatine tonsil, it is not itself a lymphoid component of Waldeyer's ring.
The lingual tonsil, located on the posterior third of the tongue, forms the base or inferior portion of the circumpharyngeal lymphoid ring.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Waldeyer’s Ring of Lymphoid Tissue... The pharyngeal tonsil in the roof of the nasopharynx forms the upper part, and the lingual tonsil on the posterior third of the tongue forms the lower part.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: An 8-year-old male presents with persistent, brisk venous bleeding following a tonsillectomy. The surgeon notes the hemorrhage is originating from the loose areolar tissue in the lateral part of the tonsillar bed. Which vessel is the most likely source?
options: External palatine vein
Internal carotid artery
Lingual vein
Ascending pharyngeal artery
Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
correctOption: External palatine vein
optionExplanations: The external palatine (paratonsillar) vein descends from the soft palate in the loose areolar tissue lateral to the tonsillar capsule, making it a common source of post-tonsillectomy hemorrhage.
The internal carotid artery is a major lateral relation but is protected by the superior constrictor muscle and is rarely the source of immediate post-op venous ooze.
The lingual vein drains the tongue and is located inferior to the primary tonsillar bed.
The ascending pharyngeal artery contributes to the supply but is an arterial source, not a venous one.
The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the primary arterial supply, but the question specifies venous bleeding in the loose areolar tissue.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): [After tonsillectomy, the external palatine vein, which lies lateral to the tonsil, may be the source of troublesome postoperative bleeding.]

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: During a clinical examination of the oropharynx, a physician identifies a mass located between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches. Which anatomical feature distinguishes the lateral relation of this mass from the mass itself?
options: The attachment of the median glossoepiglottic fold
A fibrous capsule separated from the superior constrictor by loose areolar tissue
The absence of any overlying mucous membrane
Direct continuity with the torus tubarius
The presence of tonsillar crypts on the lateral surface
correctOption: A fibrous capsule separated from the superior constrictor by loose areolar tissue
optionExplanations: The median glossoepiglottic fold is a feature of the oropharynx connecting the tongue to the epiglottis, located in the midline, not lateral to the tonsillar fossa.

The palatine tonsil is bounded laterally by a fibrous capsule. This capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle (the pharyngeal bed) by a layer of loose areolar tissue, which is a surgical cleavage plane.
The palatine tonsil is covered by a mucous membrane on its medial surface; it is not an exposed or 'raw' lymphoid mass in its normal state.
The torus tubarius is a feature of the nasopharynx related to the auditory tube, located superior to the oropharyngeal tonsillar fossa.
Tonsillar crypts are found on the free medial surface that projects into the pharynx, not the lateral surface which is covered by a capsule.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The tonsil is covered on its lateral surface by a fibrous tonsillar capsule. The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Arterial Supply of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: What is the primary arterial vessel providing blood supply to the palatine tonsil?
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
Maxillary artery
Superior laryngeal artery
Internal laryngeal artery
Superior thyroid artery
correctOption: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
optionExplanations: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the principal artery supplying the palatine tonsil.
While branches of the maxillary artery (like the descending palatine) contribute, the facial artery's tonsillar branch is the primary supply.
The superior laryngeal artery supplies the larynx and does not reach the palatine tonsil.
There is no 'internal laryngeal artery'; the internal laryngeal nerve is accompanied by the superior laryngeal artery.
The superior thyroid artery supplies the thyroid gland and the upper larynx, not the tonsils.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Blood Supply: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 5-year-old child is diagnosed with excessive hypertrophy of the lymphoid tissue located in the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx. Which anatomical structure is primarily involved?
options: Tubal tonsil
Pharyngeal tonsil
Palatine tonsil
Lingual tonsil
Sublingual gland
correctOption: Pharyngeal tonsil
optionExplanations: Tubal tonsils are smaller collections of lymphoid tissue specifically located around the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube.
The pharyngeal tonsil, also known as adenoids when hypertrophied, is situated in the submucosa of the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx.
The palatine tonsils are located in the lateral wall of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches, not in the roof of the nasopharynx.
The lingual tonsil is located on the posterior third of the tongue, forming the inferior part of Waldeyer's ring.
The sublingual gland is a salivary gland located in the floor of the mouth, not part of the lymphoid Waldeyer's ring.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1751 (Book Page): A collection of lymphoid tissue, the pharyngeal tonsil, sits in the submucosa of the roof.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Boundaries of a Peritonsillar Abscess
statement: A 19-year-old male presents with severe throat pain, high fever, and 'hot potato' voice. Examination reveals a peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy) that has displaced the uvula to the opposite side. Anatomically, where is the pus collected in this condition, and what is its immediate lateral relation?
options: Between the tongue and the epiglottis; within the vallecula
Outside the tonsillar capsule in the loose connective tissue; medial to the superior constrictor
Between the mucosa and the capsule; lateral to the palatoglossus
Within the tonsillar crypts; medial to the palatopharyngeus
Deep to the superior constrictor muscle; lateral to the internal carotid artery
correctOption: Outside the tonsillar capsule in the loose connective tissue; medial to the superior constrictor
optionExplanations: The vallecula is a depression between the tongue and epiglottis; it is far inferior to the site of a palatine peritonsillar abscess.
Correct. A peritonsillar abscess forms in the loose areolar tissue (the peritonsillar space) which is situated between the tonsillar capsule and the superior constrictor muscle.
The infection in quinsy spreads through the capsule, not merely deep to the mucosa; the palatoglossus is the anterior boundary of the fossa, not the lateral wall.
Infection within the crypts is simple follicular tonsillitis; quinsy specifically refers to the spread beyond the capsule into the surrounding tissue.
If pus were deep (lateral) to the superior constrictor, it would be in the parapharyngeal space, which is a more severe complication; quinsy is medial to this muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1761 (Book Page): A peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) is caused by spread of infection from the palatine tonsil to the loose connective tissue outside the capsule (see Fig. 12.91). ... Page 1760 (Book Page): The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: During a tonsillectomy, a surgeon must ligate the primary arterial supply to the palatine tonsil to prevent perioperative hemorrhage. From which of the following arteries does this primary vessel directly arise?
options: Maxillary artery
Internal carotid artery
Facial artery
Ascending pharyngeal artery
Lingual artery
correctOption: Facial artery
optionExplanations: The maxillary artery provides supply to the palate and nasal cavity, but the tonsillar branch specifically originates from the facial artery.
The internal carotid artery has no branches in the neck and lies lateral to the superior constrictor muscle, serving as a landmark rather than a direct supplier here.
The facial artery, as it arches over the submandibular gland, gives off the tonsillar branch, which is the main source of blood for the palatine tonsil.
The ascending pharyngeal artery provides supplementary supply to the pharynx but is not the source of the primary tonsillar branch.
While the lingual artery supplies the tongue and may provide minor branches to the lingual tonsil, it is not the primary supply to the palatine tonsil.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Blood Supply: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lateral Anatomical Relations of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: A patient presents with a deep-seated infection in the oropharyngeal wall. In the lateral relations of the palatine tonsil, which muscle lies immediately lateral to the superior constrictor muscle?
options: Palatopharyngeus
Palatoglossus
Styloglossus
Mylohyoid
Levator veli palatini
correctOption: Styloglossus
optionExplanations: The palatopharyngeus muscle is located medial to the tonsillar bed, within the palatopharyngeal arch.
The palatoglossus muscle is located medial to the tonsillar bed, within the palatoglossal arch.
The styloglossus muscle is one of the structures (along with the facial artery loop and internal carotid) found lateral to the superior constrictor muscle in the tonsillar region.
The mylohyoid muscle forms the floor of the mouth and is located inferior to the tonsillar region.
The levator veli palatini is located superiorly and medially in the soft palate, not immediately lateral to the tonsillar bed.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Lateral to the superior constrictor muscle lie the styloglossus muscle, the loop of the facial artery, and the internal carotid artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a history of persistent mouth breathing and loud snoring at night. Clinical examination suggests a significant collection of lymphoid tissue is obstructing the posterior nasal apertures. In which specific anatomical location is this tissue primarily situated?
options: Lateral wall of the oropharynx
Pharyngeal recess behind the tubal elevation
Posterior third of the tongue
Floor of the nasal cavity
Submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
correctOption: Submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx
optionExplanations: The lateral wall of the oropharynx is the site of the palatine tonsils, not the nasopharyngeal tonsils.
The pharyngeal recess (Rosenmüller's fossa) is a depression behind the tubal elevation, but it is not the primary site of the pharyngeal tonsil mass.
The posterior third of the tongue contains the lingual tonsil, not the pharyngeal tonsil.
The floor of the nasal cavity is formed by the hard palate and does not contain the pharyngeal tonsil.
The pharyngeal tonsil, which when enlarged is called adenoids, is specifically located in the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1751 (Book Page): A collection of lymphoid tissue, the pharyngeal tonsil, sits in the submucosa of the roof.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Vascular Supply of the Palatine Tonsils
statement: A surgeon performing a tonsillectomy must be particularly cautious of arterial bleeding. Which vessel provides the primary arterial supply to the palatine tonsil?
options: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
Superior thyroid artery
Ascending pharyngeal artery
Lingual artery
Descending palatine artery
correctOption: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
optionExplanations: The tonsillar branch of the facial artery is the principal arterial supply to the palatine tonsil, often requiring ligation or cautery during surgery.
The superior thyroid artery supplies the larynx and thyroid gland and has no significant contribution to the tonsillar vascular bed.
The ascending pharyngeal artery provides supplementary supply but is not the primary vessel targeted during tonsillectomy for hemostasis.
The lingual artery supplies the tongue and floor of the mouth; while it gives branches to the tonsillar region, it is not the main supply.
The descending palatine artery supplies the hard and soft palate but is not the chief nutrient artery for the palatine tonsil.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The tonsillar branch of the facial artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Relations of the Palatine Tonsil Capsule
statement: Regarding the surgical anatomy of the palatine tonsil, which of the following correctly describes the relationship between the tonsillar capsule and the surrounding structures?
options: The superior constrictor muscle lies medial to the tonsillar capsule.
The tonsillar artery pierces the capsule on its medial (free) surface.
The capsule is fused directly to the fibers of the palatoglossus muscle.
The external palatine vein is located lateral to the capsule within loose areolar tissue.
The internal carotid artery is located anterior to the palatoglossal arch.
correctOption: The external palatine vein is located lateral to the capsule within loose areolar tissue.
optionExplanations: The superior constrictor muscle forms the tonsillar bed and lies lateral to the capsule, not medial to it [Page 1760].
The arterial supply (tonsillar branch of the facial artery) enters the tonsil by piercing the superior constrictor and the capsule from the lateral side, not the medial free surface [Page 1760].
The capsule is on the lateral surface, while the palatoglossus forms the palatoglossal arch anterior to the tonsil, not fused to the capsule [Page 1753].
The external palatine vein (paratonsillar vein) is a critical surgical landmark because it lies in the loose areolar tissue plane lateral to the fibrous capsule of the tonsil [Page 1760].

The internal carotid artery is located lateral to the superior constrictor muscle in the carotid sheath, which is posterior and lateral to the tonsil, not anterior to the palatoglossal arch [Page 1760].
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue, and the external palatine vein descends from the soft palate in this tissue to join the pharyngeal venous plexus.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with a 'lumpy' feeling at the back of his tongue. Upon examination, the clinician identifies multiple irregular nodules on the posterior one-third of the tongue, posterior to the sulcus terminalis. These nodules represent which anatomical structure?
options: Lingual tonsil
Fungiform papillae
Epiglottic vallecula
Palatine tonsil
Vallate papillae
correctOption: Lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: The lingual tonsil consists of lymphoid nodules located in the posterior third of the tongue, giving it an irregular, 'lumpy' surface.
Fungiform papillae are found on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, specifically on the dorsal surface.
The valleculae are depressions located between the tongue and the epiglottis, posterior to the lingual tonsil.
The palatine tonsils are located in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, not on the surface of the tongue.
Vallate papillae are large papillae located anterior to the sulcus terminalis, not on the posterior one-third (root) itself.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue is devoid of papillae but has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lateral Relations of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: A surgeon performing a deep dissection of the tonsillar bed must be aware of the structures lying immediately lateral to the tonsillar capsule. Which muscle separates the palatine tonsil from the facial artery loop and the internal carotid artery?
options: Palatoglossus
Middle constrictor
Superior constrictor
Palatopharyngeus
Styloglossus
correctOption: Superior constrictor
optionExplanations: The palatoglossus muscle forms the anterior arch (pillar) of the tonsillar fossa, not its lateral bed.
The middle constrictor muscle is located inferior to the superior constrictor and does not form the primary lateral bed of the palatine tonsil.
The superior constrictor muscle forms the main part of the tonsillar bed; it separates the tonsillar capsule from deeper structures like the facial artery and internal carotid.
The palatopharyngeus muscle forms the posterior arch (pillar) of the tonsillar fossa.
The styloglossus muscle lies lateral to the superior constrictor, meaning the constrictor is between the tonsil and this muscle.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): The capsule is separated from the superior constrictor muscle by loose areolar tissue... Lateral to the superior constrictor muscle lie the styloglossus muscle, the loop of the facial artery, and the internal carotid artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Features of the Lingual Tonsil
statement: A 45-year-old male presents with an irregular, bumpy sensation on the posterior one-third of his tongue. Upon inspection with a mirror, the physician notes several lymphoid nodules. Which anatomical feature is characteristic of the mucous membrane in this specific region of the tongue?
options: Fringed folds of the plica fimbriata
Absence of papillae and presence of the lingual tonsil
Presence of filiform papillae for tactile sensation
Presence of large vallate papillae along the sulcus terminalis
Openings of the submandibular ducts on the sublingual fold
correctOption: Absence of papillae and presence of the lingual tonsil
optionExplanations: The plica fimbriata is located on the inferior surface of the tongue, lateral to the lingual frenulum [Page 1719, 1727].

The posterior third (pharyngeal part) of the tongue is unique because it lacks papillae entirely; its irregular, nodular surface is due to the lymphoid tissue that constitutes the lingual tonsil [Page 1727].
Filiform papillae are found only on the anterior two-thirds (oral part) of the tongue, providing it with a velvet-like texture [Page 1727].
Vallate papillae are situated just anterior to the sulcus terminalis (the boundary), not on the posterior third itself [Page 1727, 1734].
The submandibular ducts open into the floor of the mouth on papillae lateral to the lingual frenulum, not on the posterior third of the tongue [Page 1719].
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1727 (Book Page): The mucous membrane covering the posterior third of the tongue is devoid of papillae but has an irregular surface, caused by the presence of underlying lymph nodules, the lingual tonsil.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lateral relations of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: A patient is diagnosed with a peritonsillar abscess (Quinsy). During the assessment of the lateral relations of the tonsillar bed, the clinician must realize that the internal carotid artery is situated in a vulnerable location. What is the correct topographical relationship of the internal carotid artery to the palatine tonsil?
options: It descends within the palatopharyngeal arch itself.
It lies directly medial to the tonsillar crypts in the oropharyngeal lumen.
It is located anterior to the palatoglossal arch in the submandibular space.
It pierces the tonsillar capsule to provide the main blood supply to the lower pole.
It lies lateral to the superior constrictor muscle, roughly 1 inch posterior and lateral to the tonsil.
correctOption: It lies lateral to the superior constrictor muscle, roughly 1 inch posterior and lateral to the tonsil.
optionExplanations: The palatopharyngeal arch contains the palatopharyngeus muscle, not the internal carotid artery.
The internal carotid artery is a deep structure in the neck and never enters the pharyngeal lumen.
The internal carotid artery is posterior to the oral cavity and palatoglossal arch, located in the carotid sheath.
The internal carotid artery provides no direct branches to the tonsil; the tonsillar supply comes from the external carotid system (facial, lingual, ascending pharyngeal).

The internal carotid artery lies lateral to the superior constrictor muscle (the muscular bed of the tonsil). It is a vital lateral relation that must be considered during deep surgical procedures or abscess drainage.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Lateral to the superior constrictor muscle lie the styloglossus muscle, the loop of the facial artery, and the internal carotid artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Anatomical Location of the Pharyngeal Tonsil
statement: A 5-year-old boy is brought to the clinic due to persistent mouth breathing and loud snoring at night. Clinical examination reveals significant hypertrophy of the lymphoid tissue located in the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx. Which specific anatomical structure is primarily involved in this condition?
options: Lingual tonsil
Pharyngeal tonsil
Submandibular gland
Tubal tonsil
Palatine tonsil
correctOption: Pharyngeal tonsil
optionExplanations: The lingual tonsil is situated on the posterior third of the tongue, forming the inferior portion of Waldeyer's ring.
The pharyngeal tonsil is specifically located in the submucosa of the roof of the nasopharynx; when hypertrophied, it is referred to as adenoids.
The submandibular gland is a salivary gland located in the submandibular triangle of the neck, not a component of the nasopharyngeal lymphoid tissue.
The tubal tonsils are located around the opening of the auditory tube in the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, rather than the roof.
The palatine tonsils are located on the lateral walls of the oropharynx between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches, not the roof of the nasopharynx.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1751 (Book Page): A collection of lymphoid tissue, the pharyngeal tonsil, sits in the submucosa of the roof

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
coreConcept: Lateral Relations of the Palatine Tonsil
statement: During a surgical dissection of the oropharynx, the surgeon identifies the fibrous capsule of the palatine tonsil. To safely mobilize the tonsil, the surgeon must be aware of the structures located immediately lateral to the superior constrictor muscle in this region. Which of the following sets of structures is found in that lateral position?
options: Hyoglossus muscle and the lingual artery
Medial pterygoid muscle and the mandibular nerve (V3)
Salpingopharyngeus muscle and the ascending pharyngeal artery
Palatoglossus muscle and the external palatine vein
Styloglossus muscle, facial artery loop, and internal carotid artery
correctOption: Styloglossus muscle, facial artery loop, and internal carotid artery
optionExplanations: The hyoglossus muscle and lingual artery are primarily related to the floor of the mouth and the root of the tongue, inferior to the main palatine tonsil bed.
The medial pterygoid muscle and V3 are in the infratemporal fossa, which is significantly lateral and superior to the specific tonsillar bed relations.
The salpingopharyngeus is located in the nasopharynx and oropharynx walls but is not the primary lateral relation described for the tonsillar bed.
The palatoglossus muscle forms the anterior pillar and is medial to the superior constrictor, while the external palatine vein is in the loose areolar tissue medial to the muscle.

The palatine tonsil's capsule is separated from the superior constrictor by areolar tissue; once through the muscle, the styloglossus, facial artery loop, and internal carotid are the critical lateral relations.
citation: In book "Snell's Clinical Anatomy by Regions", Page 1760 (Book Page): Lateral to the superior constrictor muscle lie the styloglossus muscle, the loop of the facial artery, and the internal carotid artery.

category: Discuss the location, anatomical features, relations and vascular supply of tonsils: nasopharyngeal, palatine and lingual
statement: A 7-year-old boy presents with persistent snoring, mouth breathing, and recurrent middle ear infections. His mother notes he often sounds 'nasal' when speaking. Which anatomical relationship best explains why hypertrophy of the pharyngeal tonsil leads to these middle ear complications?
options: Hypertrophy causes posterior displacement of the soft palate, blocking the oropharynx.
Infected lymphoid tissue obstructs the pharyngeal opening of the auditory tube on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx.
Inflammation spreads directly through the superior constrictor muscle into the tympanic cavity.
Enlarged lymphoid tissue compresses the external auditory meatus from its medial aspect.
